parts.name: Chapter 1 — Whether the One Principle of All Things Is beyond All Things · pp. 1–5

lines.text: Chapter 1 — Whether the One Principle of All Things Is beyond All Things · pp. 1–5

Is the so-called single principle of all things beyond all things, or is it some one of all things — say, the summit of those that proceed from it? And do we say that all things exist together with it, or after it and from it?

For if one were to assert the latter, how could anything be outside the all? For things from which nothing whatever is absent — these are all things without qualification. But the principle is absent. Then what comes after the principle is not all things without qualification, but all things short of the principle. Further, "all things" means many things that are bounded; for the unbounded could not be all things in complete tally. Nothing, then, will show itself outside the all; for allness is a kind of boundary, an embrace already drawn, within which the principle is the upper limit and what lies farthest from the principle is the lower limit. All things, then, together with their limits. Again, the principle is coordinated with what comes from the principle: it both is called and is their principle; and so too the cause with its effects, and the first with what comes after the first. But things of which there is a single coordination, they being many — these we call "all things"; so that the principle too is among all things. And in general we say "all things," without qualification, of whatever we conceive in any way at all — and we conceive the principle as well. Thus we are accustomed to call a whole city the ruler together with the ruled, and a whole clan the begetter together with the begotten. But if all things include the principle, the principle would no longer be a principle of all things, since the principle is itself comprised among all things. The single coordination of all things, then — which is what we mean by "all things" — is without principle and without cause, lest we ascend to infinity.

And yet surely everything must be either a principle or from a principle; so all things, too, are either a principle or from a principle. But if the latter, the principle would not be together with all things but outside all things, as the principle of what comes from it. And if the former — what could that be which proceeds from all things as from a principle, standing outside all things in the downward direction, as the finished product of all things? For this too is among all things, since the conception of "all things" without qualification lets nothing escape. All things, therefore, are neither a principle nor from a principle.

Further, how are all things seen at once in multiplicity, and by what differentiation? — for we do not conceive the all apart from these. How then did differentiation and multiplicity straightway make their appearance? Or are all things not in every respect in differentiation and multiplicity: is the One rather the summit of the many, and the Unified — the monad — the summit of the differentiated, the One being simpler still than the monad? But, first, the monad too is the whole of number, even if number still folded together; on that showing the monad too is all things. And next, the One is not some one of the many — otherwise it would help fill up the many, like each of the others. Rather, however many the many are on any division whatever, just so many is that One before the division, in virtue of being altogether without parts. For it is not one as a minimum, as Speusippus was thought to say, but one as having swallowed all things. By its own simplicity it has dissolved all things together into itself and made all things one. Hence all things come from it because it is all things, itself before all things: as the Unified is before the differentiated, so the One, prior to the many, is all things.

But when we unfold our whole conception toward all things, we shall not predicate "all" in a single manner, but in at least three ways: unitarily, unifiedly, and in pluralized fashion — "from one and toward one," as we are accustomed to say. If, then, by "all things" we mean, in the more usual sense, the things that subsist in multiplicity and differentiation, we shall posit as their principles the Unified and, in still greater degree, the One. But if we conceive even these as all things, and gather them in with all the rest according to their relation and coordination with them, as was said before, then the argument will demand of us another principle prior to all things — one which it is no longer right to conceive as all things, nor to coordinate with what comes from it. For suppose someone says: even if the One is also, in whatever fashion, all things, still it is one before all things so taken, and it is one rather than all things — one in its own right, but all things as the cause of all and in virtue of its coordination with all; in a word, all things in a secondary way, but one primarily. Whoever says this will, first, be positing a doubleness within it — though in truth it is we who divide, we who are doubled and further multiplied about its simplicity; for that One, by being one, is all things in the simplest manner. And even should someone grant the point, nonetheless the principle of all things must be exempt and transcendent — exempt from all things themselves, from the simplest allness, and from the very simplicity that swallows all things, such as the simplicity of the One.

Note 4. A marginal scheme in the Hamburg copy (attributed to Holstenius) glosses the triple mode: "All things under one undifferentiated idea — unitarily; all things by their mutual relation and coordination — unifiedly; all things severally, by differentiation — pluralized."
Chapter 2 — The Soul's Divination: the Principle beyond Even the One · pp. 5–8

Our soul, then, divines that of all things, however conceived, there is a principle beyond all things, uncoordinated with all things. It must therefore not be called principle, nor cause, nor first, nor indeed prior to all things, nor beyond all things; least of all may it be hymned as being all things. In a word: it must not be hymned at all, nor conceived, nor surmised. For whatever we think or devise is either some one of all things — and this is the truer account — or, taken in its purified sense, it is all things. Even if we ascend to the simplest — dissolving everything, and ourselves dissolved — we reach only what is most comprehensive of all, like the outermost circumference, embracing not beings only but non-beings too. For among beings the ultimate is the Unified, altogether undifferentiated, since every being is a mixture of elements; and of the many taken simply, the ultimate is the One. Simpler than the One we can conceive nothing — than what is in every way one, and only one. And even if we call it principle and cause and first and simplest, these — and everything else — are There only according to the One; while we, unable to take it in one grasp, are divided about it, and predicate of it the divided things that are in ourselves. Except that we then dishonor even these, as being many and so failing to fit the One. Hence it is neither knowable nor nameable, since in that way too it would be many. Or are even these in it, according to the One? For the nature of the One is all-receiving — or rather, all-engendering. There is nothing that the One is not; and for this reason all things are wound off from it as from a single clew. And being the cause in the strict sense, and the first, it is also itself the end, itself the last: it is, quite simply, the coping-stone of all things, and the single nature of the many — not the nature within them that derives from it, but the nature before them that begets the one within them — the most partless summit of all things in whatever sense, and the greatest circumference of whatever is in any way called whole.

But if the One is cause of all things and comprehensive of all things, what is this ascent of ours beyond even it? Are we perhaps treading on emptiness, straining toward sheer nothing? For what is not even one is, in all justice, nothing. Whence indeed could there be anything beyond the One? The many need nothing whatever except the One; therefore the One alone is cause of the many — and the One is cause altogether, precisely because the cause of the many can only be the One. For the nothing is not their cause, since nothing is cause of nothing; nor are the many themselves, for insofar as they are many they are uncoordinated, and the many would not be one cause. And if there were many causes, they could not be causes of one another — because of the lack of coordination, and because of the circle; so each would be cause of itself, and of the many as many there would be no cause at all. Necessarily, then, the One is the cause of the many — the cause also of the coordination among them; for coordination is a kind of breathing-together, a unification of things with one another.
Chapter 3 — Against Resting in the One: Training the Soul's Birth-Pangs · pp. 8–9

Now suppose someone, caught in these perplexities, says that we should rest content with the principle of the One, and adds as capstone that we possess no conception, nor even surmise, simpler than the One: how then are we to surmise something beyond the very last surmise and conception? If anyone urges this, we shall pardon him his perplexity, for such thinking is, it seems, a trackless country where every device fails. Yet all the same, beginning from what is more familiar to us, we must train up the ineffable birth-pangs within us toward the ineffable — I do not know how to name it — co-awareness of this proud truth. For since, among things here, the wholly relationless is more honorable than what stands in relation, and the uncoordinated than the coordinated — as the contemplative man is more honorable than the statesman; as Kronos, so to speak, than the Demiurge; as Being than the Forms; and as the One than the many whose principle the One is — so too, among causes and effects without qualification, among all principles and all that principles govern, the most honorable is that which has stepped out beyond everything of the kind and is posited in no coordination and no relation whatever, so far as discourse can put it. For the One, after all, presides by nature over the many, the simplest over the however-composite, the most comprehensive over what is contained within it; but that — if one wishes to speak so — is beyond all this, beyond even the antithesis itself: not only the antithesis between things of the same rank, but even that of the first and what comes after the first.
Chapter 4 — The Twofold Nothing; All Things Proceed as from a Sanctuary · pp. 9–10

Further, then: the One and the Unified, and the many and differentiated things that come from them, are all things. For however many the things being differentiated are, just so many is the Unified from which they are differentiated; and however many the many are, just so many is the One from which they unroll. Yet it is one nonetheless — if anything, all the more — because the many come after it and are not in it; and the Unified likewise, because it is the concentration of the things being differentiated, before their differentiation. Whether by their coordination, then, or by their own nature, each of the two is all things. But all things cannot be first, nor a principle: if "all things" by coordination, because the last things are then included with them; and if the One among them alone, because it is at once one and all things together according to the One — and what is in every way beyond all things we have not yet found — and because the One is the summit of the many, as cause of what comes from it. Besides, we conceive the One according to a surmise progressively purified toward what is simplest and most comprehensive; whereas the most venerable must be ungraspable by all conceptions and surmises alike. For even among things here, what ever flees upward away from our conceptions is more honorable than what is more ready to hand; so that the most honorable of all would be what has escaped all our surmises altogether.

But if this is nothing — then let the nothing be twofold: the one better than the One, the other on this side of it. And if in saying these things we are treading on emptiness, then treading on emptiness is twofold as well: the one kind falls out into the ineffable, the other into what in no way and nowhere exists. For this latter too is ineffable, as Plato says, but according to the worse; the former according to the better. And if we go on to ask what need there is of it, this is the most necessary need of all: that from There, as from an inner sanctuary, all things proceed — out of the ineffable and in the ineffable manner. For it does not bring forth the many as being one, nor the differentiated as being unified, but ineffably brings forth all things alike, as the ineffable. And if, in saying even these things about it — that it is ineffable, that it is none of all things, that it is beyond conception — we are overturned by our own discourse, we must understand that these are names and words of our own birth-pangs, which dare to meddle overmuch with That: birth-pangs standing in the forecourt of the sanctuary, reporting nothing of what is within, but announcing only their own affections concerning it, their perplexities and their failures to attain — and not even this clearly, but by way of intimations, and to those capable of hearkening even to such things.
Chapter 5 — Plato's Silence: through the One to What Is beyond It · pp. 11–13

What is more, we see that our birth-pangs suffer these same things about the One as well, and in like manner are somehow distressed and overturned. For the One, says Plato, if it is, is not even one; and if it is not, no statement will fit it — so neither will negation, nor even a name (for a name is not simple either), nor any opinion or knowledge, since these are not simple, nor is intellect itself simple. Hence the One is altogether unknowable and ineffable. What then — are we seeking something else beyond the ineffable? Or perhaps Plato led us up ineffably, through the One as intermediary, to the ineffable now before us, beyond the One? For by the very removal of the One — just as, by the removal of everything else, he led us round to the One. That the One admits of being posited and known by a kind of purification, he made clear in the Sophist, demonstrating it as subsisting in itself prior to Being. And if, having ascended as far as the One, he fell silent, this too befits Plato: about things wholly unutterable to keep silence wholly, in the ancient manner. For the discourse here is in very truth a most hazardous one, should it fall upon untrained ears. There is no question that when he stirred up the account of that which in no way and nowhere is, the argument was overturned and ran the risk of falling into the sea of unlikeness3 — or rather of insubstantial emptiness.

And if demonstrations do not fit the One, that is no wonder: they are human things, divided, and more composite than is needful. They do not even fit Being, concerned as they are with forms — or rather they do not fit the Forms themselves, being discursive. It is Plato himself who declares in the Epistles that nothing among us is significative of the Form: no figure, no name, no statement, no opinion, no knowledge; intellect alone could light upon the Forms — intellect, which we who delight in dialectic do not yet possess. If, then, we put forward an intellection, but a form-directed one, we shall not fit it to the Unified and to Being; if at some point we put forward the concentrated intellection, even this, in relation to the One, is unspun with it and incommensurable; and if we put forward even the unitary intellection, the one that closes its eyes into the One itself, still this is simplified-together only as far as the One — if indeed there is any knowledge of the One at all; let that question wait for us. The result is that the ineffable and unknowable meets us everywhere — so that even the One is of this character. Nevertheless, even now, situated as we are, we go on measuring ourselves against the differentiation of these tremendous matters by means of intimations and surmises, purifying ourselves toward unaccustomed conceptions, led upward through analogy and through negations, dishonoring what is ours beside those things, guided by this road from what is less honorable in us toward what is more honorable; for this is exactly what we have continued doing even now.

And perhaps the wholly ineffable should be posited in this way: as so ineffable that we may not even posit of it that it is ineffable; whereas the One is to be posited as escaping every composition of statement and of name, and every differentiation — even that of known from knower — conceived after the manner of an encompassing ring, simplest and most comprehensive; and not only one, as the One's peculiar property, but one as all things and one before all things — yet not one as some one of all things. For these are the birth-pangs, and it is in this way that they are purified toward the simply One and the truly single principle of all things. In any case the one in us, surmised in this fashion — being nearer to us and more akin to us, even while falling short of That by, one might almost say, the whole of everything — is the readier instrument for such a surmise; for from the "some one," however posited, the passage to the "simply one" is easiest; and even if we can in no way make contact with That, still, riding upon the "simply one" that is ours, we form our surmise about what is before all things. The One, then, is in this way sayable and in this way unsayable; but let That be honored with complete silence — and, before silence, with the complete ignorance that dishonors all knowledge.
Note 3. "The sea of unlikeness": Statesman 273d, the boundless ocean of dissimilitude into which the cosmos risks sinking; here transferred to the discourse on absolute non-being.
Chapter 6 — In What Sense It Is Called Unknowable: Our Negations Confess Our Own State · pp. 14–17

Come then, let us examine this second point itself: in what sense it is said to be wholly unknowable. For if this is true, how do we write all these things about it, setting them in order? Surely we are not just spinning tales, babbling at length about what we do not know. But if it is in truth uncoordinated with all things and unrelated to all things, and is none of all things, not even the One itself — perhaps just these are its "nature," which we know when we are disposed toward it as we are, and labor to dispose others. Further: its very unknowability — either we know that it is unknowable, or we do not. But if the latter, how do we say it is wholly unknowable? And if we know it, then in this respect it is knowable — in the respect in which the unknowable is known to be unknowable. Moreover, one cannot deny one thing of another without knowing that of which one denies; nor can one say "this is not that" while in no way at all touching that. For of what one does not know, says Socrates in the Theaetetus, one could not say that it is — nor that it is not. How then do we deny of That, of which we are wholly ignorant, the things which we in some way know? It is like a man blind from birth declaring that warmth does not belong to color.

Or perhaps even he will speak justly in saying that color is not warm: for the warm is tangible, and this he knows through touch; while color he does not know at all — except that it is not tangible. For he knows that he does not know it; and such knowledge, quite simply, is not of the thing, but of his own ignorance. So we too, when we call That unknowable, are not reporting anything of it, but confessing our own affection concerning it. For the blind man's insensibility is not in the color — nor is his blindness — but in himself; and likewise the ignorance of what we are ignorant of is in us. For the knowledge of the known is in the knower, not in the known. And if someone should say that, just as knowledge might be in the thing known — being, as it were, its luminousness — so ignorance is in the thing unknown, as being its darkness or invisibility, in virtue of which it is unknown and invisible to all, then whoever says this fails to see that ignorance is a privation, exactly like blindness; every ignorance is so; and as the invisible stands to sight, so stand the unthought and the unknown to thought.

Now in other cases the privation of this or that leaves something else standing: the incorporeal, though invisible, is yet intelligible; and the non-intelligized is yet something — as whatever happens to be incomprehensible to some particular act of thinking. But when we remove every conception and every surmise, and say that this is our ignorance of it altogether — the thing toward which we close every eye, close it wholly — then we call it "unknowable" not because we are thereby saying something of it: not as "what is not of a nature to be seen by sight," which we say of the intelligible, nor as "what is not of a nature to be thought by the substantial and manifold intellection," which we say of the One — but as that which affords no purchase whatever on itself, not even the shadow of a suspicion. For we do not say merely that it is unknowable, as though it were some other thing which had, in addition, the nature of being unknowable; rather, we do not think fit to predicate of it "being," or "one," or "all things," or "principle of all things," or "beyond all things," or anything whatsoever. So not even these are its nature — the "nothing" itself, the "beyond all things," the "supra-causal," the "uncoordinated with all things": none of these is a nature of it, but they are only removals of what comes after it.

How then do we say anything about it at all? Surely thus: knowing the things that come after it, we dishonor this very knowing-in-any-way beside the positing — if I may so put it — of the wholly ineffable. For as what is beyond a given knowledge is better than what that knowledge grasps, so what is beyond every surmise must be most venerable — not as something known to be more venerable, but as holding the place of highest honor in us; this word too is our own affection, spoken of what is wholly ungraspable by our conceptions. The argument is by analogy: if what is in some respect unknowable according to the better is superior to what is wholly knowable, then what is wholly unknowable according to the better must of necessity be confessed supreme — even though That has neither the "supreme," nor the "mightiest," nor the "most venerable"; for these are our confessions about That which wholly escapes our conceptions and surmises alike. By the very fact that we surmise nothing of it, we confess it to be most wondrous of all; for if we surmised anything of it, we would seek something else again prior to that surmise — and either this goes on without limit, or we must come to a stand in the absolutely ineffable.

parts.name: Chapter 7 — Is the Ineffable Demonstrable? The Discourse Overturns Itself into Silence · pp. 17–23

lines.text: Chapter 7 — Is the Ineffable Demonstrable? The Discourse Overturns Itself into Silence · pp. 17–23

Do we then demonstrate something about That, and is That demonstrable — the very thing we judge not even fit to be surmised? Or is it rather that in saying these things we do produce demonstrations, even concerning That, yet not of That, nor is the demonstrable in That? For neither is anything else in it, nor is the demonstrable; what we demonstrate concerning it is our own ignorance and speechlessness regarding it, and this is the thing demonstrated. What then — do we not opine about it these very things that we say? And if there is an opinion of it, then it is also opinable. Or is it that we opine that it is not? And this opinion, says Aristotle, is a true one. Then if the opinion is true, there is also a thing to which the opinion, fitting itself, becomes true; for it is by the thing's being that the opinion too is true. And yet how could That be — or how be true — which is altogether unknowable? Or is it the not-being of it and its not being knowable that is the true thing here, as the truly false is true; for it is true that it is false? Or rather, such conclusions are to be drawn in the case of privations and of what in some way is not — cases in which the falling-away can still share, alongside, in the subsistence of the form: as the absence of light, which we call shadow, shares in light; for if there is no light, there is no shadow either. But to that which in no way and nowhere is, nothing of beings can belong in any way whatever, as Plato says; so neither not-being, nor privation at all. Indeed even the phrase "in no way and nowhere" is not valid in its own signification; for this phrase is a being, and its signification is some one of beings, and what is opinable is at any rate a being — even if one opines that it in no way is, still the opinable itself is one of beings. For which reason Plato does better to say that what in no way and nowhere is is ineffable and unopinable according to the worse, just as we say it of That according to the better.

But then we are opining what cannot be opined — or else, as the saying goes, the argument is overturned, and in truth we are not even opining. What then? Do we not think, and are we not persuaded, that this is how it stands? Or is what we hold only our own affections about That, as has been said many times? Yet we do have this opinion in us. Then it is an empty one — like our opinions of the void and of the infinite. For just as, though these are not, we take up opinions of them as though they were — imaginary, fabricated opinions; just as we also opine the sun to be a foot wide, which is hardly its size — so, whether we are opining about that which in no way and nowhere is, or about that of which we are writing these things, the opinion is our own, treading on emptiness within us; and grasping it, we suppose we are grasping That — but That is nothing to us: so far has it stepped beyond our conception. How then is even this demonstrable — the ignorance concerning That, just so much of it as forms itself within us?

For how do we call That unknowable? By one argument, already stated: we always find what is above knowledge to be the more honorable; so that what is above all knowledge, were it discoverable, would itself be found most honorable of all — and for the demonstration it suffices that it is not even discoverable. By a second argument: that it is above all things. For if it were knowable in any way, it too would be among all things — since whatever we know, all of that we call "all things" — and it would have something in common with all things, namely being knowable; but things that have something in common belong to one coordination, so that in this way too That would be ranked with all things. In this way too, then, it must be unknowable. Third: the unknowable is present in beings just as the knowable is; even if relatively, still it is present. As we call the same thing great and small relative to different things, so also knowable and unknowable relative to this and to that; and as the same thing, partaking of the two forms of small and great, is at once great and small, so what partakes at once of the knowable and the unknowable is each of the two. And as the knowable pre-exists, so the unknowable must pre-exist — above all if it be better than the knowable, as the intelligible is unknowable to perception but knowable to intellect. For the better cannot be a privation of form while the worse is a being — least of all a privation belonging to the intelligible; for absence and privation of that kind reside in matter, or in soul. In intellect how could they? — in which all things are present. And in the intelligible how, still more? Unless we should speak of one privation only, the privation according to the better: as the non-form, which is supra-formal; and the non-being, which is supra-essential; and the nothing, which is the truly unknowable, by transcendence over absolutely everything.

If, then, the One is the last knowable of all things in any way known or surmised, what is beyond the One is the primarily and wholly unknowable — so genuinely unknowable that it does not even have unknowability as a nature; nor do we apprehend it as unknowable; we are ignorant even whether it is unknowable. The ignorance concerning it is complete: we know That neither as knowable nor as unknowable. Hence we are overturned at every point, touching it at no point — as though it were nothing; or rather, since not even this belongs to it, the nothing. Is "that which in no way and nowhere is," then, the same as it — or is it beyond even this? — seeing that the one is the negation of Being, while the other is the negation even of the One: the sheer nothing. But the nothing is empty, a falling-away from everything; and that is not how we conceive the ineffable. Rather, the nothing is twofold: the one beyond, the other on this side. For the One too is twofold: the one last — that of matter; the other first — that which is elder than Being. So the nothing likewise: in one sense as not even the last one; in the other, as not even the first. And in the same way the unknowable and the ineffable are twofold: the one as falling beneath even the last surmisable thing, the other as rising above even the first.

Do we then posit it as unknowable merely to us? That indeed would be nothing strange. But it would be unknowable — if it is lawful to say so — even to the much-honored intellect; for all intellect looks toward the intelligible, and the intelligible is either form or being. But perhaps the divine knowledge knows it, and to that knowledge — the unitary and supra-essential — it is knowable? Yet this knowledge lights upon the One; and That, as we found, is beyond even the One. Speaking generally: if it were known, That too would be together with the others and itself one of all things; for it would have in common with the others the being-knowable, and to that extent it would be coordinated with the others. Further: if it is knowable, then knowledge — divine knowledge, no less — will encompass it; it will therefore bound it; but every bound ascends at last to the One, and That is above the One: it is therefore unencompassable and altogether unbounded — hence wholly unknowable even to knowledge, even, therefore, to the divine knowledge. Besides all this: knowledge is of things known as beings, or as existents, or as participants in the One; but That is beyond these. And the known stands in relation to knowledge and the knower; so That would have, after all, some coordination and relation to such things.

Indeed even the One runs the risk of being unknowable, if knower and known must be other than each other — even where both are in the same thing. The really One, at any rate, could not know even itself; for the One has no doubleness; there will not be within it a knower and a known. Nor will god, insofar as he stands according to the One alone and is conjoined with the One in its simplicity, be conjoined by way of doubleness; for how could the double be conjoined with the simple? And if it should know the One by the One, the knower will be one and the known will be one, and the nature of the One will admit each; so it will not be conjoined as one thing to another, as knower to known, since it is precisely this — one only; hence not even by way of knowledge. But how this stands with the One — another time. By so much the more, then, is what is not even one unknowable. For Plato says well that it is impossible to claim to know while knowing nothing; but insofar as the One is the last knowable, we know nothing whatever of what is beyond the One — so that we are merely rhapsodizing when we say these things.

Or rather: these things that we know — in knowing them we know this too about them, that they are unworthy, if it is lawful to say so, of the first hypothesis. Just as, not yet knowing the intelligible Forms, we nonetheless dishonor the images of them that form within us — their nature being partless and eternal, while these images become divided in us and change in many ways; and as, still more, though ignorant of the concentration of the Forms and kinds, yet holding its image — which is a concentration of the kinds and forms differentiated within us — we surmise Being to be of that sort: not this, but something better, and the most unified of all. And by now we conceive the One as well, not by concentrating but by unfolding all things into simplicity toward That; and this simplicity forms itself in us relative to all the things in us, falling far short of touching that all-complete simplicity. For the one and the simple in us is least of all what it is called — except that it is a token of that nature. Just so, then, taking up in intellect everything in any way knowable and surmisable, up to and including the One, we judge it right — if one must utter the unutterable and conceive the inconceivable — we judge it right nonetheless to posit that which is incommensurable with all things, uncoordinated, and transcendent in such wise that it does not in truth even possess transcendence. For the transcendent is always transcendent over something, and is not transcendent in every way, since it keeps a relation to that which it transcends, and in general a coordination within some opposition. If, then, the really transcendent is to be laid down, let it be laid down as not even transcendent; for its own name does not hold strictly true of the transcendent — by that very name it is already coordinated as well — so that this too must be denied of it. But the negation, too, is a statement, and the thing negated is a thing; and That is nothing. So it is not even negatable, nor sayable at all, nor knowable in any way whatever; so that it is not even possible to declare the negation of it. The complete self-overturning of our statements and of our thoughts — this is the demonstration, conjured before us, of the things we are saying. And what limit will there be to the discourse, except helpless silence, and the confession that we know nothing of things which it is not lawful — since it is not possible — to bring into knowledge?

Note 2. "This opinion, says Aristotle, is a true one": that there can be a true opinion that a thing is not, Aristotle, Metaphysics IX 10 (1051b) and De anima III 3 (Kopp cites Metaph. VI 5 and De an. III 3). The absence of light called shadow: a privation presupposes the subsistence of the form it falls away from. "As Plato says": Sophist 238c, where "that which in no way is" is declared unthinkable, unsayable, unutterable and irrational; cf. Republic 477a and Parmenides 142a. Damascius' point is that even this phrase, being a phrase and so a being, names its object improperly "according to the worse", while the Ineffable escapes it "according to the better".
Note 3. The sun "a foot wide": the stock example, from Heraclitus (DK 22 B3), of an appearance-opinion that misses the thing's true magnitude.
Chapter 8 — Whether Anything Comes from the Ineffable to Things Here · pp. 24–29

But would one not, measuring himself against these arguments, raise this further question? If we say anything about That on the basis of things here — since among these the monad everywhere leads a number proper to itself, for there is one soul and many souls, one intellect and many intellects, one Being and many beings, one henad and many henads1 — then presumably the argument will likewise demand both one ineffable and many ineffables; and the ineffable would have to be fertile — to speak ineffably — so that it will beget a multitude of its own. Or are these and all such puzzles raised in forgetfulness of what was said before? For there is nothing whatever that That has in common with things here; it would not even be a cause of the things we say and think and surmise; so it is neither the one nor the many, neither the fertile nor the productive nor in any way whatever a cause; nor is there any analogy with it, nor any likeness. That — or Those — is not, then, as things here are; or rather one must not even say "That," nor "Those," nor that it is one, nor that it is many. Best of all is to keep still, remaining in the ineffable sanctuary of the soul and not coming forth. But if one must after all give some indication, it is the negations of these things that we must use: that it is neither one nor many, neither fertile nor barren, neither cause nor causeless — negations which, I know not how, are simply overturned without end.

Are we then merely producing the "in no way and nowhere," babbling as we say all this? For everything we have said will fit that as well, and this overturning besets both alike — as the Eleatic philosopher also teaches us. Or is the first point not hard to resolve? It has been said before that the one is so called according to the worse, while That is posited according to the better; and the things denied are not denied of each in the same manner: above, the worse are denied of the better — if it is lawful to say so — below, the better of the worse, if it is possible to say so; for of matter too we deny even the one, but in this twofold manner of speaking. This difficulty, then, as I said, dissolves easily; the next is already tougher. If the "in no way and nowhere existent" is a falling-away from Being — the complete falling-away — while the One is beyond Being, and the ineffable more so still, then the in-no-way-existent will be encompassed by the One, which stretches out under it on this side; it will then be one, and even ineffable, since the ineffable, being beyond, reaches also to this side of the One. Or thus: if this so-called in-no-way-existent is a privation of Being, it may well undergo all this, and no wonder; for matter is altogether non-being when it stands viewed according to its one — the one above Being exists here below as well, after Being — and there is nothing absurd in its participating even in the ineffable. But if "in no way and nowhere existent" is meant thus: as posited neither as being nor as one nor as ineffable, neither affirmatively nor negatively, neither by overturning nor by contradiction, nor in any other fashion whatsoever, in no way, nowhere — for it was about such a thing that the Eleatic Stranger discoursed — then this is the falling-out of everything surmisable, in every fashion: the sheer not-anything-at-all.

The ineffable, then, most truly — like a citadel3 — is thrown about the whole of the sayable as its coping, towering over it from above and underlying everything from below as its seat. Or will not even this saying befit That? For with it there is no above and no below, nothing first of it and nothing last — for there is no procession; so it is neither the coping-stone of all things, nor does it contain all things; the sayable is not inside it, nor even the One itself.

Does nothing, then, come from it to things here? For upon all this, that must be the next question. And how could anything fail to come, if all things are from it? For each thing participates in that from which it proceeds — if in nothing else, then in this: that it is what it is, having and breathing from There its own principle, and turning back toward it according to its power. What indeed will prevent That from giving something of itself to what comes from it — for what else stands between? And must not the second always be nearer than the third to the single principle, and the third than the fourth? And if so, it departs less from it; and if so, it remains more within the horizon of that nature; and if so, it is more assimilated to it — hence more fitted to participate in it, hence participating. And how could we ourselves form these surmises about it, in whatever fashion, if there were not in us some faint trace of it, straining, as it were, toward it? Perhaps, then, it must even be said that, being ineffable, it gives to all things an ineffable participation, in virtue of which there is something ineffable in each — just as we agree that some things are by nature more ineffable than others: the One than Being, Being than Life, Life than Intellect, and so on always in the same proportion — or rather in the converse proportion, from matter up to the rational substance: these according to the worse, those according to the better, if it is lawful to say so.

But whoever posits this will make of That, too, a procession, and a certain ineffable order of things proceeded; and we shall carry everything sayable up into the ineffable as well, as being everywhere co-divided with the sayable; and we shall then make three monads and three numbers, no longer two — the substantial, the unitary, and the ineffable — and shall posit, what we earlier forbade, one and many within the ineffable, and a rank of firsts and middles and lasts in it, and further remaining, procession, reversion; in short, we shall mix much of the sayable into the ineffable. If instead, as we were saying, neither "That" nor "Those" may be brought to bear on the ineffable — since what we want is that which is above the One and the many — then neither may we posit one term before the many and another term, co-divided, in participation by the many. It is not, then, participated, nor does it impart anything of itself to what comes from it; nor is every god ineffable before he is one, in the way that he is one before he is substance. So perhaps here too the argument, overturning itself, declares That ineffable in every way — conceived in contraries from the side of the things after it. And what wonder, when about the One too we shall raise other perplexities of the same kind — and surely about the perfectly Unified and Being as well? But let these wait for us. Now, about what has been posited first, this must still be asked: what is the ascent toward That, and in what manner is it accomplished, starting from the last things? And let the account hold in common for the other principles too, and for what proceeds from them down to the very last. For as Parmenides, in his search for the One, went forth to everything that in any way depends on the One, so let us go forward together with him toward what has been posited first — or rather, beginning from things wholly sayable and familiar to perception, we shall ascend to those others, and shall bring the birth-pangs of truth to harbor in the silence that surrounds That. How then, setting out from things evident, should one make this whole ascent from the beginning? We must put forward an axiom, riding upon which we shall cross from here to there as far as our power permits, with what safety there may be.

Note 1. Henads: the divine unities of the school's theology, each god being primarily a "one." Damascius's point is that everywhere among the sayable, a monad heads a series of its own kind — soul, intellect, being, henad — so analogy threatens to demand a series even of "ineffables."

Note 3. A few words at the page-turn (Kopp pp. 26–27) are uncertain in the source's text layer; Kopp's Latin paraphrase gives "like a citadel" (tanquam arx), towering above and underlying all. The coping-stone (thrinkos) resumes the image of Chapter 2.
Chapter 9 — The Axiom of the Ascent: Neither Body nor Quality nor Their Compound Is the Principle · pp. 29–31

Let it be laid down, then, that the needless is by nature altogether prior to the needy. For what needs another is born to serve, of necessity, that which it needs; and if two things need each other, each lacking the other in a different respect, neither would be the principle. For to the principle that really is one, needlessness is most proper: if it needed anything, in that respect it would not be a principle; and the principle must be just this alone — principle. To it, then, the needless belongs, and we must confess that there is nothing whatever before it; whereas it will confess the needy if it has need in any respect at all. And if something needs one of the things before it — that is, a more sovereign principle — it is no wonder if it is still a principle relative to what comes after it, of which at least it has no need; but if it should in any way need even these, it will not preserve the dignity of principle even toward them. So let qualified body be laid down first; for this is the first sayable for us, namely the perceptible.

Is this, then, the first? But these are two things: body, and the qualification, which is in the body as in a substrate. Which nature, then, is prior? The compound of the two is needy of its own parts; but equally, what is in a substrate needs the substrate. Is body itself, then, the principle and the first substance? Impossible. First, the principle could not take on anything from what is after it and from it; but body, we say, has been qualified; so the qualification — the quality — is not from it, belonging to it as it does as something other. Second, body is divisible through and through: each of its parts needs the others, and the whole needs them all; being needy, then, and filled up out of needy parts, it could not be the wholly needless. Further, if it is not one but unified, it needs the one that holds it together, as Plato says. Again, it is something common and quite simply formless, like a kind of matter; it therefore needs ordering and form-giving, so as to be not merely body but such-and-such a body, fiery, say, or earthy — in a word, ordered and qualified. So what accrues to it perfects and arranges it, body being now the second substrate — what they call a second matter.

Is then that which accrues the principle? That too is impossible: it does not remain upon itself nor subsist alone, but is in a substrate and needs the substrate. And if someone should rank it not as in a substrate but as one of the elements within each thing — as "animal" is in horse and in man — even so each is needy of the other, this substrate and what is in the substrate; or rather the common element, like "animal," and the proper ones, like "rational" and "irrational." For the elements always need one another, and what is made of elements needs its own elements. And in general, this perceptible and vivid thing thus projected before us is neither the body — for body of itself does not move perception — nor the quality — for quality has no extension commensurate with perception, the organ of perception being itself a body. What acts on sight to dilate or contract it is neither the body nor the color, but the colored body, or color embodied: this is what moves sight; and universally, the perceptible of perception is body of a certain kind. From this two things are plain: first, that this "such-and-such" which is laid upon body is incorporeal — for if it were body, it would not yet be perceptible; so the body needs the incorporeal, and the incorporeal in turn the body, since neither is perceptible by itself. Second, that each in turn gains the advantage over the other, and neither pre-exists the other: being elements of the one perceptible, they exist together, the one furnishing extension to the unextended, the other bringing in besides, for the shapeless, the fully formed perceptible variety. And third, upon these: not even the compound of the two is the principle, for neither is it needless: it requires its own elements, and it requires whatever gathers them into the generation of the one perceptible form. For the body will not do the gathering — it is precisely what holds apart — nor will the quality, which does not even subsist without the body in which, or with which, it happens to be. Moreover, a form that is composite either produces itself — which is impossible, for it does not converge upon itself, but its whole is flung apart in many directions — or it is not produced by itself, and there will be another principle before it.

parts.name: Chapter 10 — Nature Is Not the Principle · pp. 32–33

lines.text: Chapter 10 — Nature Is Not the Principle · pp. 32–33

Then let there be laid down what we call Nature: a principle of motion and of rest, residing in the very thing that is moved and brought to rest, essentially and not by accident. For Nature is something simpler than the composite forms, and crafts them. But if it is in the very things it crafts, and subsists neither apart from them nor before them, but needs them in order to be what it is — let it keep, by all means, its prerogative over them, that it moulds them together and crafts them, as we say — still it is not needless, seeing that it has its being together with them and is inseparable within them: existing when they exist, and not existing when they do not, because it has sunk wholly down into them and cannot recover what is its own. For what nourishes and increases and begets like things — and the one prior to these three, which is Nature — will not be incorporeal in its entirety; it is very nearly a quality of body, differing only by this much, that it furnishes the composite with what seems to move and to rest from within. For the quality of the perceptible contributes the surface appearance that strikes perception; the body contributes extension in every direction; and Nature contributes the natural activity proceeding from within — whether in respect of place alone, or in respect of nourishing and increasing and begetting the like. This latter is already a more considerable nature, such as the nature at work through plants; yet not even it works through itself in such a way as to be able to pull itself up out of the things it administers: it has given the whole of itself over to them, in its very substance. There is indeed also a certain life other than the natural body, plainer than the nature sent down into body and acting from within in its own fashion; but this too is inseparable from its substrate, and needy. So Nature could not, without qualification, be a principle, having as it does neediness toward the worse.

For the wonder is not if something that is a principle is needy of the principle above itself, but if it is needy of the things after itself — the very things of which it is supposed to be the principle.
Chapter 11 — Nor Is the Irrational Soul · pp. 33–34

By the same argument we shall also refute anyone who posits as principle the irrational soul, whether the perceptive or the appetitive. For even if this soul seems to have something more separable about it, in its impulsive and its cognitive activities, nevertheless it too is bound into the body and has something inseparable from it — seeing that it cannot turn back toward itself, but its activity is kneaded together with the substrate; and it is clear that its substance too is of the same sort. For if its substance were absolute and free, resting upon itself, it would have displayed some activity of that same character: not directed always toward the body, but turning at some time toward itself — or, if always toward the body, at least critically, and with examination of itself. Thus the activities of the generality of men, even when they busy and spend themselves upon external things, nonetheless display about those very things something separable, in deliberating how to attain them, and in recognizing that there is need of counsel before doing or undergoing any of the apparent goods, or before avoiding any of their contraries. But the impulses of the irrational animals are uniform and self-grown: they move along with the organs, darting only toward the pleasant sensations that come from perceptible things and turning away from the painful ones. If, then, the body shares in the pain and the pleasure and is somehow disposed by them, it is clear that the soul-activities too come forth kneaded together with bodies, and are not purely of the soul but body-like — just as the power that dilates or contracts sight belongs not to the color alone but to the colored body; and just as cutting, Aristotle says, would belong neither to the iron nor yet to the shape, but to the two together, which is the axe, or the chisel, or the sword. So too perceiving and desiring belong to the ensouled body, or to the body-like soul — even if in these the soul-element shows through more than the corporeal, as in the former cases the corporeal prevails in extension and subsistence. But insofar as a thing has its being in another, in whatever way, to that extent it is needy of the worse; and such a thing could not be a principle.
Chapter 12 — Nor the Rational Soul, nor Even the Much-Honored Intellect · pp. 34–37

And surely, prior to this substance, we see a form that is also separate, resting upon itself and turning back into itself — such as the form of the rational subsistence. Our soul, at any rate, presides over its own activities and corrects itself; it could not do this if it did not turn back toward itself, and it could not turn back toward itself if it did not have a separate substance — as Aristotle also holds. This soul, then, does not need the worse: is it therefore the most complete principle? Or rather: it does not project all its activities at once, but is always in need of most of them; and the principle wants to have nothing needy about it, while this is a substance deficient in respect of its own activities. But the substance, someone might say, is eternal and needless, holding its essential activities without deficiency and ever running abreast of the substance, in virtue of its self-motion and everlasting life — and on that ground it would be a principle. Yet the soul as a whole is one form and a single nature: is it then to be needless in one respect and needy in another? The principle is needless in every way. So the soul — the soul, that is, which also projects changing activities — would not be the principle; not, at least, the most sovereign one. There must therefore be before it another, unchangeable in every way: in substance, in life, and in knowledge, in all its powers and all its activities — such as we declare the unmoved and eternal to be, the much-honored Intellect itself, to which Aristotle too ascended, and thought that he had found the first principle. For what could it still lack — that which has gathered into itself, completely, its own plenitudes; in which neither addition nor subtraction ever changes anything of what belongs to it, in any respect, at any time?

Or is this too both one and many, both whole and parts, with firsts in it and middles and lasts? The worse plenitudes need the better, and the better the worse, and the whole its parts; for things correlative to one another need one another, and the firsts need the lasts for the same reason — nothing, indeed, is "first" in its own right. Moreover, the one of the many is itself in need of the many, because it has its being among many: insofar as this one is what gathers the many together, it exists not by itself but with them. Much, then, is the neediness even in this principle. Indeed, even as begetting within itself its own plenitudes, out of which the entire intellect is filled up together, Intellect would be needy of its own self: not only the begotten needing the begetter, but the begetter needing the begotten, toward the entire filling-up of that whole which begets itself. Again, it is thinking and being thought — an intelligible and an intellective, its own and for itself — and the compound of the two is Intellect. The intellective, then, needs the intelligible, as its own proper object of desire; and the intelligible has need of the intellective, because it wills itself to be intelligible; and the compound of both is needy of each — even if the attainment always accompanies the need, as the cosmos accompanies matter. Still, by nature a certain neediness is of the very substance of Intellect — enough, at all events, to keep it from being the most sovereign principle.
Chapter 13 — The One-Being and the One: the Topmost Trace of Neediness · pp. 37–41

Should we then gather Intellect together into the simplest of beings — that which we call One-Being? For where nothing whatever is differentiated, where there is no multitude within, no order, no doubleness, no turning back upon itself, what neediness could show itself in the wholly Unified — least of all the neediness of the worse, from which the present argument took its start? This is why the great Parmenides ascended to this as the safest principle, as being the most needless. Yet one must by all means keep Plato's point in mind: that the Unified is not the One itself, but that which has undergone the One — that which, evidently, participates in it. And indeed, even along the present line of argument, the Unified shows itself as holding within itself both the unified element — even if what is being unified lies swallowed down to the last degree by what unifies it, still it stands there as unified — and the One itself. For if Being is of elements, as Plato seems to say in calling it the Mixed, it needs its own elements. Or suppose the simplicity of the One, slackening, came to a stand at the measure of the one — projecting itself, so to speak, thick and double-handed together with itself, its elements, I do not say differentiated, but bound by its own one and still as it were confounded, projected just so far that That is no longer one but unified: substance now, instead of henad. In this way one might defend the Mixed with precision, taking care not to make the better out of the worse, but to set the worse with the better, from it and in it. Yet even so, the one in it is needy of the One from which it is, and the compound of the two is altogether needy of each.

And if the conception of being is one thing and that of being-unified another, while the whole is at once unified and being, then these need each other, and the whole — which is called One-Being — needs the two. If the one is the better, it will need being for the subsistence of the one-being; if being is better than the one, as supervening upon it — a form, as it were, for the Mixed and Unified, as the property "man" supervenes upon "at-once-animal-rational-mortal" — then in this way too the one will be needy of being. And if — what it is more correct to say — the one is twofold, the one being the cause of the mixture, which will pre-exist being, the other that which stands upright together with being (about these, if need be, we shall say more hereafter), nevertheless neediness will not completely desert even this nature — though not, I grant, the neediness of the worse, along which the manner of our ascent proceeds.

But over and above all these, would not the One be needless in every way? It does not need what comes after it in order to be — for the really One is by itself, separated from all things; nor anything worse or better within itself — for there is nothing in it beside itself; nor even its own self. For that is one which does not have even a doubleness toward itself: not even the "toward itself" may be said of the really One, for it is simple through and through. This, then, is the most needless of all things; this, then, is the principle of all things, and this the cause, and this the first of absolutely everything at once. But if these three belong to it, it would not be one. Or rather: to the One all things will belong according to the One — these, and whatever else we shall predicate of it: the simplest, the mightiest, the savior of all things, the Good itself; and "all things," if one says it of it according to the simplicity of the One — that simplicity being all-bearing and, prior even to that, all-substance, and for just this reason all-nourishing. But if these things too are truly said of the One, then even so it would be needy of what comes after it, precisely in respect of these things which we attach to it in whatever way. For the principle both is and is called principle of what is from the principle, and the cause of its effects, and the first of what is ranked after it; the simple, again, is simple by superiority over others, and the mightiest by its power over what it masters, and the good, the desired, the saving, exist for the things that are saved and that desire.

Indeed, if it should be called all things, it will be so called according to the anticipation of all things within it — an anticipation in respect of the One alone; yet for all that, one cause of all things before all things, no other cause than this, and this too according to the One. Insofar, then, as it is one only, in that respect it is most needless; insofar as it is most needless, it is the first principle and the most unswerving root of all principles; but insofar as it is in any way principle, and the first cause of all things, enthroned before all as what all desire — in this respect it presents the appearance of being somehow needy of the very things to which it stands related. It has, then — if it is lawful to say so — even a topmost trace of neediness, just as, conversely, matter has the last echo of the needless, in respect of that in it which is one, faintest of all.

And the argument seems to carry a certain self-overturning. For insofar as it is one, it is needless — if indeed it showed itself as principle precisely in virtue of being most needless and one; and yet, insofar as it is one, it is also principle; and insofar as it is one, needless, while insofar as it is principle, needy — yet not in the same respect: with respect to being what it is, it is needless; as also bringing forth the other things and having anticipated them, needy; and this too is peculiar to the One. So that each of the two holds according to the One; and therefore neither holds in the way that speech divides them when it says "each," but there is one only — and according to this one, both all the rest and the needy itself. For why should not this too be according to the One, like everything else that proceeds from it? Neediness, after all, is one of those things. Something else must therefore be sought, which will in no manner whatsoever have neediness, not in any way at all. And such would be that of which it is not even true to say that it is a principle — not even that very thing which it seemed most august to say, "the most needless"; for this too signifies a superiority, an exemption from the needy. Indeed we did not think fit to call it even the wholly transcendent, but rather the wholly inconceivable and the wholly kept-in-silence. This would most justly be the axiom of conception now sought — of a conception that no longer utters anything, but is content not to utter, and in this way reveres that unmanageable unknowing.
Chapter 14 — A Second Way of Ascent: Potency before Act, Matter before Form · pp. 41–44

This, then, is one way of ascent to what is called in this manner the first — or rather, to what is beyond everything posited in whatsoever way. But there is also another way, which does not prefer the needless to what is needy of the worse, but ranks what is needy of the better second to the better itself. Thus what is in potency is everywhere second to what is in act: in order to come into act and not remain idly in potency, it stands in need besides of what is in act; for never does the better sprout up from the worse. Let this too be set down for us as determined in advance, meeting the common conceptions without distortion. Matter, then, has before itself the enmattered form, because all matter is form in potency — whether the first matter, found in respect of complete formlessness, or the second, which stands as qualityless body: the matter to which, plausibly enough, those who inquired after the perceptibles looked first, and which alone seemed to them to be the first substance; for the community of the differing elements persuaded them that there is some qualityless body, graspable by reason. And it is plain that the qualities, by which the differentiae are constituted, rise above the qualityless body itself, which already pre-exists them as a kind of matter. What then — would someone say that accidents are better than substance? There is nothing strange in things that exist together gaining each in turn the advantage over the other, and in the joint fillers-up of the one-out-of-all participating reciprocally in one another.

Next, the qualified is twofold. There is the substantial: fire itself — I mean the very form — and man, and each of the others, insofar as each is a qualified body; and the elements of each, as of fire the heat and the brightness, and of man the mortal and the rational, and the shape, as the upright animal has its uprightness and its articulation; and in each case the plenitudes of each thing's substance, with which, all at once, the whole form qualified the second substrate by form-making quality — "quality" being so called simply with reference to the qualityless body. And there is the adventitious and accidental qualified, which, having its substance in one thing, accrues to another by accident — and in every case it accrues to a body already qualified in its substance; so that this must of necessity be worse than the receiving substance, which is already form-endowed and antecedent. That the qualityless body is qualified first by the substantial quality is plain: when the accidents supervene, the forms severally remain, holding the underlying seat of the body; and it is around them, while they remain, that the change of accidents is observed. Reasonably, then, we rank the qualified before the qualityless body; and on this account it is something already perceptible — this visible cosmos itself. But since, among such bodies, some have their governing principle within and others without, as artifacts do, one must conceive Nature besides, as something better than the qualities, set before them in the rank of cause, as art is set before artifacts. And again, of the things governed from within, some seem merely to be, while others are nourished and grow and beget their like: there is therefore yet another cause before the nature just named — this vegetative power itself. And it is evident that all the things which supervene upon body as upon a pre-existing substrate are incorporeal in themselves, even if they become body-like by participation in that in which they are — as such things are both called and are "material," in virtue of the affection that comes from matter. The qualities, then, and the natures still more, and the vegetative life more eminently yet, preserve the incorporeal in their own right.
Chapter 15 — The Self-Moved Animal and the Twofold Soul: Does the Irrational Soul Move Itself? · pp. 44–46

But since perception exhibits yet another, plainer life — that of the things that move now by impulse and from place to place — this must be ranked before the former, as a more sovereign principle and as supplier of a better form, the self-moved animal taking natural precedence over the plant rooted in the earth. And yet the animal is not strictly self-moved: it is not such whole through whole; rather, one part of it moves and another part is moved. This, then, is an apparent self-mover; so there must be before it the truly self-moved, which as a whole moves and is moved, in order that the apparent may be its image. And indeed the soul that moves the body must be posited as the more sovereign self-moved substance. This soul is twofold, the one rational, the other irrational. That perception vouches for the rational one too is evident — or does not each man have a co-awareness of himself, more plainly or more dimly, as turning back toward himself in his self-concernments and self-searchings and in his vital and cognitive attendings upon himself? The substance capable of these things, gathering the universals too by reasoning, would justly be called rational. But the irrational soul as well, even if it does not appear to traverse these things and reason them out with itself, nevertheless moves bodies from place to place, being itself moved first in its own right; for at different times it projects different impulses. Does it then move itself from one impulse to another, or is it moved by something else — say, as some assert, by the whole rational soul in the cosmos? But this at least is absurd to maintain: that the activities of each irrational soul belong not to that soul but to the diviner one — activities unbounded and indeterminate as they are, and mingled with much that is ugly and imperfect. To say the irrational activities belong to the rational soul is the same as positing that very substance as irrational — the substance that projects the irrational activities — not to say the whole soul itself.

It is absurd, moreover, to posit a substance that is not generative of its own activities. For if there is some irrational substance, it would have activities proper to itself, not supplied from elsewhere but proceeding from it. The irrational soul also, then, moves itself toward its now one, now another desire and impulse. But if it moves itself, it turns back toward itself; and since that is so, the irrational soul is separable and not in a substrate; it is therefore rational — if indeed it looks into itself; for it will see itself if it turns back toward itself. Yet in fact, stretched toward externals, it looks to externals — rather, to some colored body; itself it does not see, seeing that vision, at any rate, is neither a body nor colored. It does not, then, turn back toward itself; it sees nothing of itself, the irrational soul. For neither does imagination project an image of itself, but of the perceptible — of a colored body, say; nor does irrational appetite desire itself, but some object of desire — honor, say, or retaliation, or pleasure, or possessions. It does not, then, move itself. But perhaps it moves thus: not as moving itself, but as moving externals from itself, without taking hold of itself — and in this sense it is self-moved, in that the motion is from itself; it is not, however, moved by itself. For this is how the school of the great Syrianus thinks one should hear the term "self-moved" in its looser use in the Laws and in the Timaeus; for this, says the Timaeus, is why plants do not move, because they have no share in the self-moved soul, as the beasts do share in it, moving from place to place. But none the less it remains necessary that everything moved be moved either by itself or by another; and the latter in two ways — either by the better, as we say of the individual and genuinely irrational activities, or by anything whatever; for it is certainly not moved by that in which it is, this being a body, and a body which, on the contrary, is moved by it.

parts.name: Chapter 16 — The Solution: Apparent Self-Motion Belongs to the Composite · pp. 46–48

lines.text: Chapter 16 — The Solution: Apparent Self-Motion Belongs to the Composite · pp. 46–48

Perhaps, then, the activities are moved by the substance, and the irrational soul is self-moved in this sense, as being generative of its own activities? But, first, this will be common to every substance, including the one called other-moved; for fire too is self-moved in this way, as a substance generative of its own individual activities, and the clod likewise, and the adze, and anything whatever that is capable of acting; for the proper activity always proceeds from the substance. This, then, so stated, would carry no weight. But perhaps, since a form of this kind is presupposed to be in a substrate, it must not be taken by itself as the agent, but together with the substrate in which it is; for as it is, so also it acts. Just as, then, what dilates sight is neither the whiteness nor the qualityless body, but the two together, so also the perceptive activity belongs neither to the incorporeal perception nor to the sense-organ, which is a body, but to what is made of both, as to one composite substance — like the substance compounded of matter and form. For the sense-organ is not the instrument of perception but its substrate: perception is in it, not using it. If it used it, it would have moved itself before the organ, in order to move the organ as well; but as it is, it subsists together with the substrate, and has no separate activity at all. Let the compound, then, be the agent — yet let the activity proceed according to the form, as the chisel's proceeds according to its shape, and as the white body's power of dilating sight proceeds according to the whiteness. What, then, in the composite is the mover, and what the moved? Does the soul move, and the body get moved? But on those terms, once again, the soul will move on its own and the body will be moved on its own; and there will be a mover prior to the moved, possessing a separate moving activity prior to the activity moved. We must not, then, posit here a mover and there a moved, but the animal as one thing — body become perceptive, or perception embodied — and it is this that performs the activity which seems self-moved.

For if the composite animal has a substance of its own, it assuredly has also a composite activity, befitting the animal as a whole — itself a kind of whole, in which something incorporeal is discerned and something body-like, blended together at once, just as in the dilating of sight the two-together is present. That is why we are affected by the white body in both ways at once: corporeally, in that the sense-organ is dilated; incorporeally, in that we apprehend the affection, taking cognizance, as it were, of it. As the agent is composite, so also the patient: sight itself is a composite, of an incorporeal optical power and an underlying body. Such, then, is the kind of self-motion we must posit as residing in the optical power, and, to speak generally, in perception: of itself it does not act — for of itself it does not even subsist — but, coming to be in the body and qualifying it, in virtue of a certain more considerable quality and illumination, it completes the whole apparent self-mover. And why "apparent"? Because it is not a partless same that moves and is moved; rather, the case is like substances separated from one another yet coming together in another manner — as the rational soul and the animal, or the shell-like body and the pneumatic, or this and the luminous; for in these interweavings too the one moves and the other is moved, precisely because the one is not a substrate with the other in the substrate. But when the composite form stands as we have described, neither does each act on its own — for neither even subsists on its own — nor, within the composition, is the one the mover and the other the moved; for then they will stand apart again in their activities, and so in their subsistences as well.
Chapter 17 — By Which and According to Which: the Two Senses of Motion · pp. 48–49

But this is another mode of self-motion, in which the compound is moved according to the one element — the form — whence this also seems to be the mover: not that the other element is moved by it, but that the compound is moved according to it; or else by something else. And if the latter, then either by the better or by the worse, and the same arguments will return; while if by itself, the same thing will be mover and moved — which befits only the partless and incomposite. Or rather: just as the self-mover here is not genuine, so neither is it true that the same thing is moved by itself and moves itself; it is apparent, because that according to which it moves the composite is one and simple, and this, as moving, is one. There is, however, both a "whereby it is moved" and a "whereby it moves": the whole form is the two-together, in which lies the "whereby it is moved"; and it is two-together in respect of each, because of the reciprocal interchange of the quasi-elements of the whole form — so that the whole both moves and is moved, yet not so as to move and be moved, itself, according to the whole: it moves according to the soul and is moved according to the body, and yet by neither soul nor body. And what distinguishes the "by which" from the "according to which" would readily be plain. For motion is twofold: the one comes to be within the moved, becoming an affection of it; the other is outside it, and imparts the former. The thing is moved, then, by the latter, but according to the former. For if it were moved by the former as well, this too would impart some motion from itself to what is moved by it; that motion, in turn, will be the affection — the one according to which the moved is moved — and we shall go on to infinity.
Chapter 18 — Life Twofold; the Scale of Separability · pp. 49–51

The same account proves true when examined in the case of life as well: the one life makes alive, imparting life to what is vivified by it; the other is that according to which the thing vivified by the former lives. For if this latter also made alive, it too would give a further life — and so to infinity. Just so, then, with the form of self-motion: the one is that by which the apparent self-mover is made self-moving; the other, that according to which it seems to be such — an affection of self-motion, inseparable from the participant. For the self-moved nature too is a life of this sort, being soul; and soul is twofold: the one begetting, the other that according to which the ensouled is given its being — which is also why the ensouled seems to be moved from within, out of itself, although what is present within it is not the "by which" it is moved, but the "according to which," which we call ensoulment. Perhaps, however, someone who has granted all this will suppose these features to be common also to plants and to soulless things; for the clod too is moved toward the earth from within, and plants likewise — the vegetative soul being in them, according to which they are nourished and grow and beget their like; and further, the irrational animals are in the same case, and the rational animals in the same — so that there will be nothing that is not self-moved. To him we shall reply that every natural and vegetative form, and every animal besides, is indeed moved from within — but not with every motion: only when it makes its motion in place; for this is the conspicuously self-moved motion, and it is by reference to this that we call the rest other-moved — all that is not moved from within with this motion. Indeed, if we discriminated the self-moved by that strict criterion by which the rational soul is self-moved, not even the irrational animals will appear self-moved; for they are not of a nature to turn back into themselves:

vision does not see itself, nor does imagination imagine that it is imagining; and spirit and appetite have, for their matter and for their every activity, an object of desire that lies outside. This is why we said that a self-mover of this kind acts from within upon the outside — not in a circle back upon itself, but, quite simply, along a straight line; for that was the form of this life, inseparable as it is from the straight-stretched body that underlies it.
