As fire moves upward and earth downward according to the nature present in them, and as plants are nourished and grow and beget their like according to the vegetative soul present in them, so the beasts too act according to the appetitive life present in their natural and vegetative body and consubstantiated with the form of the animal: it is according to this that they perform their — quite simply irrational — self-motion.

And if someone, observing that the beasts are reason-like and emit reason-like activities, supposes that they too participate in what is primarily self-moved, and therefore have a soul that turns back toward itself, perhaps we might indulge him even in making them rational — except that it is not by existence but by participation, and that of the faintest; just as one might call the rational soul itself intellectual by participation, inasmuch as it ever projects the common conceptions without distortion. In any case we shall take "the separable" as admitting of breadth, and shall say that here the one predominates and there the other. The extremes are the wholly separable, such as the rational form, and the wholly inseparable, such as quality. In between lie nature, next to the inseparable, having a small reflection of the separable; and the irrational soul, next to the separable — for it seems somehow to subsist even by itself, apart from the substrate, whence it is even disputable whether it is self-moved or other-moved: large indeed is the trace of self-motion in it, but not the genuine thing, which turns back into itself and for that very reason is altogether separated from the substrate. The vegetative soul stands somehow in the middle — which is why to some it seems to be a soul, to others a nature. But these matters must be examined more fully elsewhere; for the present let so much be said.
Chapter 19 — The Mover before the Moved: the Unmoved before the Self-Moved · pp. 51–52

We must pass back, then, to what lay before us. The self-mover of this kind, which is kneaded together with the other-moved — how could it be first? It neither gives itself subsistence nor perfects itself in truth, but needs, for each of these, something else; and there is before it the genuinely self-moved. Such a thing perception — or rather the evidence of the appearances — gives us in the human; and clearly every rational form is such: from this let us now take our start, for our present task is to grasp the properties of things in the broader strokes. Is then the strictly self-moved the principle, in need of no better form? Or is the mover by nature always prior to the moved — and, quite generally, does not every form that is pure of its opposite subsist by itself before what is mixed with that opposite, the pure being cause of the mixed? For what is consubstantiated with another has its activity, too, kneaded together with that other's; so that what is so conditioned will make itself self-moved, at once moving and moved; but mover only it could not make itself, for neither is it "only." Yet every form must also be capable of being alone; hence there must be also the mover that is not moved. Indeed, it is absurd that the moved-only should exist — body, for instance — and yet that the mover-only should not exist before the compound of the two; for it is plain that the advantage must lie on the side of the better, since even within the self-moved, that respect in which it moves is better than that in which it is moved. First, then, must come the unmoved mover; third, the moved that does not move; and between them the self-moved — which, we shall say, needs the mover in order that the mover make it motive; though let what is motive-of-itself have that from itself, if one insists. In general: if it is moved, it does not remain, to just the extent that it is moved; and if it moves, it must move while remaining, insofar as it moves. Whence, then, will it have its remaining? From itself it has either being-moved only, or remaining-and-being-moved at once, as one same whole; but the remaining taken simply — whence? From what remains simply; and that was the unmoved cause. Before the self-moved, then, we must posit the unmoved.
Chapter 20 — The Unmoved as Intellect; before the Form-like, the Unified · pp. 52–53

Let us consider, then, whether the unmoved is the most sovereign principle, and how this can be. The unmoved is, unmovedly, just as many things as the self-moved is self-movedly. For nothing self-moved can be first, for the reasons given; but each of the elements in the self-moved is a self-moved something; before each of them, therefore, pre-exists the corresponding unmoved each. To say plainly what I mean, passing over the rest, I shall make the argument bear on three. In the self-moved soul at least three things are seen — the substantial, the vital, the cognitive — and each of these is evidently self-moved; for as the whole is self-moved as a whole, so before each there is, by the same reasonings, the unmoved each. The unmoved, then, is also a plenitude of these three forms — and that neither of forms torn apart (for even in the self-moved they are unified with one another), nor of forms so wholly fused that nothing in them is differentiated; for on those terms each would stand as each only in the self-moved, and not also as unmoved — yet each must be unmoved too, each on its own, precisely because the self-moved each was not first. And besides: the unmoved differentiation must of necessity exist before the self-moved one. The unmoved, then, is at once one and many, at once unified and differentiated — the very thing we have named Intellect. And it is plain that the unified in it is by nature prior to the differentiated, and more honorable; for differentiation is always in need of union, but not, conversely, union of differentiation. Now Intellect does not possess the unified pure of its opposite; for the whole intellectual form is consubstantiated throughout with the differentiated. The somehow-unified, then, needs the simply Unified, and the with-another needs the by-itself, and the by-participation the by-existence. And indeed Intellect, being self-subsistent, produces itself as at once unified and differentiated — according to the compound, therefore; therefore, in respect of the unified taken simply, it will be produced from what is simply, and only, Unified. Before the form-like, then, is the uncircumscribed, undifferentiated into forms — what we call the Unified, which the wise have called Being: that which holds the many in one concentration pre-existing the many.
Chapter 21 — Is Being the Principle? The One before Being · pp. 53–54

Here, then, let us halt, take breath, and reckon up whether Being is the sought-for principle of all things. What indeed could be without share in Being, seeing that whatever in any way "is" is something lesser than Being itself? Or rather: if Being is this Unified, it would be second to the One, since it has become unified by participating in it. And in general, we conceive the one as one thing and being as another. If Being were prior to the One, it will not participate in the One: there will then be many only — and these infinitely infinite. And if the One is together with Being, and Being with the One, and they are of the same rank, then either they stand apart from each other — and there will be two principles, and the absurdity just named will follow — or they will participate reciprocally in each other, and the two will be elements, or parts, of a third made of both. And what, then, is it that gathered them to each other? If it is the One that unified Being to itself, as being one (for one might say this too), then the One will be active before Being, in order to summon Being and turn it toward itself: the One, therefore, subsists self-complete, upon itself, before Being. Further, the simpler is always before the more composite. If, then, they are alike simple, the principles are two; or out of the two comes one — and that one will be composite; before it, therefore, is the simple and wholly incomposite, which is either one or not one; and if not one, either many or nothing. But "nothing," if it signifies the wholly empty, would point to something idle; and if it signifies the ineffable, that is not even simple. And if many, then not simple; for the simple means to be without multiplicity, by the very privation of the many. In sum, it is impossible to conceive a principle simpler than the One: in every way, then, the One is before Being. But to be quit of these arguments too, let us simply take hold of the reasoning of the ascent itself: having ascended to the Unified — whatever it is to be called, but unified through and through — from this we ascend to the One: from the participant to the participated.
Chapter 22 — The One in Plato's Negations; the Way through the Properties Completed · pp. 54–55

That, then, is the principle of all things; and Plato, having run up to it, needed no further principle in his discourses. For that ineffable other is not a principle of discourses, nor of knowledges, nor indeed of lives nor of beings nor of henads, but of all things simply, ranked above every device of thought. Hence he displayed nothing about That, but made his negations from the One — negations of everything else except the One itself. Being he denied of it last of all, but not the one; he denied of it even the negation itself, but not the one; he denied the name and the thought and all knowledge — and what more could one mention? — Being itself, whole and entire; and, let it be granted, the Unified too and the unitary; and, if you like, the unlimited and limit, the two principles: but in no way what is beyond all these. The one he nowhere denied, in any fashion. This is why in the Sophist he posits it as one before Being, and in the Republic as the Good beyond all substance. So there remains, for all that, only "one"; and this is either knowable and sayable, or unknowable and unsayable, or in one way the former and in one way not: for through negations one might say something about it, while by affirmation it is unsayable; and again, by the simplicity of our knowledge it would be knowable, or surmisable, while by knowledge's compositeness it is wholly unknowable — and hence not even to be captured by negation. And in general: insofar as it is posited as one, to that extent it is somehow coordinated with the things posited in other ways; for it is the summit of the things that subsist by positing. Yet there is much in it, even so, of the unsayable and unknowable and uncoordinated and unpositable — but together with the appearance of their contraries; and the former are better than these. Everywhere, however, the things pure of their contraries pre-exist, unmixed, before the mixed. Either, then, the better terms are in the One by existence — and then how shall the contraries also be there together with them? — or by participation; and then they come from elsewhere, from what is primarily of that character. Before the One, therefore, is what is simply and wholly unsayable, unpositable, uncoordinated, inconceivable in every manner: the very thing toward which this ascent of the argument through the most evident things was hastening, leaving aside none of the intermediates, from those first things down to the last of all. Thus far, then, we have proceeded by the way through the properties; but the greatness and all-perfection and all-comprehensiveness of the first principles — the Unified, the One, the Ineffable — we have not yet displayed.
Chapter 23 — The Method through the All-Perfect: the Cosmos and Its Unmoved Cause · pp. 56–58

We must go on, as far as we are able, to this method also. Let us lay hold, then, of the First in its all-perfection — the very thing which the gods themselves have stretched out even to perception, as an indication of the invisible and intelligible and unitary and ineffable all-perfection. This cosmos, then, is perfect, made of perfect parts, as we see; and what we see of it is the perceptible. But it is clear that the things in us pre-subsist in it as well; for it surely does not possess the worse of the things in us — the body-like, and whatever underlies the body-like, this latter not being from itself but having its being in a substrate — while lacking the better, and that though it is the more perfect. It will have, then, a nature befitting it: not the nature that moves things downward and upward, but the one that wheels them in a circle; for that is its motion according to nature. It will have, then, also the life better than this, the vegetative — not, to be sure, the life that nourishes or feeds or begets like things which come to be and perish in a kind of inflow and outflow (unless these too belong to it in another manner, which there is no need to wheel into the argument here), but the life that holds it together and keeps it active as the same in form and in number: the connate filling and growth — not the growth that is still growing, but that which has already wholly grown — and, further, the generation of its own illuminations — the generation that has already begotten them — the cosmos doing and holding together these things, in their analogous mode, there above.

Shall we not grant it also the irrational soul — not the perceptive only, as they say, but also the soul that masters the perceptibles within, ever ranked in a celestial and god-befitting imagination; and the appetitive as well, which is there in another manner, both spirited and desiderative: the desiderative faring well amid the divine ease and the ever-gladsome condition of the animal, the spirited rejoicing in the perfect and august pre-eminence, according to nature, that belongs to the cosmic animal? But surely, if the human is a rational animal, dependent upon a reasoning soul, then assuredly the cosmos too is of this kind; it possesses, then, in far greater measure, the presiding cause that is genuinely self-moved. It makes its circular motion, accordingly, not only by nature but also by choice; and clearly a motion ever ordered, and never missing its proper end; for this is what the star-watching record of the cosmic circuit dictates. Now the self-moved soul, by its own proper changes, makes the again-the-same-and-again of the circulation, its activity coming to be now one and now another. But the selfsame, always, in the same and about the same and toward the same — utterly unvarying in the varying, unchanged in the changing, standing in the moving — what is it that furnishes this to the All? For the self-moved soul makes changing activities: in moving, it is at once moved. The unmoved, then — whence has the cosmos that? If it is everlasting, it has the wholly and always unmoved; and if it is but the longest-lived of animals — let even this be granted for the present, taken from the record4 — yet, remaining through all this time, ever in the same manner unvarying according to the same, circling back from the same to the same with one order and one circulatory manner, in so vast a stretch of time it has endured no change and no variation — unless it were conjoined with some cause that is itself altogether unmoved. It needed, then, that in the All too the self-moved depend from the unmoved, which furnishes to the cosmos its own proper order and its unmoved life.

Note 4. The clause is corrupt in both manuscripts (Kopp despairs of it); the drift, secured by his Latin, is: even granting only an immensely long-lived cosmos, observation shows an unvarying circulation that no self-moved cause alone could supply.

parts.name: Chapter 24 — From the World-Soul to the Hidden Cosmos: the All-Great One and the Ineffable Comprehension · pp. 58–59

lines.text: Chapter 24 — From the World-Soul to the Hidden Cosmos: the All-Great One and the Ineffable Comprehension · pp. 58–59

And if the soul of the All, being first among the encosmic things, is ever perfect and ever happy, this assuredly it could not have had from itself; for what it gives subsistence to from itself is the changing; rather, it has come to participate in the unmoved cause that presides over it. For if it possessed the ever-ordered and measured1 in virtue of its self-motion, then perhaps the human soul too would be ever perfect; for it too is self-moved — and, no doubt, deathless and ever-moving; yet it does not keep its transitive activities forever unvarying, because it stands far removed from the unmoved. And if it has been shown in general that before the self-moved is the unmoved, then before the cosmic self-moved there must preside the cosmic unmoved, proper to the unchanging administration that presides over the cosmos — just as each divine animal has its own, ranked together with its peculiarity. But — not to dwell now upon these things, which carry many grounds of suspicion — before the whole self-moved we shall set the whole unmoved; for it cannot be that the lower is complete-and-whole while the higher is partial. There will be, then, an unmoved cosmos before the self-moved; and by the same argument, before the differentiated, the concentrated and unified cosmos — being all things by way of union that the multiplied cosmos is by way of differentiation, including the one just now described as self-moved; and more still than can be said.

And from this hidden ordering the discourse has ascended to the One itself. Do not suppose it some least one, nor some single property — as it were one form, or one intellect, or one god, or many gods, or even all the gods together and no more — but some all-great One: the simply One itself, comprehensive of all the things that come from itself; or rather, being all those things, and being the One itself before all things — the One of the world that is called hidden. This is a more ineffable cosmos — one that no longer endures even to be called a cosmos, but is all-things-one, undifferentiated; nor even, in strict truth, "all things," but the One before all things, containing all things in its own all-perfect simplicity. And the One being of such greatness, the Ineffable too must be surmised after the same manner: as being at once one ineffable comprehension of all things — and so ineffable that it is neither one, nor a comprehension, nor is, nor is even ineffable. And here let the rashness of our discourse find its limit, begging pardon of the gods for this venturesome eagerness.
Note 1. Reading "measured" (emmetron) with the Munich manuscript, which Kopp prefers, for the printed "ensouled."
Chapter 25 — Whether the One Is Knowable: the Arguments for Knowledge · pp. 59–64

Again, then, from another beginning, we must inquire concerning the One. And first: is the One to be ranked after the wholly ineffable, in the way that, with other intervals, something intermediate must be posited between the ineffable and the sayable? Or is "the ineffable" in a certain manner negative? I say "in a certain manner," not because it is somehow affirmative or positive, but because it is neither negation nor position — neither the name nor the thing — but a complete removal, not being anything at all; for it is nothing of the things that are — nay, it is not even itself, in any way whatever. If, then, we define the ineffable name so — as not even a name — then everything that is "before the One" would be of this nature; for beyond the One we can surmise nothing. And if the One is the first surmisable, in whatever fashion, why do we seek anything more before it — there where there is neither the "more" nor the "one"? Concerning That, then, let us be released from the meddlesome perplexity and helplessness; and let us inquire once more about the One itself: whether it is simply sayable, or whether what we seek is something between the unsayable and the sayable. Much, indeed, has of necessity been said already about the nature of the One, on account of the principle beyond even this; for holding fast to the One, we kept trying to speak about That which cannot be held. But now let the leading account of the One itself be given; and this must be asked before all: whether it is in some way knowable, or wholly unknowable.

Well then: if we too are able to analyze to the very last, up to the simplest of all and the most comprehensive of all — which can only be posited as the One — then assuredly we do in some way cognize this very thing; and in still greater measure the better knowledge attains it. Second: if in conceiving the One we conceive one thing, and in conceiving the many something else opposed to it, then we have a conception of the One; and if we conceive this form-like one, then also the uncircumscribed one before the forms — the one that is one in every way, in respect of what is in every way simplest. And besides these: since each thing whatever is also some one — and to be one and to be form are not the same thing, just as neither are to be being and to be one — then, gathering each set together: as forms, we gather them into the one uncircumscribed substance of Intellect; as beings, into the one undifferentiated union of Being; and as ones, into the one incomposite unity of the One. For as, in gathering infinite points, you make one point, so, in concentrating infinite ones together, you make one — the most comprehensive one of all.

Further: everything whatever that is proposed to conception must either be many alone, with no share of the one — but in that way it will not even stand still, being infinitized, and in that way we shall conceive nothing whatever of it — or be many participating in the one; and then, together with the cognizing of the many, the one too will somehow be known — the very thing that halted the outpouring of the many toward the infinite; or else the one itself, remaining one, is proposed by itself, separated from the conception of the many so far as may be; for even if it is not easy to stand altogether away from multitude, still we are led up rather toward the One, and we purify our conception, for all that, in its direction.

Again: knowing comes about either by direct intuition, or by syllogism — which is either a certain soft and dim knowledge, seeing as it were from afar, yet leaning upon the necessity of consecution, or a kind of bastard reasoning, which does not even have the support from afar, but conceives some things from others — the reasoning by which we are accustomed to cognize matter, and privation, and in general non-being. If, then, this too is some mode of knowledge, perhaps it is in this way that we know even the One beyond all things — as Plato hands down, at one time leading us up by analogy to what is exempt from substance, at another stripping that nature bare by the negations: the nature which, at the end, he says does not even "be," but is only one, without share of being; for from it comes being; and since the name and the definition and opinion and knowledge are of being, he takes these away as well. And if intellection is of the intelligible, and the intelligible is of being, this too must be removed, as being composite and not fitting what is simplest. But if there is a unitary knowledge, such as is the knowledge of the gods, standing according to the one and above the unified, this will touch the One by direct intuition; whereas the coarser knowledge, such as ours, will barely apprehend the One by bastard reasoning. Yet someday we also shall cast our intuition upon it — when, as he says, we incline the radiance of the soul, putting forth the flower of our unitary knowledge. And that Plato posits it as knowable he showed plainly, calling it the greatest study; and in the Sophist, indeed, declaring it to be before Being, he rested the demonstration upon the conception of the one alone.

Apart from these things: if there is a unitary knowledge — as the divine possessions make plain6 — then, just as the divided knowledge of the many beings is gathered into the one conception of the one being, so also the knowledge of the many unitary knowables; for clearly to the unitary knowledge we shall oppose a unitary knowable. For surely the participated god will not know the other things and be ignorant of himself; nor will he know himself only according to being, and not also according to the one — above all with the unitary knowledge in which he rejoices, the unitary intellection which he himself possesses; for as Intellect possesses it by dependence, so also does the very one that rules before it. He will know himself, then; and he himself is the one; he will know, therefore, the one as well. And to speak generally: as the intellective is twofold, so we say the intelligible too is twofold — the one unified, the other unitary; the one substantial, that other supersubstantial; and we call "intelligible" what is knowable by intellection. There is, then, a unitary knowable also; and the knowable is some one; many, then, are the unitary knowables — including those I was just now going through. So let the division of these many knowledges be gathered up into one whole-complete knowledge of the whole-complete One — which is the simple concentration of the many henads.

We say further: if some one is knowable, does the nature of the One refuse knowledge altogether? As the simple form is knowable, because this particular form is too, and the simple being, because this being is, so also the simple one would be knowable, because this one is; for what is everywhere of a kind is such precisely as such: a certain form, but as form; a certain being, but as being; a certain one, then, but as one. And if the concentration overleaps us — dragged down as we are by the Titanic war — what wonder? For we do not know in that mode, as Plato himself says in the Letters; and yet, for all that, we seem to determine many things about those matters too, touching them somehow not immediately, but as through certain transparent bodies — the forms awakened within us.

Further still: the knowable too must begin from the One — and so the philosophers say; for all things, they say, begin from the gods; and this will be shown by us in what follows, when we come to it. So the first knowable is among gods, since the first knower is also; and where the one correlative is, there by nature is the other; for these are relatives. If, then, the first knower is one, the first one must be knowable — since among beings the first knowable is precisely the first intelligible and being itself. But above all: the One taken simply is all things; for it is not some one thing, but all things one, as Linus said, and Pythagoras; so that it is knowable as well; for the knowable is some one of all things; in the One, then, this too is pre-contained. From these arguments and the like, one might suppose that the very One before all things is knowable.
Note 6. hoi enthousiasmoi: states of divine possession, taken as empirical evidence that a unitary, non-discursive mode of knowing exists.
Chapter 26 — The Counter-Arguments: the One beyond Knowledge · pp. 64–66

But again one might raise perplexities, looking back at those arguments — and first against what was mentioned last. If the One is all things, why is it knowable rather than unknowable? For the unknowable too is there first; this also is some one of the things that come after the One — the very thing that is counter-divided against the knowable, and is one of the many. And what is beyond even the One is neither knowable nor unknowable. The One, then, is unknowable — at least by an argument of this kind. And on other grounds: if it sprang up first from the unsayable, clearly it stands least of all apart from it, and is still overshadowed by that one's unknowability. Besides this: if all things are in it according to the One, nothing in it is differentiated; so it is neither knowable nor unknowable, but only one — and all things one. Further: if it is knowable because it is all things, it will also be knowing; for this too is one of all things. And yet what would it know? Not what is before it; for that is in no way knowable. Not itself; for it would then have a doubleness, turning back upon itself, and would no longer be one; and it would be active — it, the thing before all activity and power; for these are seen in some differentiation from substance, whereas it is above all differentiation, and is just this: one only. Nor will it know the things after itself; for then it will be active, and its activity will be directed toward the worse — and that, an activity which is the first of all activities. And consider: even among the things that come after, the first knowledge is that of the better, the second that of oneself, and the third that of what comes after oneself.

Apart from these things: even if the "what-is-one" is knowable, and the "one-something," still not, on that account, the simply one. Let the unitary be known as intellective, if you like, or as vital, or as the supersubstantial one that shines down upon being; but the simply One is beyond even these; so that both the arguments from the concentrations and those from the analogy of being carry us only to this one — the one seated above being. For as the one-being among beings is the first intelligible, so the One among the supersubstantials is the first supersubstantial; what is beyond, therefore, would be unknowable. And as for the bastard reasoning — the one through negations, and the one through analogy, and further the syllogism that compels by consecution, which does not know that it knows all these things4 — perhaps it belongs to a reasoning that treads on emptiness, knowing some things from others; and in general, if it does not know the simple, it would not know the whole premise, and so not the whole syllogism either. The analogy, moreover, could be framed even about things that in no way are: as the sun is to the seen and the seeing, so this one to the knowing and the known — but the sun we know; the one we do not know; and the negation removes what we know, while what it leaves behind, we do not know. And Plato, too, does not think the One knowable without remainder: first, in the Parmenides he says "therefore it is not even known," removing knowledge universally; and in the Republic, though he seems to make it familiar, he says nonetheless that the knower and the known stand in need of the light, in order that the apprehending power be flooded by the light, the knowable becoming, as it were, more distinct — for the knowable also looks toward the knower, awakening it, as it were, to its proper activity. If, then, the One is knowable, it must be flooded by the light; and yet how could the One be flooded by its own light? For the light of truth, among those beings, flows off from the One itself.

But perhaps our conception of the One, in apprehending what is determined over against the others, apprehends it together with them — which is why it co-manifests the apprehension of the many; so that even if we perform the gathering, we are still riding upon the same conception, the one opposed to the many. But the conception of the One ought to be without opposite, and one, and complete; even the concentration falls short of the unitary. And "all things according to the one" belongs to a one of that derivative kind — since Being, too, is all things according to the unified; and the simplest in that mode is what stands proximately before the many; for the simple means to be free of multitude. But That is beyond the many henads themselves, since differentiation comes only after it; for as, among unified things, the simplest is the wholly unified and undifferentiated, so, among the ones, the simplest is the supersubstantial unified — a "unitary unified," if one must speak so; while what is called the simply One is above even this unfolding; so that even the last term of that unfolding would be the one which indeed we call unitary.

Note 4. I.e. discursive inference holds its conclusions without the direct acquaintance that would make them knowledge; the text is compressed. kenembatein, "to tread on emptiness," repeats the treatise's signature word for thought stepping where there is no footing (cf. Chapters 5 and 7).
Chapter 27 — Neither Procession nor Reversion: Union beyond Knowledge · pp. 66–69

It must be examined, too, whether even the Unified is, as yet, knowable; for the knowable is gathered up in it and, as it were, confounded undifferentiatedly with the rest, so that all is one together — a single concentration of all things — and the knowable is not yet some one thing showing itself by itself. Such, then, are the perplexities one might raise against what was said. But apart from these, considering the problem itself by itself, we ask whether the One, at least, can simply be familiar to knowledge. If, then, the One is itself only the one, and nothing else of all things — neither by participation, since nothing is before it; nor by existence, since it is one; nor by cause, since it does not even have in itself a cause of anything that comes from it, for nothing is there beside the one — how shall we say that it is both one and knowable? For neither is it itself both knowable and one — these are not the same — nor, if the knowable is something other, is it still one. And again: if it is knowable, it is so either by participation — and then the knowable-by-existence will be before it; or by cause — and then it is not yet knowable, but the knowable comes after it and from another; or by existence — and then That is not by existence ; rather, the compound will be the one knowable, so that it is one by participation — if indeed the by-existence resides in the compound.

Further: if that One is all things and the all, as both Linus and Pythagoras said, while to be all things is not to be some "what" — and to be knowable is to be some what — then the consequence is plain: what is all things is not knowable. Further: the knowable is the desired of the knower; knowledge, then, is a reversion of the knower upon the knowable; and every reversion is a conjoining; and the effect conjoins with its cause either by knowledge, or by life, or by being itself. Before the cognitive reversion, then, is the vital; and before this, the substantial; and before the ones thus divided is the simple reversion-and-conjoining — either identical with simple knowledge or, what is truer, the union even before this; since the one is prior to intellect and to life and to substance, and prior, I say, to each of their unitary counterparts. Union, then, is beyond knowledge. What reverts to the One, therefore, is borne toward it neither as a knower nor as toward a knowable, but as one to one — through union, not through knowledge; for each thing must revert to the first through the first reversion, and knowledge is not first, but at the least third; whereas this union is the common root of the three — or rather, what is truer, the union sought is even before the common.

But perhaps this very thing deserves inquiry: whether it is possible at all to be conjoined to That through reversion. For nothing can proceed from it — so that something might also revert after the procession. How could anything proceed without being differentiated? And how could anything be differentiated from the One, and not fall out into the nothing? For whatever has in any way stepped outside the One is nothing. And if each thing comes to be one-and-not-one, so that the not-one may remain and not be scattered into the nothing — as being bound fast by the one — still, precisely insofar as it is one, it exists together with the One; or rather, it did not even proceed from the One in respect of the one; no, nor yet in respect of the not-one; rather, the one always anticipates the differentiation, however it arises, of the not-one; so that neither does anything revert toward the One — from which it never proceeded. Further: the differentiated is differentiated from a differentiated, as other is other than an other. If, then, something reverts, it has been differentiated just so far as it reverts; then the One too has been differentiated from it; the One, then, has undergone differentiation, and is not only one but differentiated as well — therefore not one. Next: what would be the cause of the differentiation in it? Either the One itself — and how the One should be a cause of differentiation is hard even to feign; for the One is cause of union; of differentiation, the many — or whatever else it may be; but of this hereafter. Or, if not itself, something else will differentiate it: either what is before it — which is absurd, for then the differentiating power will stand before the unifying, the worse before the better; or what is after it — and how is the cause to be affected by its own effect? Besides, what is this "after it" that has proceeded? The argument is in danger of being overturned into the same place, every procession differentiating, and the cause of the differentiation being sought, always, in between — and this to infinity. Nothing, then, proceeds from the One, nor does procession begin from there; rather it begins from that first thing which can differentiate both itself from what comes after it, and those things from itself; whereas the One, contrariwise, is itself united with what comes after it, and does not allow those things to be differentiated from itself. If, then, nothing proceeds from it, neither does anything revert upon it; much less, then, through knowledge — much less as a knower toward a knowable; for these stand in the greatest differentiation toward one another. And even if some faintest differentiation from it should be devised — belonging to the first thing proceeded — certainly the differentiation from That will not become so great as to require a cognitive reversion. Such things one might say in denying the stretching-up of cognition toward the One.

Who, then, shall be appointed arbiter between such arguments, disputing with one another about matters so great? The truest concerning these things the gods themselves know; but we too must dare to bring our aporetic birth-pangs to term, so far as divine providence grants of the truth that is sought — and so far as our own power allows.

parts.name: Chapter 28 — The Not-One Rooted in the One: Differentiation without Reciprocity · pp. 69–75

lines.text: Chapter 28 — The Not-One Rooted in the One: Differentiation without Reciprocity · pp. 69–75

What, then, the procession of the things that come from the One is, and in what manner it is accomplished, and how one might escape the perplexities raised against it, we shall pursue hereafter — very soon indeed; for now, only so much must be taken: that after the One there are all things; for That is not alone, but the things after it are many and various. And that these are not That is evident; so they are differentiated from it — and if not insofar as each is one, then insofar as it is not-one. Now this "not-one" is not a negation, but a position of what is beside the one; and this too, nevertheless, is one — yet not insofar as it is not-one and beside the one, but because not even this has stood apart from the One altogether: it is, as it were, rooted in the One, and the not-one exists through the one. So, to one who looks closely, the not-one is differentiated from the One by its own nature, being differentiated by the nature of the not-one; but its one still holds to the One and does not stand away from it — not even by so much; since the not-one too (or whatever it may be, beside the one) is nevertheless still one by participation, through having become not-one. Does it not, then, make itself not-one, while the One makes it, and makes it as one, anticipating its differentiation by its own union? The not-one, accordingly, is differentiated from the One, in that it becomes not-one; but the One is not differentiated from the not-one — the One which makes one even the not-one, even what has stood apart: so far is it from being differentiated that it is not let go even when the other lets go, but forestalls, by its unifying participation, the differentiating existence of that other; for there could not even be an existence of anything without the one — so that the participation constitutes the very existence; that is to say, the union constitutes the differentiation. And at this we shall not greatly wonder, nor so much as distrust what has been said, if we consider the nature of the One: that it is of a nature neither to effect nor to undergo differentiation.

Let us examine the matter also in the case of the visible corrector of all truth, the sun. To the opened eye that does not see, because of a glaucoma, the sun is present, just as to the seeing eye; but the eye is not present to the sun, because of its own standing-away. And let us not fear the demands of logic; for these have their place among things of one kind, where the relative terms are of roughly equal worth, or kindred. Why, even the form is other than matter; is then matter, too, other than the form? But otherness is a form! Matter, then, is not "other" in the form's own manner: the form is differentiated from matter without matter's being differentiated in its turn; the differentiation has remained in the form, unable to pass over into matter. If, then, something was differentiated in this fashion from what is not differentiated, what prevents the differentiated itself from healing its differentiation by reversion — so that not only is the One present to it, but it also to the One? And clearly according to the measure of its differentiation, from near or from far; for as each thing is of a nature to be differentiated from it, so far also can it revert toward it. And as the One remains undifferentiated relative to each thing differentiated, so also relative to each thing reverting it remains the same, and is one end of all things, undifferentiated. But as, being the same, it is present with each thing that proceeds, it is called by that thing's peculiar property — substantial one, vital one, intellective one — being itself everywhere one, surnamed from the participants, not itself divided, I say, by the many properties of the gods; rather, I contemplate the simply one in each thing before the particular one, though I name it, all the same, from the things to which it is present, undifferenced though it is. Thus, surely, each thing too, meeting it as an end proper to itself according to its own differentiation, names it from its own perfecting that comes from There, positing it to be of the same kind as that which it met — and as that which fell to its lot. For That also, being all things according to the existence of the one, is present with each thing as its own proper root, and appears to each as its own proper end. For all the things that exist dividedly — those things That is, according to the one: not in potency, as one might suppose, nor by way of cause, as of things not yet; but, if it is lawful to say so, by an existence that both is and is of things that are — yet one existence, and one of an all-bearing nature.

As, then, with each of the others, so too with the knower the one is present, as a knowing one; and it stands forth as knowable — not by being either of the two, but by the compound above each; or, to speak more exactly, above the compound. For it is all things not from differentiation, but before differentiation; thus it will be, in truth, all things before all things: not loosely, as in potency, nor by way of cause, as being not yet all things, but all things by the undifferentiated existence — not the unified existence before all things, but the existence super-simplified above all things by its own simplicity, being all the things, in kind and in number, that have proceeded by differentiation. And That is what is all things in the strict sense; for the differentiation has dimmed the things differentiated from it, by its own nature. Moreover, each of these is more sovereignly its own self within the one coordination of all things, and, falling away even from this, becomes ever more partial and inferior; except that, among the properties, some stand more akin to the lesser differentiation, others to the greater — which is why different ones are uttered in different regions. But about these matters this is not the moment to pursue the precise examination. The One, then, all things before all things, is both knowable and knowing — and each of the others; though not, as I now speak these words, and as each is each (for those are in differentiation, and counter-divided against one another), but as the one co-existing, in its own peculiar way, with each of the differentiated things with which it co-exists: the one of man is the truer man; the one of soul, the truer soul; the one of body, the truer body; so too the one of sun and of moon — the truer moon, the truer sun; and yet it is none of these differentiated things whose truer reality it is, but only the one, seated above its own self. And gather for me also the one present-with-each, which seems to have been divided, into the remaining and undivided and really one; for perhaps it was never divided at all, but, remaining the same, is present to all and to each as its own — not divided, because, being all things according to the one, it has no need of division. Does it then know? Or is knowing proper to differentiation? Then neither is it known; for this too belongs to differentiation. Or is this also true, that knowing is set in opposition to being-known — and nothing of that kind fits That? For neither does "one" fit it, nor "all things"; these too are opposed, and divide our conception. If we look toward the simple, we lose the all-great all-perfection of it; if we conceive all things together, we obliterate its one and simple. The cause is that we are ourselves divided, and look to divided properties; yet, yearning all the same for whatever knowledge of That may be had, we weave together all things at once, in the hope of being able even so to lay hold of the great nature — guarding, for all that, against the multitude of all things that creeps in with them, or against a straitened isolation of the one. Thus it is that we bring forward the "one" itself, for the account of the eldest principle, as a kind of symbol of its simplicity — as the "all things" is a kind of symbol of its comprehension of all; while what stands upon both, or before both, we can neither conceive nor name. And what wonder if we are so affected about That, when even its differentiated knowledge is unitary — a knowledge we do not perceive? About Being, too, we have undergone other things of the same kind: attempting to see Being, we let it go and run round its elements, limit and unlimited, as they say; and if we conceive the truer thought — that this too is a unified plenitude of all things — the "of all things" carries us down into multitude, while the "unified" obliterates the "all things." But not even this is yet to be wondered at; for when we wish to see each of the forms, we run round its elements; and when we long for its one, we lose the elements; each form is at once one and many — not one in one respect and many in another, but through and through, as a whole, such; and being unable to seize it all at once, we are content to cast ourselves upon it with the dividedness of our own conceptions.
Chapter 29 — The Sudden Light; the One between the Knowable and the Unsayable; the Birth-Pang of Knowledge · pp. 75–80

Climbing ever up the steep toward what is more undivided, we somehow have a co-perception, even within division, of the uniform; at any rate we hold division cheap beside the gathered apprehension of That — and we could not so much as think this together, were there not some trace of the gathered intellection quivering within us. And this is the light of truth that is kindled of a sudden, as from fire-sticks rubbed together; for the divided conceptions, mustered together and exercised against one another along the summit that converges upon the uniform and simple, end as it were in a meeting-point — like the meeting at the center, in a circle, of the ends of the many straight lines pressing from the circumference toward the center; and though they remain divided in their condition, yet, as they are thrown against the undivided, some trace of knowledge of that form is shaken loose in us beforehand — just as, the center being invisible, the single coincidence of the circle toward its middle, conceived as equal from every side, furnishes a certain dim presentation of it.

In the same manner we ascend also to Being: first conceiving each form — which strikes us as divided — to be not only undivided but unified, confounding (if one must speak so) the many in each; then, taking all of them together in their distinctness and removing their circumscriptions — as one might make of many waters one uncircumscribed water — except that we conceive the unified itself out of all of them into the one water before all, as the form of water is before the waters that have been marked off. In just this way, then, we are unfolded into the One as well: first gathering together, and then letting go of the things gathered, into that One's pre-eminence, super-simplified above them. Have we then, in our ascent, met it as the knowable? Or, wishing to meet it as such, have we been dissolved into the unknowing? Or is each true? For from afar we meet it as knowable; and when we are unified with it close at hand, having passed beyond the knowing-of-the-one within us, we are brought round into being one — that is, into being unknowing instead of knowing. This conjunction, then, is of one with one, above knowledge; the other was of a knower with a knowable. And how should it be knowable, if it is only one? Not, certainly, in such a way that knowledge could press against it; nor yet knowable by the bastard reasoning in the manner described, by which we cognize even matter — though matter does not possess the knowable; for the knowable too is a kind of form, or some one of the things that are, whereas matter is the non-being and formless. As, then, they say the crooked is known by the straight, so by the knowable we surmise, beneath it, the unknowable; and even this, nevertheless, is a mode of knowledge: That also, then, is knowable just so far — namely, that it does not abide the approach of knowledge. From afar it presents itself as knowable, and gives forth its own token; but the nearer knowledge approaches, the less — not, as with other things, the more — it knows that which it approaches; for the knowledge is unstrung by the One into unknowing. And reasonably: since knowledge stands in need of differentiation, as was said before; but as it draws near the One, the differentiation folds itself up into union, so that the knowledge too dissolves into unknowing. So, surely, Plato's analogy itself demands: the sun is the first thing we attempt to see, and from afar we do see it; but the nearer we come to it, the less we see it; and at the last we see neither other things nor it, becoming, instead of an illumined eye, the very light.

Is then the One unknowable by its own nature — even though the unknowable is something other than the one, while the One wills to be by itself, and with nothing else? Rather: what is counter-divided against the knowable is the unknowable; but what is beyond the One is ineffable in every way — that of which we confess neither to know it nor to be ignorant of it, but to have toward it our very ignorance surpassed; by whose neighborhood the One too is overshadowed: for, lying nearest the unmanageable principle — if it is lawful to speak so — it remains, as it were, within the inner sanctuary of that silence. This is why, in Plato, the discourses about it overturn themselves; for it lies near the every-way self-overturning of the First. Yet it differs from That in this: that it is one simply, and is, according to the one, also all things together; and this is above the one and the all, simpler than both; while That is not even this. Insofar, then, as it has stepped forth from the ineffable — yet not the determinate one (for that is completely knowable), but the all-things-one; nor again "all things" so far as they are marked off (for these are still more knowable, being many forms), but the together-all-one, which from the "one" has its simplicity, purified clean of the many, and from the "all" has its refusal of the one's determinateness and narrowing: each of these is knowable, and the compound of the two, as knowable-in-two. But what is before both — the very thing we indicate by means of that compound — does not, of itself, abide knowledge; it is known through the image of the compound, as being, before the compound, of such a kind as the compound is together with it. And if one must speak by division: the really knowable is what is contemplated within some determination — which is also, by now, in a way a form; for this, by its own circumscription, abides the knowledge that circumscribes; and that is why knowledge begins from things of this kind. What runs clean contrary to this is the wholly unsayable, which suffers no handle at all. And of what lies in between, one part is before the knowable — namely the Unified, escaping even this determining or circumscribing knowledge; the other is before the unsayable — namely the one simply, and all-things-according-to-the-one, affording about itself a slightest and dimmest surmise. And if there is something in between even these, we shall attend to it when we come to distinguish each of them.

For now we say this, setting it as a seal upon such a one: that what we say, it is not; nor do we know it as one and as all-things-together; but what from this we labor with — I mean a cognitive birth-pang — that it is; for the knowledge of it has advanced as far as the birth-pang; but when it tries to issue into utterance and articulation, it falls away from That, into offspring of its own. And this is what the philosopher Proclus, in the Monobiblos, has called the ineffable axiom — the axiom answering to the knowledge that labors toward That — as the sayable axiom is the one answering to the knowledge already articulated. This too is the cause of the ever-equivocating assay and judgment concerning it, now as knowable, now as unknowable — for in one way it is the former, in another the latter. And for this reason Plato, in the Letters, takes away from it the "of what sort" and the "what," and accuses this of being the cause of all evils — the division proper to ourselves, into the what and the what-sort; for in very truth this is the Titanic affection we suffer; and yet even this affection we attempt to carry up to what is holiest of all and most undivided of every whole. If, then, the what and the what-sort must be removed from the knowledge of it, the "one" too must be removed; for this is a "what" among all things; and "all things" likewise, for the all are certain "whats" — each of the all is a what, so that together also they are certain whats. If, then, it is known neither as one nor as all, what would it be? Away, man! Do not bring in the "what": this very thing blocks you from the knowledge of That — that you expect to hear some "what"; whereas, if you take away the what and the what-sort, it will appear to you, so far as may be, what it is; for it is precisely the not-what and not-of-what-sort, but before these — the very thing that can neither be said (for every name is a what, and indicative of some what) nor easily thought (for every thought is of a what and of some what-sort; and even if you gather all things together, they are of-what-sorts and whats, being of certain qualified things). And so intellect itself, as intellect, being a contemplator of qualified whats, labors indeed with a conception of that nature, but cannot bring it forth — not even intellect; rather, on the contrary, it gathers the birth-pang in upon itself, and leads it up toward what is simplest, wholly uncircumscribed, and altogether unqualified by the circumscribing quality, whether common to all together or proper to each — the very thing that Plato, in accord with the Oracles, exhorts us to do: if somehow we might be able, forgetting our own conceptions, to run back up to that birth-pang. Or rather: that pang is of a nature to recognize That, but to report it to no one — except that it removes the obstacle that stands in the way of such a projection, namely the thinking of it as a what-sort and as a what. And if someone compels it to teach concerning That, it will put forward in place of itself a second or third conception, which, uttering the together-things in their distinctness, seems to utter That: as, that the simplest is the principle, and the first, and the all-containing, and the generative of all, and the desired of all, and the mightiest of all — and whatever else one will enumerate in order, of which That is the cause, or rather the mightiest and most honorable of all such terms, as those just named, and above all "the one," and "all things," on the grounds already given. But when these have been said, a conception better than this one will take hold, declining the determinate and multiform in an account of the principle, and concentrating all into one uniform nature, and judging this — the unified — worthy to be set before the determinate. Yet the first birth-pang of the cognitive power, the one that remains within and does not go forth, will not accept even this concentration, as being pregnant with the multitude and not yet having brought it forth; itself laboring with the one that is simple through and through and seated above all multitude — which, unknowable as it is, nevertheless labors-forth the knowable, if it is lawful to say so: not as something added to that One; rather its nature, not being wholly ineffable, hands over to surmise an unarticulated knowable, answering to the birth-pang — the surmise not going forth into knowledge, the knowable not going forth into being known.
Chapter 30 — How the One Is All Things, and How the Unified: the Mixture in the Third God · pp. 80–81

Come then: since all things are — there being nothing that the One is not, as we say — let us inquire into this very thing. First, in what way it is true that the One is all things; second, whether it is all things equally; and third, what the difference is between the One's being all things and the Unified's being all things. For each of the two is all things undifferentiatedly — I mean the supersubstantial being; or rather the unitary one; for this too is all things according to the one, the one seated above being, which would also be said, before that being, to be unified, having pre-grasped the everlastingness of the mixed. Or rather, this latter already shows forth the supreme union out of many, and the first birth-pang of the mixture of multitude; or rather of multitude's mixture; for before it the multitude shone forth, as did the one; and from both, coming together into it, it projects the one unified and mixed existence upon them — which has become its existence, the existence of Being: not the one, nor the many, but the mixture of these, shining forth in the third god. This is the very thing which the mixture and the mixed are — which indeed we call the Unified, what is twofold. If, then, this too is all things, still it is all things unifiedly; since before it, too, the multitude is all things — and is all things more sovereignly than the one; for the multitude is all things in that the all are many, whereas the one is all things in that the all are one, and all according to the one.

But perhaps someone might raise a difficulty: if the One too is all things, will there not be, before it, the only-one as well — since "the one" has a simpler conception than "the one that is all things"; for "all things" is an addition to "the one"? And if one wishes, one may go to meet the objector:

calling the multitude "one-all" — one by existence, all by participation — while the one is one only, and not yet all. Yet, for all that, it is truer to say this: that the multitude too is in the One; for this also is from it, of another sort, by way of cause — a cause not marked off from that in which it is; for there is as yet no determination there. Rather, because the One is such, before all things, as the all things after the One are, the One is even more all things than the all things are; for this is the cause of the all things' being all things: the One is. In another way, then, the One is all things before the multitude; but in its own respect it is the only-one, and the simplest of all; for it is simplest precisely because it is most comprehensive — and therefore all things.

parts.name: Chapter 31 — All Things Equally — More than Equally: Order without Order · pp. 81–84

lines.text: Chapter 31 — All Things Equally — More than Equally: Order without Order · pp. 81–84

Is it then equally? How not? For all things are according to the one, and there is nothing that is not according to the one; and the according-to-the-one is even more than equal — "more equal than equally," if one may really speak so. But the things from it are according to an order, one before another; whereas in it they are without order, because order belongs to differentiation. Nay, the order is not even by way of cause; for then differentiation too would be by way of cause, and the causes would be differentiated — unless indeed the order there, and the differentiation, be not by way of cause but in a greater manner than by the cause; for it is according to the one, and the wholly-one; and on this account all things are equally.

Why, then, are some of them more proper to it, others less proper — as we say: the One itself, the all-together, the simplest, the first, the beyond-all, the Good, and whatever wishes to exhibit the single principle? For these a man of sense would say about it; but as to what man is, or any of the more dishonored things — the very last, or the effect, or matter, or any such — no one, unless he were mad, would dare to say. The cause of this is that none of those determinate terms holds true of it — not the first, not the last, not any of the means; but, seeing the order of these very things, which they have toward one another (how some produce and some are produced, some order and some are ordered), and wishing to indicate, from the things we know, something about that which we do not know, we dedicate to it the terms elder by nature: the causes to the pre-cause, and the things that first proceeded from it to what never proceeded — inasmuch as these too proceeded least of all. What then? Did That also produce the first things first, the second second? For so the order would appear in it too. Or does That produce all things together, while they do not come forth together, but the one produces itself earlier, the other later? And how are the better separated from the One earlier than the worse? Or, even if they are prior because more strongly braced toward self-subsistence, still they are not on that account separated in a greater degree, but least of all, by that same power; for what proceeds through weakness — perhaps the prior things would be left behind as second to the One — which is just what the weaker souls undergo, standing away from intellect before the stronger, which are second perhaps and only with difficulty. As it is, the procession from the causes comes about according to power; and some things are more self-sufficient toward subsistence, while others are by nature not able to produce themselves at all, but the whole of them is given subsistence from elsewhere. And if That produces them, it furnishes the things more like itself before the more unlike, and the things more like it — not because it has pre-grasped the order, but because from it is the order too, as also all the other things. This, then, is so. And we name it from the things more like it. The things produced, then, are unequal; but the producer is equal toward all, and still more than equal; for it is one only —3 both as itself, and as being all things, and as producing all things; for it is according to the one, whatever you might say about it.

Note 3. en gar esti monon, "for it is one only": the producer's equality toward all rests on its being one — the same one as itself, as all things, and as the cause of all. The argument closes the second question (whether equally) and opens the third.
Chapter 32 — More than the All: in What Sense the One Is, and Is Not, All Things · pp. 84–85

But the first of all the things inquired must now be resolved: in what way is it all things? For perhaps it is not even possible for the One to be all things. And what need is there for it to be all things? For the only-one suffices for being the cause of all; and if it is the cause of all, it would not be all; and if the all are many, the one at least would not be many. It seems, then, that those who said "the One is all things" said it in defense of the conception — against the more facile one, which ranks That as some one among all things; for it is not some "what," but all things, and more indeed than all things. "For the principle," they say, "is half of the whole" — or rather the whole — but, more truly, more than the whole; and these things the children of the Pythagoreans philosophize. For in truth, if we mean the whole — both the principle and what is from the principle — and the principle is the counterweight to the things from it, then the principle is half of the whole. But if the whole is more sovereign than the principle, while the things from it are, as it were, an imitation of it and, as it were, a thing hung in suspense from it — and this too is true to say — then the principle is the prior grasp of the things from it; for not even the causes in the producer are the producer itself; rather, what is productive even of the causes in itself would be the principle, more than the whole. But if it follows that we say these things, then the One would not, in truth, be the all things, but the all things would be after the One; for we do not even deposit in it the causes of all, that in this way at least it might be all things, by way of the totality of the causes. In no way, then, is the One all things, strictly to speak. But it is said so that we may conceive not the least thing, but the most comprehensive of all and the greatest; and not this as the cosmos, but as the simplest of all; and not even this as one of the things in the cosmos, like the last rim of the fixed sphere, but as all things poured back into its simplicity and no longer willing to be all things.

Or, the names being rightly given, is it right to hymn That also as all things? For of each multitude the unified is an undifferentiated concentration — the multitude being, as it were, the differentiated; and before the unified, everywhere, is the one of each; and the one is just as many as the unified, since it proceeded into just so many; for it is so many because it proceeded into so many. For the One did not step down into a one, but into a unified; nor did the unified step into a unified, but into an all-differentiated — there, precisely, where we clearly think "all things." But as in the center the circle is folded up, and all the lines from the center, so also in the Unified is the whole multitude of differentiation; and by the same proportion, in the One, both the center itself and the things folded up in the center are all alike simplified. And thus we say that all things are one, and that the One is all things — and still more, because all things are according to the one; and the all things are not altogether one, whereas that One is altogether all things.
Chapter 33 — The Fore-Appearing Conception and the Determinate One: the One as Principle and as Good · pp. 85–89

Upon these things it is worth inquiring how the fore-appearing conception differs from the determinate one. And concerning this — of which we speak, the one incommensurate with our conceptions — does the ready conception ring true of the ready one, or the determinate conception of the other things? Clearly it will not fit that undetermined one. But if this conception is removed from it, we have no other knowledge of it; so that in vain do we even call it "one." And again: of this one, once it is cognized, we conceive nothing simpler; so that this would be the first principle of all things; for the Good, too, seemed to be most first — wherefore nothing can be mightier than it; so that this too is a principle of all things; and on this account our conceptions bring us to the same point, the One and the Good. And how is the first thing in determination and counter-division? And how is the first a form? For "the one" and "the Good" are some one among the many forms. Besides this: as motion and rest are a single opposition, and otherness and sameness, and many others of the kind, so too "one" and "many" are a certain single opposition; and in each opposition there is the better and the worse, as one pair, though the better and the worse stand in a coordinate account; and indeed the opposites mutually participate in one another, as is shown in the Parmenides, so that the one and the many too are in one another. Is it then not a principle, because the many are unified with this one? Yet insofar as the many are unified, this is one; and the one in them is participated, whereas the one by existence and upon itself is before the many — before all things, therefore; therefore this one is the principle of all things. For even if the many are set over against it, still not as coordinate, but as effects toward the cause.

Apart from these things: if the One is a gathering-together of all things — for its proper work is the making-one, and it is the cause of the mixture; and the one-making and gathering-together of all things is elder and more honorable than the things gathered and made-one — it is manifest that the One is the principle of all things, above which it is counter-divided against all, as cause against effects. And this is what we cognize as one. But is there not some other one, namely the one spoken of as genus? It must be said that the one spoken of as genus, we cognize as being some one of all things — as the many: I mean the form, and the good, and the beautiful; for the determinate conception is of a determinate thing. But that One is to be taken not as one-making, but as all-making; for it is both multitude-making, and good-making, and whole-making — and not even one, since it makes being by its own single simplicity. And if the one-making is not to be called "one" strictly — and if there is no proper name of it — then each thing is to be called it: not only one-making, but also multitude-making; and "one," if you wish, and "many"; or rather, all things before the many and the all.

What then? Does not Socrates, in the Philebus, gather together all things and make That the cause of the mixture? All things, surely; but putting it forward in respect of the one property only, the gathering and one-making; for of this the mixture had need. Since the limit too was one, and the unlimited one, and the mixed one — and That is the cause not of the mixture alone, as it seems to be said, but also of the elements. And that Socrates does not bring his thought to bear upon this one, but as upon something august and ineffable, he made plain: letting it itself go, as wholly hidden, but bringing forward, as its tokens, the three monads in its forecourt — the three of the One. And yet it was easy to conceive this form-like one, and to cast into the mind the gathering and one-making of the many, and this rather than truth and beauty and symmetry. Further, then: not the limit only and the unlimited were the elements, but also the one and the two; and if these alone were the elements, so that the one was taken as an element —

upon these, what was being sought? The elements, both the others and the one, lay ready before; but the mixed out of these was being sought, how it came to be. The mixed, then, is all things together — the elements and the compound of the elements; wherefore it had need of the cause of all, that it might become all things for the sake of all, as that cause is before all. And how could it have participated in this, unless the things coming together were commensurate and sympathetic toward one another, and brightened by the same light of truth? For these were, as it were, forerunning traces, the causes of the common — the cause of all things. And the determinate one suffers something from the many — either as underlying its property, in respect of its constitution out of many, or as set over against them, since rest too is moved and motion stands still; whereas That is wholly simple. Therefore it is not worthy even to be called "one," because we conceive the one over against the many, and conceive being and being-moved and standing and other and same, so that it is many by participation, but one by the existence of the property.

But the most first of the things perplexed-over is most true: that we do not have a conception of That, complete and one; wherefore it is not even to be called "one" — except in such a way that it is no less to be called "all things"; which Socrates too made plain, through the three monads fore-appearing in its forecourt in whatever manner — truth, beauty, symmetry — symmetry furnishing the order among all things, beauty the mutually-sympathetic blending, and truth the existence; while of That, in truth, all things are present together, ineffably.

Note 4. pantopoion, "all-making," against henopoion, "one-making": the supreme cause is not merely the source of unity (which would make it a member of the one/many pair) but the source of multitude, goodness, and wholeness alike — and so "not even one."
Chapter 34 — Whether Anything Proceeds from That: the Trace of the One in All Things · pp. 89–94

It would follow, upon these things, to inquire whether anything proceeds from That into the things after it — anything at all — or whether it imparts nothing to them; for one might reasonably raise a perplexity either way. If it imparts nothing to the things set forth from it, how did it even produce them, standing so unrelated to it as to enjoy nothing of its nature? And how is it their cause according to its own nature, if it does not impart that nature? And how do those things revert toward it, and how do they reach out after it, if they cannot participate in it — it being in every way unparticipated? And how would the things that have proceeded be preserved, if they are not rooted in their own cause? Does not Socrates, in the Republic, call truth a light, proceeding from That, that constitutes the intelligible and the intellective? He too, then, knows the thing that has come and is participated from There. And if matter carries off its last trace, then assuredly the things before matter possess it too — the participations of every kind, made proper to each according to the measure of each thing's subsistence. Nay, something pervading will appear in all things; for each thing is — among the indivisibles and the wholes, the mortal and the everlasting, the solid and the form-like — not many only, but also one before the many; before division, the undivided; before the differentiated, the unified; and what each thing's all-things is, that — before all things — is the concentration of all, which we call the Unified, which we name Being; and before the Unified, clearly, the one — each thing's all-things standing according to the one, as Being is each thing's all-things according to the unified, as all-things-in-determination is according to the differentiated. There is, then, in each thing, the something that answers by analogy to what is before all things; and this is itself That one's procession into all things — the all-perfect subsistence pre-existing, according to the one, in each region; or rather, the root of each thing's subsistence.

But if it proceeds, one might perplex again: in what manner could it proceed? For what will be the cause of its differentiation? Since every procession is with differentiation, and of all differentiation the multitude is cause; for the differentiating is always multitude-making, whereas That is one before the multitude. And if it is even before the one only, much more is it before the multitude; its nature, then, is altogether undifferentiated; it is, therefore, without procession. All things, then, proceed from it into another nature — and it produced that — but it itself proceeds into nothing, nor imparts to anything something from itself; for the imparted must be lower than the imparter, and not be that very thing, but of-the-sort-of that, and not the simply so, but something with a measure for each. Now lowering, and measures, and anything of the kind, are seen in some multitude, and with determination, and according to a flowing and changing of the same — even if no other thing falls in between; but that nature is before every appearance-in-multitude, however it be multiplied; for once the many begin, there is room also for procession, whether uniform or non-uniform. That, then, is in every way without procession, not even putting forth from itself an illumination into any of all things; for the illumination too is differentiated from the illuminant. Further still: not even Being — which we posit as wholly unified — would this proceed either; for this too stands fixed before the substantial differentiation, nor does Parmenides say it moves; for the wholly unified being, in no way differentiated, stands still; it would not, then, differentiate itself into the procession of the many. Nor yet would it differentiate any of the things before it — those that are — nor, indeed, of the things after it; for what could the second do toward the prior, or the effect toward the cause? Being, then, does not proceed into the many, neither by lowering nor by division nor in any way by procession; for 'it will not cut being off from holding to being,' as Parmenides says; wherefore he said that Being is also one; nor, then, would anyone say that it proceeds, if indeed it cannot be cut off. Much more, then, neither does the One. Further still: the measures of the one engendered in things — the traces before the other traces, which supervene through the processions according to others and from others — either are unified with one another completely, so as not to be cut off, the one from the One (and thus all will be one, and nothing other than the One itself); or they are somehow differentiated from one another — and that either spontaneously and without any cause, which is absurd, or by a cause, which is absurd; or, then, by the multitude after the one, and the procession will not be proper to the one but to the multitude — or it will be according to the one; and how is the one able to accomplish, or anything before the one, such as we judge that to be which is called, before all things, all-things-one, which is none of all things but all things before all things, as we said — whose procession we are seeking? But That is neither differentiating nor differentiated; neither many, nor multitude-making; nor yet one, nor one-making; so that that nature neither proceeds, nor remains, nor reverts, being all things by what is above all things.
