Besides this: if it proceeds, and there is in each of the things that are and that come to be a measure of That, it is plain that it imparts to each what falls to it; to the perishable and mortal, then — if it imparts nothing, how is it hymned as their cause too? But if it imparts, not the same thing it imparts to the eternal or the everlasting, then what is imparted to these is perishable and mortal; and what perishing could there be of the one — or rather of the not-even-one? — which cannot so much as be imperishable; for the eternal too is far down from it, and so is Eternity itself; wherefore, concerning the first Being, the same perplexity awaits us; for this too is before Eternity, and so before the eternal — much more, then, before what is everlasting in another way; it stands, then, farthest off from the perishable; the trace of the One in each perishable thing, then, would not be a perishable one, an echo of that One. But perhaps it is with That as with matter; for matter is on this side of the other things, and is, as it were, a kind of matter itself; partly the one in matter itself, partly the one before matter — and each is in potency, imperishable and perishable, but neither is in act. Yet the argument is not about this — the thing fallen forth to this side — but about what is before matter and before the whole-in-potency, present with the forms themselves. For it is plain that, before the last things, the middle things participate in the one principle of wholes.

Note 2. The chapter's affirmative pole: a pervading something (epexion ti) appears in all things — the one before the many, the undivided before division — which is the One's own procession into all, the root of each thing's subsistence.
Chapter 35 — The One Imparts Only Itself: the Single Undivided Participation; the Root and the Center · pp. 94–97

Perhaps, then, it is so: that the One is itself imperishable, and that at different times different ones, among the perishable plenitudes, are constituted around-and-about, changing about the unchangeable. Or rather, this — the participation — is not proper to each, as of this reed-pen that writes these things, and of this paper on which they are written; but it belongs to some good proper to each, if indeed the things proceeded from the principle not undifferentiated. Then again: the perishable itself, as perishable, does it participate in That, or does it not participate? For if it does, That would not be the cause of this perishability; but if it does, what is imparted will also be perishable; and one might reason the same about the imperishable. But perhaps the participation is of the everlasting things only — of the wholes, say. Or, first, as has been said, not even the everlasting belongs in any way to That; and then, what is this allotment, that some of the things from it should participate, and some not — and that, though it is above all the imperishable and all the perishable? Perhaps, then, all things participate in it, but the participation is one, undivided, the same present to all — as the light of the sun is present, the same, to all, even if not whole, because it is divisible and body-like; whereas That, being above the undivided and above the whole, is reasonably participated as the same by everything, the differentiation lying in the participants, not in the participated. For thus Plotinus claims that Being should be conceived: the same everywhere, present whole, in common to all and to each of the many. But even if the participation is undivided and one for all — both that of Being and that of the One (for let the manner of both be alike) — still it is a participation proceeding from the existence and being differentiated. What, then, differentiates the second from the first? For it makes no difference to speak of differentiating the one from the One, and many such things in series; for that nature refuses the differentiation. But perhaps there is never any other participation of it than its existence; for it gives nothing else from itself to the participants, but itself, which it is. Does this, then, belong to the whole — and, to speak generally, to the elements? For it gives itself, and so it gives to what comes from them, of which matter comes to be the element-like. Or, if one will not say this, still matter, having nothing after itself to give, gives itself to the cosmos. Or rather, this — matter — does so according to the worse; whereas That, perhaps according to the better, gives itself to all and to each, not as matter — nor as form, but as the first participation of the first cause; which is the same as to say, an existence, present in the participants, not even willing to be differentiated from them, even if they proceed from it; and insofar as it participates in the multitude, so that the procession is not from it either, but is generated from the multitude; while from That all things are one, and all things, again, are being — as the root alone, before the outgrowth of the branches and of the trunk itself, is already the whole tree; or as a center, in which also are all the ends of the many straight lines together, and the one is all things before the spreading-apart of the infinite straight lines; but after the center comes the spreading-apart — and the center is not the cause of it, but the flowing of the continuous toward the one.

And there is, indeed, in it something multitude-making — a cause and principle even of the processions: of the substantial, the substantial; of the unitary, the unitary. But these are august things and surpassing nature, agreeing with our other conceptions as well — both those that lead all things from the One, and those that judge there to be ever in the effects a trace of the cause, present not from outside only but, beyond this, made-consubstantial; since, even if the sun's light is common, for participation, there is also in the eyes a sun-like radiance, already proper and not common; and it is by the proper that we are conjoined to the common. And does not Plato too say there is a certain radiance of the soul itself, which, having inclined, we must conjoin to the light of truth? But further: from the one principle of all things there flows off, too, a certain common participation still, which he has called truth — corresponding not to the sun, but to the sun's light. But perhaps Plato kept silent about the precise examination of these matters, because of the many; and in the same place, taking the multitude-making cause as well, had room to differentiate the many from the one. Our present argument, however, contemplates separately, if it is lawful, the one principle, which he did not name; and separately the multitude-making cause; and that Plato passed over such a differentiation he made plain, not even setting the multitude-making cause before the mixed — though he took up many elements of it, and laid down three principles instead of one; and perhaps he did not even indicate, in those, the one we now speak of, but the one after the two principles, according to which the mixed comes to be; for this too is one, and the division of this is the three monads — not of the really first principle.

These things, then, again, if there be need. But our conceptions do not articulate the first principles precisely; rather they simply posit the same thing as cause both of union and of differentiation, not even seeing that the differentiating is other than that which preserves the undifferentiated; this latter being first differentiating itself from the One, then becoming the cause of this for the others as well; whereas the One is cause of all things — yet it makes all things one, and does not even make; for neither is it active, since activity is somehow differentiated from the agent; nor yet is it potent, for potency is, as they say, a kind of extension of substance, and That does not even will to be substance; for substance is third from it, according to the mixed — the unitary substance, I mean, and according to the unitary. But these things later. What the argument now says is this: that the one principle is so far from differentiating that it does not even unify; for neither does it make anything; for the unifying too is some one thing, like the differentiating; rather it makes all things one — each thing; but of the one the multitude-making and differentiating cause is the cause, while the elder, prior to each thing, makes all things one, so to speak; for neither is it all things in truth, since the all are in differentiation — there where even the whole is; whereas the one is all things according to the one above all things, in that all things are one.

parts.name: Chapter 36 — The All-Making Cause beyond Cause and Effect: the One That Differentiates Nothing from Itself · pp. 97–105

lines.text: Chapter 36 — The All-Making Cause beyond Cause and Effect: the One That Differentiates Nothing from Itself · pp. 97–105

Such, then, being the perplexities set before us, let us take up the argument from the beginning — having here too, as it were, called upon the Savior. That One, then, being all things, and not only the one — and being all things according to the simplest — and this very simplicity, which is the resolution of all things, and the one before all: this is not a unifying one; for the unifying belongs to determination; nor a multitude-making one, for the same cause; it is not the maker-proper of any of the other things, but a common-making cause simply, and an all-making — not making the differentiated things all together; for neither does it make the unified things; for of those and of these there is the same cause, and before both; it is, then, the producer neither of anything unified nor of anything differentiated, but of all things simply that have subsisted in every manner. Its nature, then, is neither differentiated from anything, nor unified with anything, nor changed-along-with any of all things; for it would no longer be all things, but that thing from which it was differentiated, and would have become proper; but it refuses the proper; nothing, then, is parceled out from it into each thing in a proper manner, nor in any way whatever.

But perhaps a common and single participation of all things proceeds from it into all? Then the participation is differentiated from the existence — and there is as yet no determination of anything: not of cause, not of existence, not of participation; nor, then, would anything proceed at all from it; for nothing is in it that might also proceed; for the remaining is always before all procession; and the undifferentiated things are not yet from the differentiating nature. Do not, then, all things participate in it? Quite so, I will say; does it then give itself to them? Quite so, I will say — the most honorable of all things, itself, as existence; but not a participation from itself. Will it not then become the participants' own, no longer its own? Or is it neither its own, nor the participants', nor those things' own; neither thrust out, nor coordinated — since not by existence, nor by participation; for all such things are in determination — whereas it is wholly undetermined; and is neither of all things, nor of none; for, in truth, it is neither in all things, nor before all things, for these too are certain determinations; rather it is simple and undetermined, and this very thing, all-things-one; for we cannot name it uniformly — that it is also the one — for it is other than all things, and the all things are other than the one. About That, then, and after That, the other things make their manifold determinations in the many-numbered causes from it; it itself, then, is neither participated nor unparticipated, but in another manner, the manner before both, it both is, and preserves the other things, and perfects them, and produces all things together according to its one all-making act — which must be called neither productive nor perfective nor any other of such things; for these too are in determination; rather it is all-bearing, but according to a single nature; all things, then, hang suspended from it, and enjoy it in every way, holding fast to it; nothing, then, from it is such-as-itself; in no way; for neither was it possible for it to stand apart from itself by a lowering, no other thing having appeared to make the standing-apart; nor was it lawful for the differing nature to come to be in some difference toward itself, nor for the simplicity of all things to proceed into some doubleness. How, then, is matter its limit and last trace? Or is it not so? For neither is there in That anything determined as one — as we say matter to be — nor is there from it a first and middle and last; for these too are determinations; nor the in-potency and in-act; nor, in general, anything of the characteristics of matter; for matter too is some one of the elements of the generated; it is determined, therefore; far off, therefore, from the undetermined nature, sprung from somewhere hence in its own property — whence comes generation, and that, indeed, from this principle: not in the first nor in the middle products, but in the last echoes. All things, then, are determined round about That; and the last determination of all marks off, after all things, the dregs (as they truly are) of all things. But about matter it will be possible to speak again, and, having raised the perplexities, to resolve them in season. For now this must be added: that this principle here set forth has comprehended even the last matter, flowed away as it is, within its own undifferenced comprehension of all-complete simplicity.

If, then, nothing is from it, how is it the cause of all things? Or is it thus: that as a determined cause, and according to the conception determined as 'cause,' it is not a cause? For neither is it productive — something else is before this; nor paradigmatic — for something else leads this too; nor, as one might think, the final cause itself — for this too is some one of the causes, and is determined off from the others; nor yet the three causes together, as one all-cause; for the three too are determined off from the many things that are not causes; but There is nothing of the determined things; rather, before all things is That, and cause of all, as cause even of the causes — and not even this, as something beside the one simplicity; but as one from the things below, so surely also cause. And of what is it cause, if cause at all? Of all things, I will say — not of these, and not of those; nor in this respect cause, and in that not; nor any such determined things, beside That. Does something, then, come from There? Quite so — all things; but not such-as-That, but the things after that nature. The generation from it, then, is non-uniform; and before this, the uniform, as more akin; and each thing proceeding from the whole, not from any of the causes determined within it; just as the uniform — and still more, the most common — generation is of all the gods. For the non-uniform is not of all — as if certain of the gods were called maidens and unwed youths; but the uniform is everywhere, and he who does not bring it forth is barren — which is true of matter alone, if even of that. If, then, the procession of all things from That is non-uniform, assuredly the uniform too will pre-exist — which was shown impossible. Or: to divide the two processions upon That is not lawful; for, being altogether undetermined, it would not make its generation from itself determined — whether uniform, or the two at once; rather there belongs to it, if it is lawful to say, the procession before both, undetermined. But, second, if one should wish to rest in the determined causes, one would conceive both at once as the generation of all things from it: as being all things according to the one, it produces all things uniformly; as being before all things, non-uniformly; and at once, as being the same, both is all things and is before all things; at once, then, it makes its single procession both uniform and non-uniform; for it is all things and produces all things — this uniformly, and is before all things; and produces them this non-uniformly. But in another way again: as wholly simple, the not-simple things wholly non-uniformly; as super-simple, these not-simple things uniformly. Does it, then, produce? For so it would be active; and before activity is potency, and before potency, existence; perhaps it is neither potency — much more so — nor still more, activity; for such things too are in determination, and are somehow differentiated from one another. It does not, then, fit the wholly undifferenced to exist and to be potent and to be active. Or rather, these things are not present to it as we say them; but as the one, though not present, we nonetheless refer up to it, and yoke all things to the one, for the causes often mentioned, so we would speak, of it, the to-be-active and to-be-potent and to-be, as the three undetermined from one another. For it does not make by being, as one might say; for this would be one making, counter-determined against others; nor because it is That, on this account are the other things; for thus it would be cause of nothing, unless it produced them; rather, according to the all-bearing simplicity, before activity, before potency, before existence, it is the midst of all things. And is it cause simply, and determined off from the effects? Or is both the cause and the effect, after That, determined off from the determining cause — whatever that may be — while That is only unto all things? And if it is cause too, it is the cause in all things, so that all things are effects from it, as in the wholes, this too being comprehended; whereas That presides — neither as cause nor as effect, but simply and undeterminedly, as one all-things of all things.

Is it not, then, determined even in this way — as such-a-thing, from the not-such? But even if the things after it are determined off from it, the determination is not from it; rather the things that proceeded determined themselves off from That — as the moon stood apart from the sun, that one not standing apart. But if not That, what is the cause of the differentiation? For surely not all things are causes of this, even if all stood apart. Or, of the things that proceeded from That, which will the argument declare, as it goes on? That, then, first differentiated itself from itself, then the other things also. Let That, then, be first differentiated by itself, beginning from its own activity, and yet differentiating — and it is plain that, in the differentiating, the differentiated is differentiated. Or is even this not necessary? For when we close our eyes to the sun, it not standing apart, and the sun is bent back — the god being everywhere — we are separated by the unfittedness of our life. And from matter, too, the form is differentiated, though matter does not possess the differentiation; for differentiation is some form, and the form, they say, is other than matter, matter not being other; and the image is like to the paradigm, though the paradigm is not like to its own image. Or must one not say these things are 'other'? For if by the account of the paradigm the likeness of the image falls short, by this very thing the likeness of the paradigm exceeds the image; the likeness of coordinate things stands equal toward the reciprocal turning, but the likeness of better and worse turns back indeed, yet with the exceeding and the falling-short. If, then, the image is like the paradigm not equally but by falling-short, what prevents the paradigm too from being like the image — but by exceeding? And there is this: that the image is likened to the paradigm, and is thereby like, and the paradigm likens the image to itself, and is thereby like. But these things would belong to another harmony of discourse; nor, indeed, is the form other than matter because matter is not other, but only not-whole; for otherness too is differentiating of sameness, and matter is not even otherness; but form and matter are in no way the same — for matter would not be the same — nor again is there otherness in things related to one another; one must say that matter and form are separated from one another;

and the separated turns back toward the separated, so that all things too are separated from that one nature, itself separated. It is determined off, then — this nature too — from all things. How, then, has it undergone determination? For surely not from any of the things after it, above which we call it the determining cause; and how was it itself differentiated, the wholly undifferentiated being agreed upon? Or, as one must not call things 'other' in which there is no otherness common to both, so neither 'determined off from one another,' nor 'differentiated,' in which there is no common thing and name, differentiation and determination; since the determining or differentiating cause turns back toward its own effect not from the equal, but as maker toward made; the effect is differentiated from the cause, as participating in the differentiating cause; but the cause is somehow differentiated from the effect, as producing it from itself and differentiating it — for thus we judged the like, of image and paradigm, to turn back. But what is beyond all determination, one could in no way say to be in any way determined; since it is even determined off, in that it is in every way determined off; yet it has also something common, one. There will be, then, in the second something from the first, of-the-sort-of That which we despaired of; and if That very thing is both in the second and in all, as we were saying, there would not be a common thing and at the same time a determined one; for in the one and the same these too are determinations — the common and the proper.
Chapter 37 — The Ever-Laboring Birth-Pang; the Second as Potency Welded to Existence · pp. 105–106

How, then, must one speak — and in what manner dispose these simple and truly tremorless apparitions of this surpassing truth? For either there is nothing after That, and it alone is; or, if there are also other things after That, it is in every way one thing, and stands toward That, assuredly, in a determination. Or should one take even this as from the things below, for a dim indication — an indication, too, belonging to that birth-pang about That which is ever in travail but never able to give birth, possessing its giving-birth in its laboring, in whatever fashion? As for an indication of this, then, let there be determined a certain manner most unapparent, and least of all distinct as a determination — the most primal additional-determination of all, I mean, and one all but swallowed up by the undetermined — so that the second seems to be a potency of the first: a potency welded fast to the existence, as certain holy discourses already hint at this. Or, if anything is more uniform even than this, one might conceive it among the things whose nature is before all existence and potency; and let the second be called 'after That'; but That, rather 'than-after-which'; and 'of it' rather than 'from it' — and as many such excesses of speech as one may find.

Are then the other things too, after the second, present to it in the same manner — even the last of all? And are all things of equal honor toward That? But that is absurd. So that, even if it is not differentiated from the second, it is sufficiently differentiated from the others, and most of all from the last? Or have all things come forth together — first and middle and last — holding, indeed, their mutual comparison among themselves, yet, as all together, standing toward the one-all as one: as effects toward the cause;

while the further procession and order comes upon them all from the other causes; from That, these too indeed come, but as items within the all. Wherefore That alone is cause of all things; other causes are causes of other things among these all.
Chapter 38 — Cause of All as All Together: Iamblichus on the Ascent with All Things · p. 106

That it is the cause of all things as of all-together, its all-perfection makes plain; plain too its indefiniteness — being no more of this than of that; and plain, further, the yearning of all things for such a cause, as of all: for it is surely not the leading cause of some one thing while failing to be the cause of all together, as all. And if it is, what other cause could there be beside the one set before us? Or does it differ from all things just so much — if it is lawful to say so — as the all are all in every manner of way, while it is all in the simplest manner? And that these things can chime with Iamblichus too, I take this as my evidence: that he says the leading-up to That is not attainable for each single thing, unless it should rank itself together with all things, and run back up, together with all, to the common principle of all. If, then, all things together are of a nature to stretch up toward it, while each by itself is not so of a nature, apart from the others, it is plain to everyone that all things also came forth together from There — each not by itself, but one from another.

But if all came forth together, still some are far and some near. Yet these things too were determined after that nature; at that point there was as yet no far and near. Speaking, then, as one ordering the highest things from the things below, one might speak thus; but, to speak according to the truer birth-pang: neither were these things differentiated from That, nor That by these; nor yet are they unified with one another; they are neither the same, nor other; neither like, nor unlike; neither one, nor many; neither of the same rank, nor of a different rank; for not even 'before all things' fits That — and so neither does 'after That' fit them all; neither first, then, nor second; neither cause, nor effect; for such terms stand toward one another within some determination; whereas That is the undetermined — not the opposite of the determined, but the in-every-way simple, and all things undifferentiatedly; for all things are according to the one, and That is the one which is all things, and not one only.
Chapter 39 — Neither Proceeded nor Not Proceeded: the Unitary Procession; the Three That Are One · pp. 107–108

Let no one, then, raise the perplexity whether, if the other things proceed from it, they were separated from it, and That, accordingly, was separated from them; or whether, if they are unified with it, they did not come forth. For it is not as we conceive it: they neither proceeded, nor did not proceed. For other is that manner of the unitary procession, which we do not yet conceive together, divided as we are into remaining and procession and reversion; whereas That is above the determination of such things: it is neither necessary that it be unified, if it is not differentiated, nor that it be differentiated, if it is not unified; for That has obtained the undetermined nature before both — while these stand as opposites. Nor again let anyone inquire whether it produces and the others are produced. For if it is active, it is also potent, and exists; the all, then, would be three, not one — existence, potency, and activity; but it has been said that That is before activity and potency and existence; for it is one, not three; and it is before the others as one even of the three. It is from the helplessness of our intellection and exposition that we nevertheless say it 'produces'; but the manner of the producing must be purified clean, as being unkindred to us, and as accomplished neither by being-active, nor by being-potent, nor by existing, but by the ineffable manner before the three.

Nor let anyone say that some participation flows off from it — neither one becoming proper to each thing, nor one common participation of all — so that the things proceeded from it might participate in it, and That might give something from itself to the things that came forth. Nor, if not this, that they do not even have their being from There, and that there is nothing common between them and That; for then either That must be something, or be in these — and so not by itself; or these must be in That — and so nothing beside it. This kind of perplexity, one must say, has force over the things that produce by way of differentiation; but just as we posited the procession of the things from it to be neither according to union nor according to differentiation, so also the perfecting from There, and the participation of That, is neither as of one giving something from itself, nor as of one withholding the gift; neither as having the given illumination itself as something common with the others, nor as being wholly determined off and in no way communing with them; for all such oppositions are within determination. But That is, as has been often said, undetermined; so that all these things together must be affirmed of it at once — and again, none of them alone, taken by itself as determined; or, what is truer, not even all of them: but the one before all things, simplifying all of these together.
Chapter 40 — The Light of Truth and the Henads; the Root That Proceeds with the Branches · pp. 108–111

What, then, is the light of truth that, according to Plato, is sent forth in advance from it? That Plato utters these things about it in a manner nearer to our conceptions, he has made plain elsewhere — judging it right to station not truth alone, but beauty and symmetry too, in its forecourt; and then, indeed, he has not taken up at all that One before all things, but that from which Being proximately hangs. Wherefore he says this light is what binds together the knowable and the knowing — that is, the intelligible and the intellective — as seated within the intelligible, and making true at once the intellect and the intellected. But this must be examined again hereafter. If, however, we should call truth a light even of That — the truth from it — we shall say that it is the procession of the divine henads, as the philosophers hold. Have these henads, then, nothing in common with one another, in virtue of which all the gods both are and are called one god? Assuredly they have, I shall say; but either as from one and toward one — so that this too is many; or, if there is even some undifferenced one, like a single root of the many gods, this is nothing like That; it is a participation of That: a root of the things that have come forth, proceeding together with the things that proceed — a monad, if it is lawful to say so, of the divine number. And as for the one of matter — if someone should bring forward this too, as some last trace of That — he will miss the whole. For matter is determined off against form, and the last against the first; but the nature of That is before these; and in general, everywhere form is present together with matter; whence form proceeds, from that same order matter proceeds also. But this too belongs to a later inquiry.

What has been said upon all the perplexities already raised is this: the concentration, in each thing, of all things — before all the things in each — does answer to That by analogy; yet it is not, as it were, an image of That, nor its light, but belongs to what has proceeded; and this is crown and root, having come forth together with that whose root it is, in the manner native to what springs from There — just as the one common root of all things also proceeds. But That was not a root, but before all things; nor a root only, but all things together with the root: it is itself one-all and before all, while the all proceed from it, root and branches at once. How then could that root — whether the one or the many — be an echo of That, when we have confessed it to be at once root and branches, having confessed That to be the undetermined one-all before all? For the root is determined off against the branches, and the crown against all the rest. The illumination from There, then, was not, after all, the uniform one that is before all things in each of the multiplied things; this, at any rate, would be in some manner multiplied by its ranking, and somehow determined off from what illumines. Yet it does not follow that, because the others do not participate in it in this fashion, they do not participate at all, and that we shall set That apart, exiled from everything; one must endure the second wave of perplexities also — perplexities that war against the manner of participation customary in other things, but which, taken simply, do not hold good. For let it be: as the surmise of its subsistence is of its own peculiar manner, so too of its procession — neither according to union nor according to differentiation, neither uniform nor non-uniform, but before both; and likewise of the participation: neither coming about by its presence, nor by an illumination separated off from it, but before both. It will not be fitting, then, to say that what is given is common or proper; for this too is beyond the two; no, nor that it is given, nor again not given; for these too are somehow opposed; and That is beyond all opposition — even the contradictory one; much more, then, beyond every other; so that it is neither perishable nor imperishable, but deserves to be called what is before these — if indeed there were any appellation proper to its own name. But how could there be, for that to which not even the proper belongs — nor the common? We are in no way likened to it — to that in which no property resides — but to the first after it; since neither are we unified with That; rather, even union comes after it; while That stands at the one and, so to speak, before the one — the before-the-one and before all things.

parts.name: Chapter 41 — The Radiance of the Soul; the Only Knowledge of That: Dishonoring All Our Conceptions · pp. 111–112

lines.text: Chapter 41 — The Radiance of the Soul; the Only Knowledge of That: Dishonoring All Our Conceptions · pp. 111–112

What, then, does Plato intend by the radiance of the soul? That it is conjoined to the light that is from That — but not to That; or, if to That, is not the light itself conjoined, the light from it? Or is it conjoined according to the image of the analogy, but no longer according to truth? For That does not abide conjunction with another — That which does not abide even the conjoined. But how is the immediately-after-it related to it? Either in that it shone forth first of the others, or in that it has not wholly stooped forth from the inner sanctuary. But about Plato's statements, later; and further, about the second after That, whatever it may be: insofar as it is from That, it proceeds together with all things in the wholly undetermined manner, without the opposition that goes with determination; but insofar as it is a second principle, it will put forward for us other conceptions, about itself and about the things from it. For it is plain that we must liken our conceptions, so far as we can, to the things themselves.

For indeed we formed our surmise of it thus: we attempted to gather up, from the simplicity of the One before all things, the soul's conceptions that are by nature divided — or rather our torn-asunder surmises — even though our impulse strained to awaken against the contrary; striving emulously to fit them to the one that is in every way one, and that has embraced all things in itself no less (if not rather more), or — better — to the one that is beyond even existing; and perhaps better still, to the one that does not even exist, but is above this: the all-things-one. Hence too arose the great tumult, the divided discourse being ever in danger either of tearing the One apart into many, or of losing altogether its own proper nature and potency and activity. Accordingly we gather also these conclusions, which follow upon those: that of That nothing must be said of all that is said in such determination — nor even all of them brought together at once: as, that it is cause of all, that it is first, that it is the Good, that it is the simplest, that it is the beyond-being, that it is measure, that it is the desired, that it is end, that it is principle. For the conceptions of all these are determined ones, and to That no determination is appropriate — no, not even as the undetermined that is the opposite of the determined; but if there is anything before all these — one, indicative of all — this alone is to be surmised in its case. For one-and-all-together were the two, as one before the one and the all; it has no conception proper to it that is at once complete and simple — much less an appellation; yet it demands such a one as we are at a loss to offer. Wherefore the only knowledge of it that we achieve is this: that by which we dishonor all that is ours, as unfit so to be fitted to it; and whatever we posit about the things after it, these too we dishonor; and we judge That to be neither some one of all things, nor all things together (although we account it cause of all and in every way simple), nor simple in such a way as to be some one of all things, nor as simplicity itself — for this too is some one of all things — but simple in such a way as to be at once all things, and all things in such a way as to be at-once-simple; nor again all things in such a way that the all are many, or a whole out of many; but all things thus: as one before all things.
Chapter 42 — The Second after That: Neither Differentiated nor Unified; Remaining, Procession, and Reversion Denied · pp. 112–113

But since That has been declared to be of such a kind, it would be next to inquire about what has proceeded after it — whatever it may be. This, however, must wait for us; rather, only in respect of its being from That and after That must it be inquired: one thing, whether it was differentiated from it; another, whether That remains while this proceeds — for the remaining must always be before the proceeding — and whether it proceeds remaining, or only proceeds. Let us begin from above. If, then, the second was differentiated from the first, assuredly the first too was differentiated from the second; for the differentiated is differentiated from a differentiated. But if this is so, then either it has suffered the differentiation from the second, which differentiated itself — and how is the cause somehow altered by the effect, or how has it suffered anything at all? — or it had this from itself: in differentiating the second from itself, it also differentiated itself from that. And how is it differentiating — That which we did not judge to be even one-making? And how, in general, is it differentiated from the second? Or is it even unified with it — That which abides neither union nor differentiation toward anything whatsoever? But if it is not differentiated, how is the one cause and the other effect? And how is the begotten not in every way indistinguishable from the begetter?

Perhaps, then, it is safer to say: the first, without union and without differentiation — being beyond both one and multitude — produces all things, as was said before, in the manner unkindred to us; and it is separated from all things, and present in all, in another manner of the same kind. From wherever differentiation begins, from there also begin the exempt and the coordinated, and in general the prior and the second; and we say even these things about those natures wishing only to indicate something concerning the wholly undetermined; so that neither anything else, nor what seems to be the second, is either differentiated from That or unified with it — for then it would be a thing unified with That. As, then, we do not judge it right to say of it 'other' or 'same,' because sameness and otherness are not yet, so neither 'being unified' nor 'being differentiated,' because union and differentiation are not yet. Neither, then, is any remaining of That determined, nor procession, nor reversion — for the same cause. We shall not, then, justly raise the remaining perplexities either; but later we shall inquire where these terms are to be affirmed, and what, in those natures, is the remaining, or the proceeding, or the reverting — and whether they are the same with respect to the whole subsistence, or are themselves three subsistences.
Chapter 43 — Groping in Darkness: That as the Remaining; the First from It as the Proceeding; the Third as the Reverting · pp. 113–114

But if one should wish — groping, as it were, in darkness — nevertheless to contemplate these things in those natures too, by analogy, not by way of indication but in a manner better than the truth that can be indicated: let That answer by analogy to the cause that only remains; what proceeds from it first, to the proceeding — the ruler of procession in the strict sense; and the third from it, to the reverting. And if we set apart these very terms, such as we surmise them to be, we shall know that the analogy runs in their favor.
Chapter 44 — Whether the Remaining Is Other than the One-All: the Regress Halted · p. 114

Except that, from this very point, it must now be asked whether 'the remaining' is something other than the one-all posited from the beginning; for that was in no way determined. Of the three that come after it, one might say the first is 'the remaining'; for even if each of these too is all-perfect and undetermined, still one of them would by now rather give indication according to the remaining, another according to the proceeding, another according to the reverting. Or, even if one should wish to indicate these things in their case, the one-all suffices for the indication of the remaining — inasmuch as even the first thing that came forth from it did not remain, but proceeded from it; whereas That in no way proceeds, because before it was the Ineffable, of which nothing could be said, not even by way of indication; nothing, then, proceeds from That; so neither does the one-all proceed. And the unproceeding, in this very respect, would be said to remain — as by analogy; since even what comes from it might be said to remain, seeing that this also proceeds from it insofar as it is after it; in which respect it will be necessary to posit something remaining even before this thing's procession, if indeed we judge that the remaining is before the proceeding. Either, then, we shall seek another, and this to infinity, or we shall make the one-all the remaining — the very thing we posited as remaining before the proceeding; since, if this is not before the things that in whatever way remain, neither will what comes after it be first among the things that in whatever way proceed. And let this be carried thus far.
Chapter 45 — Two Principles before the Intelligible Triad? Iamblichus, Porphyry, the Pythagoreans, and the Oracles; the Monad from Remaining · pp. 115–118

After these things, let us put forward this for examination: whether the first principles are two, before the first intelligible triad — the wholly ineffable, and the one uncoordinated with the triad — as the great Iamblichus judged in the twenty-eighth book of his most perfect Chaldaean Theology; or whether, as most of those after him approved, the first triad of the intelligibles comes immediately after the ineffable cause; or shall we descend below even this hypothesis and say, with Porphyry, that the one principle of all things is the Father of the intelligible triad? How the Oracles of the gods intend it would belong to another occasion to distinguish; for the present let us pursue these matters too in the more philosophical manner which we have taken in hand. Well then: the uncoordinated cause, the one common cause of all, wholly ineffable — how could it be numbered in with the intelligibles, and be called father of one triad? For that father is already the summit of beings, whereas this cause has stepped beyond all things; and from the father the paternal intellect peculiarly depends, whereas of this cause nothing is peculiar; and the father is in some way intelligible to his own intellect, whereas this is altogether unsayable. Further, on the basis of what we have said, one would call the father of the triad either something more common, or the one-all; but not even this is of equal weight with that hypothesis — much less the more common. Perhaps, then, it is better to speak with Iamblichus. For whether it is monad and indefinite dyad and upon these the triad — this being the whole intelligible triad, as the Pythagoreans say — the One would be before these, as those men also say; or whether it is limit and unlimited and mixed, before these too Plato presupposes the One, which he says is for the mixed the cause of the mixture; or whether it is father and power and intellect, there would be, before these, the one father before the triad. For 'in every cosmos shines a triad, which a monad rules,' says the Oracle; and if in the cosmoi, much more in the abyss above the cosmos; for it least of all befits That to be ruled by multitude. If, then, before the triadic is the uniform, and before this the wholly unsayable, as we were saying, the consequence is plain.

For again: if the one-all is a second principle after the unsayable one — and this is no more some 'this' than 'that,' but all things equally — while the ruler of the triad is rather existence, as the second is power and the third intellect, it is clear from the very things that the One must be set before the triad, prior to the monad — as belonging indeed to every number; for every number is one, yet the One is not a monad, as we were saying. For either it is a monad — and then the One will be before it, and before this again the unsayable will pre-exist; the monad, then, will be first of the intelligible number, being third as principle — or this alone is called One, and after it again there will be the monad ruling the intelligible number. And one will make much use, on Iamblichus's side, both of the Oracle cited before, and of the argument that posits, after the one-all, the remaining principle — to which, surely, both the name and the thing of the monad will be altogether fitting; for it is from the remaining that the monad is named; and so the dyad is processive — and reversive; and thus a triad, so called not according to multitude, but according to its own peculiar nature. Nor will the remaining deign to proceed at all, but only to come to be by itself, in the recess of itself, after the in-every-way one. It has not proceeded, then; nor is it right to speak of procession in its case. And what comes after the remaining is by now the really proceeding; for from it, first, procession begins, as from the third begins reversion; wherefore this third is also the first intellect.

Upon these things, letting go of these pre-occupied names, let us say that there must indeed be principles after the one principle of all — the principle posited by affirmation, however purified, and declared to be all-things-one. There must, then, after this be another principle: either no longer being all-things-one, or not all things equally, but in some proper manner; and again after this another, of its own manner, and stepping down below even that. For each is all things — since each intelligible principle in the sequence is still all things; and perhaps each ordered world, even down to the intellectuals, is all things. Yet There all things are undeterminedly — whether according to the unified or according to the one — so that one must conceive some other difference among those principles. After the principle that is simply all-things-one, then, must be ranked the principle that is all-one in a certain respect, and not simply; so that some property must now be added — clearly the eldest and most generic of all; and then, in the same way, to the third principle a third property, more common and second by nature. This principle, then, will hold a certain opposition toward that one — which I think the ancients also saw when they named them: some, limit and unlimited; others, monad and indefinite dyad; the theologians, father and power. If, then, these principles, of whatever sort they are, lean toward something in a proper manner, the principle that leans toward nothing, being all-things-one, would be simply the one common principle before them; and before even this is the Ineffable.
Chapter 46 — The Argument from the Two Columns; Damascius's Verdict: Determined Names Must Not Be Carried Up · pp. 118–121

Nay more, one might establish the same conclusion also from below, as from a piece of evidence. Seeing in beings two columns counter-divided against one another — the one better, the other worse; the one one-like, the other multitude-like — from these we are sent back up to two principles as well, the One and the Multitude (I mean for the things counter-determined), or to others, as one may wish to suppose; each column, at any rate, having its own proper principle, from which the common element is present in each member: in the one-like, the property of the one; in the multitude-like, the trace of multitude. For even if the two series split off from one single principle, still, before the series, their principles too stand apart. And if the two series have also something in common with one another — for they are surely not torn asunder in every way — in this respect, at least, they proceeded from the uniform and single principle. And these things I say in the strict sense, not by way of indication, led up from the things determined in Intellect — or rather even in soul. Since these are here, the causes of them must be presupposed, intelligibly, in the intelligible also, so far as may be by way of indication. From the undivided and uniform column, then, we shall come to the one principle before all, upon which we conferred 'all-things-one' for want of its proper name; and instead of the divided two, to the principles opposed in whatever manner — analogous to those that are truly counter-divided — which one may call however one pleases; we shall not quarrel with him over the names, if what he says bears any indication or analogy whatever toward those principles seated above wholes.

Are we then to posit in this way two principles beyond the intelligible triads — and, to speak generally, beyond all beings — as Iamblichus judged, alone, so far as I know, of all before us? Or must we follow all the others who came after him? The truest about matters so great, god would know; but if I must say what seems to me, these arguments do not seem to me firm for the demonstration proposed. For if, being led up from determined thoughts and names, we presuppose such things There also, we would indeed rightly force this conclusion — that the One is before limit and unlimitedness, for each of the two is one, and among determined things this must be so; but that one absurdity will follow: that limit and the unlimited are themselves placed There. For why not also monad and indefinite dyad, according to those who say so, or father and power? Each of these too we conceive, and they are no whit less honorable than unlimitedness and limit. Instead of two principles, then, or three, we shall make many There — as many as the most generic of the determined things; and if not all, at least those laid down by the various schools; and, what is harder still, determined ones. How, then, will the summit of the intelligible still differ from the genera distinguished within Intellect? Or should we carry up to each of the two principles not 'limit,' but the common element of the whole one-like file, and not 'the unlimited,' but the common element of this kindred genus? But even so there will be determination There, and counter-division; so that neither of the two will be a principle of all things, nor all-before-all; each will be all and of all, yet more of this than of that — the one according to the one, the other according to multitude. We shall need, then, to set a cause over the more-and-less as well — and over any counter-division whatever between coordinates. And apart from these things, we shall set before limit and unlimitedness not the One only, but also the Multitude — or whatever the multitude-making or differentiating cause must be called; for as each of the two is one, so both together are two — or not-one. What, then, is the cause for them of such a common element? This too must be ranked before both, if they are coordinate — and if the one proceeds from the other, the second from the first, together with the properties that of necessity co-subsist in this manner; for the first, producing itself first according to its own peculiar nature, thereby begins to produce the other first things as well.

Besides this: if everything is taken from the determined, then the One too will be a truly determinate one — the one which, drawn on by our conception of it, we set before the two, the monad and the dyad. But if this is determined, how will it differ from the genus? For the genus too is all things according to its own proper one. How then is it all things simply, and in such a way as to be above all? But if we use these thoughts wishing, from 'the one,' to seize the in-every-way simplest and beyond all; and from 'all things,' to escape the least one and the one determined as some one thing; and from both, to give indication of the one principle of wholes, beyond all and stepped forth from all — then it is plain that the principles after her, too, must be sought by us in the same manner: from determined conceptions running up, so far as possible, to the all-perfect ones; not resting in the determination of the conceptions, nor being content with it, nor carrying that determination There. It is as if someone, wishing to exhibit the simple intellection of Intellect by setting it beside the soul's, should use examples — for the intellective, the casting of sight; for the rational, the reception of hearing — and then, when one ought to press on from the examples to the truer conceptions about those things, should demand of the exhibitor that, just as there is a common sense prior to sight and hearing, so there be some community of substantial knowledge between the intellective and the psychic — failing to conceive that the psychic proceeds from the intellective as image from paradigm. So too those who avail themselves of determined thoughts and things for the indication of the all-perfect and undetermined principles could not justly be required to carry up to those principles what accompanies these: as, that these are many, so those too are many — and not two or three only; that these are set against one another, so those too must be supposed opposed; and that, since the one among these is before limit and unlimitedness, therefore the single position of the One stands before the two principles. Indeed, the very fact that different men have used different names to indicate the two principles — each school speaking well, but each darting upon them by a different intuition — let this be our evidence that those determinate things are not to be deposited There, but that from them, by analogy, one is led up beyond.
Chapter 47 — Monad, Limit, Father, Existence, Aether: Symbols of One Nature; the Egyptians' Unknowable Darkness; Pythagoras and Plato on the One · pp. 121–123

As, then, monad and limit and father and existence and aether — if you will — are, among these determined things, each something different, just as their names also are, while There all are paradigms or symbols of one nature: so too the one, even if it is something different as used by each of these schools, is There an indication of that same nature; and similarly let the many — belonging to the other nature, ranked after the one we have spoken of — stand, by a certain analogy, as an example of her: of whom the unlimited too, and the indefinite dyad, and the power, and chaos are examples, and whatever else one might devise for a more familiar presentation. The one principle, then — someone might say — must not be before the two principles, seeing that it is opposed , whereas the first is before all opposition. Or, first: they are not opposed as things of the same rank, in the way of limit and unlimited; for opposition of that sort belongs to the counter-divided; but if they are opposed at all, it is as cause to effect — as the intelligible cosmos to the intellectual, the whole to the whole. Then, even if we too shall concede that there is the one principle — the one which, seeking it in what went before, we found to be unsayable — yet the one that Pythagoras celebrated is such as we posited the second to be, calling it one-all; and after it he set monad and indefinite dyad. But I shall say this: that each, wishing to give indication of the principle beyond all things, lays down now one token of her, now another — or rather a symbol, to speak most truly: some, 'the One' simply; some, 'God' simply; some, 'Time,' or 'the critical moment,' or perhaps yet another such name. We for our part posited an unsayable principle; or rather, the Egyptians too hymned it as ineffable: for they have named it 'unknowable darkness' — thrice proclaiming this over it. So then Pythagoras also wished to set some name beneath her, though at a loss before the demands of philosophic teaching; and therefore after her he marked off the monad, calling this too a symbol of her, and not some proper disclosure; since the monad, in truth, is where number is; and number is among determined things, not in the undetermined plenitude of beings. Plato, however, is open to dispute as to how he uses the names. In the Sophist he sets the one before all things; in the Republic he makes it an unknowable nature; and in the Parmenides, by the first hypothesis, he seems indeed to leave the one without being — for he removes, as it appears, the 'is' of the one — yet not so simply; rather, perhaps, through the complete negation, and the removal of everything knowable, he gives indication of the Unsayable. But this it will be more timely to examine elsewhere. In the second hypothesis, at any rate, this one is clearly posited — the one which we too have now posited affirmatively as one-all, so far as was possible: the very one that is also simplest of all things; whereas that one, which Pythagoras placed before the monad, and Plato in the first hypothesis, is a symbol of the unsayable principle — each having named her in his own different way.

If, then, someone should say that the one-all is all-one equally in every respect, while the elder of the two principles is existential rather than productive — or limit-like — just as the second is rather the contraries, and yet each of the two is nonetheless all-one: we shall know that he who says these things is still held fast among the determined things — positing more-and-less in those principles, and marking them off by properties that differ from one another, such as the stable and the processive, or the existential and the potential. Said by way of indication, these would meet with just pardon; but said simply, in this fashion they will work dreadful confusion. For even the base of the intelligibles will be shown to be all things equally, although it is already, in some manner, projecting determination within itself; and let it be known that we too suppose the Unsayable to be all things equally, before all things, in accordance with her being wholly unsayable.

parts.name: Chapter 48 — The One-All Heads the One-Like Column; the One above All Procession; the Paternal and the Maternal Principle · pp. 123–126

lines.text: Chapter 48 — The One-All Heads the One-Like Column; the One above All Procession; the Paternal and the Maternal Principle · pp. 123–126

Further still, in the third place: the one-all, so called in respect of the very one — for 'all things' is set forth as common in each of the principles, toward the disclosure of their all-perfection — this too, then, will head the one column, the one-like, just as multitude heads the opposed column; for multitude too is a principle, and not the mere form of multitude: not some single property, but the principle that is all things according to multitude; so that the one-all, in turn, leans rather toward the stable and one-like nature of beings. Moreover, let him who reasons out the difference of the one from the monad be reminded of what has been said: that neither monad nor one is in those first principles according to truth; so that neither must their difference toward one another be posited by us in them; rather, each of the two can be led up toward the same supposition and the same indication. And he who cuts procession off at the second principle, positing the remaining before it, even he is still held in the determination of the conceptions — counter-dividing remaining and procession in those principles, instead of unfolding even these into the all-perfect manner of indication; nevertheless, even he will agree with us when we call the second principle processive, and the prior one stable and remaining — which we say is the one-all: not proceeding from the unsayable through procession, but through remaining. For That was unsayable; whereas what comes to be one is no longer unsayable to us — it is one. Yet neither did it proceed. For all procession is dyadic, while the one is above all procession: the one is ever unsplit, even amid multiplied begetting; it is unitive, at any rate, of the multitude in whatever things it supervenes upon; so that the one is in every way without procession — that, at least, which is completely one. If, then, the one stepped down beside the unsayable, its stepping-away is not a procession — or rather, there would not even be a stepping-away; for the one is unitive of all the other things, both toward one another and toward their proper causes; and, so far as rests with the one, all things would be one; so that neither did it divide itself off from the unsayable. Wherefore, even when it is supposed to be one, it is nevertheless shown to be one unsayably; and being such, it is in no way a proceeding thing — and perhaps not even a remaining one; for the remaining is other than the one — unless it be called remaining only by way of indication.

'But the remaining,' he says, 'either remains in itself — and the one will have a certain doubleness; or in what is before itself — and there will be something sayable in the unsayable, for the remaining is somehow sayable; or in what comes after itself — which is more absurd still, for this does not belong even to all souls.' But we shall say that That is not the remaining thing, but remaining itself, by analogy; for it is the cause, to the others, of their remaining. And even if someone should add that it does not itself remain, I permit him to say it: That is before what remains in another and in itself — neither affording remaining alone, nor soaring off in its train; and just as it is called one, and limit, and existence, and aether, so too it might be called remaining — by analogy. But if someone demands, by way of procession, that the two opposed principles proceed from the uniform principle, leaning toward either side; or sends the downward scissions of beings back up to those principles from one still-connate monad: then, if he speaks thus counter-dividing them — as two after the one and from the one — we do not accept the opposition; but if he posits the one above all, as one; and another after this, herself also embracing all things, yet not, in that first way, all things unsayably; and beneath this another, by now in some manner bringing herself near to the things that come after her: then we agree — the one unsayable; the one-like after her; and the multitude-like third upon these; this last, however, not opposed to the former as multitude is opposed to the one among determined things, but rather as dyad to monad, and power to existence — or rather, in truth, not even so; for power is something of the very substance, while the dyad has been far torn away from the monad; but as a second whole cosmos toward a prior whole: the differentiated toward the unified; except that each of the two is all-one — the one, as it were one; the other, as it were multitude. These things, then, we shall articulate hereafter — presently, indeed, with all speed, so far as may be.

For now, simply, against the last of the arguments attempted by Iamblichus, we say this: that we too begin from one principle of all things, and after the one we rank the two — on the analogy of the double column splitting from one connate growth, and not counter-divided: the one principle not yet willing to come forth from the unsayable, but rather swallowed up by it; the other by now proceeding, and given her form by the slackening alone, because proceeding is consubstantiated with her. Wherefore she has become, for all things, the cause of their being differentiated in whatever manner — just as the other principle is the cause of their having grown together with their proper causes; so that each of the two is a principle of all things: the one, of all things' growing together with one another, in breadth and in depth — wherefore she is called one, by indication; the other, of their being differentiated in every manner whatsoever. Let no one say, then, that the one rules the one file and the other the other; rather, each rules both; and of the unified that is before both — being in a certain manner from both — the one is, so to speak, the paternal cause; the other, quite simply, the maternal. But if, letting go the Oracles that advocate for us, one must demonstrate our own position itself, by itself — the position whereon the other philosophers also take their stand: that there is one only principle before all things, and after the one the two, limit and unlimited, or however one may wish to indicate and signify them — from this point, at last, must the argument begin.
Chapter 49 — The One and the Unified; the Not-One; the First Syzygy of One and Many; the One King; the One Not Wholly Unsayable · pp. 127–133

Other is the Unified, other the One — as Plato says, and the common conception bears witness besides. For the unified is of such a kind as to have been affected by the one; while that which is only one stands above the unified. Not, however, that either is torn from the other completely: the unified participates in the one; there is, then, a certain relation viewed between the two, like a composition of the extremes. Taking these in order: if the one, and what is above the one, are without relation, there will be one principle, the unsayable; while the so-called two are the one and the relation — which is the power; for power is first of all relations; and third is intellect, even that Being which we hymn. But this demonstration has been written by Syrianus and by Proclus, on the Parmenides; for the One posited at the opening of the second hypothesis signifies the triad. You may grasp it also, more natively, from the very nature of the unified. The unified is not only one — for then it would be the same as the one from the beginning — but also not-one; nor again only not-one — for then it would not be unified, a name which signifies its having been affected by the one. As, then, because it is also not-one, it has before itself that which is purely one, so also — because it is one, and yet not purely not-one, but a not-one that has been affected by the one (for it is of a nature to be unified precisely because its property stands according to the both-together, if one must speak so) — for this reason there will be before it the purely not-one, so called as subsisting in its own peculiar subsistence: not, to be sure, like 'the nothing,' for that is without subsistence; but as a certain nature that manifested the not-one among beings — through which the first Being also is not-one, just as it is one through the one, and unified through itself. And this not-one some will call unlimited; some, chaos; some, indefinite dyad; and some might say even multitude. Wherefore Being too is called mixed: because it is unified out of one and not-one. But of this, again, hereafter.

Now we say once more: Being is either one, or many, or the both-together. One it is not — for the conception of being and of one is not the same; nor many, by the same conception; whence we speak both of 'Being' and of 'beings,' as one and many. And if it is the both-together, surely not according to existence; for one and many are not the same, nor is it one according to existence, seeing that it stands together with many; nor are the many consubstantiated with the one in such wise that what is of both is an element, as it were, by participation. As the one pre-exists, then, so too do the many. And if the one is other than limit, and the many other than the unlimited, it will follow that the principles are more numerous than we wish; but if the unlimited and multitude come to the same, then limit and the one will also come to the same — according to the indication of the undetermined from the determined. Further: as limit seems to be set against the unlimited, so the one against multitude; and if the one is before limit, multitude too is before the unlimited; and if the one is before the monad, multitude too is before the indefinite dyad; and if before the intelligible father, then also before the power. The first syzygy of principles, therefore, is the One and the Many; all the others either give indication, every one, of this same single reality, or are ranked after it — and then the principles before Being are two no longer but many, which not even those who say these things intend. Besides this: the one, in that it is one, is in no way of a nature to proceed; for neither being-differentiated nor differentiating belongs to the nature of the one — if indeed differentiation is contrary to union. If, then, union is of the one, differentiation would assuredly be of multitude. These two, then, are principles; and in this way they will take the lead of all things, while seeming to be set against one another; and the principle of the one is not before all opposition — among determined conceptions, at any rate; neither, then, by indication, among the undetermined.

Further: everything that first does something, and first suffers it, becomes for the others the cause of being such — the first beautiful, of each thing's being beautiful; and the first beautified is cause, to the others, of their being beautified; and on all cases the argument is the same. If, then, something first differentiates, or is first differentiated, this would become for the others the cause of each respectively; and the first multitude — being also the first multiplied — of their being many and being multiplied; and with the one it stands likewise. Now if each thing does this very thing to itself — the thing which it is — beginning from itself in its own proper activity, so as also to suffer it from itself, then the form sought would in each case be one: the first doer-and-sufferer. But if the doer is one thing, and what suffers under the doer another, the firsts will be two, divided by doing and suffering — as the first beautiful does, and the first beautified suffers. And the argument we were just stating holds true on either alternative: if the one, by its own nature, is without procession, the many would begin procession, as the first to proceed — just as the dyad, for the Pythagoreans, rules all procession; and the power, on the Chaldaean hypothesis; for she first stands away, be it ever so little, from her proper existence. And what would be the cause of differentiation, of whatever sort, but multitude? For what is it to be differentiated, if not to become many instead of one? From what has thus been agreed, then, this first conclusion must be drawn: the one does not proceed; for if it should proceed, it would itself be what begins all procession, so that even before the one we shall need the principle that does not proceed but remains — and so to infinity; or else multitude, or whatever one may wish to name the cause of all procession. And a second: that multitude, displaying differentiation through itself, would itself be what begins differentiation — whether multiplying and differentiating itself, or being itself only multitude, and differentiative, while it multiplies and differentiates the others; for whichever way one puts it, it would be what begins the procession. This, then, is what all who posit the two principles intend the second principle to be; so that they will posit the one as the former of the two; for the one is set against multitude. And this is the much-rehearsed syzygy of the two intelligible principles laid down after the one.

So that, even if someone should suppose that there is one principle before the intelligible triad, and that this one is the very one-all — for this, he will say, is also the unsayable; and Plato speaks thus in the Philebus, positing the two principles, limit and unlimited, and the one before these, which also supervenes upon the mixed in the unsayable manner (for it is unsayable in such wise as to be made known through the three monads seated in its forecourt); and Pythagoras judges likewise, setting the one before the monad and the so-called indefinite dyad; and assuredly all those philosophers think so who posited one principle before the two. Nay, one might contend the same from the opinions of the blessed men: the two are set against one another, while the one must exist before all opposition; and one would call to witness, besides, the common conception — that praised even by Aristotle — which declares the Homeric verdict, holding that the lordship of many is not good, and seating one king over wholes; for by this argument it will be necessary that the truly one rule all things whatsoever. Wherefore Plato too everywhere gives the elder honor to the one first principle: in the Sophist he sets the one before beings; and in the Parmenides, by the first hypothesis, resolving all things away from it — and 'is' besides all — he leaves the one itself alone, stripped bare of all the others. If, then, someone, reckoning up these things and the like — and knowing, at the same time, the opinion of Iamblichus — should suppose the one to be a single principle before the two, we shall meet him by bringing forward what has been said: wherein the many were set against the one, and the unlimited and the indefinite dyad were driven together into identity with the many — so that the monad too, and limit, come into identity with the one; so that the one becomes one of the two principles; and the second of the two is, in a manner, the fore-cause of all procession, while the one already gives a glimpse of the stable element in beings — insofar as it is by nature without procession, and set athwart differentiation, without which there would be no procession; and whatever else one might conclude from what has been said toward this hypothesis.

Yet further, in addition to these, those points too must be stated. One: that the one is not wholly unsayable, but only not sayable by discourse; for it is grasped neither by affirmation nor by negation, but perhaps by some simple intellection — and that neither rational nor intellective, for everything of that kind is form-like and composite; nor by the substantial intellection at all, for not even substance is something truly simple; but by the unitary form of knowledge, and by the flower of such an intuitive thrust of the soul. To us, however — or rather to the blessed beholders — it gives itself only to be surmised; and this only as far as the birth-pang alone, and all that has been said before concerning it. Since not even to the unitary knowledge is it knowable through and through — because what is only one, and nothing besides, is not even knowable; and if, in addition, it were also knowable, it would no longer be one in the strict sense. And yet even such a purgation of it draws somewhat near to its nature; and while it is still near, it wipes off for itself a certain knowledge of it; but having drawn close, it shuts its eyes — and there comes to be, in place of knowledge, union. But these things were said before as well. And it is plain, even now, that the one would not be the unsayable principle of all. For again: she is in every way placeless, ranked in no manner whatsoever together with all the other things; whereas the one, even if it be all things, is all things by the one, and is posited as one, and is, as it were, the crown of all things. And apart from these things: if anyone should wish in any manner to name what is by nature nameless, or to speak the wholly unspeakable, or to signify the signless, nothing prevents bringing to the one unsayable principle the mightiest of names and of thoughts, as symbols — the holiest that we have — and calling her too 'one,' and the manifest common conception that deems the principle of all things worthy to be one; knowing, however, by the stricter reckoning, that this name is not befitting to her, but is proper to the elder of the two principles — if indeed even to her it belongs, as has often been said, only by indication. And perhaps the common conception of all does reach as far as this principle that is in real truth one — if indeed even to her, yet only in that she deserves to be called something more common, and a principle; but not to the unsayable; since she is unkindred to all our conceptions whatsoever, and altogether beyond conceiving. And if the opposition of the one toward the many demands, once more, a one before the one, we at least would not place that opposition There, but somewhere below, among the determined things — from which we lead up to those principles the opposition that only seems.
Chapter 50 — The Case for the Dyad after the One: Orpheus, the Oracles, Philolaus; Iamblichus's Middle One · pp. 133–136

Come then, let us now say something about this second principle as well. Is it the case that, as well-nigh all the philosophers — and even some of the theologians — appear to posit a dyad after the one hymned principle, so we too must posit it, speaking with the precision we are now attempting? And why indeed not? — someone might say. For what needed to come forth after the one, if not the two? and after the monad the dyad, and in this way the remaining number? So, at any rate, Orpheus brings forth aether and chaos after Time; and the gods themselves, after the one god, show forth father and power as a dyad only; and all the theologies together have been handed down doing the same thing. And apart from these, the argument itself demands it: since Being is from limit and unlimited, as Plato says in the Philebus, and Philolaus in his books On Nature; and in general, since the conception of the one and of being is different, Being would not be the very thing that the one is. Yet it certainly participates in the one; it has, then, something that is also not-one. And this, as has been said, is either nothing — which is absurd — or many. If one should wish only two, they are limit and unlimited; if more, then all the genera of Being must pre-exist There seminally — since if one wishes to place simply all number in the monad, nothing prevents it. Being, then, is many; and of these, some fall to limit, the others to unlimitedness.
