One must therefore, someone will perhaps say, presuppose the causes both of the one Being and of the dyadic nature of the elements within it: the pre-divided dyad of principles, then, is cause of the dyad we have spoken of — just as the one before the dyad, which Iamblichus posits before both, pre-exists as cause of the one Being.

And indeed, to speak generally: if we divide all beings into the unified and the differentiated-in-whatever-manner — even if the counter-divided members stand toward one another as cause and effect — the same will result; for from two files, even so, of the one whole counter-division, we shall ascend assuredly to two principles; before which the one summit pre-exists, being cause of connate growth, while the two principles, with the two channels of all the opposites that grow out doubly from them, are parceled out according to every opposition. For such things he too used to say who championed the principle of Iamblichus, placing it midway between the two and that which is wholly unsayable. And he added this besides: must the two principles be participated by Being? Let the unitary stand before the substantial: the participations in Being, then, are the first elements of Being as mixed — namely limit and unlimited; wherefore Being is also unified, save that by its own property it has entered together with them into the same; but everywhere the elements are counter-divided, so that their principles too have something counter-divided — and so the cause stands even before Being's counter-division. For this argument claimed at once to advocate both the hypothesis of Iamblichus and the counter-division, in whatever manner, of the two principles; since one might say this also follows from it: that the henad before the two principles was all things together before all, but all things equally; while the first of the two is herself also all things, but according to the more limit-like; and the second all things likewise, but according to the more unlimited.

Further, one may see the same thing from below as well: all things being unified and differentiated, the one principle leads as of things unified, the other as of things differentiated, and the one before both as of things simply. Or perhaps it is better to speak in some such way as this: the one — the limit-like — is as of things remaining; the other as of things proceeding; and the third, which also takes its stand at Being, as of things reverting. But before these there must be the common summit of all, being simply one — the crown of all things: not as of things in any way presided over, but only as of things subsisting. For again: if someone should say that the two — or the three together with the third — are principles of all things simply, how will they differ from one another, all being all things in like manner? And if you say they will differ by the more and the less — what, among those natures, is the measuring-out of more and less, where there is no form-like difference at all? And in general, the more and the less is seen within one property; and again, the principle of the one property is one, and not many.

parts.name: Chapter 51 — The Two Channels and the One Cause of Their Connate Growth; the Regress of Middle Principles · pp. 136–137

lines.text: Chapter 51 — The Two Channels and the One Cause of Their Connate Growth; the Regress of Middle Principles · pp. 136–137

Against these things and all such, this is ready to hand to say: that all our conceptions are sent back up from the determined things to the undetermined principles before all — both the conception of the one, someone would say, and that of all things; but, purifying our conceptions nevertheless from the determined to the undetermined, so far as we can bear them, we say the one and the all together: breaking off from the one its partial character by the addition of all things, and dissolving the composite character of all things by the addition of the one's simplicity.

In another way, then, must the counter-division also be viewed There — the counter-division of all things together that are counter-divided in whatever manner, whether as coordinates, or as causes and effects. For there is something common to them all according to the most generic division; so that, the things counter-divided in whatever way being taken in two files, two causes pre-exist, and these, as it were, counter-divided. And there must, the two being thus opposed, also be the one cause of the connate growth of the two principles — and of the whole file of the things that grow together, down to the last, out of the pairs of counter-elements that arise at every level; and it is no wonder if this whole file should be superior to the two files, since this is the law among those natures: the whole proceeds before the parts, and the unified before the differentiated, and one principle indeed before the two. This, then, is the simply one, which Iamblichus places midway between the two principles and that which is altogether unsayable; while the two are Limit, say, and Unlimited — or, if one wishes, One and Many; but the One that is opposed to the many, not the one before both, which is without opposition.

If, then, someone should so contend, making the two principles opposed and ranking the principle of the one before both, we must say to him, first: that thing which he named last of the middle file — the cause of the connate whole — what ever is it? For if what is before the two is one, being of the connate, it will itself also be connate; so that it is not simply one, but the connate-out-of-two, even if it be before the two; and so before it, in turn, there will be the simply one. But if it is simply one, it will be the cause of the one of that kind at every level, but not of the connate growth out of two. And if the connate growth of the two principles — the one that arises between them according to their participation of the one — is itself the principle of the whole connate file, it will be necessary to make this a one before the two, according to the connate; and before this, the simply one; and from it, the two principles: so that, either way, the middle principles will turn out to be two — between the unsayable and the so-called two principles — and no longer one, according to Iamblichus. But, he will say, the simplicity of the first is not one thing, and the connate growth now being purified another: they are the same; for there is a single summit of the double counter-division. Very well, I shall say: it is one nature, holding together in the same the twin procession. But if even the partition of one procession, gathered up in one partless nature pre-existing according to a single uncomposed nature, does not lead us up to the simply one — what must one think about the leading monad of the double column? Surely, that it cannot be the simplest one. What then will he say? Do we not call it all-things-one? — and yet, for all that, one. Let it, however, be called also the connate growth of the two files, in which all the other things too are strung together — or under which they are ranked.
Chapter 52 — The Refutation: Ascent from All Things, Not from One Opposition; Dishonoring Even the One; the Egyptians' Darkness beyond All Intellection; the Fount of Founts · pp. 137–140

But first: it is better to be led up from all things, in utter completeness, to the one super-simplified simplicity of the one of all things — and not from a single counter-division, even if all things are contained in it; for it would present all things in itself according to the properties of only two characters; whereas one must be wholly unfolded back from all things upon the one cause of all.

Second: not even does this generic counter-division embrace all things. For the common-natured procession from the two — the procession that everywhere goes forth before each partition, and gathers it up — this the counter-division has not comprehended; since every counter-division is a partition, while before every partition the partless is viewed: and this is not the one, but, as it were, a fount of the things partitioned from it — as the monad is of all number, being other than the simply one. Then he says that neither does this persuade us: that one of the principles is, as it were, a monad; another, as it were, a dyad; and another according to the one before both — for so, he says, Pythagoras too declares. Or rather: Pythagoras gave covert indication of the unsayable principle by the one, having nothing else by which to utter her to another; but we now dishonor even the one, dishonoring it in comparison with that position — since she will appear more august, made august by us with the Unsayable alone, if it be lawful to say so. Thus, at any rate, the Egyptians also called her unknowable darkness — proclaiming this three times over her — and, further, darkness beyond all intellection; and, further still, hymning her as the great concealment: making a high tragedy, rather, of our own states of unknowing, and by these attempting to give covert indication of her.

But indeed the many, too, are before monad and dyad — and, in general, before all number, as he shows in the Parmenides — being elder; and from these one is led up to the first principles: clearly, from the one to its own cause, and from the many to the cause of multitude. And one should observe how we have ascended to the two sole principles from before monad and dyad; hardly, then, would we ascend to them from monad and dyad — or from the one to the single principle before them; for the one is counter-distinguished from the many, and this whole opposition is before that one. — But this I have made as a parenthesis of the argument. —3 Again, returning to the matter from the beginning, this must be said third: that we shall be in danger of driving these two channels of the procession-by-every-counter-division out to infinity. For this too is a certain counter-division — that of the one-before-both toward the dyad of channels; and we shall need to conceive yet another before this one as well; and before that, perhaps, to presuppose another still.

And fourth: every division is the offspring of multitude — that is, of the multitude-making dyad. Carrying the whole of what is called counter-division, then, of whatever kind, we shall refer it to that single principle, the multitude-making, which leads off all differentiations. And its summit, which we call one, is not really one, but, as it were, the monad — or connate growth — of the counter-division: a monad pointing toward the simply one; the very thing that Limit, and the truly all-things-one, means to be. For as the counter-division is an offspring of the principle according to the Unlimited, so its connate growth will be the offspring of the principle according to Limit — and we may call the one also the things ranked with limit, as we call the other the things ranked with unlimitedness; and above all the most principle-like of these, namely the one and the many. Connate growth, however, and counter-division — and differentiation in general — is, in Being, unified according to gathering: not yet differentiated, but being the sole connate growth of all things before all differentiation; whereas in the intelligible intellect determination first shone forth, in whatever manner — whether differentiation, or any multitude whatsoever. For the middle order, as was said before, means to be in the preparation of differentiation: seen as in the very act of being differentiated, and not yet bearing anything differentiated; so that counter-division in actuality begins, in a manner, from the third of the intelligible world-orders. For the first differentiation and division is fontal; and that order is hymned as the Fount of founts.

Note 3. The parenthesis: in the Parmenides the one and the many are elder than monad, dyad, and all number — so the ascent to the two principles runs from one-and-many, not from monad-and-dyad; and the one of that pair, being counter-distinguished from the many, cannot itself be the single principle before both.
Chapter 53 — From All Partition to the Union-Mass of All; Existence, the Many, and Chaos; the Orphic Metis, Fount of the Fontal World-Orders · pp. 140–143

Fifth, then, in addition to these: from partition we ascend everywhere to the partless; so that from the common partition of all things we shall be led up to the common partless of all. And this is the gathering of all things — or, to speak most justly, the union-mass of all. For that which is all things unifiedly and undividedly — as the fount of the many channels is an undetermined union-mass — this would be such as we often surmise Being to be. For what has been affected by the one, yet is not one, would be Being: being both one and not-one, though these are not yet determined in it; wherefore it deserves to be called only Unified. If, then, from the complete differentiation-mass of all things we ascend to the complete concretion of all things, and from the multiplication of all to the union-mass of all, it is clear that, attempting to climb beyond even these, we shall stand off far more greatly from all counter-division — passing, as it were, from a complete cosmos undifferentiated and unified to a complete cosmos that deserves to be called not even undifferentiated; for it is not even unified, but simpler still — many, or unlimited, or dyad. For the unified carries the appearance of both many and one, even if these are not yet determined within it; but that principle is many only, insofar as she is at all; wherefore she is also unlimited by herself; for multitude conceived without the one is infinitely infinite — the unweighable gaping void of the unlimited. The unlimited too, indeed, is one — but by participation; her existence, and as it were her property, is many only and unlimited only: not many in this sense, as being some several things, so that a unified should arise out of many blended with the one; rather she is one-many by her property. And before the many, the one assuredly is one wholly: one only by its property, and one according to existence, being nothing at all by participation. Wherefore that principle is named Existence — because it is only according to existence.

And the second, participating the first, thereupon projected as her own property the multitude-making existence of the first; wherefore the dyadic first appeared in her, and the processive — because she first proceeded — and the property of Chaos, because she first contained the one before her, and first stepped out of the one, in whatever manner. The Unified, then, is not yet either of those two — nor yet is it the mixed without more; for the mixed requires at the least two pre-subsisting properties, and one that gathers them. It stands, accordingly, in the third place from the first: that in which are two participations — one of the one, and one of the many — gathered together by the existence of the unified, of Being; and the third is indeed a triad. And this third is a complete whole cosmos, and the single root of all things; while each of those two principles is a cosmos more greatly complete — or rather a cause of complete cosmoi: the one, as of cosmoi unified; the other, as of each multiplied; and a cause of the very first of all, which for this reason is called hidden — the wholly hidden cosmos — such that it is not even a seed of the hidden cosmoi that proceed from it, but is still beyond the seminal principle; since before every seed stands the one undetermined nature that has gathered up all things in herself. Wherefore the theologian hymns Metis first, bearing the seed of gods — Metis, who is also called, by the gods themselves, fount of all the fontal world-orders. So far does he stand from that counter-divided opposition, that the single connate growth and union of the whole of it is his, together with the intelligible appearance that is in labor with differentiation. And if Metis is such, much more so the Metis yet in the womb — or perhaps it is finer to say: the intelligible middleness that is pregnant with the metis; and before even her, Being itself — the world-order that is hidden in very truth.

Still more greatly complete, then, is the cause of this; but it is no longer a cosmos — it is a cause of cosmos, in that the cosmos is all things; just as the principle before her is cause in that the cosmos is also one. For that third too is a certain one-and-many, but as it were undifferentiatedly. Let us bring on, then, the sixth generation of the demonstration as well: that each of the three is all things, and before all things; but the third is all according to the union-mass of all; the first is all according to the one, as one complete simplicity; and the middle is all according to the all themselves. For she too is all things — as many, which is just what all things are; for surely not as some things, since those would be a particular many; she was many simply: therefore all; but all things neither determined nor unified. For she is not the participants, but manyness itself; so that she is all according to existence — just as Being is all by participation, while the Unified is all according to existence, as the one is one according to existence but all things according to cause, if it be lawful to say so. Not that the one is at once also the cause of all — for so it would be not-one; rather it is the one alone, solitary, all-bearing. So it will be fitting to distinguish them by their very names: the first principle is the One before all; the second, All things; the third, One-All according to union. Let so much, then, be essayed toward the indication of the first two so-called principles.
Chapter 54 — Neither Two nor One: the Misuse of Names; Intellect Folds Its Intellections Together (Iamblichus); One-All, All-One, and the Unified · pp. 143–147

And it is plain that the two principles are not of the same rank — even if this is often said, by way of certain indications drawn from the more familiar; nor are they two, if indeed all number is below — even the monad itself; nor are they determined off from one another; for not even in the third principle is there ever determination, but only a fore-union of the things that will be determined out of her. Nor does otherness take them apart, if indeed sameness is not in those natures either. Rather — as the gods themselves, conversing with men, declared — the three principles stand toward one another as Intellect and Power and Father would: the existence, the power of the existence, and the intellection of the power. Yet it is altogether plain that not even these things are truly true of those principles; for the determination of these appears — intelligibly, and hiddenly — in the third of the intelligible world-orders; whereas in the Unified even these are unified; for not even the determination of cause and effect is in those natures — no, not in the summit of the intelligibles; for not even Iamblichus judged the principle there to be determined. For one is the intelligible continuity of all such things — and not even a continuity opposed to determination; for then there would again be another division before both, and yet before all of it, union: among the intelligibles everything is made fast from the one and about the one. For whatever is surmised as multiplied There — insofar as the unified is not the very one — even this must be viewed within the uniform. For neither could the union There be called the union opposed to multitude; for with that union the counter-divided multitude would coexist; rather, the union before both is one. And if we judge thus in the case of the intelligibles, what must one expect in the case of the two principles that lie before the whole intelligible? Is it not that they are unified far more greatly? Or rather: before the whole unified substance, the two are assuredly — one.

How then are they two? Surely not according to the dyad; for number is not yet There, nor determination at all; for neither is the monad There; for not even the one itself — that which is called one — nor the many; for these too are counter-distinguished toward one another. We misuse the names, nevertheless, in their case, since we possess no appellations worthy of them; for neither do we have intellections of that kind; nor are the very intelligibles graspable by our intellections; for not even by the watchtowers of intellect is the summit of the intelligible intellected, according to Iamblichus; rather, intellect must fold its own intellections together into the intelligible, if, being gathered, it is to cast itself, in whatever manner, upon the wholly gathered. We must not say, then, that the principles are two — nor indeed one, as men counting; rather, surmising according to the property, which we declare to be dyadic and monadic: a dyad, in that she is dyad-like; a monad, in that monad-like; and one and many in the same fashion — not by number, nor by quantity at all, nor by some quantified nature, nor by the principle of quantity, nor by that of qualified substance, but beyond all such conceptions; for each of these is partial and determined. Nor are we content with these: we avail ourselves of yet others toward the indication of that nature; and not one of them hits the truth; but out of them all we compel our surmise to flee up into the undetermined and the more nobly born — since we even say that the principles are two, and subordinate the one to the other according to procession, though There is neither dyad nor any procession at all.

It would perhaps be better — if this too were granted — not to make them two in such a fashion, as two monads, but to make the two one dyadic thing, as one might conceive the one of the dyad. But not even this fits those principles; for this one is some particular one — one one consorts with one number, another with another. It is better, then, to take up that one which is common to all things; and, having made it two-formed in just this respect — that it is containing of all things both as unified and as differentiated — so to fit it to the nature of the two so-called principles. Whence we attempt to make them clear, or to give indication of them, in the manner that is possible: at one time from the two columns, purified from below and brought to a joint crest at the very top, toward that twin single summit; at another time, more magnificently, from the whole plenitudes that are everywhere, and from the whole cosmoi, as multiplied and as unified — these ever subordinated to those — sending us up by steps thus great to the all-complete precedence and subordination of the first principles. And grander, perhaps, even than this ascent, and more worthy of the height, for indication, would be the one that leads up simply from all things — from things in whatever manner existing, and in whatever manner viewed as causes and as effects; and in however many ways one may wish, or be able, to surmise somewhat the things There, let him not surmise them as these things, nor as such as these hint at, but — still more greatly — as principles and causes of these, which have not yet appeared There; and not even these: I mean the very name and thing of principle, and of cause. For these too are determined, intelligibly, in the limit of the intelligibles; in the middleness they are in process of being determined, according to the still-laboring birth-pang of the differentiation of all such things; while in the summit all things are gathered up into one — the union-mass of all.

Before this, therefore, stand the two principles: proximately, the second, according to the birth-pang of all things; and above her, the first, according to the simplicity before all — in respect of which the one is imaged forth, just as the many are imaged according to the birth-pang of all things. For — if it be lawful so to define — the first is one-all, and the second all-one; for the first, being all things through herself, is nevertheless all precisely insofar as she brought forth the second; while the third has the one from the first, and the all according to the property of the second — so as to be multiplied according to this latter and unified according to that former; and to become the first composite; and to be made complete as the union-mass of all things; and to project this from herself: the Unified — which indeed we also call Being; whose property is the one as having-been-unified, just as the property of the principle before it is the all, and of the yet earlier, the before-all; the second showing forth all things as one — the all; and the third the one-all: the unified, out of one and all. But of these things again, when we speak concerning the third — presently, very soon indeed.
Chapter 55 — On the Unified: Why the Third Is Called Mixed — Philolaus and the Orphic Egg; Out of What Is It Mixed? · pp. 147–151

Accordingly, let us now approach the third problem of the discourse — or rather, the third principle of all things; for we shall be seen to stretch out from her toward the two first principles as well. Let us inquire, then, into the Unified, which we have constantly ranked third. What ever is it? And why do we place it third? And how is it called Mixed by Plato and the other philosophers of the Platonic school — and, still earlier, by Philolaus and the other Pythagoreans? Not only because it is compacted out of limiters and unlimiteds — which is what Philolaus says Being is — but because, after the monad and the indefinite dyad, they posit as third principle the unified triad; and every unified is mixed, if indeed the unified carries the appearance of both one and multitude; so that we must also inquire out of what it has been mixed. For Orpheus too says: Then great Chronos fashioned in divine aether a silvery-white egg. For 'fashioned' indicates something crafted, and not a begetting; and the crafted-not-begotten is all-mixed, out of two at the least — matter and form, or the things analogous to these. Further, then: whether the Mixed is superior to its own elements, out of which it is filled up; and whether the elements come from forefather principles homogeneous with them in property — for Plato seems to intend these things — and whatever perplexities must be raised about these matters and conceived, so far as is possible, concerning things so great.

Before all else, someone might inquire this: why is the Unified not immediately after the One? For the unified has first been affected by the one; it should therefore come right after the one. — But the unified requires also being many; for a certain multitude appears along with it, as it were swallowed up by the one. — Then the principle of the many is herself both a multitude and a participant of the one: she, therefore, is the unified — having wished to become unlimited, but having been fettered by the participation of the one! — Or rather: the unified means to be such as the mixed; but nothing is composed out of existence and participation; for the participation in a thing, and its existence, would not be elements or parts of anything; since the existence would stand, as element, pre-underlying in the role of matter, while the participation supervenes, like a form upon a single element. And in general, elements are somehow of the same rank; but the participant and the participation are not of the same rank, nor from a single counter-division. Apart from these things: the elements are two at the least; but the second principle was a dyad as one dyadic thing, and many-and-unlimited as manyness and unlimitedness — each being only one, though by property many and unlimited; there are not yet, therefore, elements of the unified There. For the one, supervening upon several things, works the unified; for it is the one that unifies — not, surely, something else, the one being itself only one and simple — but there must also be several; and the several are not yet There; for it is by participation of manyness that the several come to be, manyness being divisive; and it is the divided that are unified; and these come after the multitude-making principle. In the third, first, then, the several are imaged forth; wherefore also the union of these is in it first; and that is the unified before all things. Before this stands the second principle: she participates the one — for she too became one — but, being many by her property alone, she does not have union. For union is where there was division of several. This, then, one could not surmise otherwise.

In the third, then, what several do we say there are? — Elements of the mixed. — And what are these? — It is ready to hand to say: the participations from those two principles, the one and the many, which came forth into the third — or, if you wish to say limit and unlimited, or monad and indefinite dyad — into the subsistence of the unified triad; for the triad too will be triad by her property alone, and not a composition of several, nor a number; but nevertheless, even so, of such elements: of the monad and the dyad. — But if one should suppose it so, first we shall need yet another principle before the two. For if these are the principles of the two elements, and the mixed is before its elements, it will be necessary to make for the mixed also a principle of its own peculiar manner — itself named mixed, at least by indication — pre-existing as the as-it-were property of the truly mixed; just as we pre-suppose the one and the many, of the homonymous elements in the mixed, as something other, and before the mixed, again, the two principles. For every mixed has something one-like and something multitude-like. And in this way we shall go to infinity, forever presupposing principles of principles. Yet not even those philosophers themselves who do these things — who make limit and unlimited elements within the mixed, and the mixed prior to the elements, as Plato does, and beyond the mixed again limit and unlimited, the two principles of the elements — not even they think it right to make, before the two principles, another single principle, the mixed. Next: neither does each of the two principles stand partially, so as to be the principle of one element — the one of limit only, the other of unlimitedness; rather, each is principle of all things: the one as of things divided and many and unlimited, should it so chance; the other as of things unified, and as of ones, and as of limit-like things — of them all. For, in general, the principle of the many, being multitude-making, is somehow divisive of the elements — whether of the first two, or of more, or of the simply multiplied plenitude in the third; while the principle of the one, overtaking the union-mass before the many, makes that which the mixed is: composed, as it were, of parts and of whole — of the many and of the one.

Do the participations of the two principles, then, complete the mixed? For the argument runs back up, once more, to the one and the many as being elements — the very thing for which we did not accept the philosophers when they do it. — Or is the third one according to the participation of the one, and many — and as it were manyness — according to the uniform procession from the second principle, and not yet the mixed? — Rather, this third is brought forth from the first principle as it were uniformly; from the second as it were dyadically — in which respect it is also named mixed; and from both heteroform-wise, as mixed from unmixed; just as, homoform-wise, it comes from both as one-all and as many-all. And since the participations act back upon one another, having become as it were of the same rank, the one was multiplied and differentiated into several, and the many were gathered up and became homogeneous. And this latter affection became union — being a being-affected of the one in multitude; and the former, differentiation — being a being-affected of the many in the one. And thus, in the third, union and differentiation came together; out of which the whole mixed was compacted. Further still: according to its self-subsistent procession, the mixed projected itself from itself, and within itself co-divided the elements ranged against one another. For the whole apportions its parts within itself and from itself; and likewise the element-source, which is what the mixed is: pre-existing its elements, as being superior to them, it further differentiates the elements within itself and from itself; for before the divided, always, the undivided subsists.

parts.name: Chapter 56 — The Mixed without Elements, Parts, or Wholeness: One Water Much-Divisible; the Congealing of the Flow; the Prayer to the Gods · pp. 151–156

lines.text: Chapter 56 — The Mixed without Elements, Parts, or Wholeness: One Water Much-Divisible; the Congealing of the Flow; the Prayer to the Gods · pp. 151–156

And if you should view them also in this way, proceeding from the principles, you would not throw far from my hope: the one would bring forth the union-mass of the mixed — I mean the mixed itself; while its elemental multitude is brought forth by the hymned principle of the many; and as the one principle is supportive of the other principle's subsistence, so too the union-mass co-establishes the multitude of the elements. But the elements are a this-here and a this-here — limit and unlimited, or one and many, the counter-ranged. As being such, what is it that produces them? Again, the better comes from the better principle, and the worse from the worse; and again the two principles are principles of the counter-divided elements — or else these elements are homonyms only of those principles, the manner of their subsistence being other, or by analogy. Perhaps these too were brought forth alongside from the two principles — yet not the one from that principle and the other from this; or the mixed itself gave them subsistence and differentiated them, according to its own twin single nature: for being one-many — and, to speak simply, unified — according to the appearance of multitude it brought forth the many, and according to the dominance of the one, the one. Or, if you wish, the second principle too divided these within the third — but the many according to herself, and the one according to the unity present with her from what is called the one. The two, at any rate, have grown together, and the connate growth is before the growing-apart: insofar as the mixed has grown together, it comes also from the higher principle; and perhaps each element comes from her too — the one insofar as she is herself, the other insofar as she consorts with the one;

and again each from the second — the one insofar as she is herself, the other insofar as she has taken up the first beforehand. But this, surely: both are in the mixed — the multitude of the elements, and the union-mass before them.

Should we not rather make the mixed of these two — of which each is all things: the one the gathering of all, the other the differentiation-mass of all — the whole mixed out of both? For as intellect, whole and every form, is neither its many only nor its one only, but the both-together, so too the first mixed would be neither the one nor the other, but the both-together. — Or, doing thus, shall we go to infinity? For the both-together will be counter-divided against each of the two, and again another both-together must be sought; since the whole, too, is before the parts only. And if the whole itself is out of whole and parts, we shall need yet another wholeness; and if out of this and those two, the whole will again require a third set as well — and this to infinity. If we must come to a stand, let us remain at the first wholeness, saying that there are whole and parts only, and the element-source together with the elements. — Do we not, then, conceive the Whole as one thing, the parts as another, and the both-together as yet another? This first mixed is not from things of the same rank; nor from elements; nor from parts; nor is it a whole, nor a composite — nor, therefore, mixed in those senses. It would be like compounding something out of cause and effect — for that too would be a both-together of a kind; or out of user and instrument; or out of paradigm and image. For such a yoking is viewed in some relation, and not in the co-ordering that is according to substance. But if this both-together should be in one — as, in intellect, its unified and its differentiated — how is the one intellect not out of both? It is out of both in this way: as the unified projecting the differentiated from itself. For such a thing seems to be a mean between the two: between the both-together as of elements, which is before its elements, and the both-together of cause and effect, where nothing is common according to substance, a relation only lying between, and that stretching from the cause into the effect — namely, the unity of intellect, which has co-established the connate whole of two plenitudes, the unified and the differentiated. For intellect is the all; and those two are not counter-ranked parts, but plenitudes, the one co-subsisting out of the other — as heaven stands to the sub-heavenly place. For always, what pre-subsists from the separate cause further differentiates the second plenitude and co-establishes it with its cause. Composite, nevertheless, is the both-together even of these; but as composite, a whole; and toward those plenitudes, parts — even if parts of a more whole-like kind; for of the cosmos too the most generic parts are two, heaven and everything sub-heavenly — or so much as is immortal and so much as is mortal; since the material cosmos, too, is filled up out of the three material cosmoi, which hold the ratio of parts to the whole.

Or rather: such a thing is neither composite, nor a whole out of elements, nor out of parts; but it is, as it were, the procession of a series, stepping forward by descent through firsts and middles and lasts; and it does have a certain co-ordering, appearing as one whole — yet not as of a wholeness toward parts, nor as of a mixed thing toward elements, but, as has been said, according to the connate mutual inter-holding of the seconds, always, with their antecedents, and of the produced with their producers. But such a forward-stepping has not yet appeared in the first mixed — it being first, and not yet having stepped down into a first and a second plenitude. Otherwise even the first plenitude will be mixed, and the second likewise mixed; for in intellect each of the two is indeed mixed, since intellect is a mixed out of mixeds; but the first was the simplest mixed of all, and not out of mixeds. Wherefore it would be imaged as mingled rather as out of elements only — for not as out of parts; the partition of parts is greater, parts standing in distance toward one another; whereas elements mean rather to be gathered up, and as it were con-fused, the property of each not showing forth in the mixed — just as the forms do the contrary, each circumscribing itself according to its own shape; and the parts hold the middle station: they are divided — wherefore they are even called parts — yet they are eager to dissolve their partition by the upward glance toward the whole. Proportionally, then: the forms have shone forth in the third order of the intelligible; the parts in the middle; and the elements in the summit — in which nothing proper to anything is truly differentiated, but all has been drunk down by the single union of the mixed. Since not even the several elements There are yet differentiated, so that one might know a this-here; rather, as in the wholly unified, the multitude-like is merely imaged forth, because of the simplicity of the first mixed; for it is much only, and not several things — like one water, much-divisible; and the multitude There, being of that kind, is nevertheless itself also gathered up, and hidden away beneath its union.

Not two plenitudes of the mixed, then — a union-mass and a differentiation-mass, as in intellect; rather, the whole is one only — and truly unmixed: the property of mixed shown forth first. For it is not as of several things blended into the same — this one could not justly bring even to the mixture of our own soul; nor as of several things There co-appearing with the one in truth; for it is from intellect that we drag these differentiative surmises onto That. But just as we viewed the many according to one complete property — the one property being nevertheless all things — so also the mixed is one simple and incomposite property, being nevertheless all things within the simple — save that it is so according to the peculiar manner of the mixed of all. For the mixed is all things in the proper sense — yet before all the things that are properly called all according to differentiation; for That is all things undifferentiatedly, according to the union-mass of all. The second principle too is all things, but more simply; for she is all not only undifferentiatedly, like the unified, according to co-ordering and compaction, if it be lawful to say so, but according to the simply unco-ordered unlimitedness of the many, and the indeterminacy superior to every bound; for even the embrace of all things is a kind of bound. And the first, again, is all things — simpler even than that undetermined and unembraced principle which is nevertheless all — according to the very simplicity of the one before unlimitedness: a one not even poured out into the many, but exempted far more greatly from the unified co-ordering of all things in the mixed; in which mixed the unified subsisted according to the as-it-were congealing of the outpouring of the many and of the unlimited nature — an outpouring which we suppose to be a kind of flowing of the one; and this flow, congealed, we say is the mixed, and the first unified. So that all we said before, differentiating the things within the mixed in order that we might conceive it as mixed, we now gather up, by a single argument, into the one undifferentiated property of the mixed — the truly intelligible crown of all things. And I call upon the gods to be forgiving for the weakness of such conceptions — and still more, of the expressions. For without this counter-rampart of arguments, and this frankly metaphorical necessity, we could not have given indication of anything whatsoever, in any way, concerning the most primal principles. May the gods, then, be truly gracious.
Chapter 57 — The Same Doctrine through Limit and Unlimited, Monad and Dyad: the Mixed as the Monad before Number; Father and Mother of One First-Born · pp. 156–159

In the same manner also, if one makes the two principles Limit and Unlimitedness, as Plato holds, we shall view the mixed coming to be from these: pinning down the outpouring of unlimitedness, by the limit-like bond, into the one other property of the Limited, in which are both limit and unlimited. For the limited is neither limit nor unlimitedness, but the both-together. Let it be conceived, then: as the unified is simple and incomposite, so also is this mixed of limit and unlimited — as before both; for not even the division of these is yet There; That is of such a kind before the two. And the same account will hold both of the composition, conceived along with it by our weakness, and of the simplicity of the mixed as it is being purified. And if one makes the two principles monad and indefinite dyad, from these he views the unified triad — not composed out of some three, but being the very one of the triad, and for this reason being one triadic property, furnishing all things according to this one. In this way, then, we shall declare the third to subsist from the first principles — itself first, beyond all the things that are called unified and mixed; while from below, from the things proceeding out of her, we are led back up to her by resolution: from all things together, because she too is the crown of all; folding together, always, and gathering up the many differentiations into the many unions, and the one differentiation before the many into the one union before the many, and the counter-division of these toward one another — whatever it may be, and howsoever it stands — into the single and simple and wholly undifferentiated and un-opposed unified summit, which has gathered all things together at once.

And, if you wish, I call the mixed the union-mass of all — being before all the things that are being mixed; and all things are in it; all things, therefore, are mixed, and this mixed is before all: as the monad is every number, even the unlimited number ever being set forth; for the number that steps forward from her will never unroll what has been gathered up in the monad. Wherefore the mixed is from unlimited and limit in this respect also: that it is super-simplified beyond all the things after itself, and has gathered up, without limit, the unlimitedness of the things that come to be upon it. And it is, nevertheless, a monad in the truest sense — not the principle of number, for that monad is many removes below this one, but such by indication: as the one of the first principle is such, and as the many of the second. For the monad before number is a concretion of the one and the many, just as that nature is of the two principles. And such will the intelligible number also appear to us, of the same kind as the monad herself. But let this be deferred to another occasion. That the monad has both the one and the many is plain to everyone, since she has also every number; she is the first number — but gathered and undifferentiated; wherefore the one in her is the more distinct, and the multitude the more exact. For she has multitude simply, and the unlimited; wherefore also every number — whose unlimitedness generation, in unrolling it, would never find a limit of the unrolling. Wherefore the monad too is mixed, out of the things said in whatever way to pre-exist as many in the mixed — I mean all the things that are differentiated from her and after her, but which are in her undifferentiated, according to one unified all-generative nature: a nature not containing many causes of the things after her — for neither is there a differentiation of the many causes There — but one all-working cause; or rather, no cause other than herself. For she is the nature now made known: the fount of all things — not according to the one cause contained within her, but according to her own existence.

Is then the multitude There unified as having been united out of forms? But that is the mixed of intellect. As out of parts, then? But that was the gathering of the whole — or, if you wish, of the middle. It remains, then: as out of elements. But, first, that will not be the simply mixed, if it is the from-elements; and, next, it is perhaps possible for something to be out of many, or to be many, while there are not yet either elements, or parts, or forms, but only many; for each of these is many; to be many, then, is common to all the manys. And third: the principle of the many was multitude-making only — not of elements, nor of parts, nor of forms; so that even if there is multitude in the mixed, it is only multitude — not the such-like multitude of forms and genera, nor of parts, nor of elements. But even if one should concede this too, not even so will that be the simply mixed, nor the one undifferentiated crown of all; nay, the principle of the many will not be simply the cause of all things, but only insofar as the all are many. And yet many was said by indication — not because she is out of many, or many; nor out of elements, or elements; nor, of the rest, those things. For these are determined first in intellect — I mean their first causes; wherefore I defer speaking with precision about them for the present. But that mixed is as out of all things alike — many, and elements, and parts, and genera, and forms; for indeed out of composites and wholes, all of them; but, as has been said, it is the before-all that is the all. And if one should make it a mixture out of the two principles, as proceeding from them as from a father and a mother — one offspring, the very first-born of all things, from parents — he would not throw far from the surmise that is possible concerning the third principle, insofar as she is called mixed. And if also as out of the all-one and the all-many, in this way too it would have the indication of that nature which baffles inquiry and exceeds it. This, however, does not deserve to pass unmarked: that the appearance, in whatever manner, of multitude is not a differentiation of the unified, but belongs to the still simpler many — and to things coming to be in that way — out of which the unified is, the already-composite; whereas the differentiation of the unified itself is many unifieds, arising after the first unified; for that first, in this respect at least, is undifferentiated, and as it were one, the unified. But about these things, too, more precisely hereafter.
Chapter 58 — In How Many Ways Being Is Said: the Four Senses; the Nameless Mixture of the Body; Humanly, Horsely, Lunarly, Solarly · pp. 159–164

Now let us speak again, from the beginning, about this principle — what it is — no longer according to the conception of the mixed and unified, but in that the philosophers, speaking from true conceptions, declare it to be Being and substance: the simply so, and the first substance herself. For even if we do not refer the third immediately to substantial Being, as they do, but before this to the unitary, still: why is the third henad said to be the first Being and the first substance? Before all else, the significations of the names must be divided. For Being is said, first, as some one of the genera of Being, opposed to not-being and counter-divided from the other genera — this Being is eidetic, one of the simple forms along with the other four genera; and in the Parmenides, before the hypotheses, he ranked this too among the generic forms. In another way, Being is said as the connate-whole plenitude of the genera — which we peculiarly call presence, with Plotinus; and it is so taken in the Sophist, when he makes Being many things affected by the one. Being is said also as the whole that subsists before soul, as in the Republic; and he calls this substance, though as he proceeds he ranks together with it the genus of soul as well; and accordingly he thinks it right to call soul the first generation in relation to this substance. And Being and Substance are said, lastly, as the summit of the whole intelligible — that which is also the simply intelligible: the very thing which in the Sophist he shows to be unmoved, and which in the Parmenides, according to the second hypothesis, he takes as Being first; and, having celebrated it as One-Being, he derives from it all the things that in any way are, or are said to be, or become, or are not, as is said There; and he hymns it as substance too, beginning at the very opening of the hypothesis.

From which of these, then — and according to the conception of which Being — do we ascend to that Unified? From the genus, as we were led up from the one to the simply one? For this Being is simple, and its conception befits the first Being. But That was all things; and the substance composed out of all would resemble it the more, by so much: being not some one thing, but a complete whole cosmos. For as this substance is all things together, so the third principle is all things undifferentiatedly. We would ascend, accordingly, not from one of the things that have proceeded from her, but from all the things differentiated after her. Or perhaps one must gather both together in her case as well: the simple, from the one genus; the entire and all-full, from the substance composed out of all; so that we should justly call the unified principle by both names, Substance and Being. For before every multitude, surely, there is always the gathering of that multitude: of the forms, the eidetic gathering; of the genera, the generic — and so with the rest.

Of such natures there is no name according to truth, nor any concept of the kind that belongs to divided things; for names are in differentiation, and all of them assuredly eidetic; whereas That was in every way one, and all things must be gathered up by its own singleness. How, then, could the straitened peculiarity of names suffice for the disclosure, or the embrace, of the complete unified simplicity that is before all? — when not even of the divided forms, nor of the last things all together, do we possess a common name, or project some concentrated and entire concept; and hardly could we do this in the case of the highest and all-pervading crown. Why say much? When even of the partial gatherings we can name not a single one — except perhaps as gathering, and mixed, and whatever is of that sort. For example, our own body, which has been compounded out of the four elements: what proper name could it have? Body belongs also to each of the simples; and earthy, or wet, or pneumatic, or airy, or fiery, or warm names the whole from some one of the things within it; while the whole itself has no common name as common — though perhaps the human, and the generic, such as animal. Another mixture is vegetal; others again soulless; and the particulars of these likewise. And humanity is some one of the many properties in the mixed, and it supervenes upon the mixture as form upon matter; while matter, by herself, is nameless. And what wonder? — when even some of the forms partake of namelessness, as that man says of the genus of hotness and coldness. Just so, the mixture of the elements also goes unnamed.

But further: the common property that supervenes upon the mixture — the one that gives form to the mixture — is it, as it were, an element of the whole, as of a whole from matter and form? For it is simple, as each element is. Or not so: rather, it is the property of the mixture, according to which each of the composite forms is named — these being so called in contradistinction to the elemental and simpler genera. And the property of each genus, too, is simple; while the other mixture is of the others, by participation either of priors or of co-ranked things. So too intellect, and life, and Being itself assuredly: of which each is all things — but the one according to the peculiar character of intellect, the second according to that of life, the third according to that of Being. Is Being, then, also a simple peculiar character — say substancehood, as lifehood in the case of life and intellecthood in the case of intellect? Or does it rather seem to be something between an element and the whole composite form — like the whole intellectual plenitude? For the elements come from one place into another, and are ranked in the role of matter toward the form-giving property; while she characterizes, and gathers, and alters the elements toward herself, sufficing for them all and stretching alongside them by her own simplicity. Wherefore she means to be entire, more than any of the elements whatsoever. For each of them belongs to her, and is by-named from her; and the others stand according to her: the four elements subsist humanly, or horsely, or lunarly, or solarly; and the whole of both together is the form, or the genus, or the intellect, or the animal, or life, or Being — which last we posit as the first of all the things subsisting in this manner.
Yet one must not suppose that we are asserting composition in their case: each form is one and many — one, insofar as it is a peculiar character;

many, insofar as we call them so from the elements seated together within it: the many proceeding from the one and remaining in the one. For intellect, beginning from its own gathering, brings forth within itself its multitude of genera and forms; and indeed each form, imitating the whole intellect, begets within itself its own multitude of genera and forms; and these are many, as proceeding from one; elements, as from a unified; parts, as from a whole; genera, as from composite substance; forms, as from intellect. But these things belong to a later stage.

parts.name: Chapter 59 — The Mountains Seen from Afar: Names as Taperings-Off of the Plenitudes; the Root That Never Leaves the One; Iamblichus on the Intelligible in the One · pp. 164–166

lines.text: Chapter 59 — The Mountains Seen from Afar: Names as Taperings-Off of the Plenitudes; the Root That Never Leaves the One; Iamblichus on the Intelligible in the One · pp. 164–166

For the present, taking the argument back up, we say that there is no one name for the entire plenitude; and we must be content to name the bare properties — since even to conceive them is barely within our power, as they come to us beforehand, narrowed from afar into the differentiated and, as it were, atomic character of our conceptions. In the same manner, I think, the mountains also, from afar, appear smallest and still unarticulated to our sight; and of the stars, and of sun and moon, the lights — the most visible of all things to our eyes — are driven together into something narrow and faint and commensurate with us, because of the efflux of the appearances, as from the greatest distance. Some other such thing, we suppose, the eyes of our soul suffer with respect to the radiance of the forms that shines forth toward us. Are these simple properties, then, as they are imaged, narrowings — certain taperings-off of the plenitudes There, which are entire? Or rather: these, as they reach us, are indeed of that kind; yet the simple properties are not only such; among those natures too they shine forth — more richly there, and more distinctly — and simple nevertheless, dominating all their companions by their own light; and for this very reason they win through even to us, so far off, in whatever measure they do, while the rest are quenched and do not fall out to us along with them. For of mountains too, and of all else that is seen from far away, the more general features run on ahead, while the more particular lie hidden.

But the original point must be taken up again: we name the summit of beings Being and Substance not from some property marked off and, as described, shining forth ahead — for all the properties are in differentiation — but because it is all things, and the principle of all, and the principle before all: as the unified principle of differentiated things that are, and live, and know, and subsist in whatever manner. As all these are severally, so is that nature all of them in concert: so great a gathering of all things is she. Yet she is called Being, by indication, from one of the things after her and from her — the one that was allotted the second nature after the One; for that name befitted the first principle. Let our ascent, then, be made: as from the differentiated to the unified, so from all the things that in any way are, called thus or thus — to nothing else than the single fount, undifferentiated still, of the many and diverse subsistences that are divided off from her: a root that has never departed from the one, and for this reason unified, set over the things that grow out of her like countless branches. And there is also something like a trunk from her, which is not yet branches — though what is so viewed is assuredly already partial; but these things are not yet so.

And that the intelligible has its substance in the one and about the one, Iamblichus also proclaims in many places. And as the One is not this determined thing, nor that upon which any conception of ours casts itself as upon some one of all things, but, by the indication that runs through this name, leads us up to the before-all — even to that which is the one simple nature of all things: so too what is constituted from That and about That — Being — is none of the many, nor unified to any one of them, nor is it what is viewed according to being alone; rather, by indication, and this the indication of the nature that has gathered all things at once, and is all things. And we call all things beings from the one Being, and that Being so, because it too has been gathered up within itself; while the whole-together has no proper name, since every name is differentiating, and barely lays hold of one property — exactly as definition does. From all things, then, one must ascend to the one crown of all: to the unitary crown, from the henads as they are differentiated; and to the substantial, from the substances.
Chapter 60 — How the Third Proceeds from the Two: the Flight of the First Principles from Being; the Titanic Monad; Being Draws Nigh to Being · pp. 166–170

Come now, let us view how the third proceeds for us from the first two principles, according to Being. That the unified is the one and the many, we gave indication earlier. But how was Being first constituted — how did Being come to subsist, as it were compacted into being? Each of the principles before it fled away from being, and in the better manner: the second into the gaping void of multitude — as it were poured out to infinity, nowhere able to come to a stand, or rather not enduring to, in her longing for the unlimited nature; the first into the simplicity and partlessness of the one — having wished to be nothing other than one, as indeed not even having wished to be. Wherefore the third, first constituted and eager to subsist, furnished the principle of Being: through which everything that subsists is neither one only nor many only, but one and many — or rather unified and multiplied; or the unified alone suffices, since it has within itself the appearance of the multiplied as well. For in the third, neither did the one remain unaffected by the many — it was somehow differentiated in its co-ordering toward the many; nor did the many preserve their own unlimited outpouring — they were twisted together, according to the necessity of the one, which ever bounds what proceeds. Out of both, the unified came to be; and Being bloomed forth upon the constitution and the subsistence. And again in another way: the many are of a nature to bring forward the differentiated, and the one to gather these into union. As, then, the second principle is immediately after the first, so the many, in proceeding, proceed about the one — the things from it and by it — and are bound together and called back toward union, because the second principle, too, is seated in the first. What comes of both, accordingly, is neither one only nor many only, but one and many. And this we call Being: having stood out from the one, having stood out from the many, becoming an other, a third, after both — possessing no proper name; for neither were its principles called by proper names; and as they are named, by indication, with the names of the determined things that come after them, so this third principle too is hymned as substance and as Being: because it is the first unified, and one-and-many, as each of the beings is seen to be.

But if the unified is Being, and each of them is double — either unitary, if by its property it is being and unified, or of itself and according to subsistence being and unified — what is it that has set each apart from the other? For how would the first unified differ from the first unified — the unitary from the substantial? And how could there be a unified according to existence at all, if what is called unified is the thing that has been affected by the one — while the supersubstantial one has not been affected, but wishes to be the very one? — Or rather, it is as body is double: this body here, which stands apart in three ways, and the wholly unextended and bodiless — yet a body nevertheless, according to the paradigmatic property; and soul likewise: the one is she who is called the first generation, the other is intellect and god, according to the stationary property. And the paradigm too — say the beautiful itself and the just itself — is either some intellectual form and a substance, or the preconception in god, and god, as Parmenides says: which is not a substance, but a supersubstantial one — yet beautiful, for all that, and just: the unitary before the eidetic. So also the whole intellect: the one is substance, the other a henad projecting the character of intellect; and life likewise. Just so, then, both Being and the unified: the one will be unitary, the other substantial; yet each is mixed, and out of several — or rather, the unitary is mixed according to the property alone, and out-of-several in the same manner. For it is not because it has several — it is one only — but the one according to the property of the several. And a unitary multitude is as the one number of each: a triadic One, and not the simply one. Indeed it is simpler even than the arithmetical one; and since multitude, too, is simpler than number — because number is out of such things: for number is out of many monads, whereas multitude is filled up out of henads; and the monad is many removes below the henad, if we take it as eidetic, together with the number that accords with it. That unified, then, and the several within it, and the mixed, are according to the property alone; and it is a one of such a kind, third from the first — and for this reason a triad, and for this reason the mixed. But Being itself is unified also according to subsistence; and the several in it are differentiated — if not according to number, then according to multitude; or rather not even as the scattered, but as what has grown together within it and is utterly unified.

But if several are conceived in each, in whatever manner, what would each of them be? A monad it could not be, for the monad has been isolated toward determination — the monad is somehow Titanic; whereas each of the several There does not even wish to be each, but also all the others — or rather, one in place of all, yet having gathered all things; for those are the first fragments of the one, and for this reason each is at once encompassed by the union and compacted together, if it be lawful to say so, before the differentiation; for it is only in labor with differentiation; and the whole differentiation of the several There belongs to the what-it-is. Is it then still one, and not yet the unified? Or is the unified itself the birth-pang of the one toward differentiation — being, it seems, nothing else than the one that has conceived the many, and for this reason has stood out from the one? Why, then, must each of the several There be each, rather than unified? But no partition of the unified has yet come to be; for it must pre-exist the things partitioned beneath it. Each, then, is one; and if this, then the whole-together also is one — yet not a unified built of them; for the many points are not a line. And in general: is this one self-complete, or incomplete? If incomplete, how did it proceed There, and from what — the incomplete? But if self-complete, how are the many gods — the third — hymned as one god, and as Being? And how is Being many substances, when we say that it is all things undifferentiatedly? And one might raise this difficulty besides: how shall the several be conceived beforehand, where the mixed is what is spoken of? For the common is always before the proper There; and the unified, or Being, before the differentiated, everywhere and in every way; for even in the last generation there is also the procession from the more complete to the less complete.

Let us speak, then, calling upon god to take part with us, and indeed to be indulgent to the discourse — which strains, always, after the truth of the single nature of those things, but is dragged aside, through its own weakness, now to these conceptions and now to those. Let us say, then, with regard to the unified: That is the first unified, and unified in the highest degree — so that it is not in any way either differentiated or being-differentiated. It is not, therefore, one-and-many in this sense, as the many after the one; nor mixed in this sense, as the one out of many; but one nature — which, being able to call it neither one nor many, we posited by folding One and Many together, according to the unified: which appeared many just so far as the one stepped down, and one just so far as it transcends the many of differentiation; and this is nothing else than the unified — not wishing to be composite, as one might suppose, but a mean between the one and the many that stand in some differentiation; wherefore it would carry an appearance of differentiation, though not, in reality, differentiation. For why should a mean need to subsist between the things already being differentiated and the wholly one? — a mean which is one still, and yet undifferentiated. And this was the unified; wherefore it also seems to be the first Being — insofar as the conception of Being is neither some simplest thing, nor does it refuse what is in any way multiplied, as the one does; nor yet does it admit differentiation — being one only, and simply Being. For being draws nigh to being, says Parmenides in his verses; wherefore he also calls it one, because only by the one could it have been affected, as Plato would say; and it is none of the many beings, but Being itself. And Being, therefore, like the unified, is immediately what comes after the one, and before all the things that are being differentiated. The unified being supposed by us to be of this kind, the perplexities no longer have any room.
Chapter 61 — Existence, Power, Activity: Iamblichus On the Gods; the First Activity Is Reversion; the First Intellect of the Chaldaean Triad; Amelius · pp. 170–173

Come now, by another approach let us demonstrate the third principle — what relation it would have to substance and to Being. We say, surely, that that is, which can do something and act; for what is, as it might seem, but does not act — this we say not even to be. The first principle, then, is viewed according to existence, as in the Oracles; the second is plainly so called according to power; the third, therefore, will take on activity as well: it will be at once existing and empowered and acting; and this is called substance, and Being. And this is why substance comes after existence: because it is with power and activity; while before these is existence — being itself the subsistence-making cause of all things, as power is the empowering cause of all, and as the third principle is what awakens all things into activity, being itself the begetter of every substance that at once exists and is empowered and acts. And surely every substance is before power and activity; for these come from it; so that the simply substance should not yet have either power or activity. Or rather: she does not have these that come after her, which we posit to be her stretching-out; for in that there is already a certain differentiation; but she has what one might say to be one with the substance that is before power and activity — a power and activity con-substantiated with her, according to which she begets and projects the power and activity that come after herself. This one might leave with the first substance even more connately — power and activity; wherefore before her is power only, with existence; and before power, existence only — in no way whatsoever either power or activity, but the simplest of all things: existence.

Is then existing something other than being? — as the philosophers seem to make it, and Iamblichus himself, both elsewhere in many places and in his treatise On the Gods. Or rather: being is denominated from substance; while substance — even if you take the one before power and activity — is con-substantiated out of three peculiar characters: the subsistence-making, which we also call existing, and which is sometimes called being as well; the powerful, which is the fertile element of existence; and the active, which by now stretches out toward the things outside and displays its own use. And as these are separated in conception, we are led up to what is simpler, by indication, concerning the first principles: from existing alone, to the first — to which we were led up also from the one, and from limit, and from several other names; and from power, which also has existence, to the second. In this way, then, existence is other than substance: as one property stripped bare of the others, toward the indication of the first principle. But, to speak according to subsistence, existence would even be the same as substance — wherever, that is, it has truly subsisted together with power and activity. For the things before these are before all existence too, and one only, as has been said many times; whereas existence and power and activity subsisted from Being, and in Being first — save that in Being, both power and activity are according to existence, as we said; while in the second order of the intelligibles, both existence and activity are according to power — for all things stretch out into what is being differentiated, in whatever manner; and in the third order, both existence and power are according to activity — which is by now a limit of the intelligible, and in a certain manner stretched toward what is outside. Wherefore the first activity is that of the intelligible intellect. And what, indeed, would be the first of all activities, if not the one that reverts from the third to the first? For that of the second is not yet activity — for there is not yet any standing-away from being, but only, as it were, a preparation; just as that of the first is not even a preparation for standing away, but being only — needing neither power nor activity.

In this way, then, one may view these things according to the more manifest and transitive form of conceptions; but to speak more unsayably, and by indication: the hypostasis of Being — which is the subsistence of the third principle — holds the third rank according to activity, since in it is the active, even though that active is what has grown together with existence. This, then, as it were gives form to the third; the second is power, because she is the first stretching-out, in whatever manner, and not yet proceeding into activity; and the principle of the one is conceived as the first existence, by indication; for the one is what gives subsistence to all things, while to it nothing gives subsistence. For it would no longer be one, if it were itself something, and participated in a giver of subsistence before itself. So that through all these considerations it is plain that Being is the third principle.

In the same way it will be shown, too, that the first intellect is the third principle, according to the triad hymned in the Chaldaean manner. For intellect first stood away from its cause, and turned back toward it, and exercised this first activity. For what is still in the act of proceeding has not yet stood away; and what does not stand away has no need of reversion; for reversion is the setting-right of the standing-out. For if Being is the third, it is the first to act; and this acting is to revert toward the cause; and what is of such a kind is intellect: what follows is plain. And if the third is intellect, it is the first intelligible; and the intelligible is substance: the first substance — which they call existence. And if the first is existence by indication, it is plain that the third, too, is intellect by indication, as standing toward that first intelligible. And if the third is the first intellect, this is what first proceeded from the one and turned back toward the one — and this is the first unified. And if the third was the first to escape the principles of Being that pour over it — limit and unlimitedness alike — having itself first become a determined one, and as it were congealed into subsistence (and this was Being): then the intellect so called by indication would come to the same as what is properly the first Being. Wherefore it is hymned also as substantial intellect — characterized not according to intellection, but according to being; and if Amelius wishes to speak in this way, let him call intellect this.
Chapter 62 — What Do We Mean by Being? The Sophist's Power; Strato of Lampsacus; the Etymologies of Existing and Subsisting · pp. 173–175

Come, let us examine again from the beginning: what do we even mean when we say Being? What is this property? What else, I shall say, than the one signifying the being of each thing? For there is no other way to conceive the properties than through themselves; and they are more distinct when made known through themselves than through other things. For man signifies what it is, more than rational mortal animal does. And in the case of the simple genera it is not even easy to define through elements; for there are properties, some simpler — such as those of the first forms — and some more composite — such as those of the things composed out of the former, as the animal is from the genera of Being, or whatever things are composed from these. Being, then, will be what furnishes to each thing its very being, and that whereby it is being. And as the is is a bond of the other verbs and nouns, so Being is for you a bond of all the forms — like a root of every form, from which each and every form grows out and is settled; save that the one is a root even of this root, a simpler one.

Concerning the order of the forms, or of the genera, it is not now proposed to inquire. But Plato, in defining Being, attempted to make it known from activity; for what is able to act and to suffer — this, he says, we call Being. Then — whether being wary of giving the cause its subsistence as standing or as moved, he declares it to be neither standing nor moved; or because, being unable to seize, in the double character of this activity of acting and suffering, anything common to both — in the way that the being-able goes forth as each before each — he fled down upon the power, and made this to be Being: as if one should attempt to make even power known from activity. For power is of such a kind as activity still remaining within; as activity is power that has already gone forth toward the outside; and substance is of such a kind, remaining wholly within, as power preparing itself for motion. Looking to this, it seems to me, Strato too declared Being to be remaining — since he saw that power is the stretching-out of Being. But he ought to have observed besides that even if remaining coexists with being, it is nevertheless not the same; as the conceptions clearly distinguish, knowing being as one thing and remaining as another. For a thing must first be, and then remain or be moved. And remaining is opposed to being-moved — for remaining and standing are the same; whereas being either has no opposite at all, or only not-being, as Plato in many places sets them against each other. So that one would straightway define Being to be subsistence. But this conception is carried back to the same point as Strato's; for to subsist is something denominated from standing; and if anyone makes subsistence carry a proper signification of its own, let him say from what this disclosure has been formed — if not, surely, from the is; but that signifies being: so once again the thing is explained through itself.

But perhaps being should rather be called existing; for substance is existence, as we say. Yet if the thing is to be pursued according to the name, this would signify some second principle, subordinated to the prior one; and perhaps Being would then be a second principle, coming after the principle of the one that is ranked before it.
