And if, by a certain usage, we should take the word as signifying being, we cannot say from what it has been formed, such that existing should be the disclosure of being; so that I would not come to know being through existing, but the contrary. Perhaps, indeed, only being discloses the nature of the thing together with the conception; since the other names are taken from the properties that sit alongside it or are conceived along with it — properties which There are undifferentiated, but which in our intellections are differentiated shapelessly: such as existing and subsisting — the latter as not yet having made procession; the former as ranked under the very first principle. And in this way you would find each of the other names, too, affected from some property — even the stranger among the names: such as to-come-to-be, because it runs toward a telos, and the telos is somewhere near — wherefore it is even disputable of what the striving is: of being, or of the One alone; for the striving after well-being is for the both-together. And to-be, because it draws nigh, and wishes to be near, the one. And to-be-preserved: for being is somehow of this kind, because it is intact and sound, and nothing is lacking to it; for it is all things. And to-attain, if ever it should signify being, even when said by itself: because, before all things, it is attaining of the common telos, and filled full of the good. But of such matters, enough.

parts.name: Chapter 63 — Being from Going: the Cratylus Etymology; the Philosopher's Dream; All Things Become of One Another by the Exchange of Friendship · pp. 175–178

lines.text: Chapter 63 — Being from Going: the Cratylus Etymology; the Philosopher's Dream; All Things Become of One Another by the Exchange of Friendship · pp. 175–178

But the name Being itself — whence does it come? Or is it from the source that Socrates in the Cratylus divines: from going? For it would be going (ion); and — the hovering of the sound being still more analogous — it should be written with the diphthong; whence Homer says: let us go, as he commanded, up through the thickets. Of this verb, they say, the participle would arise — both ion and on; which means that Being is this: what is of a nature also to act, like the acting thing — as that definition says, the able. What then: is Being alone the acting? Or also the beautiful, and the good — and indeed the one and the many, the as-it-were genera, and rest, and motion? For every form whatsoever has some power and some activity. But perhaps: insofar as each is being, in this respect it is also acting — or is it a substance? Yet motion and rest also act — a motive activity and a static one; and in the same way each is also able, with a power of its own peculiar manner, apart from its substance. Or rather: the name and thing of Being is in this way common over all — not according to the conception of the one genus, the Being which we say is counter-divided from the other genera, but according to what is said to be of each thing in actuality: whether this be said relative to the in-potency of each, or relative to the becoming of each — which the having-already-become being discloses; as a certain dream also disclosed to me, saying that Being is this: what of each thing is the in-actuality. And this is by now common to all things, as being according to the substance which we are accustomed to counter-divide against power and activity. For if there is, properly, an activity of each of the forms or genera, why not also a substance, according to some common disclosure, as there are each of those? But perhaps this substance, too, is by-named from Being — as activity is motion, and named from motion.

Perhaps, indeed, power too is motion; for each of the two is a stretching-out of substance; but rest also acts and is able. Or does it act because it too participates motion — as, participating Being, it is substance by participation? But, first, the genera participate one another according to their own subsistence, before power and activity — sameness and otherness at once, one and many, limit and unlimited, according to their substances first — and hence rest and motion likewise; motion, therefore, does not lie in the activities and powers alone. Next, the powers and the activities also participate the other genera, and Being itself; or rather, each substance participates each of the substances, each power each of the powers, each activity each of the activities. Further: substance is counter-divided against activity, and power is the mean of these, spoken toward each of the two; whereas motion is spoken against rest alone — neither against substance, nor as some mean of rest and motion. And further still: we do not project the same conceptions when we hear to be moved and to act; for conceiving standing, and resting, and sleeping, and all such things as acts, we conceive them not as movements but as the contrary; for standing is contrary to being moved; and if acting belongs to both, being-moved could not be its contrary. And if we call the common element motion, what shall we say standing is? For rest must always be set in opposition to motion; and if power is motion, what would rest be? For there is nothing that is opposed to activity and to power except substance, in a certain manner; substance, therefore, will be rest. And this, I suppose, is the thesis of Strato — which did not seem sound. And if substance is generative of power and, after it, of activity, while motion is some one of the many genera, just as rest is: then motion is counter-divided against Being; it is not, therefore, its offspring and a kind of stretching-out of it — since the one does not participate the other any more than the converse. For each of them, by itself, is what it is; and thereupon all things become of one another, according to the reciprocal exchange of friendship; so that Being, too, participates both motion and rest; so that motion is not from Being, nor is it the activity of Being as its source. For how shall the effect impart anything to its cause — the begotten to its begetter?
Chapter 64 — Activity Is Not Motion: Suffering as Work; the Dancing and the Dance; Every Form Has Its Activity · pp. 178–179

Apart from these considerations: acting is a kind of activity — but suffering, how could it be an activity? Yet suffering, too, is a motion; and the patient has its acting in just this — in suffering: its suffering is its work; as one might say of matter that its one and only work is to suffer, though acting does not even belong to it. Now activity is the fulfillment of the proper work; and power is the preparation of activity. But if activity is conceived as this — the rendering of the work that accords with nature — then we must inquire what the work is: whether it is something other than the working, or the very same thing. If the same, then substance too will appear to be activity — and so, on this showing, rest as well, and every form and genus; and motion will not alone be the work; and the argument will demand the whole rendering of the work over and above the work, and so it will demand activity likewise; and activity, therefore, is not motion, but rather work. But if the work is the former — something other than the working — then there will be a work of motion also: to move the things that are; there will therefore be an activity of motion as well, being the rendering of its work. And if this rendering is the work itself, it is no doubt absurd to say that activity — being the laborious fulfillment of the work — is the very work. But if the work lies in the rendering, and the work is itself the fulfilling — as the dancing is the dance — still there will be some product of such an activity, for the sake of which the activity is projected; for every activity is for the sake of something, and is not itself, in the primary sense, that for whose sake. Indeed motion, too, moves; for motion imparts this its peculiar character, as rest imparts standing; so that motion will act, exactly as rest does; activity, therefore, is not motion.

And if motion, insofar as it is motion, is nothing other than motion, while activity connotes, by its very name, also the work that is being accomplished — and is, moreover, as numerous as the things that act: the activity of a man is a man acting, and that of a horse, a horse; for activity, too, is a kind of whole form — how could it be motion, or motion only? Or will one say that activity is not the motion that is a property, but a kind of composite form — even if it is given its form rather by motion, according to predominance? Or rather: activity can be both composite — the activity of composites — and simple — that of simples; for, in general, motion too has an activity: both the simple motion (not insofar as it is being), and the composite, supposed as a form. These things, then, have been said even beyond measure, because of the disagreement concerning them with the philosophers, who are accustomed to say constantly that this — activity and motion — is one thing. This, however, it is necessary to add: if activity is not motion, is it some form, itself as well, so that the others act by participation, just as they are moved and stand through motion and rest? Or is it the stretched-out element of each of the others — as it were a procession of each thing from itself into itself, or toward another?
Chapter 65 — The Same Difficulties about Power; the Three Folded Together in the First Mixed; Being, the Most Unified of the Genera; Mixedness · pp. 179–182

One might raise the same difficulties about power as well. If one should give the second answer, whence does this property — the being-able, and the acting — come to the others? For in each thing, the being what it is, and the being-able, and the acting, are different. But if the first answer, then activity and power are not the procession of each thing. Or rather: procession too is one property; and so is differentiation; and everything that has some marked-off conception is assuredly a property; for it is some differing thing, and this from a principle of its own peculiar manner — not to be saved out of the spontaneous — if indeed there is a difference of things, and not of names only. And further, the philosophers themselves say that power begins from the first Power, as existence from the first Existence, and activity from the third and mixed principle — because in this the activity appeared third, as having proceeded after power; whereby it is also plain that activity is not motion; for the genera of Being are not yet There. Are then activity and power and existence in the first mixed? And yet that, surely, was unified! Or must we confess that these too have been unified — that no stretching-out has yet proceeded, but the three are folded together and unified with one another; or rather, that they have not yet even been differentiated, the three being one — the so-called mixed, as was said before.

Accordingly we say that being is the activity of Being — although it signifies, rather, its nature; and if it also makes-being, still its character is being, and its making-being is in this manner. For the activity of intellect is clear — concurrent with the substance and as it were compacted with it; but the activity of Being is the substance itself; while that of life carries an appearance of separation; for we say that life lives, and the living seems to be something other than life, and yet it is, for all that, itself upon her; for it signifies being-life. In the case of souls there are both the activities that run concurrent according to substance, and others that have flowed from the substance — as with the enmattered forms, where the substances themselves have flowed out toward the exterior. But these things belong to another discourse. As to whether being is the same as Being — as the activity of the substance gathered in the middle, together with its power: Being is one of the genera — for this is what we conceive — and being belongs, determinately, to this genus; but That we named from this by indication, as has been said — or rather from each substance, against which its proper activity and power were counter-divided. So it is plain that the genus Being, too, is unified — since in its case as well being is the same as the being, and the activity the same as the substance. The unified, then, would not be exempt from the summit of beings, nor from the intelligible union-mass, as we were saying — since it belongs even to the genus, which is by now a form, or something near a form; just as we conceive nothing simpler than the property of the one — and yet the one is a genus, marked off from the what of the others; and it is by now composite, if it is some one of the genera or forms, though by its property nevertheless simple. As motion is one thing and rest another, so Being too is, in one way, unified by its property — and Being the same as being; yet it is, for all that, some one of the many genera, and counter-participates them.

Then indeed it will even be convicted of not being a true unified — because it is counter-divided against the others, and has suffered division toward them; so that it is also divided. And further, it counter-participates the others, so that the others appear plainly within it, just as it appears in them. How then is it exactly unified? For in this way the one, too, is caught out: not being really one, since it participates the others and is determined against them; and yet it wishes to be the very one — what it is according to its own fore-shining nature of peculiar manner; wherefore it seemed best-natured of all toward the indication of the cause that is all things — or rather, that is beyond all — according to one all-bearing simplicity. So too, then, this Being — the most unified of all the genera — would justly be indicative of the principle that is unified according to the single summit of all beings. And perhaps, the principles containing all things and being all things, the things that come from them are wound off from them, each different according to a different property, being differentiated and brought to a stand. For that unified summit does not stand according to the unified that is counter-divided toward the differentiated — for so it would not be complete — but according to what is above both, and, to speak more truly, above all things, and has gathered all things in itself; since the one, too, that was indicated before all, was not determined against the others, nor simple as against some composite, but is what has snatched itself away before all things — before the composites and the simples, the many, and the one that is set against them. But since of such transcendences we possess no conception to bring forward, we are content to give indication of those natures from what we have — compelling, by the argument, the things we conceive to take the lower honor beside the self-sufficient positions surmised of those most venerable principles. If, then, the one is simple — yet as among genera, and as among forms, and according to the property alone, as the form is good by its formhood, and beautiful, and whatever else of the kind — in the same way it is also one, and unified, and Being.

One might pause, however, on whether the unified is some property of its own apart from Being — and Being participates it most of all things; unless, indeed, the participation of the one is what makes the unified, as that of multitude makes the multiplied. If this be so, Being would be the first participant of many and one — and most of all, of the one. But if the mixed also takes its beginning from some source, and there is some existence of such a kind, through which every form is mixed, then the unified too would be something of its own — the summit of this mixed. And how should there not be the simply mixed, if the particular mixeds exist — man, horse, and animal; and, in general, the substance mixed out of the genera; and, to speak universally, the composite form, from which being-composite comes to the other composites; and one is justified in calling a thing mixed and composite according to the simple property of the form or the genus — a property which might be called mixedness, set in opposition to simplicity. But about these things hereafter.
Chapter 66 — The In-Actuality as Each Thing's Standing; Partitioned about Her; Neither One nor Being — Plato's One Being and the Middle Nature of Soul · pp. 182–185

Running back at last to the beginning, let us say to ourselves: Being is according to what of each thing is in actuality — whereby not Being alone, but each of the others also is being: motion, and rest; for each of these is a substance, against which activity is spoken, and power — each of the two from the substance; and what each thing is, is activity even according to its existence already; for the in-potency stands somewhere before the in-actuality, and not after it, as in things that advance from the less complete to the more complete. The in-actuality, then, means the already-proper existence of each thing, according to which it stands. And before all the severals of this kind there is the simply Being itself — which is also simply activity. For That stood first according to its own activity, as what is before it stood according to power, and what is still before this according to bare existence — to speak by indication only; since these coexist with one another: existence and power and activity; and this is substance — an existence at once powerful and active; which is substance in actuality, and with activity. For what else does in actuality disclose, than already with activity — as in potency means with some power? The in-actuality, then, comes to the same thing: to a being that acts in this manner and first projects activity. But There the three are still unified — activity, power, existence; for she is existence alone, having, in mere existing alone, both the being-able and the acting; for by being she both is able and acts; and the three are being alone.

And what wonder, if the summit of beings stands thus, when even Being the genus seems to stand thus, as was said — save that the genus, perhaps, does so according to the character of its property (as the one is simple, though not simple), whereas That does so according to the complete, undifferentiated subsistence before all things; and in the middle of the intelligible even these are being prepared toward differentiation. In the third, therefore, substance is first as such, and in some manner stretches itself out toward power and activity — wherefore intellect is said to intelligize, and to revert toward the intelligible, and to be king of the intellectuals and, in general, of the things that have proceeded from it; and yet even these activities are compacted with the substance and never depart from it — activities none the less. For how else is intellect of such a kind than as being in activity by its very substance, as that man says? But in the summit of beings, power and activity are drunk down by the existence — being one with it nevertheless. Wherefore the existence There is not bare, but already substance, as was said before. And what is there strange in this, when not even one thing is transparent in That? For it has nothing of the determined things appearing in it part by part; it is one all-holding gathering above all things — which we do not yet know, because we are unable to bring forward, for the conceiving of it, an intuition complete and made equal to it; and setting ourselves to conceive it as we are able, we partition it — or rather, we are ourselves partitioned about it.

And again, from the beginning, we gather her up, toward the indication of the complete and, at once, before-all single crown; and if we claim just this of her, she is neither Being nor substance — since she is not characterized according to these either, but is beyond these, as beyond the rest; so that That is not even intelligible. What then would it be? Surely not one; first, because it is distinguished even from the one; and if one calls it so by indication — in what would the third principle differ from the first of the three? for that, too, is a one of this kind. Must we then say: the unified itself, alone? And indeed, how should there fail to be some mean of the one and Being — the mean which one would call the unified, for lack of a proper name? For why are there meannesses of all the other things, though they differ by a whole genus in procession, and yet none of the supersubstantial and substance — of one and being? Since Plato too, as it seems, having seen just this, in the Parmenides has called it neither one nor being, but the whole One Being — through lack of a proper appellation, wishing to present the mean from its extremes; just as he makes the soul, too, known from the things lying on either side of her — she being a mean — calling her between the partless substance and the substance that is partitioned about bodies; although she also is one single nature, and not, as it might seem, compounded from the extremes. Just so, then, the One Being also is not some composite, nor two things — the one leading and the other following, as the philosophers expound it — but one nature of both, in the middle of the one and of Being: already slackened from the simplicity of the one, and not yet projecting the gathering of Being.
Chapter 67 — Why Being? Why Intelligible? Iamblichus on the Intelligible about the One; the Plain of Truth; Orphic Night, Nurse of Kronos · pp. 185–187

But why do we call That Being, when we call it all things? And why intelligible, when it has taken in the intellectual and the sensible as well, by the power of cause? For it is not even the unified, as was said before — this thing we conceive as not yet being differentiated, and as set against them — but, by indication, the before-all. How else does Iamblichus, expounding the intelligible, say that it has its subsistence about the one, and is never-departing from the one — unless he too conceives along with us what we call the unified and the One Being: as not yet really being, nor yet some one, but ranked through the middle of both? And besides this, after the One Being he sets substance over against the one, having differentiated the two at the summit of the intellectuals — where he also brought to light, together with them, the divine otherness; so that, before these, it was not possible to determine that one of them is the one and the other being, lying under the one; rather, the both-together is One Being — not as a mixture out of each, but as a mean of both, and, as it were, a forward-stepping of the one into Being. Indeed, when Plato made his cutting of it, did he not divide the whole into one and being? — and he made each of the two portions a one-being; and if he says that the one and being are parts of the One Being, nevertheless, proceeding a little, he made it quite plain that neither is being without the one, nor the one without being. And if each seems to be determined as participating the other, still this serves as disclosive of the nameless meanness — as if one should say that the partless in soul is one thing, and participates the partible, and the partible another, participating the partless: whereas each must be conceived according to the single both-together nature, which is somehow unmixed, and simple relative to the partible and the partless.

And if one calls it intelligible, we shall say that this is another intelligible — or it is as we say that Being is knowable; for the knowable is counter-divided against knowledge; but That is all things, and counter-distinguished against nothing; nor is it the one alone — which alone escaped intellection; and besides, let it be intelligible in this way: as Being. But neither does it have Being transparent in it; for it is all things undifferentiatedly; and the intelligible, accordingly, is of the same kind; for its being is not one thing to itself and another to its intelligible — since then it would not be truly unified — rather, it is all things, the intelligible included; and the most venerable things are drunk down within it; or rather: Being, and the intelligible, and the most venerable and honorable things, are the more appropriated and assimilated to it; wherefore it even seems to be these very things — though it is not, in truth. And perhaps in the Phaedrus, too, he gives indication of this very point — saying that the souls, having taken their stand upon the circuit of heaven, behold the things beyond heaven: that substance, surely, which is without color and without shape and intangible, beingly being — which he justly called also the plain of truth; and that the soul is nourished from the meadow There — the intelligible substance being There. And still more plainly in the Cratylus he says the same; for having made heaven the one that looks upon the things above — and clearly the first that does so — it is plain that he means by what it sees, the first visible, that which lies proximately above it.

And Orpheus, too, seems to know Cronus as intellect — as both the whole myth concerning him shows, and the epithet crooked-counselled; and to know Night as the first substance and nurse of all things — hymned, for this very reason, as having nursed Kronos himself above all: as being, in the station of the intelligible, the nurse of intellect; since for the intelligizer its intelligized is nourishment, according to the Oracle. The theologian says, at any rate: And out of them all, Night nourished and reared Kronos. Since even if Zeus drinks down him who is before him, yet he does so through her, and him who abides at her side; and perhaps it is also in labor with something intelligible — the consummation of the unified. But of these things, enough.

parts.name: Chapter 68 — The Contrary Hypothesis: One and Being Yoked without an Entering-Wedge; Vehicle and Rider; the Battle about a Name Only · pp. 187–189

lines.text: Chapter 68 — The Contrary Hypothesis: One and Being Yoked without an Entering-Wedge; Vehicle and Rider; the Battle about a Name Only · pp. 187–189

One might also advocate the contrary hypothesis, saying: after the supersubstantial, what would one take other than substance and the unified? What else could one name it than the being that has been affected by the one, as says the Eleatic Stranger in the Sophist? And how is the unified not the gathering of all beings and of all substances? And the one substance is also the gathering of them all, as we were saying; wherefore it is one being, because unified — for there is also something differentiated. And if it is as henad and being, the both-together according to one nature, the middle one — still, because the one stepped down, while Being, as first, is most one-like, it is not easy to distinguish the vehicle and the rider — or rather the haver and the had — because everywhere the firsts resemble, as closely as may be, the things before them. For this reason, then, he called the both-together not one and being, but One Being — giving indication of the unspeakable union of the unified being toward the one; since he made it plain that it is not as something ordered, by saying that the one participates and the other is participated. Moreover, in the first of the hypotheses he takes being away from the one, and posits the one, for a while, without being; then, indeed, he removes even this. And as in that hypothesis he removes two, so in the second he posits two. The One, then, and Being are yoked together, being two, to one another; and they hold of each other so connately as to leave no entering-wedge for what would differentiate them; for so there would be otherness; but where otherness too found room — the union having been slackened because of the procession — there substance was counter-distinguished against the one, as a vehicle against its rider; and she became the principle of the intellectuals, which have their being in differentiation. Wherefore each of the things here has become one and many; and for this reason, in this order, substance too has become pure, stripped in some manner of the one; and the many subsisted from that point — whereas before, the multitude was in the unified by appearance only. Whence Iamblichus also declared that the intelligible remains in the one, because it is the more unified toward it, and is given its form according to it rather than according to Being.

Assuredly, nothing is determined within it — not substance, not intelligible, not anything else; but in this it has its being: in being all things according to gathering; and this is its character, and the intelligible of Being is all things; for it is — but intelligibly, says the Oracle; for it gathers all our intellections into one, and makes one complete intellection, taken together out of them all, undifferentiated and truly unified — such as Iamblichus wishes the intellection of that intelligible to be. And if elsewhere he indicates that substance is the summit of the intellectuals — whether he, or Plato, or any other of the divine men — there is nothing strange in it; for the pure substance, even according to Iamblichus, appeared in this order; and this would be the intellectual summit, being intellectual substance; and that means: determined by itself, and turned back under the one as other to other, according to the substantial and unitary otherness that shone forth There.

And yet, while seeming to contradict much, we appear to be waging the battle about a name only. For if we call substance that which is already being differentiated, the unified would not be substance of that kind; rather, substance is that which, after the unified, has become one and many; whereas that was one-many as unified. But if one should call this too substance, according to the indications we have stated, there is nothing strange in supposing that, before the substance that is differentiated into many through otherness, there is the wholly unified and un-othered substance. Wherefore, otherness not yet having shone forth, the One did not seem to stand apart from Being, but to be as it were con-fused toward it; and this is the meanness we were seeking, of the one and of Being — the connate growth of the two. Or perhaps, between the one and the unified being, the many stand in the middle: being one still, not yet unified, but many as one still and in process of being unified — if indeed as participating the one, insofar as they are many by property; while the unified stands between the one, however spoken, and the determined substance. Or rather, in place of all these, that must be said which is most true: that what is called the supersubstantial one is neither being nor one — not, in truth, the one that is counter-divided against Being, as a rider riding upon a vehicle, or counter-divided in any way at all — but above both: even that which someone says is both One and Being. There is, however, the one before both, viewed in one simplicity as the both-together; and as this is one, of such a kind is That unified — not one of the pair, nor the unified of the pair, but the unified before both, as that was the one before both. For as the one leads each of the two, having pre-taken each insofar as it is simple, so the unified too has pre-taken the unified of them toward each other — their connate-grown union — and leads both the one and Being: as before both, and the union-mass of both. The one before both, then, is both according to the simplest — which is also simply supersubstantial; while the unified before each is both according to what is connate-grown of both, above both, so as to impart these to them. Third comes the connate growth as of things now other; wherefore otherness also co-appears with it. Above stand the two — but according to the unified before both; and highest of all, above both — but according to the one. Wherefore Plato, after the One Being, differentiated substance and one from each other — by now through a certain otherness.
Chapter 69 — The Mean as One Nature: the Blending before the Blended; Body, Soul, and Intellect Mounted in Order; Plato's Three Hypotheses Vindicated · pp. 189–192

The mean, then, is neither one nor being, but One Being: as one nature that has pre-taken both — the things differentiated below — according to the unified. Let no one say, accordingly, that this meanness is simply substance, nor simply one; rather, either a meanness of both, imaged toward each of the two as the other; or one as being at once, and being as one; or the both-together One Being, according to the as-it-were blending that is before the things blended out of differentiation — so that it is at once substance and one. But insofar as it is one, we have no name to utter — unless someone should say unified One, the one being shown forth in this together with the unified, which latter was an appearance of Being. Yet neither is the one in this by participation, nor being according to existence; for it is not yet being, nor yet one; for what is before the unified was neither of the two, but itself the both-together, according to one simplicity capable of carrying both. Wherefore after it, and from it, each of the two proceeded — the One separately, and Being — the one leading, the other following, having stood apart from each other in some manner through otherness; just as from the demiurgic intellect, which is all things together, there proceeds the whole bodiform nature, and the soul riding upon this, and, further, intellect mounting upon her. And if the three are in the demiurge according to cause, why should not the one and Being likewise be in the unified — though not by determined causes? For There is no determination as yet, but one cause-form existence of both — the existence of what is truly unified. So that, summing up, one should claim: what is called One by indication is not even one, in truth; the many spoken after it, by indication, are a meanness, and as it were a forward-stepping of that toward the unified — a descent of the first principle into the subsistence of the third; and the summit of the unified is this third principle, being the unified existence of the whole unified order. For after her comes what is being differentiated of it — of whole and of parts — as expressive of the unified: as if one should call it a birth-pang of the unified's differentiation, and as it were a preparation of it. And after this meanness is the base of the intelligible — the differentiated of the unified nature; wherefore even the things There that have in any way stood apart are unified still; and each of them is such that it falls short in nothing of the two sections — neither of the one nor of being — as says the Platonic Parmenides. And the intelligible intellect — which is what is intelligibly differentiated — must be viewed as divided into unifieds, not indeed into forms; unless one makes the union-masses paradigms of the eidetic paradigms. This, then, must be surmised to stand thus.

And that Plato too plainly embraces this hypothesis — namely, that he posits the first as neither of the two, the second as the both-together according to the unified, and the third as each separately — he showed: by denying of the first both being and the one; by gathering together, in the middle, the One Being; and, upon these, by setting the one and being apart, together with the otherness — of whatever kind, and operating in whatever manner — that makes them stand apart. Since only thus, indeed, would we barely escape the ancient perplexity. For how could anyone rank what is primally Being — which we claimed to be also the unified — completely, as substance, before life and intellect, there being no determination There; although life is determined off from intellect, and substance from life? How could there be determination, otherness not yet existing? And how could the wholly first unified be determined against an other? So it is plain that substance — as substance alone, relative to life — has appeared as what is viewed together, by this alone, with the peculiar character of life, along with a certain property; whereas the truly unified is neither life as yet, nor intellect, nor substance — except by some analogy, or by that cause-form appearance which even the philosophers sometimes intend when they say this — but all things, undeterminedly, and according to the unified pre-eminence before all; wherefore the unified is counter-distinguished against nothing, being all the things that are determined, part by part, in our conceptions. Concerning the unified, then, in relation to one and substance, these things must be conceived, so far as is possible.

And if, in what went before, we posited the third principle as unified according to Being, and made this double — the substantial and the unitary — yet now, having folded the two together into the one before both, and having ranked the differentiated two lower than the intelligible, we have seemed to speak in accord both with Plato and with the intelligible itself — wholly unified, and wound up together about the Good, according to Iamblichus — to which we have dedicated the most august of our conceptions. And further, we shall easily transfer what was then syllogized to what has now been decided; for all those things were said concerning the first mixed; and the first mixed, in the present arguments, has appeared to be the as-it-were both-together before the one and Being.
Chapter 70 — Is the Unified Knowable? The Great Iamblichus; the Oracles on the Flower of Intellect and the Turned-Away Eye · pp. 192–196

Since, then, drawn on by the argument, we have ascended in due course to the most august and most unified crown of that subsistence of things which is never divided, come now, let us justly inquire in what sense we call it intelligible. That it is graspable neither by opinion, nor by discursive reason, nor by the intellective intellect, nor by intellection accompanied with reason, nor even by the complete watchtower of intellect; nor is it seizable by the flower of intellect, nor by intuition at all, nor according to any determined leaning-upon, nor according to embrace, nor knowable in any such manner — all this we must concede to the great Iamblichus when he claims it. But first he must himself be asked: shall we say that it is knowable at all? and that the intelligible — that which fulfills intellection — belongs to the same nature: the unified intellection pre-supposed, before all intellections, in one intelligible simplicity? Or is it unknowable — as being fixed fast, as he says, about the unsayable principle and the Good — yet fulfilling of intellect and generative of it, ranked in the portion of the Good relative to it, and wishing to be the desired of intellect: of intellect not as intelligizing, but as being? For since this man seems to be carried toward each side — or rather makes us be carried about, partitioned around his single intellection — and the argument, if moderately put to the test, will have much pull toward each, consider: At once, we say that the knowable is being; but That is above being — even above the being against which the unified stands counter-determined, the unified we placed before both. It is not, then, knowable at all, since it is not even being, simply. Further: if it is knowable before substance, substance too would have to be somehow knowing, so that with knowledge she might revert toward the knowable. But the knowing — intellect — is third from substance, life being the mean of the two, even she in some manner knowing substance, as having something intellect-like toward the intelligible, and as coming after the intelligible; or else substance too must be allowed to have something knowing, as having stepped out from the intelligible — if the unified is of that kind. The knowledge of intellect, then, is of a nature to revert through life toward substance; for intellect belongs to her, and not to the unified — nor is the unified that in which it dwells. Third: if the unified is intelligible, as the knowable stands to the knowing, then the intelligible intellect will know the unified before itself; it will not, then, itself be unified; for knowledge is an activity determined off from substance, even if concurrent with substance; and, in general, the knower stands in much determination toward the known — and no such thing could arise in the unified. Intellect, at any rate, having stood away from substance, is content to return through knowledge into substance; but if the unified should be known, it will not be unified only, but also knowable; it would not, then, be unified, the knowable being determined within it; and if it should not be knowable of itself, but should have even the knowable undifferentiated along with the rest, it will not be known of itself; rather, there will be union alone — the contact with it, and the reversion. Further: many are the reversions, and three are first — according to substance, according to life, according to knowledge; the last makes the knowing, the middle the living, the first the substantiated, and that which submits to being knowable; but the unified is before all of these; it will have, then, neither the knowing reversion, nor the knowable, nor the middle one. And perhaps the unified is not even of a nature to revert at all — for neither does it proceed; every reversion belongs to what proceeds, and comes after procession; but it stands thus, undifferentiatedly — so that it would be even before substance and before the one, at least the one before substance. And, upon all these: knowledge wishes, in circumscribing, to embrace the known; and everything circumscribed is a form; but the unified is uncircumscribable — completely unknowable, therefore.

But on the other hand: even if one should suppose That to be unknowable, the argument is baffled; for already we ourselves seem somehow to surmise the unified — that it is before substance, and before the one that is before substance, and, before both, the both-together. And even if we do not yet, still the divine intellect assuredly knows the unified — whatever it means to be — according to the one nature before substance and one. Next: as the unified is before substance and one, surely there would also be, before the unitary knowledge and the substantial, what would be called simply knowledge — being before both, according to the unified nature. For life too being double — substantial and unitary — there would also be the simply life before both, as there is the simply subsistence; and nothing prevents us from speaking of the both-together signified in yet another way: the simply life as a subsistence, and substance likewise — the one according to the summit of the unified, while according to its middle stands what we have called the unified knowledge; and this is the truly intelligible knowledge, and the intelligible life, and the intelligible substance — each having the intelligible in common; and this common element is the unified; for it is all things — but intelligibly, says the Oracle — and that means: undifferentiatedly and unifiedly. There is, then, an intelligible knowledge, and this is the simply knowledge; for it is neither unitary nor substantial, but before both — which is the same as to say, before all knowledges. For the first determination is that of the one and substance; and That is simply life, and likewise substance, according to what is common to the unitary and the substantial. And this intelligible knowledge is of the simply intelligible; and simply intelligible is what is before the intelligible that is determined as unitary against substantial: so that the unified, too, is known — by the unified knowledge. Again: if the unified is wholly unknowable, then the one before the unified is still more greatly unknowable; and in that case, by what shall we say that unsayable principle differs from this one, or from the unified? Or are these, too, wholly unsayable? And yet we do conceive how the unified differs from the one, in the way we said before.

Apart from these things, the gods themselves plainly declare that the intelligible is known; they are not only said to be intelligized, and to intelligize. The philosophers, it is true, expound these matters in another way as well — saying that the intelligible lies before intellect not as known but as desired, and that intellect is filled from it not with knowledge but with substance, and with a whole intelligible perfection; for so, in many places, both Iamblichus and those after him maintain. Yet not always so: elsewhere they leave knowledge too in the intelligible and about it — as, in his Chaldaean writings, Iamblichus confessedly does. They call the gods themselves to witness, in the verses where the gods speak to the theurgist: For there is a certain intelligible, which you must intelligize by the flower of intellect; for if you incline your intellect toward it and intelligize it as intelligizing some thing, you shall not intelligize it: for it is the power of an all-round-shining strength, flashing with intellectual cuttings. You must not, then, intelligize that intelligible with vehemence, but with the subtle flame of a subtle intellect that measures all things — except that intelligible; and you must indeed intelligize it: for if only you incline your intellect, you shall intelligize it too — not fixedly, but bearing the pure, turned-away eye of your soul, to stretch an empty intellect toward the intelligible, that you may learn the intelligible: since it exists outside of intellect. For these things are said plainly about the intelligible, and about the knowledge that will be able to know it: he instructs what kind of knowledge it would be that shall lay hold of the intelligible — not the vehement knowledge, pressing hard against some known thing, nor the one that hastens to make the intelligible its own, but the one that lets itself go to That, toward the unfolding of itself into it, and is eager to be intelligible rather than intellectual; for it knows that there is no differentiation standing between, in the middle: it presses to be laid up, unified, with the unified, having denied every determination — both its own and that of what is intelligized — declining them not as being, but as not being; nor seeking after anything: being knowledge, the simply and first and most properly so — because it has grown most connately together with its known; not such, however, as the intellectual knowledge, but such as one would truly hymn as intelligible, gathered up into the undifferentiated of the intelligible: Clothed in the all-armored vigor of sounding light, having armed intellect and soul with three-barbed strength, to cast into the heart the watchword of the triad of the All, and not to frequent the empyrean channels scatteredly, but massively. Such things too the oracle-chanting god says about this knowledge; whence one must not be afraid that the circumscription of knowledge, as eidetic, is being brought against the unified; for knowledge of this kind is not such as to circumscribe the intelligible — rather, to be circumscribed by it, and bounded, just so far as it gives itself over into the vision.
Chapter 71 — Knowledge Poured Out Whole into That; the Hidden Triad in the Unified; Know Thyself, Ninth from the First Substance; Knowable and Unknowable Together · pp. 196–200

What then — is knowledge not an embrace of the known, and a kind of circumscription? Every knowledge, rather, is itself given form by the known, more than it gives form to the known; and the unified knowledge of the unified does not even subsist in any other way, except by unfolding itself together with the union of That — or, to speak more justly, by letting itself go and being poured out whole into That: attempting, with its own uncircumscribed, to seize the uncircumscribed of That, and making the intelligible the same as itself, it has itself come to belong to the intelligible. Nor, indeed, is the peculiar character of reversion alien to the intelligible. For even if it is unified, still there is also a unified procession of it within itself — being, as it were, a birth-pang of the procession below; and likewise what is common with the remaining; and the reversion There will be, as it were, a cause of reversion — itself also hidden. For, to speak generally: the unified, relative to what is called the one before it, has proceeded — so far as it is lawful to say so, and so far as a procession can come from the one; but relative to the principles determined in whatever manner, it still remains about the one and has grown together with it. For it has proceeded only so much as to remain within itself and in no way to have proceeded. And if the unified has its substance according to the remaining in the one — as, according to the procession from it, the middle race of the gods, and according to the reversion, the race of the intellectuals — still, viewing these too as within the remaining, there is also of That a first and a middle and a last, as it were by cause, and altogether hiddenly — and this is the very thing we mean by unifiedly. Some reversion of it, then, will appear in truth — the intelligible reversion — though perhaps not the intelligizing one; for it is not knowable in the ordinary way, because even the knowable in it has been gathered up, and as it were drunk down, together with the rest, by the union. Much more, then, is there no knowledge in the unified; for knowledge stands many removes from the knowable — from it, knowledge seems to be a kind of third. And the cognitive is also third among the reversions, if before it is the vital, and before that the substantial; and we say that according to this last is the self-subsistent, according to the middle the self-living, and according to the final one the self-knowing — and the Know Thyself; and the three reversions stand to one another in the proportion that intellect bears to life, and life to substance. Knowledge, then, is ninth from the first substance, which we say is the knowable. And what argument could turn anyone back to supposing so great a differentiation in the unified?

Or rather, against arguments of this kind, that must be said which was said: that it is we who are partitioned about it — giving up the knowing of all that it is, and how great; not yet projecting intelligible intellection, we who cannot purely and firmly project even the intellectual kind, nor the last kind — I mean the rational — pure and well-jointed; and if we do at all, it is a knowledge hoping to descry from afar something of the truths, and in mere hopes fore-taking, artlessly, the end of its whole eagerness. But the intelligible is all things — but intelligibly, according to the Oracle. There is, then, of it the summit — as it were substance — being the unified of the one and of substance, but before both; and the middle, which is before life, and before the one determined according to life — a certain unified life, homonymous with each of the two below it, because it is neither of them, while pre-existing both. And so the third is the intelligible intellect: being a union-mass of the intelligible and the intellectual one, the both-together before each; whose knowledge is neither unitary nor of the appended intellect, but is itself also one and unified before both; for, standing in any other way, it would not in any manner have fitted the unified. Just so, the knowable too is knowable neither by the unitary knowledge, nor by that of the intellect-according-to-substance, but by the unified, as has been said. The knowable, then, belongs neither to the lower substance, nor to the one that leads her; it is the knowable before both, and the really simply knowable; for this belongs to the simply Being; and such is the unified — if indeed it is neither the unitary one, nor as the vehicle of this one.

Is then to be unified the same as to be knowable? But in that case it would not be knowable of itself; and if it is the same, how is the knowable not determined There? Or rather: divided it must not be — for all things are unified; yet this too, the knowable, is there along with the rest — not in potency but in actuality, according to the gathering that precedes all division. As, then, being one, the whole is knowable by the property of the knowable; for every form is knowable as a whole by the property of the knowable — as it is whole by that of the whole, and beautiful and good by the beautiful and the good. Is it then also unknowable, by the property of the unknowable? Indeed: least knowable, and most unknowable, would be what is beyond all the divided things; and in general the generators are always unembraceable by the generated, and super-simplified beyond their substance — let alone beyond their knowledge. There is in That, accordingly, something unknowable as well — and this rather than the knowable; and yet that first nature is, as we say, intelligible. So it is even most intelligible: by knowledge it is of a nature to be known as most knowable; but far beyond knowledge lies its unknowable — whatever that knowledge be, and of whatever sort it happens to be. But the knowable-and-unknowable is both in Being, and present in the one, and, before both, in the unified according to the both-together. So then the knowing element too is There according to the unified — pre-existing both the unitary and the substantial knowledge. For as the knowable is unified, so is the co-ordinate knowledge — the intelligible knowledge of the intelligible; and knowledge accompanied by some differentiation comes later, while There both the knowledge is unified and of-the-unified, and the differentiation likewise; for even There, intelligibly, there is a first and a second and a third. If, then, the third should revert, and should know — what wonder? Nor is it necessary that substance be cognitive because the unified stands before her; for it is not the case that, because That has all things intelligibly, according to the Oracle, all things are thereupon in each of the determined things; for all things are wound off out of the unified, each according to its proper determination: the one, substance, life, the one of life, intellect, the intellectual one. And substance is not, on this account, life. There is also in the unified the life, according to the analogy of the unified before both; nor, then, is substance intellect, nor cognitive, merely because in the unified the third element is cognitive; for from the knowable above is made manifest the knowable below; from the knowing, the knowing; and from the middle, the middle. To the perplexities, then, one might respond in this manner, so far as is possible.

parts.name: Chapter 72 — How Was the First Other Differentiated from Other? Relatives That Do Not Convert; Otherness Is a Form — Matter Is Not Other than Form · pp. 200–202

lines.text: Chapter 72 — How Was the First Other Differentiated from Other? Relatives That Do Not Convert; Otherness Is a Form — Matter Is Not Other than Form · pp. 200–202

Again, beginning from another starting-point, let us speak about the knowable and knowledge — and, still before these, about remaining and procession and reversion; for from these accounts it will appear both what the use of knowledge is, and what the knowable; and from these, further, we shall raise the difficulty whether there is any remaining and procession and reversion in the unified. And before everything it must be asked: how was the first other differentiated from an other? For take the first term that is being-differentiated, or has-been-differentiated — let the argument concern the latter: the differentiated , before itself, that from which it has been differentiated — which must itself also be differentiated. But that is not yet the first differentiated; rather, the first differentiated stands third from the unified, the being-differentiated being the middle. How then could the first unified be the first differentiated? For it is from this that the first differentiated thing was differentiated. Perhaps, then, it is among coordinates that the converse of relatives holds true; for among these, mutual subsistence too is true; but with cause and effect it is not in every way true that they convert. For the effect does not make the cause a cause; on the contrary, the cause makes both the effect, and itself the cause of it. But if it does not also mutually establish, let it nevertheless be relative according to the synonymous relation, as the equal is equal to an equal.

Or rather: the differentiated differentiated itself from the first within itself — and not within that first — having made the differentiation by its own stepping-down; just as the material body was differentiated from the immaterial by the form's inclination toward matter, while the immaterial nevertheless passes even through the enmattered, not admitting the differentiation. In this way, then, body stood apart from soul; yet intellect passes through all the seconds, and soul likewise. Or this is true, and nevertheless intellect too was differentiated from soul, and soul from body, by the change of their subsistences — so that, once again, the differentiated is differentiated from a differentiated, even if the mode of differentiation is different for each. For the beautiful is other than the just, both being others; but the otherness is not the same, except in the genus of the property; for in the very respect in which the forms differ from one another, so too do the genera that fill them out. But surely the other is not always other than an other; rather, only when each of the two is a form. The form, at any rate, is other than matter; yet matter is not other than form — because no otherness fills her out; for otherness is itself a form, and she is formless; so that the form was differentiated from matter, but matter was not differentiated from form — because differentiation, too, was a form, and a thing arising only in forms. And above, likewise: the first differentiation is the form's, from the super-eidetic — which remains undifferentiated; for being super-eidetic, it could not suffer anything form-like; and being-differentiated is such a thing. The differentiated, then, is not in every case differentiated from a differentiated; the first differentiated — or the last — would not stand so.

What then? Does not each of the two stand from itself — the one matter only, the other form only; and the one, if it so chance, being only, the other intellect only? Indeed, neither of the two is the other; rather, by as much as the second stepped down into a differentiation of nature, by so much the first is exempted into an unconfused pre-eminence relative to the second; nor shall we be at variance — provided only the mode of the differentiation is not the same. For the immortal is differentiated from the mortal, and the mortal from the immortal; yet the differentiation is not the same in each, since in the one it is immortal, in the other mortal; and in the eternal both the differentiation and the otherness are eternal, while in the temporal each of the two is temporal. So it stands also with the ungenerated toward the generated, the paradigmatic toward the iconic, the rational toward the irrational; for all things are in each according to its own peculiar-natured manner. So, then, differentiation everywhere stands, and otherness — and indeed sameness as well, even if she seems to work connate growth. For if man and horse are the same insofar as they are animals, still the animal is other in each; so that the form of sameness too, whatever it is, is one thing in horse and another in man; and indeed in the form it is eidetic, in matter material — that is, in potency — and in the super-eidetic, super-eidetic — that is, by cause. But as for the relation: if the one term is in potency, so is the other; and in some respect each is unlike each; for they are in activity together, and according to existence, since they have co-subsisted; and so the cause is at once with the caused — even the sameness of matter being in activity; for the in-potency relative to form was, of matter herself, the in-activity; and the by-cause There stood, relative to form, as existence — the cause having gathered up in herself the differentiation too. But if the differentiation is gathered up, so is what is said to be differentiated according to it; for if it is determined as first and second, the differentiation would already be separated within it — so that what we still call unified would be differentiated even within itself; for the differentiation, determined within it, would co-differentiate with itself the rest as well. For what allotment would explain that, of the genera or forms within it, the differentiation alone got determined? And it is absurd that anything whatsoever be determined in the unified. In general, we confess things to be determined by just this: that we posit the one to be unified, and the other differentiated.
Chapter 73 — The Unified's Privilege: Not Its Own, but the One's; Differentiated Only So Far as to Remain Undifferentiated · pp. 202–204

How then is the unified, of all things, differentiated? For what is said looks like a contradiction; and the perplexity is greater if we compare the unified to the one as something that has proceeded from its producer. Or rather, this is precisely the exempt privilege of the unified nature: not to admit differentiation toward the one, nor procession from it, but to have grown about it; and in this consists that famous being-unified — in not being its own, but the one's. But in cases where we clearly posit being-differentiated of the one term, the reciprocal naming of the differentiation, when it is demanded for the other term of the pair, furnishes much perplexity to inquirers. Perhaps, then — the nature of relatives being abundant and of every sort — there is among them also a relation of such a kind as to equalize by the conversion, while by the nature of the converted terms it does not furnish the like: as the different differs from a different — yet the one term has the difference according to form, while matter is formless according to the difference; so that the difference itself is both of the formless and of the form. For so, too, the image makes its counter-comparison toward the paradigm as toward a like; for the likeness is common according to the rough whole of the property, yet not the same for all that: the one paradigmatic, the other iconic. In the same way the unified, too, is united to some united thing; so that, if it is united to the one, the one too will be unified — and then no longer one. Rather, the being-united must be asserted only insofar as they are yoked — according to the relation alone — since the one is above the unified. For in just this way the caused, too, is yoked to the cause: not according to a common nature of the relation, but according to one that differs in truth. The relation in the cause, at any rate, is cause of the relation in the caused — as the one nature is of the other nature.

Simply, then: both what is in the unified, and the unified itself, are united; and so, in the unified, the unified too is differentiated from the differentiated — yet as unified. For there is indeed the difference of unified toward differentiated; and this is: the undifferentiated toward the differentiated; for the undifferentiated does stand apart from the differentiated — differentiated only so far as to remain undifferentiated, and so far as to stand counter-distinguished toward the differentiated. So far, then, does differentiation of this kind stand from differentiating the unified, that it even guards it undifferentiated — or rather, it is differentiated by the differentiated; and this is, once again, to be undifferentiated. So that the differentiation is common in name — the name and thing of the relation being imaged as roughly the same — while it is not the same: standing here according to the differentiated, there according to the undifferentiated; here differentiated, there undifferentiated — the differentiation itself remaining undifferentiated. And if we name even differentiation itself, as though it were some one of the others, pardon must be granted; for names belong to things determined and eidetic; wherefore also, when we say that matter is differentiated from form, we syllogize truly — yet we do not name truly. So much, then, concerning these matters.
Chapter 74 — Remaining and Procession: the Engrafted Property and the Root in the Earth; Compelling Our Intellections to Unfold; Everything Both Remains and Has Proceeded · pp. 204–209

Since the differentiated proceeded from the undifferentiated, and we say that everything which proceeds makes its procession while remaining in the producer, and again reverts toward that from which the procession came; and since, in general, we say that these three stand in succession to one another — remaining and procession and reversion — come, let us raise the difficulties about these very things. And first: is it necessary that what proceeds, proceed while remaining in the producer? And, still before this: what do we mean by remaining in the cause? Surely not as in a place, nor as in a vessel, nor as a part in the first; for how would it then still be a thing that has proceeded, in any way at all? Let our discourse now concern the procession of what has proceeded; for it will be possible to view the same points upon the middle as well, in respect of its being-differentiated. Is it then in the first, the cause, and in this respect remaining — while it has already become third, and in that respect has proceeded? But that is impossible; for it is either first or third. Does remaining, then, signify this: that it does not stand out of the property of the producer, but, holding this within itself, engrafts upon it its own property, in respect of which it proceeds — as the man within the animal, and life within substance? For life is a substance of such a kind, and intellect a substance of such a kind together with life; for its own is always grown onto the common, or is projected from it; and what has proceeded remains, accordingly, within the property of its begetter. But if this is so: first, it is not the proceeded that should be said to remain in that, but that common element to have proceeded together with the proceeder. Next: this proceeded thing — the common we speak of relative to the begetter — has it, too, itself alone proceeded? And this goes on to infinity. So it is not necessary that the proceeding remain in proceeding; so neither is it necessary that the proper remain; and if the common does remain, still, that which we say has proceeded — does this not remain? And the thing in question was whether the proceeding remains — not the remaining. I forbear to say that it is not even in every way the case that something of like nature proceeds from the producer; this we shall show a little later to be enveloped in much perplexity; and it will perhaps be shown not to hold simply, nor of all things, if indeed it holds of some.

Perhaps, then, the proceeding — or the proceeded — has its cause in the producer; and this is the remaining in that: to have its root in it, namely the cause from which it grows out; for the plant, too, sprouts up from the earth while remaining in her only by its root. Or will this also appear irrational, if one should test it precisely? For the cause is not the very thing that is produced from the cause: the one is second, the other first; for in the first is seated the cause of the second; indeed, the cause of the produced is a certain substance of the producer — not a part of the produced, but of that; nor is it analogous to the root, but rather to the principle of the whole plant — a principle that is whole, and en-substanced in the nature of the earth. If these things appear to stand so, the same refutations will arrive: for neither does the remaining proceed, nor the proceeding remain; for neither is the produced still in the producer, nor does the cause proceed from that into the produced — for then it is no longer cause, but from-cause. It must not be said, accordingly, that the proceeding remains, but the cause of the proceeding. Perhaps, then, what the saying means is this: that, that remaining, this proceeds? Or not that simply, but the cause within it remaining. And since the from-cause is of like form with the cause, the remaining and the proceeding are somehow said to be the same — and they are the same in the rough-whole sense, by property and by form; but in truth not the same, nor in subsistence. But if one should suppose it so, first he will tear the produced apart from the producer — if nothing is common to them according to subsistence, and the proceeding things are not continuous with their producers, but are begotten from them severed, as man from man. Second: if it is by a rough-whole account, and not a true one, that the proceeding necessarily remains, the axiom would not be true, but apparent only — since the sameness too is apparent, being indeed only the community of the relation. And from thirds: this account will say nothing august, if what it says is this — that the first is not the second, nor the second the first; or that the begetter is not the begotten, and conversely; that the one remains and the other proceeds, and neither at once both proceeds and remains.

Perhaps, then, the proceeding is of such a kind as to be mastered by neither — neither by remaining nor by procession alone — but to have something at once remaining and proceeding together, which both-together, we say, constitutes its being; for the both-together belongs to the very nature of the begotten. For so the proceeding would rightly be said to remain: if it should at once proceed and remain the same. But if we say this of the middle — which has its being in proceeding, and not in having-proceeded — well; whereas the proceeded, which has already stood apart and been let go from the first, as third — how could it still be said to remain in that? For it is a contradiction, if the proceeded has not proceeded. Or rather: it has both the remaining and the proceeded — as it were having planted itself firm above, and then stretching itself down toward what is below. But in this way the former arguments will come at us: that neither does the proceeded remain, nor has the remaining proceeded; and, besides these, it will not be whole proceeded — that which we say subsists in having-proceeded — nor does it remain whole — that which, remaining, we say has proceeded; and it will differ in nothing from what subsists in the first, if it is whole in each of the two ways. And if it remains by one part and proceeds by another, it will be partible, in addition to all that has been said — if indeed it is wound off from above into what is below. Or rather: does our conception partition even the impartibles? They must nevertheless be conceived as those things ought to stand, and not as we conceive them; and the human intellections must be compelled back, and accustomed, to unfold themselves and to broaden out, so far as is possible, into the truth that befits those natures.

Whole, then, I say, is the proceeded — and it remains in its begetter in just that respect in which it has proceeded: because the proceeded itself, by its own peculiar-natured nature, is most like and most akin to the producer, and is, as it were, the producer itself according to the third measure, so to speak, of the stepping-down. For even if one form comes from another, yet the change-over is close-knit and of like nature, and the standing-apart is not so great as that which we carry up to those natures from the dis-spannings here below. For such is intellect toward life, soul toward intellect, life toward substance, that to one who saw it at the first cast, the second would seem to be the very thing before it — most of all the most proximate, but then even the farther, even if it be the last of the things proceeding from one source. For nothing among the produced is, in any way whatsoever, of another tribe toward its producer; nothing is un-akin; nothing is not embraced by the begetter as its own. And if the difference of the names, and the differentiation of our partible phantasms, deceives us into supposing complete standing-apart in those natures too — this is nothing against their truth. For everything begotten There, simply, in one respect — as itself — has proceeded from its begetter; in the other — as from that — it remains; for the from-that is not an accident, but is itself the substance of the proceeded; and the itself is no less after that: a genuine offspring of it — as if a son should be most like his own father: a son assuredly, and the other the father, but the form almost the same. And if There the begetting seems hetero-form, one must know well that There the things that are other in form have grown together with one another more than, here below, the things that are the same. Intellect, then, as intellect, has both proceeded from Being — a third from the first — and, though the first is something near, it has taken on the third rank; for the third itself, and the triad, is the very nature of intellect; and as many and of what kind the first is, so many and of such kind is the second, in a certain manner — save that There union dominates, and here differentiation.

And to speak generally: if of coordinates and counter-divided things we predicate union together with differentiation, sameness and otherness, much more of begetters and begotten shall we say that they are both other and the same — both differentiated from them, and at once unified toward them. Insofar, then, as things are the same and unified, each is justly said to remain; insofar as other and differentiated, to have proceeded. On the whole, accordingly: each thing both remains and has proceeded — beginning from the firsts, down to the things that have proceeded to the very last; but now in greater and lesser degree: here with remaining dominating, in those things in which the differentiation is hard to find; there with procession, in those in which the union is non-apparent. And it is setting out from these last that we falsely ascribe, even to the first processions, the complete dis-spanning — which is not complete even in the last. Everything proceeded, then, remains both in the nature and within the bounds of its own causes; and what does not remain — that is, what is in no way and nowhere this from which it is said to have proceeded — this has not even proceeded; for who would say that what is in no way and nowhere the being's has proceeded from the being?

Chapter 75 — Reversion: the Longing for the Ancient Nature; Procession Substance-Making, Reversion Perfection-Making; Two Rests between Two Motions; the Three Elements Blended in the Third · pp. 209–214

Let this, then, be procession, and this remaining; and let each have grown together always with the other, as has been said. But what is reversion, added upon these? What is it, and what use does it furnish to what has proceeded? That it belongs to this latter is plain; for it seems to be a return; and every return is of what has proceeded; for what has not yet proceeded, but still remains in the first — what need would it have of any reversion to the first? Remaining, indeed, is better than reversion; and what possesses the better — what need has it of the worse? Reversion belongs, then, to what has proceeded. But what is it? What else would one say, than the return of what has proceeded to its begetter? For it is set against procession, and is, as it were, its setting-right and resolution. Accordingly, soul resolves her own procession through reversion. But if this is so, it will no longer be a thing that has proceeded; for it will destroy this, if it should revert. Or rather: with soul, now the one and now the other comes to pass; but with the eternals, each holds at once and in the same respect. Is it not, then, the proper work of every reversion to assimilate the begotten to the begetter, as from procession comes the making-other? For procession is differentiative, and reversion gathering — an up-leader of the third to the first, as that is a forward-leader of the first to the third.

Come then, let us see what we even mean by saying that the proceeded reverts. We say that it reverts while remaining in its being-proceeded; the reverting, then, in the portion of the proceeded, comes nearer to the producer; and the reversive is taken on in addition, after the processive; for let each of the two be supposed according to substance — and what ever pre-subsists is better than what supervenes, so that the processive is better than the reversive: it does not, then, come nearer to the begetter insofar as it reverts than insofar as it has proceeded. And if the proceeded also remains, as has been shown, what need has it of reversion, being already assimilated according to its remaining? And if reversion is a recovery of remaining, it would itself be a remaining — though after procession; and reversion signifies nothing third, if it works nothing besides the remaining. And yet reverting is, in conception, other than remaining: for according to remaining, the begotten wishes to be the very thing the begetter is; as, according to procession, it wishes to be the very thing the begotten is, after the begetter; according to reversion, however, the begotten longs for the begetter — itself remaining, and that one remaining, each within its proper bounds. For the desiring holds onto the desired as other onto other; and the other comes always after the proceeding. Perhaps, then, reversion is the desire of the third, in its yearning? For in remaining there is not yet desire; for the desiring has not yet stood apart from the desired. Nor yet in having-proceeded; for this is just the standing-apart and differentiation of the two, in order that the one be desiring and the other desired — or rather, in order that the third, having stood away from the first, should afterward desire it, in longing for its ancient nature. Wherefore reversion does not work the remaining, but the enjoying-from-afar of the begetter, now revealed as desirable; whence, also, reverting is finer than proceeding: for having-proceeded is substance-making of the third, while reverting is perfection-making.

But the desiring hastens to become the very thing the desired is; so that the third strives to become the first — and becomes so through reversion; yet it became so first through the remaining, by its very remaining in the first. Or does it have the one before procession, and the other through reversion, after procession? But it is absurd, as was said before, that what it already has, it should take again — and the more absurd, that it should do so through the worse activity. But perhaps it is not the thing itself that it gains through reversion, but some image of it — which will then appear even worse than procession? Yet nothing desires the image, nor at all the worse of that very thing whose better and elder subsistence and enjoyment it already has. It is like one who, possessing the most complete health, should then desire the inferior kind; or one who has acquired the contemplative virtue praying to obtain the political.
