So what remaining furnishes, and what reversion furnishes, are not the same in form; for remaining and reversion are not the same in form. What then does it take on through reversion, which it possessed neither through the remaining nor through the proceeding?

And upon these perplexities there naturally grows also that further inquiry, which supposes the remaining to be double; for not only the proceeding, but also the reverting, does what it does through a remaining — the latter its reversion, the former its procession. For there are two motions — the one from above downward, the other from below upward; and between two opposed motions there must be two rests, as the natural philosophers say. And indeed we said just now that reversion is not a resolution and destruction of procession; rather, the thing makes its reversion while remaining in having-proceeded. Either, then, we must make two only in genus — rest and motion, or, if you will let me say it, remaining and way; or four in species: procession and return, and remaining, in its turn, double — the one holding above, and the other below: this latter belonging to what is about to revert, that former to what is about to proceed. What then is this much-rehearsed counter-division of the three — remaining, procession, reversion? Perhaps someone will say that the three were divided relative to the one first, according to the three relations toward it: that in which, and that from which, and that toward which; and it is plain in what respect each is made proper. But I shall say that the in-which is double — the one above, the other below; for the thing both remains in the lower form, and is roused up from it according to the reversion, and stretches toward it first according to the procession; for on either side the remaining is the mean — but here projecting the procession, and there projecting the reversion. And to such inquiries this also justly attaches: if reversion is double — the one of a thing toward itself, the other toward what is before itself — what does each give to the substance of the reverting thing, and how do the two differ? And where the second is, is the other also? And further: why is not procession also double, and remaining likewise — the one in the better, the other in itself; and again the one from the better, the other from itself? For if these three activities are always of the same rank, then as the one stands, so the others stand likewise. And let this too be inquired: whether, where the one shows itself forth, the others also appear within it; and whether to the third belong the three, to the second two — remaining and procession — and to the first one only, the remaining? For remaining seems to belong properly to the first, procession to the second, and reversion to the third, as having already proceeded. Marking off their properties from above, then, let us state the appearances; and may grace lead us toward the truth.

Remaining, then, is the nature of the first as in-mingled with the third; and procession is the third's standing-away from the first; and neither of the two is unalloyed: neither is the standing-away bereft and torn from its proper cause, nor has the first's nature, within the third, drunk down the procession — nor does it allow the proceeded to vary into another genus, even that very thing which is said to have proceeded; rather, out of both, as out of elements, the third was brought to completion: a genuine offspring of the first, and one that bears that nature within its own variation. And the reversion is the constitution and circumscription of the third viewed in itself — neither as remaining nor as proceeding; or rather, it is the union of the two elements into one another, and the reversion of the processive into the stable, according to which arises the blending of the two elements — the blending according to which the character supervenes, and the form of the third. Wherefore reversion, too, belongs to the third alone; and it is called property-making; and it is also a stretching-up of the proceeded-and-third toward the first — because the proceeded, according to its remaining element, is in the first. And you see that, according to substance, in the third the three have been blended together with one another like elements; and the whole has the three, and acts toward itself in a triple manner: remaining in itself, and proceeding from itself, and reverting toward itself; for the three are elements of its substance, and each stretches into the whole — all of them toward one another. It remains, then, through the stable element — the whole and the parts; and again it proceeds through the processive, and reverts through the reversive. Accordingly the third remains in itself according to the in-mingled property of remaining, and proceeds from itself, and reverts toward itself. But the three are said to act also toward the first; what then is the difference? It is that the differentiation is double: the one from the first, whereby it is third; the other from itself, whereby it is multiplied within itself — becoming not simply a third, but triadic, according to the triad that has appeared within it. But every triad is also a monad — or rather, before it there is assuredly a monad; so that according to the triad it proceeds from itself, according to the monad it remains in itself, and it reverts according to the union of the triad toward the monad. And if one should put it even so, he would not throw far from the truth: that the triadic in it is cause of the reversion — for reversion is third; the dyadic, of the procession — for procession is second; and the monadic, of the remaining, because remaining is first of the three. But these things belong to another discourse.

parts.name: Chapter 76 — Toward Itself and Toward Its Prior: One in Subject, Double in Relation; the Three Elements Gathered in the First, Dividing in the Middle, Divided in the Third · pp. 214–216

lines.text: Chapter 76 — Toward Itself and Toward Its Prior: One in Subject, Double in Relation; the Three Elements Gathered in the First, Dividing in the Middle, Divided in the Third · pp. 214–216

Toward the first, then: the third remains in it, because it has not in every way stood apart at all; and it reverts, because it joined what had parted to what had not parted, according to the reversion we have described. Is the reversion, then, one, or double — the one toward itself, the other toward what is before itself? Or is it one in the subject, and double in the relation? For insofar as it circumscribed itself, as has been said, through reversion, it turned toward itself; but insofar as it stood whole, circumscribed according to itself and complete, it was likened to what is before it — because that, too, before this one, is complete according to itself, having been allotted a proper nature of its own; and insofar as it is third, it gave itself subsistence toward that first. For this, too, is a kind of reversion; and there is, before these, the fact that the begotten was brought to completion such as the begetter wished it. By becoming, then, the very thing that it is, it has been turned at once both toward itself and toward what is before it. And as the reversion stands, so also the procession: for the very thing that it is, it both proceeds from itself, according to the differentiated within it, and from what is before it; for according to each it is what it is; for according to each it has proceeded; and indeed it proceeds also from the cause according to the both-together; for the proceeded itself, whole, is what it is according to the both-together; since its being differentiated from the first, according to the third differentiation, showed it differentiated also within itself. In like manner, then, the remaining too is the same in the subject, differing only in the relation. For its not standing wholly apart from the cause — this is what made it not stand wholly apart from itself either. By the same stable element, then, it remains both in itself and in what is before it; and by the processive it proceeds both from itself and from that; and indeed by the reversive it has been turned both toward itself and toward that. And this is the third element, in that the processive is bound together with the stable. Out of these three, then, is the proceeded — not insofar as it proceeded simply, but insofar as it is this determinate thing: say, intellect.

The three are present also in the proceeding, and not only in the proceeded; they are present also in the remaining, before the proceeding — but in this last they are gathered together and undifferentiated; in the third they are divided; and in the middle they are in middle manner, and only being-differentiated. But if they are undifferentiated in the first, then not even remaining could justly be predicated of the first: as possessing the stable element it could not be said to remain — for it does not possess it in truth as something marked off; but as not proceeding it might be said to remain, by analogy, relative to the third — or at any rate to the second. And likewise the proceeding, relative to what has gone forth, might be called both proceeding and remaining; in truth, however, neither; for not even in this middle are the elements yet determined. In the third, then, the three are determined off from one another; the third, therefore, is properly the first in which they are so — and it remains, and proceeds, and reverts toward what is before itself: toward the proximate — which was the second — according to the variation and subsistence that come from the second, that is, from the being-differentiated; and according to the subsistence that comes from the undifferentiated, it does so first toward the supreme itself. For intellect, let us say, has the triple relation both toward life, and toward Being, according to its generation from that. But about these matters, again, hereafter.
Chapter 77 — In Every Intellect the Three; the Lower Remaining a Participation of the Higher; the Necessity of the Division: Variation, the Begetting Form, and the Presented Offspring · pp. 216–217

In what has first become third, the three, having appeared, go forth also through all the things in succession. I mean, for example: if they appeared in the first intellect, the three are in every intellect as well; yet remaining dominates in the summit, giving form to the others; in the last, reversion; and in the middle, procession. Wherefore, in each intellectual triad, the first is the more stable, the second the more processive, and the third the more reversive. Accordingly, upon these grounds the double remaining was not supposed otherwise — if indeed to remain is not to stand wholly apart from the begetting cause, nor from its nature; while to revert is to circumscribe one's own subsistence within having-proceeded together with remaining: so that the same thing may be at once proceeded and not proceeded — neither of the two torn apart, but becoming a certain both-together through the reversive property. For, being of such a kind, what other remaining could the whole third have, besides this reversion, or this procession? — unless, perhaps, toward the things after it, the things produced from it; for what produces from itself, in its own form and its own rank, the things that come from it, would have the stable from its con-substantiated remaining. Unless, indeed, one should not even say that the producers remain, but rather that the produced remain — in their producers and in themselves; or else the remaining of the producers must be viewed in their not proceeding along with the things they produce.

What then? Does such a whole not revert toward the first — or will it make a reversion? First: if it should revert toward its begetter, it must be a thing that has proceeded — and then it does not remain, as the perplexity runs. And if someone should say that it remains in having-proceeded, he would be calling that same remaining an intensification, and as it were a confirmation, of having-proceeded — not the remaining that is counter-divided against procession and reversion; since reverting, too, is a proceeding: it is a certain advance — only not an advance from the cause. And if one should view a participation of each in each — since the stable proceeds into the third; and if it also proceeds, it also reverts; for in this way procession, too, has something reversive, if indeed it also has itself proceeded; and reversion will have something stable, if indeed it has also something processive. Supposing it thus, we shall agree well; for the three, being of the same rank, will participate one another; and the perplexity will have no place; for the division was not made of the properties according to existence; the lower remaining, accordingly, is a participation of the one named above.

What, then, is the counter-division of the three? For proceeding and remaining are contradictory — the thing is said to proceed and not to proceed; but reverting — what is it, relative to these? It is that proceeding discloses only standing-apart and variation — not yet any twisting-together and constitution of the character, in which the proceeding came to a stand and was circumscribed; this, then, is what reversion, added upon them, brought in besides: so that the one term is disclosive of the standing-apart — or variation — from one thing to another, namely the processive property; the stable is disclosive of the begetting form; and the reversive is presentative of the begotten. Whether the begotten participate their begetters, and how they participate or do not, we shall inquire after this. For now, only the necessity of the division of the three has been rendered: the two are viewed at the limits, and the one at the middle; for the thing remains in the producer; and it reverts according to the produced, which is what it is; and it proceeds into this latter from that former.
Chapter 78 — The Three Reversions — Substantial, Vital, Cognitive; the Self-Subsistent; Intellect Steps into Its Own Bound and Is Made Akin to Being · pp. 217–219

But since these matters have been determined universally, come now, let us take them up in the things themselves. For each of the three is divided in three ways — remaining and procession and reversion alike; for each is either substantial, or vital, or cognitive. That there is reverting according to knowledge is plain; for the knower knows both itself and the things before it. And that there is reverting according to substance, is shown by the necessity that there be something self-subsistent, and not only subsisting from elsewhere. For either we go to infinity; or nothing is self-subsistent; or else, immediately after what has wholly stepped out of subsistence — so as to subsist in no way, neither from another nor from itself — we shall posit what subsists from elsewhere, and shall look down upon what subsists from itself, although it is a mean by its very nature; just as we agree that the self-moved is a mean of the unmoved and the other-moved. For even if what subsists from elsewhere is, in one way, better than what subsists from itself, still there is also a sense in which it is worse — which it is true to say of the bodiform things; and the by-nature better must exist, if indeed the worse does. But that the self-subsistent is, we shall inquire hereafter — both this, and what it happens to be, and in what order it shows itself forth. Now this giving-subsistence-to-itself is precisely a reverting of the thing toward itself according to substance; and it will be self-living too, by the same causes, in that it makes itself live, and does not receive its life from elsewhere only. Toward itself, then, it displays the three reversions in this manner.

But toward the first — how? The cognitive reversion of the third toward that arises because it knows that; the vital in a certain manner; while the substantial, perhaps, shows itself forth more plainly. For we said in what went before: since the third proceeded, and came to be according to itself, and got from itself its proper bound, in this very way it was turned toward the first — having become another thing of the same kind in the third rank, as that is in the first: as that is Being simply, this is intellect simply; and as that is unified substance, so this is gathered intellect — with the gathering that befits intellect, not the gathering that befits Being. Wherefore intellect, by stepping into its own bound, was made akin to the bound of the first, which appeared as the bound of all things. This, then, is the substantial reversion of intellect toward Being. And what would the reversion according to life be? Since life comes after Being, and the contact of life with Being is immediate, what reverts vitally toward Being presses into that contact with it which life herself, before all others, joined toward it. So the substantial reversion makes the reverting thing such as that; the vital makes it only joined to it, immediately, according to life; while the cognitive knows it from afar, and leads it back from the third rank to the first; and this — the third reversion — is the one proper to the third, as the intellectual reversion is proper to intellect. For great is the standing-apart of intellect from Being, and of the knower from the known; for the seer stands in notable differentiation toward the seen; whereas life is almost substance, coming immediately after it; and the living is not far from the substantiated. But of these things we shall speak again — presently, very soon indeed.
Chapter 79 — Intellect Three-Formed throughout the Whole of Itself; To Live Rather than To Be Life; Turned toward Its Cause Not as Its Own, but as Hers · pp. 219–220

Now we have rendered the reversions of intellect toward Being — of the third toward the first; in like manner we shall render also those toward the second: of the third, and of intellect toward life. For intellect knows life, if indeed it knows Being, and in the like manner; and moreover it will also step into her bound — which is her substance — according to which intellect becomes intellectual life, just as it becomes intellectual substance according to its assimilation to Being, and just as it is intellect according to its own third property. For conceive intellect for me as being third — as having become three-formed throughout the whole of itself: being and living and intelligizing; gathered, and being-differentiated, and differentiated. Life, then — even in the way she is differentiated, so far as the being-differentiated can be within the differentiated — intellect is assimilated toward her, and is, as it were, set into life; and this is the substantial reversion toward life. And what would the vital reversion toward life be? Is it not one thing to stand according to the bound of life and to become life — and another to be an other, standing according to itself, which is to be joined to life as a third to a second: to live, rather than to be life; and to desire life, but not now to become life?

And let the same stamp fit us everywhere for the three reversions — wherever they may be, and of however many things, or toward however many of the pre-existents; for the reverting thing reverts toward each of the things before itself, whether from near or from afar, and is assimilated to every one of those toward which it reverts: whether according to the proper characters — of plenitudes or of elements — that flow together into it from the things toward which it reverts (these being either con-substantiated with the receiver, or becoming adventitious in other ways); or according to the different existences within the reverting thing itself — existences that are its own, and have not come from above, yet are analogous to those natures of its elders, toward which, accordingly, the reversion is accomplished by analogy. For the argument, as it went forward, seemed to say each of the two: at one time assimilating intellect to Being by its proceeded and third bound; at another, leading it up to the unified before it by the unified within it — I mean the gathered element of Being. Whether each is true, or neither, or the one — whichever it be — or all of these, in what way and how: I defer to the discourse concerning the participations. For now I determine only this much, rather briefly: that it is one thing to be the very thing one is, and another to be likened to another according to the very thing one is. For example: intellect is from itself, remaining what it is, according to the reversion into itself, having circumscribed itself substantially and vitally and cognitively; but this very thing that intellect is has also proceeded from life — possessing all things from There too, as many as it possesses from itself. Every intellect, then, and wholly, has been turned toward its cause — not insofar as it is its own, but insofar as it is hers; it desires, accordingly, to be joined to the producing cause, and to be, in some manner, that very one, so far as it can, and to see her as ranked before it, and as separated. And so it stands toward Being also, and toward each of its producers — even if the productive causes be many — toward each alike.
Chapter 80 — The Ten Aporiai: the Triadic Counter-Division Itself; Self-Known, Self-Living, Self-Subsistent; the End of Knowledge; Who Acts on Whom · pp. 220–223

The argument next demands, raising its difficulties — first: why have we divided each of these three in only three ways — reversion, I mean, and procession, and remaining — calling each substantial and vital and cognitive? For one could also speak triadically: undifferentiated, being-differentiated, differentiated; or unitary and multiplied, and a certain mean, which one will think fit to call unified. Indeed it is possible to view the matter in many ways: for in each cosmos there is, for each, a remaining and procession and reversion of its own peculiar manner; and in each form, one proper to the form and by-named from it — not only in these three, intellect and life and Being. And perhaps one might raise the further difficulty: what is this triad itself, and whence did it get its counter-division? For knowledge is counter-divided against the knowable — and let there be a mean, if you wish: knowing and known; but this is not yet life, nor is the knowable in every way Being. For many other things, too, are knowable — every form is knowable, and intellect itself is knowable. Why then is intellect, as knowing, counter-divided against Being as known? And whence does substance lie over against intellect, so that we should also rank life in the middle? For if life is motion, what would be the rest set in opposition to that motion? Either intellect appears even outside the counter-division, or substance is the same thing taken according to rest — and intellect outside the antithesis. First, then, as I said, the difficulty must be raised about the triadic counter-division itself.

Second: whether the reverting is in every way the third — as the argument seemed to hold when it began; for it spoke of the third's reversion toward the first. Or does the second also revert toward what is before itself — as the argument wished intellect to revert toward life, which lies proximately above it — so that one will expect life, too, to revert toward Being? And yet what has not proceeded, we say, does not even need reversion. Third, upon these: whether not only reversion is viewed in three ways, but remaining and procession as well — substantial and cognitive and vital: the one from itself and in itself, for each; the other from what is before it. Fourth: how is it that in the cognitive reversion there are these three — knowing, known, knowledge — while in the substantial reversions there are no longer such, nor in the vital? And if in some manner there are, of what kind would they be?

Fifth: why is the self-known that which knows itself, while the self-living and the self-subsistent is that which makes itself live, and be? For the proper work of each reversion, one must say, is to incline the thing together toward itself only — not, however, to make it live; for this belongs to life, or to something life-making, and not to reversion, which wishes only to turn the thing toward itself. Likewise the substance-making is alien to reversion; for the knowledge of oneself is not knowable-making, nor productive of the knower — and yet it seemed admissible that this reversion too be taken according to making, if indeed those others are. Sixth, then, in addition to what has been said: why, among the reversions toward the more ancient, does the cognitive stand in like manner with the reversion toward oneself? — for it only knows that prior, just as it knows itself, according to the reversion; whereas the vital and the substantial are not in the same manner; for what reverts by them toward itself substantiates and vivifies itself, yet does not act in any way whatsoever upon the things before itself.

Seventh, accordingly, it must be asked: how does it know what is before itself? Does intellect, by knowing itself, know also what is before it — just as, by standing itself within its own bound, it assimilates its own substance to that of the producer, as we were saying; and as it reverts in substance, according to the proceeded, into the producer, so too, by the knowledge of the proceeded — which is the knowledge of its own nature — does it come to recognize the nature of the producer? Or does it, letting go its own, lay hold of hers — and says, indeed, that she surpasses this one, as one who also reckons in the difference? But if this, the cognitive reversion is better than the substantial — if the latter is accomplished according to the bound of the proceeded, and the former according to that of the producer. Eighth: what is the end of knowledge? And what accrues to the knower from the known? Is it the form of the known, arising within the knower; or the in-potency of the knowing, becoming in-activity according to the knowledge? And what is august in either of these — or what profitable? Ninth, worthy of inquiry: whether the knower acts upon the known, or the known upon the knower; for whichever one should say, the worse in nature — and the caused — will act upon what is better than itself, even upon its cause; for the known is better than some of those that know it, and worse than others. Tenth, then, upon them all, it must be asked: what is knowledge? what the knowable? what the cognitive? And is it present everywhere with the third? or also with the second? or even with the first, insofar as it is first? — for the first intellect is cognitive, as indeed is every intellect. And, so far as it bears upon what is proposed, the difficulty must be raised about life and substance as well: what is each of the two, and in what do they differ from knowledge?

Chapter 81 — The Whole Cosmoi: Substance, Life in Travail with All Things, Intellect; Knowledge the Consolation of Standing-Apart; the Shining of Being; One Gathering of All Knowledges — Substance toward Substance · pp. 223–232

Come then, climbing back in reverse order, from the last to the first of the problems posed, let us examine what must be said to each. The substance, then, which we now set against life and knowledge, we shall say is neither life nor knowledge. If indeed the three were of the same rank — whether as species, or as genera, or as parts, or however one might put it — nothing would have prevented them from participating one another; but as it is, we mean by the first, substance; by the second, life; by the third, knowledge; and the one is their cause, the other the caused, the other the both-together relative to one and to another; the priors, accordingly, will not participate the posteriors: life, then, is above what possesses knowledge, and Being and substance above life. And further, in this way too: we do not call these things genera, nor species, nor certain more partial subsistences, nor such as come after the first principles — which these names wish to signify — but whole cosmoi, and these the first of all the things that seem synonymous or homonymous with them: as, for instance, there lies before us now the first intellect, which contains in itself all the intellectual world-orders; and life, accordingly, the one before this, is a whole-complete cosmos, full of all things life-wise — of all that intellect has intellect-wise; so that substance too, about which the argument runs, is a whole cosmos: the eldest of all cosmoi, and the most embracing of the things disclosed by the names before us. It is no wonder, then, if intellect has taken part of life and of substance — and what this participation may be will appear as we go forward. Life, however, would not participate knowledge, if indeed knowledge is the prerogative of the third — or, to speak more commonly, of what has proceeded; and substance would have neither knowledge nor life, being neither proceeded nor proceeding — if indeed life too belongs to the middle, and to what is proceeding. Substance, then, is a whole-complete cosmos that has gathered all things together in the undifferentiated; intellect is a whole-complete cosmos subsisting in the differentiated of its nature; and life is a whole-complete cosmos in the being-differentiated of the middleness — in travail with all things. The first is itself uncircumscribed, and embraces all things uncircumscribably; the third is itself circumscribed, as having proceeded, and has inscribed the things within itself, as many as have proceeded in it and been differentiated; while the middle one, the one according to life, has neither been fixed fast in the uncircumscribed nor settled together in the circumscribed, but is, as it were, amphibious, and as it were in motion from this to that — whence they name this one life, as a stirred, and as it were seething, substance. For the eidetic life too, added to each form, brings upon it this seething and stirred character.

For just so the unmoved nature of Being, having stepped down a little, relaxed that fixed and undifferentiated character, and projected a certain procession, and an appearance of differentiation; but when it had now proceeded, and been differentiated, and come to stand in its own form, it was circumscribed according to the differentiation, and differentiated and circumscribed the things within itself — the most whole-like, and eldest of all. For it was not differentiated with the differentiation that goes out into all things, but with that which is nearest the one — to speak generally, the first differentiation, and the differentiation of firsts. Whence, since a standing-apart had come to be for it both from the things before it and from itself — for it was differentiated also itself within itself — for this very reason it took in hand a certain setting-right of the standing-apart, and as it were a consolation: knowledge. For knowledge exists among things that stand apart from one another, or from themselves, and are taken asunder by otherness; for without otherness there would not be the one term knowing, the other known, and the mean, knowledge. Fittingly, then, it was in what had proceeded and been differentiated that this subsisted — just as the other determinations also begin from there, and the other relations, as many as are differentiated. Now the other relations too have something binding of the things that stand in relation; but most of all does knowledge join the knower to the known; for it stretches the knower out into the known through love of the true, and it sets the knowable within the knower through the lightning-flash that leaps across from it into him. And this was the cognitive reversion of the proceeded into the producer — even in the very respect in which the one is differentiated from the other; for, otherness not existing, neither is there knowledge; so that substance could not know herself, being united in every way; nor could she know another, being nowhere differentiated so as to have the knowing as one thing, and the known, and indeed the knowledge itself. And life is called intelligible and intellectual from the extremes, but is neither of the two in purity; rather, insofar as it is only being-differentiated, so far it has both knowledge and known and knowing — not differentiated, but still being-differentiated; and that means: dawning from beneath.

In intellect first, then, is the first knowledge — since the first circumscription also is in it: of itself toward itself, and toward the things before it. Insofar, then, as it was differentiated toward those, by so much it was joined to those, from afar, through knowledge; and insofar as toward itself and from itself, in this respect it is joined together within itself through knowledge, in a certain standing-apart toward itself; and the things within it, toward one another and toward the whole itself, each stood apart and were circumscribed — for which reason they also know one another, and the whole; and the whole, having come to be entire in differentiation and circumscription, fittingly entire and whole is filled with knowledge: it was made true, and became intellect according to intellection, and was gladdened by the light of intellectual truth — first projecting within itself the eye of knowledge, in order that, beholding that from which it proceeded, it might return again to it, and might lead itself back toward it, so far as is possible within the standing-apart. For the substantial reversion also joined it — but according to the first standing-apart, by which it stood away and was bounded in its subsistence; and the vital joined it too — but according to the second differentiation, by which it was being differentiated from the substantial subsistence into the cognitive; and the cognitive joins it according to the farthest — being ninth from the undifferentiated, and third from the differentiated; for reversion being third after remaining and procession, the third reversion is the one that comes about through knowledge. Wherefore, having stood away the greatest distance, into its own last — the third, as it were, of the third — intellect is content to be joined with the joining of things that stand apart; and this is knowledge — which has been called a reversion, and, this too has been said, the last reversion.

What, nevertheless, is knowledge? An apprehension of the known within the knower? But we do not yet know any of the things we are saying. What the knowable might be, or the cognitive, it is not easy to know while knowledge itself is unknown. Knowledge, then — as the name half-reveals — is a coming-to-be knowing, which is intellection; and intellection is so called because it goes toward being and the is, and returns thither — so that it would justly have been called a going; but as it is, giving the word solemnity through the eta, and making it well-mouthed by the contraction, we call it noesis. So intellect, too, is named because it goes toward Being; and it goes the substantial return as well, and the vital; but in the third rank, and as it were from afar, it goes through the cognitive intellection; and insofar as intellect is cognitive, it is so in a certain manner through activity — but the activity neither of substance nor of vital power; wherefore this intellection is, rather, one that is coming to be. And this one is more evident to us, because it is most differentiated; wherefore most of the philosophers give intellect its form according to this. But one ought, before this, to name the differentiated and circumscribed subsistence also an intellection — this prior one, before the cognitive — as being the first return, into Being, of what proceeded from it; from which return intellect also has its name: already inclined toward Being, and returning, before knowledge. And perhaps knowledge wishes to be a generation of being and of substance; for the knower is substantiated by the return into Being according to knowledge — not the first substantiation, but an as it were coming-to-be one; wherefore intellect is the things themselves, as Aristotle also says. But let each fit the names to the things as well-naturedly as he can. That intellect, at any rate, subsisted according to the return into Being, and that knowledge has been projected — every return belonging to what has proceeded and already stood apart, and for this reason needs the return: a return that does not dissolve the standing-apart, but leads the very thing that stands apart, in the manner and so far as it stands apart, back up to that from which it stood apart — this is plain even from the name of knowledge.

What then is knowledge? Is it a shining-round-about, and as it were a light's fore-escorting, of the known within the knower? For sensation subsists according to the sense-datum, and imagination according to the imprint, and opining and intellection — the one according to the thing opined, the other according to the thing thought; universally, then, knowledge subsists according to the gnosma, if one may so speak. And the gnosma is the known itself — but now en-substanced within the knower. Knowledge, then, is the attainment of the knowable as knowable; for even if it is of Being, yet it is of Being as knowable. What then is the knowable, and in what does it differ from Being? Is it that a thing is knowable relative to another, while in itself, what it is, it is being? Or is this indeed added, while the nature of each has not yet been determined? Or rather: the one is the subsistence, and the other the shining of the subsistence. For to the enmattered form, let us say, its subsistence is one thing, and its being sensible another; and its sensible is that of it which falls forward and fore-shines from it as far as sensation — and is commensurate with sensation, becoming in a manner sensation itself. Just so the shining of Being is like a light of it, escorting forth as far as the knower, and going out to meet him as he strains upward toward it; commensurately it grows together with him, and perfects, and satiates his desire of Being, by the filling of its proper light. Intellect does not, then, know Being — but the shining of Being; or Being according to the shining; and Being according to the knowable. And assuredly it desires Being; or rather, it desires it as Being, but attains the same as knowable. And perhaps even the desire must be said to be of Being according to the knowable; for the natural desires are of the same things of which the attainments also are; and confessedly the attainment of Being comes to the knower according to the known.

What then do we say this shining is? It is the appearing that holds itself out to the seconds, and furnishes itself into commensurability for those who wish to enjoy it, and to embrace its forth-escorting light, for those who long for it. Not the whole, then, is knowable, but only the light — as to sight only the color is visible, and not the substrate. Or rather: it is no wonder at all, but even necessary, that something of the firsts be always ungraspable and unsayable to the seconds; for so the wholly stepped-out was unsayable simply, toward all things; while each of the others has its own unsayable toward the seconds only, and becomes unsayable relative to something. This then, as I said, is nothing paradoxical; but that, perhaps, one might raise as a difficulty: whether in real truth intellect knows the fore-escorting of Being, and not Being itself — and yet it was said to be knowable according to its shining. Let it know, then, this fore-escorting of Being — yet not as some efflux from it, as the earth-encircling light flows from the sun, but as one who sees the sun itself according to the brightness of nature that is within it. Does it then know only the surface, if it should know the shining of Being as a kind of color? Or must the shining be conceived as going through the whole — there being nothing of it that does not shine through, and hasten toward shining-forth: as if you should say that glass, or any of the diaphanous things, is visible as a whole, because the nature of the visible has gone through the whole of it. Yet even so the body is one thing, and the through-and-through shining another; so that even There the shining would be present — but not beside Being; and first, the same difficulty will come back — that the knowledge is not of Being, but of the shining, which is other; for of the wholly diaphanous, too, it is not the body that is visible, but the color only; and next, we shall be determining, within the wholly undetermined, one thing as the shining and another as Being — as the substrate to the shining, or however else differing from it.

Or rather, this must be said in answer to these things: Being itself, what it is, in one respect is only itself, and only undifferentiated; but in the other respect intellect stood apart from it, having been differentiated from it; and it became not only undifferentiated, but also a differentiated's differentiated; and since the differentiated held it as an undifferentiated standing apart from the truly differentiated — to just that extent the knowable dawned forth in it. For in intellect, according to the differentiated, the cognitive showed itself forth; so that in Being also, as in a manner differentiated, something correspondingly shows within it — not, however, the cognitive, because this belongs to what proceeded from it, but the knowable: because to the proceeded, through knowledge, That became a knowable it could attain. And the knowable is not in Being itself as some determined property; for neither is the differentiated in it as some property; for it was, according to the undifferentiated, a differentiated's differentiated — a thing which would neither have subsisted nor been named differentiated, so far as from its own nature, if one may so speak, had not the really differentiated been differentiated away from it. Thus, then, it appeared and was named knowable not according to something among the things within it, but according to the counter-comparison toward intellect. For intellect, having seen itself differentiated from That, while That remained undifferentiated, named the stepping-out from That differentiation — a differentiation existing within itself, but in That only according to the undifferentiated, and according to the not-having-stepped-out-together. Thus, then: because intellect, having proceeded, became cognitive of that from which it proceeded — in the very respect in which it proceeded — projecting the cognitive reversion, as was said before, it made that which it desired through knowledge be named knowable; or rather, it shone forth the knowable that was in it, though not determined; for the differentiated is not in determination There; for it is not in it as something beside life and intellect; for all these — both the names and the things — belong to the eidetic nature; but that nature was wholly undifferentiated, as we say; in the middle nature it is being-differentiated, in a manner; while in intellect both the rest were differentiated, and the knowable and the cognitive and knowledge; and the properly knowable is intellect, being cognitive of itself. For form is both formed and form-like; wherefore with every form there coexists some knowledge, of whatever degree; and every form is a living thing — or a corpse of a living thing, having suffered the privation at once of the living thing and of the form: as stones, and timbers, and the dead among bodies; since the things that are in their natural state are living things, and have a certain con-sensation, even if the faintest, and to us imperceptible; since even the plants are living things — though of another kind, says Plato; and rocks, and metals, and the whole earth, and each of the other elements, that they are not soulless in every way, is shown both by the life-generation of the things contained in them as living, and by the whole-completeness of their form-giving. But these matters would need another discourse.

And intellect, having been differentiated within itself, became, whole through whole, both cognitive and knowable; for, differentiated from itself and standing in the differentiation, it is joined to itself through knowledge — which is the law for things that stand apart, toward that from which they stand apart. Properly, then, as I said, the knowable and the cognitive and knowledge were differentiated from one another in intellect; and insofar as it is the thing differentiated, it appeared cognitive; insofar as it is that from which it was differentiated, in this respect it is knowable, prior to the former; for what proceeded desired to return; and returning through knowledge, it made its return as a cognitive toward a knowable; and it is itself both the from-which and the to-which: itself, then, the knowable and the cognitive, and in the middle of these, knowledge. As I was saying, then: properly these belong to intellect and are in intellect; and yet also from Being — in another manner; for intellect was, all the same, differentiated from it, so that toward That too it set out through knowledge; for this was the last contact of the things that have proceeded. And wishing to be joined to it and fitted upon it, it gathered its own knowledge into one gathering of all knowledges; and having wrought one unified knowledge, with all its speed — as one might say — it set out toward the undifferentiated, the knowable in very truth; not making the cognitive stand toward the knowable as one toward one in differentiation, but, having in a certain manner shown its knowledge to be substance by the great union, it cast itself upon the knowable as substance; and it desired, indeed, as a cognitive desires a knowable — because of the from-afar; but having been joined, and having attained, it knew the contact to be not of a cognitive, nor toward a knowable, but of substance toward substance. So that toward That the return is rather substantial; while toward itself it is rather cognitive.

Why then is intellect both — cognitive and knowable at once — while substance is knowable only, although she too is seen in a certain differentiation, as has been said? It must be answered: the knowable wishes to be a certain desired thing, and the cognitive a desiring thing — in differentiation, however it be — and these stand toward each other just as intellect and substance; and substance is the desired, for she is the better; and intellect the desiring. So it is plain that the desiring and the cognitive belong by nature to the more needy, while to the better belong the desired and the knowable. And if intellect is both knowable to itself and desired by itself — or by the others that come after it, or have proceeded from it — what wonder? The more needy participate the things before them — not, however, conversely. Accordingly substance is not intellect, while intellect is both substance and intellect — but the latter according to existence, the former according to participation; substance, then, is knowable, and intellect is knowable according to participation; while intellect is cognitive — such, therefore, according to existence. Against the perplexity, then, these things suffice. And perhaps one might suppose even substance to be cognitive — if indeed she is all things according to her proper gathering — yet not according to the determined knowledge; for in the same way she is also knowable: but undeterminedly, and in what is relationless toward another; but when intellect had proceeded from her, and a relation had arisen toward something before it, as of cause toward caused — since the caused appeared, having become cognitive, substance too projects something knowable: just so much as the property of the relation fore-appeared, counter-divided toward it. Let so much, for the present, be said about these things.
