lines.text: Chapter 82 — The Cause Acts into Itself and the Caused: the Phaedo's Rod and Number; Substance Breathes Desire into What Stood Away; Knowledge the Guide, an Eye Fore-Escorting Desire · pp. 232–235

Ninth from the top, then, among the problems posed, was this: if things subsisting according to relation mutually establish one another, how shall the caused not also act somewhat into the cause, and the desired into the desiring, and indeed the knower into the known? For if each of the two comes to be in actuality together — still, how is it possible for the caused to act into the cause? Among things of the same rank this might perhaps be true; and yet even with these one might raise the difficulty, whether what does not touch acts at all upon that which it does not touch, by the mere drawing-near of the relation; and whether the patient, though itself changing nothing, is nevertheless said to suffer from it. Or rather: the things that approach, or are separated, hold the rank of matter; and the form of the relation straightway shines upon them — whether both, or only one of the two, approaches or departs. For men, coming together, attain a certain number that supervenes upon them from without; and the one rod, cut into two, participated a dyad instead of a monad. These things Socrates teaches us in the Phaedo. But if the caused stood counter-apart from the cause in the procession, and either two came to be instead of one, or the one became the knowing and the other the known — that something should come from each of the two into the other, the argument of Socrates does not allow even in the case of coordinates; and that what belongs to both should come from one of the two, rather than from what is before both, has no account in those cases where there is nothing before both — as with the first knowable and the first cognitive, or the first cause and the first caused. Rather, it is plain that all things that are in the caused come to the caused from the cause, together with its very substance. For the producer makes the produced stand away from itself, and differentiates it from itself; it is the cause itself, then, that gives the differentiation both to itself and to that; for in this way, too, the paradigm is assimilated toward the image — because it assimilates the image to itself; and the desired lies before the desiring and is set over against it, because, when this latter stood away, the desired breathed into it a desire of its own rank. Thus, then, substance, having begotten intellect, fore-shone herself forth as knowable to it, and made within it a power cognitive of herself — and not in potency only, but the in-actuality as well; for such things do the higher impart to the lower. For a thing is knowable in just this way: as filling the cognitive with knowledge; and it is desired in just this way: that it raises the desiring up toward itself, and fills what desires with itself. So too does Iamblichus take the intelligible in relation to intellect: that it has filled intellect with the intellection of itself. The caused, accordingly, does not act into the cause; but the cause acts both into itself and into the caused; for together with the substance it also co-produces the relation of the counter-position; and, if one may so speak, before making the produced — the caused, and the desiring, and the cognitive — it pre-makes itself knowable, and desired, and cause, and producing. This, then, could not stand otherwise.

The eighth from the beginning of the things inquired demands the use of knowledge — what benefit it furnishes to the knower, or to the known, if one should wish to demand this besides. Let it be said, then, first: knowledge furnishes to the knower its very being. For it has its being in knowing — that being, I mean, which is substantiated according to knowledge; for intellect is in intelligizing; so that intelligizing is the substance of intellect; and what works the intellection within produces the substance of intellect; and this is the intelligible and knowable. Next: according to the counter-position of himself toward the intelligible, intellect shines forth the knowable in That — even if it does not give it subsistence, as we said before. And a third benefit, upon these, intellection furnishes to the intelligizer: that it gives form to intellect according to what is intelligized, and sets it — third, or second, or however far it has proceeded — within the form of the producer. And this is most august: that, in the manner that is through knowledge, it even adorns the caused with the forms of the causes. But if the things known happen to be worse: where there is sympathy of the knower toward them, the assimilation to the worse makes the knower bad; but if the knowledge of the seconds — or, generally, of the worse — is without passion, then in another manner it leads the worse back up toward the better, and sets them within those; or rather, it leads those forth into communion with the worse, according to the projection of the form-giving of the worse that takes place within knowledge.

And if one should seek the beneficial itself, and the good: let him consider the kinship of all things toward one another that comes to be through knowledge, according to the recognizing of the common kinship; and, still further, the road of all things as they set out toward the one principle, as toward the Good — on which road knowledge sets right the wandering, and is established as guide for those who are setting out upward. For it is like an eye fore-escorting, and leading, the desire as it hastens toward That — kindling its proper light. Wherefore knowledge is, of the things that lead toward the end, the most accomplishing. And further: giving form to the worse according to the cognitive form-giving of the better, it becomes reversive of the lower into the better — and into the mightiest of all at once, through the common leading-back into Being. For it is not to the Unsayable that we are joined through knowledge, but to Being; That has been joined to the Unsayable through total union; so that through this mean it would join the rest as well.

Chapter 83 — How Intellect Knows Its Prior: the Imitation Found in Knowing Itself; Her Tender Love for Her Offspring; Knowledge a Recognition, a Greeting Stretched Out across the Standing-Apart · pp. 235–239

But let us go now to the seventh of the things inquired; and first let us make a defense of the ranking — of the reversion according to knowledge and the reversion according to substance — namely, that the latter is better than the former. For as intellect, standing in its own bound, imitates what is before it as standing according to its proper bound — even if its bound stands toward that one's as the unbounded toward the bounded, and the undifferentiated toward the differentiated — so intellect, having known according to its own bound, imitated that of That which is seated above knowledge, in the knowable alone. And this is, confessedly, a second bound — not of subsistence toward subsistence, but as of knower toward known; so much, universally. If there is a substance of intellect, and a circumscription, as of a thing proceeding from itself, there will answer to this the cognitive reversion according to which intellect knows itself; and if it has proceeded also from what is before it, then to the procession from the subsistence above would answer the knowledge that knows what is before it; for it has been turned toward That with both a substantial and a cognitive reversion.

Next let us see the second part: how does it know That? Does it, by knowing itself, know That also? Or That, letting itself go? Or neither alone, but the both-together? For it knows neither That alone, apart from itself; nor through itself alone, as one who does not look toward That before it, but only toward itself. All must run together at once: for according to subsistence it proceeds, all its own, from That — so that also according to the knowledge of all itself it will know That; for knowing itself, it finds itself the imitation of what is before it — itself, and the as-it-were That; and again, knowing the imitation and the as-it-were That, in knowing itself it knows That. Only, in the one way it will know the likeness, and in the other the unlikeness: that the one is itself, and the other generative of itself; the one That's own, the other from That; or the one cognitive, and the other knowable. It must be said, then: just as intellect was differentiated from Being as the differentiated, and showed That forth, apart from itself, as undifferentiated; so, knowing itself, by the knowledge of itself — its godhead being circumscribed — it knows the uncircumscribed nature of Being; a nature that does not know, but is known only; and this because she submits to be made commensurate toward intellect, by, as it were, a tender love for her own offspring. Intellect does not, then, look toward its cause in the way it looks toward itself; rather, having stood away from her, it was inscribed toward her; and, having wished to seize her, instead of this it knew her; or rather, it seized her in such a way as not to become her, but to embrace her cognitively; and this is: to have its eye flooded round with the light of her light. For such is the contact of the knower toward the known: not to become that, nor to be that's, nor to receive an efflux from that, nor itself to be led back into that. For all such intuitions confound the things that have once been differentiated, and no longer allow even the form of knowledge to stand — the form which subsists in a differentiation standing according to the bounds of the known and of the knower: being a recognition of things that have stood apart, and a welcoming greeting stretched out in return, together with the standing-apart.

But by the such within, they say, we know the such without. Then, I shall reply, intellect did come to be outside of Being, by the variation of its nature; yet, having proceeded, it is nevertheless such — as far as may be — as the substance that remained; for the differentiation alone changed over; so that with the whole of itself intellect would know substance — no less than if it contained in itself a trace of substance. And if there is in it, before the differentiated, the gathered plenitude, this would be an intellectual image of the unified substance before it — an image, as it were, by which it will know the paradigm, as by the paradigm the image; and yet great is the differentiation of the image toward its own paradigm. And if something even of the unified nature itself — that of Being — should be present also in intellect, whether simply or in some manner, whether connate with Being or con-substanced with intellect, and where, and how: these things we shall seek in the discourse concerning participation, a little later. If, then, some such thing is present in intellect, by this intellect will know That as well; for the nature being in a manner one, the knowledge of it will also be in a manner one. These matters we hope to pursue more precisely in the discussions concerning intellect — the intellect truly so called — when we have added the discourse on participation.

But the sixth had been proposed to us upon these: how does intellect give subsistence to itself according to the substantial reversion toward itself, and yet not also to what is before it, according to the like reversion toward That? And the same difficulty was raised about the vital; for the cognitive we see standing alike in the toward-itself and the toward-That: it acts nothing in either case, insofar as it knows. For even if knowledge were a working thing, still, insofar as it acts something and gives subsistence, it is no longer knowledge, as of a known, but a poietic cause of some made thing. For making is not proper to the knower — only the knowing of what already is; whereas giving-subsistence belongs to substance and to life: or rather, to substance belongs the substantiating, and the furnishing of a first subsistence; to life, the as-it-were stirring of substance and rousing of her toward a certain procession — or the giving of the poietic nature of this. Why then does the substantial reversion into itself give subsistence to intellect itself from itself, while the reversion into what is before it does not give subsistence to That? And how indeed could the cause be given subsistence by the caused! Such a reversion, then, is not substantial, if it is not substance-making? Or rather: it is substance-making of the substance of intellect — as of one begotten from what is before it; for according to the substantial reversion into That, intellect, as proceeding from That, circumscribed itself by the turning toward That, receiving its being-from-That; for just so must the substantial reversion toward itself also be conceived: as giving subsistence to intellect as proceeding from itself. And supposing the same things about the vital reversion, we shall justly preserve the analogy in its own right.

And indeed the fifth we shall resolve easily: agreeing that the proper work of reversion is the inclining-together toward some other thing — toward which the reversion turns the reverting — or toward itself, if the reversion be toward itself; while the inclination comes to be, in the case of substance, together with the property that gives itself subsistence, and in the case of life, together with the life-making one. For reverting and making are not the same; but the maker assuredly reverts toward what is coming to be; and we wished to recognize the form of the reversion from what accompanies it — from the substance-making, or the life-making; since reversion is other than knowledge too: the inclination, as has been said, is toward another or toward itself; whereas knowledge is, as it were, an assent, and an agreement that each thing is what it is. And to the fifth must be joined the fourth; and the same divisions must be made for the three reversions: there is, even in the case of life, what answers to the knower — plainly, the living; and what answers to the known — that life which the living lives; and to knowledge — the act-of-living. So one may say in these cases too: the vital, the livable, the act-of-living; and so also in the case of substance: there is the substantiation and subsistence; the being-substantiated, the subsisting; and the substantiable — that which in intellect is substantiated, and according to which intellect is substantiated. For, to speak more plainly: the reversion is seen at the middle; and of the extremes, at the reverting end will be the cognitive, the vital, the substantiative — that is, the knowing, the living, the substantiated; and at that toward which it reverts: the knowable, the livable, the substance-making; for each of the former is desirous of one of the latter — the one of the knower's object, the other of the living's, the third of the substantiated's. And let us not pass over in silence what deserves attention: that in the case of knowledge the names have been differentiated — inasmuch as knowledge subsists in a notable differentiation; while in the others they are not laid down, because great is the union of the living toward its life, and greater still that of the substantiated toward the substance by which it is substantiated, and toward which it reverts in substance. Wherefore knowledge is both an activity and a passion — for we say I know you, and I am known by you; whereas I live and I am are spoken in neither voice, and are viewed by the grammarians as standing in simple subsistence — unless one should take on the making besides; for in those the transition arises, as I make-live, and I am made-live.
Chapter 84 — The Double Procession and the Threefold Remaining; Being Only Is, Simply; Life a Birth-Pang and an Advance; as in the Chaldaean Triads, the Power · pp. 239–243

To the third, then, we shall say that procession is double: the one is the procession of the proceeded — which one would see as third: as of the knowing, proceeding from the knowable; as of the living, from life, or from the cause of life; as of being, from the first being; while the other is the procession viewed in the very proceeding — according to which alone we say that life subsists; since of this latter the three could not be differentiated; or, if they are in any way differentiated, and project some appearance of their counter-division toward one another, at any rate in the substance that is coming to be it is impossible to divide, in any manner whatsoever, the substantial and the cognitive and the vital. If, then, one views and names only the remaining — that settled state bereft of procession — he could not divide even this in three; but if he means the remaining of what has proceeded, he will see this too divided three ways: for intellect remains both in the knowable, according to knowledge; and in life, according to its own life, or in the cause of life; and in Being, according to its not standing wholly out of Being — as we said in what went before.

So that toward the second also it is easy to say something from these: the reversion belongs to the proceeded; for this is what needs the return — the very thing that made the approach; not the proceeding, if it still proceeds; and much less the remaining before the procession; for this does not even proceed. Is then the reversion only of the proceeded? Or also the proceeding, and the remaining? For the very thing that remains has proceeded; and the middle holds the having-proceeded, and, remaining, holds the procession; in general, the three stand in determination toward one another, as has been said many times. In what has its substance determined, therefore, are the three — and this is the proceeded; whereas Being could not fittingly be said to remain — it, which does not even proceed, and in which nothing is determined; so that neither is remaining in it as something determined. In another way it is called unmoved: as wholly undifferentiated, and unified, and abiding in the nature that is before all things and without procession. And in the same way, neither does what is called life have remaining or procession or reversion viewed in differentiation, but those which are still dawning from beneath in the being-differentiated. The three, then, seem to be together with one another: in the unified, undifferentiated according to union; in the differentiated, according to a certain determination and counter-division already projected; and in the middle, plainly, the in-between — the being in a manner and not being in a manner, determined or undetermined. That, then, in the proceeded the three are present in this way — as differentiated according to form — is evident from these things.

But what — is Being not reverted toward itself, and self-subsistent, itself proceeding from itself and remaining in itself? Or rather: it appears to us to be such — to us who are partitioned about its single simplicity — while it is itself, wholly, none of these things; it has been allotted the one communion of the three, and this, moreover, gathered up within the whole communion of all things. For what exists according to some reversion, or procession, or remaining, must be in some particular manner; but That only is, simply; for each of those is not simply, but a substance of such-and-such a kind — remaining, perhaps, or proceeding, or reverting — and, to say it whole, determined. Whereby it is plain that in the proceeded are substance and life and knowledge, as counter-distinguished by division toward one another; while the middle nature is not yet any of these — neither substance, nor life, nor knowledge — but, by now, a certain birth-pang of these, and an advance; and in what is called Being, not even a dawning. But what is the proceeded? Always the third, and whatever comes after the third? Or sometimes also the second — even if not the second from Being, which we call life, but, say, the second intellect? Or rather: after the first intellect, and the first differentiation that shone forth in it, the seconds also, in succession, are ever differentiated from the things before them — participating the differentiation already projected above; and there are things which are seen also in the being-differentiated, in a certain manner, toward the things before them and the things after them, by analogy — as, in the Chaldaean triads, the Power.

Upon all these we shall examine the first thing inquired: what is the necessity of the antithesis of the three toward one another — whether of remaining and procession and reversion, or of substance and life and intellect, or of the unified and the being-differentiated and the differentiated? Perhaps, indeed, it is finer to make the counter-division thus: undifferentiated, being-differentiated, differentiated; or again: one, multiplied, and the mean of both — that which has slackened from the one, or has projected an appearance of multitude; for these stand diametrically, the one and multitude in antithesis, and in the middle of both that other. This triad, then, has been divided with likely reason; and the one before it is furnished both by the sensibles lying before all eyes — of which some, we say, only are; others also live; others also know — and by the definition of the animal, which marks it off as a substance living and knowing. The animal, accordingly, is out of the three; knowledge being removed, it becomes living substance only; and life too being left aside, it is established as substance alone. But leaving the things themselves, if you will, let us survey our own conceptions, which we have concerning them: what do we say to be signifies? what to live? what to know? This last stretches toward another; for knowing subsists according to the desire toward the knowable; while being is by itself, and of itself, and only itself, without any doubling; and living is, artlessly, the middle: still in itself and toward itself, insofar as the living lives; yet already, in a manner, being roused up from itself, and being differentiated toward itself, and as it were over-seething its own substance — not yet, however, stretched out toward another; wherefore it is not yet carried into activity and passion, as holding much to substance. For life is the up-standing of substance; wherefore it seemed to be motion, or the cause of motion; and differentiation, or the in-being-differentiated, or the cause of such differentiation; but it is none of these; for neither is substance rest, or the cause of rest, nor gathering, or the cause of gathering; nor is intellect knowledge, nor the cause of knowledge alone; for these are forms, and determined toward one another — for life and substance, as forms, are determined; whereas intellect is all things — the first intellect — and a whole cosmos, by now ordered, and sphered, by its proper circumscription and its proper differentiation. But the nature before it, which we call life from the eidetic life that resembles its middleness, is not yet ordered; for it is not yet differentiated, nor circumscribed — since circumscription too is a kind of differentiation; but it shows these from beneath, as flowing upon them from Being; and it is nothing other than only flowing — neither having remained above, nor having proceeded below. And before this is the wholly-complete subsistence of Being — so wholly-complete as not even to admit of the flowing, nor of the forth-pouring into the middle.

Justly, then, has this triad been counter-divided toward itself, according to the sequence of the determined conceptions. For substance discloses only this: what each thing is — and one would view knowledge too in this way, as itself a kind of subsistence, and life, and intellect; the good, then, the beautiful, the just — everything insofar as it is substance — belongs to that first. And the living of each thing — of each substance — its life is its seething: everywhere both up-standing, and strengthening itself from itself toward the outward activity — if this too can avail for the indication of what we mean. And when it is interwoven with another form, and stretches toward another, other activities and properties are seen within it — and indeed knowledge among them. Wherefore, relative to substance, life holds the rank of power, and knowledge of activity; and yet there is also a cognitive power, and a substance likewise, as also a vital one. With the by-itself, then, substance has co-subsisted; with the toward-another, knowledge; and with the middle — neither stretched toward another, nor at rest by itself — that which, from this very seeking and seething, is called life. And how is intellect third? If it is substantiated according to knowledge, then intelligizing is knowing — since knowledge was set in antithesis toward life, as has been said. And if intelligizing, and intellection, signify a return toward Being, as was said before, and the return is a reversion, or a differentiation, it is plain in what way intellect is third, after life and substance: for she is uncircumscribed, while intellect is circumscribed, and life holds the middle disposition; likewise intellect is differentiated, having become many instead of one and unified; substance is single-form and undifferentiated; and life holds the middle disposition of these as well. It remains to add this: in what way have remaining and procession and reversion been counter-divided toward one another? The same thing, if we take it, will have these three activities: either it keeps its quiet; or it changes some change; or it desires again the quiet. For the body, too, either is healthy according to nature, or is being led away into the contrary-to-nature, or is being led back up into the according-to-nature. And if we take what is divided three ways relative to the same one thing, we shall say that it either is together with it, or departs from it, or returns to it.

parts.name: Chapter 85 — Many, Parts, and Elements: Forms That Strive to Be Themselves; Parts in the One Mutual Inter-Holding; Elements Pressing into Union; the First Substance Has No Elder Elements · pp. 243–249

lines.text: Chapter 85 — Many, Parts, and Elements: Forms That Strive to Be Themselves; Parts in the One Mutual Inter-Holding; Elements Pressing into Union; the First Substance Has No Elder Elements · pp. 243–249

Upon these things it must now be inquired, concerning the intelligible — that which we have called the wholly unified — whether it has within itself any differentiation, and an order of first and middle and last plenitude: whether as the philosophers say, of substance and life and intellect; or as the theologians, who multiply the intelligible principles, each school in its own way; or as the Chaldaeans, who celebrate the paternal triads. But if we are to settle these things, we must first push our argument back, in due measure, into the inquiry concerning the many and multitude; for in this way it will perhaps appear whether multitude befits that intelligible, or not; and in what way it does, and in what way it does not, according to the juster account. Those things, then, are clearly seen to be many, and are so called by all, which have stood apart from one another, and each of which has come to be by itself, in its proper circumscription, wishing only to be what it is and is called — as we say the forms strive to be. But the parts also are called many; for one part of anything cannot by nature be — two at the least; the parts, then, are many; but they differ in this: that they do not wish to be by themselves, nor their own, but altogether one another's, and the whole's; and according to the one mutual inter-holding they subsist within the whole — having begun their differentiation according to the partition, yet not having flown apart into proper circumscriptions, but still con-substanced by the inclining-together toward one another and toward the whole; as appears most of all in those parts which are called like-parted. And in a third sense the elements are called many; for not even can one element alone fill out the elementated, but two at the least.

What then is the difference between parts and elements? One is this: that the parts consist of the same elements as the whole; for the parts are of the elementated — as these four elements are the elements of sinew, and indeed of each of its parts; whereas the elements are simpler even than each part — as fire, say, and earth are simpler even than what seems the least of parts, the sinew. Another: that the parts preserve their proper partition, according to which they subsisted — or, if they do not preserve it, they would not even be parts; whereas the elements do not abide any standing-apart whatsoever, but are poured together into a blending, and press into union, and have their being elements in just this: in nowhere showing forth their proper partition, and much less their circumscription. And a third difference between them: that the elements are not of the same nature as the elementated, except insofar as they are called its elements; I mean, for example, that the elements of our body are not, according to the form of the blend, bones, if you like, and flesh; rather they are elements of bones and of fleshes, whenever they become commensurate, and are made proper to this form; in themselves, however, they are of another subsistence. And so too with substance: if there be any elements of her, they would not be certain substances; for the elementated was substance, and the element would not be the elementated. The extremes, then, are: what has been circumscribed into its proper subsistence, and what has been blended together into the one common union of all; and the meanness of both is the parts, and the partition of these — of things already in a manner standing apart, but not yet being circumscribed.

But if these things stand thus apart by nature, how are these four elements still certain forms? And how would the so-called genera of Being not be forms — and yet they are called both elements of substance, and genera; and they belong to Being for this reason, that substance has been blended together out of them. And if someone shall say that these are forms and not elements, what then would the elements truly be? For what could we find simpler than the genera of Being? Yet they seem, all the same, to be forms as well, preserving their proper circumscriptions; for in substance there are both motion and rest, manifestly, and each member of each of the other antitheses. And how are head and hands and feet parts of man? And how is the whole composed of whole parts — of sun, I mean, and moon and the rest, of which each is a whole form? And our own parts have been circumscribed, in a manner, by certain eidetic differences — as many of them as are unlike-parted. To these things it must be said that the lower always participate the higher; so that the forms are also parts and elements; and the parts, in turn, are also elements — not, however, conversely in every case. For among the forms, some are simpler than others, and the simple become elements of the composite.

Further: whatever within the whole are unlike parts, are at once forms and parts: forms, because unlike; parts, because they are not by nature able to be by themselves, but within the whole — such as our parts called organic; and such as, in the heaven, hemispheres and quarters and certain different zones; and further, poles and centers and axes and circles, marked off by certain demiurgic cuts, yet unable to be by themselves. And in souls, the reason-principles happen to be parts of this kind, and all the causes and participations of the different forms are of such a nature; while the existences are as of the self-complete — save that of these too there come to be gatherings, as out of elements, and wholenesses, as out of parts, as has been said before. In this way, then, some things are forms and parts; and forms and at once elements are all those forms that are blended together into the undifferentiated constitution of one form — such as the composites among the animals, which show forth the composition whole through whole: mules, and ostriches, and all such; for these have been constituted out of different forms, as out of elements poured together into some one form. In the same manner we shall see parts as well; but parts alone, in this strict sense, are those which jut forward from the gathered nature, and yet have not stood apart, each circumscribed, complete, itself from itself; for such, confessedly, are the like-parted: having partitioned the wholeness, yet remaining all the same in the same form, and for this reason sharing one name with the whole and with one another; and there is, further, what is just now jutting forth into the unlike-parted, and yet remains within the whole, and within the common naming of the same nature — the very thing that the ordered animal has undergone in each of the forms: for it is still animal, and a part and measure of animal; but already, in a manner, the one is human and the other equine — not only by the commensurability toward each (for this the like-parted also underwent), but by the projection, and the inclination, toward man and toward horse. And parts as forms are such as lie on either side of the forms that are circumscribed each according to itself: either toward the worse, as our organic parts; or toward the better, as the parts of the cosmos; for these latter are rather the whole's, even if each has been eager to be its own; while the former cannot subsist by themselves and upon themselves, through the incompleteness of their proper nature. And there would also be parts that become elements — namely, such as fill out the wholeness that is called the wholeness from parts. For that the wholeness is filled out from parts — if not every wholeness, yet this one at least — is evident; and that it is as from elements, is shown by the one form being brought to completion out of many that vanish into the one of the many, and no longer preserve their partition in the form-giving of the whole. And I think also that the forms, viewed in the genus as in a whole, are viewed as parts — for they are not yet circumscribed there in their proper circumscriptions; and, being parts, they become elements of the genus. For the gathering of the many animals — a gathering of this kind — is the one animal, or has its subsistence in the one animal. And perhaps like to the foregoing is also this: that the genera of Being, even if they seem in a manner to be forms, are rather parts of the whole blending; yet for this very reason they settle also into the elemental nature, according to the one substance which they all constitute. These matters may be worked out more finely hereafter.

But which of the forms, or which of the parts, can become elements, and which cannot, must be said. For not all, as it seems — for instance, the last of the forms; for if these too were elements, there will be something even after them, composed out of them. And this too must be sought: whether the elements are in every way of a superior and simpler nature, retiring back toward the subsistence of the more composite things? It seems indeed to stand so in most cases — yet not in all. For our body is gathered together out of pre-existing things; and the man and the horse — rational mortal animal, and irrational mortal animal, let us say — out of the more whole-like; and the soul is blended from substance and life and knowledge, which pre-exist; but the whole body of the All is out of the four elements — which, however, no longer pre-subsist; nor is the first substance out of elements elder in nature. For before her, the elements are nowhere; for the elementated always wishes to be better than its proper elements; and the elements are not even by themselves, but always in the elementated, and with one another, as the parts are with the whole and with one another; since the elementated even uses its own elements as matter — being itself like a form supervening upon them. If, then, these things stand so, the first elementated would not be out of elements elder than its own nature and ranked before it, but out of elements first shining forth within it — more incomplete than the whole form, and for this reason conceived as simpler; though perhaps, in truth, not even simpler, but only more incomplete and more partial; for so stand the parts here, and the forms as well; for the more whole-like seems more composite, because more embracing; but it is not so — rather, it is both simpler and better.
Chapter 86 — The One Slackened into the Subsistence of the Many; the Threefold One; Life Seething and Boiling Up — Whole and Parts before All Forms; the Elements of the First Substance · pp. 249–255

What then is the so-called simplicity of the elements, and relative to what composition? Or rather, the elementated is double: the one as the supervening form — which is, in real truth, both simpler and better; the other as the mixture and blend of the concurring elements — which is presupposed as one composite matter; relative to this latter, then, the elements are simple, and not relative to the common property that gives the mixture its form. Substance, accordingly, is the former kind of nature; while the substance according to the mixture is substance in potency; and each of the elements is a part of the matter; these, then, are not yet substance, but substance-like nevertheless, and near to substance, though more incomplete. What then — is even the first substance from matter and form? And whence did the matter subsist, if not from the things prior in nature? For the matter here with us comes from the elder principles, as they say. There must, then, be There also the participations from the elders, taken up in the rank of matter and of elements. Or rather — concerning the participations I defer the busy inquiry till later; but, the elements being viewed in some multitude and some determination, substance — being before all substantial determination — could not be second to her own elements. Subsisting first, therefore, she shone forth, together with herself and within herself, her proper elements — as the wholeness its parts, and as this cosmos its own elements within itself; and I mean not the matter (though perhaps that as well), but the elements of the form — such as the four, whatever they are and however one may determine them: whether wholeness projected them as four parts, or whether the visible and the tangible, and the means of these — being everywhere, and seen in all things — these too were differentiated off from the one and single-form constitution of the cosmos. For every one is, by its own nature, before its proper multitude; and from it the multitude as it were grows out, according to the partition of that one into these; for — so to speak — the One is slackened into the subsistence of the many: that one not being used up into these, but furnishing room to these also for their subsistence; and even if the one be inseparable from the many, such is its nature. And if the many are threefold — either as forms, or as parts, or as elements — assuredly the one also would be triple, and for each multitude there is its proper one: the eidetic gathering, one form before the partition; the whole before the parts; the elementated before the elements; and the differences of the one go forth in proportion. For the one of the forms is a many-formed one; the one of the parts appears, indeed, to be many-parted, insofar as the whole stretches alongside all the parts by its embrace — yet what is before the parts is impartible, even if it should preside within the parts; for it gives the parts also room for the subsistence that is partitioned within it; while the elementated is more complete: it has been squeezed together into union, and it con-fuses the elements and unites them toward itself, and does not allow them, in truth, to be ranked after itself, but compels them to make sail toward its own proper subsistence. Wherefore, being many by nature, all of them nevertheless become one; and the mixture is not one thing and the elementated another — as we just now distinguished them for clarity's sake, turning the matter many ways. The elementated, rather, is one and many — but the many squeezed together by the one, and not permitted to be simply many, but unified, and drunk down by the one, and standing in the undetermined of the one; for thus the elements everywhere appear to stand, both toward one another and toward the elementated; and these are not the matter of that — for neither are the parts matter of the whole, nor the forms of the all, if all be said instead of whole — but only analogous to matter; and as the multitude of each form stands toward its one — out of which the whole form is constituted, one and many — so too the elementated is one and many: the many, however, blended together through the dominance of the one. Whereas if this one should relax its own simplicity, and be as it were mastered by the many that have risen in faction against it — or, to speak more truly, that have imitated it, each according to its own circumscription — then the many are established as forms instead of elements, and the one has become somehow many-colored and variegated; and instead of elementated and elements, or blend and blended, there is a monad and numbers — the one in the forms being one and many, the both-together.

The parts and the whole must be viewed in the middle manner: a certain relaxation having come about — and for this reason the parts having subsisted according to the partition that was dared — yet an inclining-together having come about as well: of the one toward the parts, by its taking-up of the partition and the distribution; and of the parts toward the one, by their taking-up of the one, and their partible reception of it; and the thing is established as a mean of the whole's and the parts' peculiar manners. Wherefore upon these the doubling, and their single relation, are both manifest; while at the extremes, even if both exist, they hold them more faintly: in the eidetic one-and-multitude, the single relation and joint-appearance is less apparent, because they do not much incline together, nor are they, nor are they said to be, one another's; while in the elements and the elementated, not even the doubling is clear — because the multitude of the elements does not show itself forth determined within the one; for their multitude appears rather by inference, through the con-fusion, if it be lawful so to speak, of the elemental properties. And what wonder, if the first elementated, substance, works the undetermined into her elements — seeing that even the forms, when they are blended in the rank of elements toward others, as we said before, are themselves also compounded toward one blend; even if each somehow escapes the blending, and shows forth its proper activities now and then, and in some manner. For things that are forms cannot be made wholly one; wherefore the visible and the tangible are each everywhere, wherever the other is — and yet the one remains one thing and the other another; and in soul, the substantial and the vital and the cognitive are everywhere throughout the soul — yet these too are determined in some manner. And such, in intellect, are the genera of Being; for these too are elements of that substance — not of the super-eidetic and simple substance, but of the eidetic; for these too are certain forms — though more elemental than the others, and simpler, and for this reason common to all forms, and to the one eidetic nature that is before the many forms; whence in this nature too their properties somehow show through. But not even these are yet forms, insofar as they are taken as elements; nor have they yet become parts.

For there is, even in the eidetic cosmos, first what stands as eidetic substance — a certain single-form gathering of the forms; then a certain partition of her, and the wholeness that gathers the partition — itself also an eidetic nature of whole and parts; and upon this, according to the differentiated of the eidetic subsistence, the forms themselves stood apart, and that which gathers the forms — the many-formed one, as has been said: a monad, and the number fastened upon the monad. Before the elemental and gathered eidetic substance, accordingly, there is the subsistence — in real truth — of the whole and the parts, seen in the being-differentiated; the first substance, and really being substance, which for this reason we call life: as already swelling into dis-stance, and being stirred into differentiation, and — as the name signifies — seething, and boiling up; not yet, however, poured out into the subsistence of forms, but viewed in the seething and the seething-up; whence also we hymn her as whole and parts, before the whole eidetic nature: because, remaining, she is moved; and, unified, she nevertheless suffers something of being-differentiated — being, by the unified and remaining, the whole; and by the being-differentiated and moving, the parts. Wherefore the whole and the parts are one nature, because one is the nature still being differentiated, and already being so: the latter, as no longer wholly unified; the former, as not yet completely differentiated. One, then, is the meanness, which we call by two names — whole and parts — viewed according to the both-together. And before even her is substance: a unified nature, simply, and undifferentiated — yet not as the one, but as the unified; and this is out of many and with many; so that the first elementated also is out of elements — she is it; for the simply substance is she, through whom also the particular substance is everywhere the particular elementated. For what is everywhere gathered we call substance — as the being-differentiated, life; and the differentiated, form; even if each of these be the last of its kind, for instance the bodily: substance is the con-blend of the four elements; the stirring of this blend, roused toward the differentiation of its proper activities, is a certain life of it — for it is a motion, and a preparation toward the eidetic activity, and a subsistence before the activity; and the figure that has stood apart is the form. And if every substance is gathered according to a wasting — or, if you will let me say it, a joint-perishing — of the elements, then assuredly the first and simply substance also is a gathering of elements; and her elements are the most fully, and most properly, elements of all: not blended together by a con-fusion of their proper circumscriptions, like the elements here — as Aristotle also says; nor united only at their own summit, letting the rest go into differentiation — as we said the forms are blended together, becoming elements of the eidetic substance, wherefore they also show forth, somehow, their proper determination within her; but as having nothing determined, nothing eidetic, nothing con-fused by any force — but being, whole through whole, simply elements, by nature such, of the substance that is properly unified and stands according to union. Not the forms, then, nor the genera of Being, are her elements; for these too are certain forms.

What then are they? For beyond these we have nothing else to name; nor, indeed, are the simply-parts these things; for the parts too are super-eidetic; what then the parts also are, must be sought. Or rather: they are the genera of Being — but not subsisting eidetically, in the way they are named by us, and conceived; for all our conceivings and namings are eidetic — I forbear to say that they are not even intellectual and true, but one must be content if they happen to be even psychic; yet nevertheless our names and thoughts are of the forms. From the things thus brought forward, then, one must render up the eidetic, and what is determined by circumscriptions of properties; and we leave them only the partition; for we call the forms also parts — but they would not be both forms and parts There. Parts, then — qua parts — are the genera of Being; they, then, are what are called the as-it-were parts; or rather, not these — not the ones that have taken on the eidetic in addition to the partial — but those before these, being such as these are. They are parts, then: but parts only, and simply parts; so that the so-called genera of Being subsisted as parts before being made proper by circumscriptions. And the elements, accordingly, in the like manner: stripping from them the necessity of the partition, we shall posit them as those very natures growing together toward one another, and being united into one blend — and in this respect seen as elements. These, then, are elements according to existence; while the parts become elements according to participation; for they too have something that grows together into the subsistence of the whole; for the whole is a connate growth of the part-wise summits, blended into one — the whole — according to which summits the parts become elements. Wherefore also the oft-raised perplexity — how the wholeness is from the parts, and how the parts are after her and from her, being parted off — yet parts according to existence, because each has its being in the partition; while the forms, circumscribed according to existence, become the others by participation: parts, more proximately, by the inclining toward the one, and by a certain departure from determination; elements, higher up, by the union, and the riddance not only of determination but of partition. The same things, then, are the genera of Being — subsisting in three ways, differently and differently.

Have then the genera of Being alone received this triple nature? Or, simply, all things that are forms — even the last of the forms — are ever contained in the firsts; but different ones are differentiated at different stages, some earlier, some later: because some have circumscriptions more whole-like, consorting with more of the undivided; others more partial, consorting with more of the divisive. Nevertheless, all that is differentiated below also exists above, gatheredly; for whence are the differentiated, if all were not gathered above? And procession is nothing other than the differentiation of the gathering — not all at once, assuredly, but little by little, different things shining forth at different stages, the more whole-like before the more partial. For why ever should all things be in intellect, differentiatedly, and yet not all in substance, unitedly? For always the unified is before the differentiated; so that also the all unified is before the all differentiated. And why should only the genera of Being be gathered There — being elements, as they say, of substance? Or limit and the unlimited alone — for the philosophers say this as well? In that case the other forms would not pre-exist There, in the unified-before-all; and so That would not be the principle of all things, but only of the everywhere-couplings of limit and unlimited, or of the extended completions and mixtures of what is called Being. But if the summit of each form is a gathering of the whole multitude that belongs to that form, how is not the one principle of all things, likewise, a gathering of the whole multitude of all that grows out from her, and is differentiated upon her? Why then — if all things are elements in substance, and all parts in the middle rank, just as all are forms in the third and differentiated, the intellect — do we nevertheless call some of the forms elements, such as the genera of Being, and others from-elements, such as animal and plant and the more composite of the forms? For why should not these too be elements? For the animal is an element of man, and man of the land-dwelling man.

lines.text: Chapter 87 — Subaltern Forms, Elements and Elementated at Once; the Individuals: the Same Form Set Whole in Many Matters; Socrates Not Other than Plato by Form; the Double Generation · pp. 255–259

Perhaps, then, even the last of the forms becomes an element in the individuals — itself also, with others, filling out the particular man? Or it must be said: that all things that are forms should be also parts and elements is no wonder; but of the forms, some are more whole-like and simpler, and for this reason better-natured toward the blending — as having circumscriptions neither deep nor manifold, but just now dawning from beneath, and not yet rolled up together into many; whence they are easily united, and as it were con-fused toward one another; but by as much as the procession happens to descend further — deepening, and being built up with circumscriptions and partitions — by so much the harder do the forms contribute to the blend of an elementated, no longer making the union exact, but as it were cleaving it toward differentiation. Whence the things nearest the unified nature appear to be elements rather than forms; the farthest, forms rather than elements; and the middles stand at the mean of the extremes, of composition and of simplicity. The genera of Being, then, are rather elements; the last of the composites rather forms — man, and horse, and, to speak generally, what are called the most specific of the forms; while the middles, which are also called subaltern, hold the rank of elements toward the things that come from them, and of elementated toward the things before them: the same things, then, are equally elementated and elements.

Are then the most specific forms, in any manner, elements of the individuals? Not, surely, of other forms; for then they would not be most specific, and last of the forms; but surely not of the individuals either; for the common must be present together with other differences; and what would be the individual differences of each — the accidents? But accidents do not fill out a substance. Or perhaps these differences too are substantial? Then they will show themselves as first, if indeed they are proper to the individual; so that they will have proper ideas, individual as they are; or there will be some form which comes to be, whole, and perishes — a form neither monadic nor embracing of individuals. Perhaps, then, the manner of the differentiation is double: the one dividing the One into many — into whole forms — by form-making differences; the other stamping the same whole upon many matters; wherefore the individual is the more properly called atom, because it is whole everywhere, having no single differentiating variation. Is then the difference of the individuals due to the matter alone? And what difference of forms could there be beside the matter? Or beside her there is none. Yet if she were endowed with form, then, beside what is in her, some differing form might arise — as the likeness of Socrates in stone differs from the one in bronze; for the form con-substanced with matter is somehow co-altered along with its substrate. But if she is formless, and differs in potency, the difference comes about according to the in-potency and the in-actuality — except that no eidetic difference is added on her account. But let these things be dismissed for the present.

This, however, I say: that in many substrates nature has set the same form whole — the same, received in many places, without difference. What then — is not one individual other than another individual? Or rather, only insofar as it is here and there; while the form is nevertheless the same; so that if one should take away the matter, the whole form would have appeared one. Not other, then, according to the form; not other, then, by otherness — if by matter; for otherness too is a form. Or they say other in number; but number too is a certain form, and undifferent on either side; and the otherness of the two monads is likewise undifferent. How then is the whole form predicated of all, while that of Socrates is no longer? Or rather: it has been narrowed not insofar as it is form, but insofar as it is a particular; for man is predicated alike, according to the subsistence of the form; but it differs by the a-certain-one and by the universal. The particular, then, toward the particular, is undifferent; for each of the two is a what. Socrates, then, is not other than Plato — for all the same attributes are rendered, conversely, of each. But why, man being one, is the one universal and the other individual? For not in vain did the one participate the whole, and the other the particular — or the individual, whatever it is. It must be said: the universal is the reason-principle from which there is, in the individuals, one participation common to all — what we call the common form in the many, which is predicated of all together, taken as common; while what is in each of the individuals is the same both with the common, and with the each-of-each — in its property, and in the whole and entire nature of the form; for there is nothing of it that is not everywhere, and eidetic in each; but, being the same in all respects, it has been partitioned in its subsistence, and stands apart — itself dis-spanned from itself into determination; as body stands apart from itself into a kind of continuous bulk, while the form is everywhere the same and undifferent.

For nature seems to have gone all the way through, from the firsts to the lasts, along the diameter, and to have arrived from the opposite at the opposite; in many places this may be seen, and it comes to pass in what we have been saying: at the top, each form is one only, simply — for that there be two first is impossible, as Plato shows; while at the last extremities the individuals are many the same — many images of one and the same, not differing in form, yet many for all that, the one form being generative, everywhere, of the same things. And perhaps the generation is double: the one according to the form-making differences of the divided forms; the other according to the different scatterings of the same — whether by continuity, as with bodies and qualities, or by partition, as with monads, and men, and horses, and all such forms; and each suffers, or works, the undifferent multiplication of the many individuals. And not only the most specific of the forms do so, but also the differences within them, and the genera seen upon them; for there is in me an individual animal, and an individual rational, and mortal; and plainly the generation of these is undifferent; and this is the individual constituted by differences; and many other things suffer the same — for instance the genera of Being; and every nature proceeds, down to the individuals; and all procession is eidetic. But it must be examined hereafter, concerning the elder principles, whether they too make some procession; and concerning the things that seem to proceed, in what manner they make the procession. What we said at the beginning, then: the most specific forms are not present as elements in the individuals, as though in compounds of them; rather, the whole elementated structures themselves are, in many places, the same — just as the blend of the one body, being an elementated, is both whole in the part, and, in this part, the whole compound of the four elements, standing apart in many places. Concerning this, I do not know whether anything further is worth drawing out.

Chapter 88 — Elements and Parts Co-Proceed with Their One; All Things Both Pre-Exist and Do Not; the Double Procession of Forms — Parmenides the Great on Part and Whole; the Titanic Differentiation; One Chorus with Its Leader · pp. 259–265

Running back up to the perplexity from the beginning, let us see whether the elements are not, in subsistence, lower than the elementated — insofar as they are elements — and yet, in the nature of their property, superior: as the animal, before man, is common and whole-like, but in man is an element of him, and more partial. Do then the synonymous properties pre-exist each of the elements in this manner? Or would it not be even in this way? For the elements, and the parts, and the forms stand toward one another in a certain division; but the division is different in different places: as the triad is out of three monads, and the tetrad out of four — not that, out of those three and another added to them, as it might seem, but the division is proper to each of the monads; so that even the monads of the numbers lesser in quantity are more whole-like. For of the whole monadic form, the division into two is one thing, that into three another, and that into four another; so that of animal, too, the differentiation into two is one — if one should say the one part is rational and the other irrational; but if, taking the rational animal — not the whole animal — one should divide it in its turn, as it might chance, by the immortal and the mortal, he will make three elements of man: animal, rational, mortal — counter-divided by the mortal according to a third rank, and no longer the same, either in form, with the former ones — neither the rational, nor the animal; and this triad of elements shone forth first in man, and was differentiated off from him, as being properly his own.

What then — are not the seconds always gathered up in the firsts, and the more partial in the more whole-like — so that the three elements of man, too, are in animal, let us say? Or rather: there too the elements are gathered together with the whole; for man also is There, in the gathering; for the seconds are always in their priors — primarily the wholes in the wholes, and, together with the wholes, the parts also in them; and likewise the elements, and the forms, and, to speak universally, the multitudes in their proper monads. Just so substance also is contained in the unified, being undifferentiated from her proper henad; for so too the henad is contained, undifferentiated from substance; and so the elements of either are themselves also taken up together There, undifferentiated from one another; wherefore There they are neither elements nor an elementated; for there is no determination at all. And so the parts also are pre-taken in the elements — but according to the elemental gathering; and so the forms in the parts — but without circumscriptions, according to the partition alone. So that, in this manner, the elements of the cosmic body too are impartibly in the hypercosmic light, whatever it is and however great; and the elements of the human body are gathered up, undifferentiatedly, in the sublunar cosmos; for those elements are common to all animals and plants and metals, all pre-taken in one gathering; and below, the proper ones are differentiated in each thing — the elements of each. Either, then, these pre-exist — and I say these, because not according to this differentiation, nor according to this form-giving; all alike, then, both do not pre-exist, and again seem to pre-exist — to one who views the matter more in the gross, and views the gathered and more whole-like manner of the form-giving.

But one must mark this: that the elements everywhere proceed together with their one elementated, and co-exist with its existence; and the parts, likewise, are everywhere together with their proper wholeness; whereas the forms, not inclining together in this way toward their proper one, but being wholly form-given by circumscriptions, and striving to be upon themselves, justly made for themselves a double procession: the one as the parts —

when the form also takes up the rank of parts; for so stand the forms in intellect: they fill out the multiplied aspect of it, as the reason-principles of soul fill out the many-formedness of soul, and those of nature the multitude of nature. And there would be, even of the one bodily form, such a many-colored multitude, answering by analogy to the many-formedness of nature and of soul and of intellect. Such things we called unlike-parted parts, by-named from the whole form — for they are human, and equine; just as the reason-principles are natural, and psychic, and yet each reason-principle is not soul, nor nature — nor is each a man, or a horse, as it were a head, and a hand, or a foot — yet completing into the whole man, and each into its whole: so that the part is neither the same as the whole, nor other, but in a certain respect and manner — as Parmenides the great requires. Such forms, then, both are, and proceed, together with the common and one, just like the parts and the elements; but another procession of theirs comes about when each is separated, self-completely, from the whole and from its counter-divided fellows — a procession that seems, indeed, to be more complete, but in truth belongs to the needier ones: to those that have relaxed the con-spiration, and the inclining-together toward the one and toward one another, and for this reason have proceeded scattered, so far as may be.

At any rate the reason-principle in the soul — and likewise the one in nature — is better than this apparent man; and the reason-principle of the human soul, in the more whole-like soul, is better than the psychic substance that subsists by itself. There is, then, also such a procession of forms — subsisting not as a swarm, but, as it were, autonomous. But since the titanic differentiation did not wholly prevail over them, these too keep some ordering toward one another: the figure of a chorus filling its scheme, or of an army-camp, or — to speak generally — of some whole cosmos which one would say consists of wholes; but that is parts and whole; so that it is better to say: a monad, and a number wound off from the monad — a chain flowing down from its proper principle, changing over, by descent of forms, with their proper differences. For so, perhaps, the cosmos also stands: one, and then many after the one; and if all together are one — yet as one chorus with its leader. But how these things stand we shall examine again, when we make the discourse about all procession, inquiring after that of the first principles — whether it is, or is not.

For now let us gather this together: the elements proceed always with their substance, and with one another; the parts, with the whole and with one another; and of the forms, those that have come to be in the rank of elements subsist with their proper elementated, and those in the rank of parts, these too with the whole; while those that, in the eidetic procession, have subsisted as forms, by themselves and upon themselves — these are the ones that proceed scattered, autonomous; each, like a number, depending from its proper monad — the more whole-like from a more whole-like one, the more partial also from a more partial. Yet not even these are wholly autonomous, nor only differentiated from one another and from their proper monad; for each participates the communion that is as of parts; and the monad participates that of the whole nature; whence the same things seem also to be parts of the single-form cosmos — this, according to the partitioned aspect; but according to the whole union of the eidetic summits — as of straight lines grown together in the center — according to this they become, as it were, elements of their one common substance.

Chapter 89 — The Simply Many, Multitude of the Simply One; the Unlimited Multitude of the Parmenides; the One Many — Fount of Founts, Seed of the Gods, Cosmic Aiōn; the First and Simply God · pp. 265–272

Again, then, let us say from the beginning: the many, everywhere, are either elements only, or parts, or forms; and of the forms, some are unified into an eidetic substance — which we also call eidetic elements; others are viewed in partition — which we call eidetic parts: the first, as in the case of the four elements of our body; the second, as in the case of its parts, and of the like-parted; for these too are parts, and eidetic, even though they have the same form, partitioned — and still more so the unlike-parted; and others are each upon themselves — as a man and another man, and sun and moon. And again, by a third remove, these last being taken in three ways: at the summits, the elemental nature is conceived; according to the filling-out of the one, and the inclining-together toward it, whole and parts; and according to the released circumscription of each, the peculiar-mannered form — as a number from a monad, and a chain from a principle, and a filling-out of a self-complete from self-completes, shows itself forth; and further than this, nothing proceeds. For the further would be the complete dis-spanning of all things — un-kindred, and altogether torn asunder — in which disorder also will supervene, all things being no longer ordered toward one; and this affection does arise in the All, yet it is led back again into one, and ordered toward the one. But the discourse concerning processions, as I said before, let it be deferred for the present; since this too must be deferred to that discourse: whether each multitude is double — for instance, of the forms, the one connate with intellect, as a multitude of intellect; the other, the multitude of the many intellects after the one intellect; for of souls also there is one multitude, that of the many souls after the one soul, and another, the multitude of the psychic reason-principles in the one soul — to which corresponds, we shall say, the multitude of the forms divided within intellect; and it must be sought, likewise, of the parts and of the elements, whether the one multitude is constituted within, and the other without. Let these things too be dismissed for the present.

But since the many are said either as elements, or as parts, or as forms, it is clear that to be many is not, for them, the same as to be forms, or parts, or elements; each of these, then, is a multitude, and a particular multitude; but that which is only multitude — the simply many — what would they be, and of what, and where subsisting? Before the triply-divided many, surely, and before the three manys; so also before the elements — and therefore before the elementated as well; for this is connate, and of the same rank, with its own elements. Of what, then? As the elements are of the elementated, the many are of what? Of the One — as the parts of the whole? For the one is not so related to them, as some one of the many, but as the before-the-many, and as it were a monad of the many, and one-the-all; being all of the one, then, the many are — themselves also completing into the subsistence of such a one, as the parts into that of the whole, the elements into that of the elementated; for we do not say that the one and the many are two substances — no more than the elementated and the elements, or the whole and the parts, or this one monad and the number of forms within it — but, according to the both-together, one and many; so that the simply one, too, must be conceived as many of this kind — as each form is one and many. What, then, are the many? Monads? But the monads are forms; and the many are before the forms. Parts, then? But the many are before the elements also; and the elements before the parts. Are the many, then, elements? But the elements are blended with one another toward the mixed substance of the elementated; whereas the many wish to be the multitude of the One. Do they then not blend with one another — or rather, do the many stand apart from one another more than the elements? This, surely, has no account; yet neither do they fail to blend; rather, being still more impartible than the elements, and more unitary, instead of being blended they are unified; and instead of making the mixed, they make the One; for the many were of the one, and not of substance. Are they, then, determined from one another, or continuous with one another? Or rather: the continuous and the determined are among the forms, and are truly forms; so that not even of the parts is it true to say either of the two; for the parts are seen in the being-differentiated of the forms, not in the having-been-differentiated; and much more do the elements escape the continuous and the determined — yet these things still attempt to differ from one another in some manner; for one of the elements contributes one thing and another another, and still more the parts, and most of all the forms; whereas the simply many do not wish to bring in many differences; for then they would be many differing things, and not simply many; but they are nothing else than only many. Wherefore, whatever of them one may take — even if all together — he will see nothing other than many; for theirs is neither the other-and-other, nor the together, nor the all; for these are differences, and differing properties; but only many, and only multitude — a multitude, however, that is not its own, nor by itself; for neither are the elements, nor the parts, nor the many forms, themselves of themselves; for no multitude is self-constituting, but is always multiplied about some one — either a monad, or a whole, or a mixed; just so the simply many, too, are multiplied about the simply one; and the multiplication is of the one, as the partition is of the whole — being, as it were, an affection of it, and a procession within itself, and constituting its all-complete nature; whence also whatever is taken is straightway many; and the many are everywhere together with the one.

And perhaps this is the unlimited multitude hymned in the Parmenides — unlimited for this reason: that it has no limit which is not multitude, but is everywhere many — even without the everywhere; rather, many-where; and not even the many-where as some other thing, by relation, but the many only. And perhaps this is the One Many, from which the negations of the first hypothesis begin — that which also first rules all the determinations that are in any way differentiated; whence it is also called One Many, as having gathered up, according to its own many, the all-bearing cause of the things that proceed from it according to any partition whatsoever; whence the Chaldaeans celebrate it as fount of founts; and Orpheus, as mixed, bearing the seed of the gods; and the Phoenicians, as cosmic Aiōn — as having gathered all things in itself.

But these titles we are accustomed to apply to the limit of the intelligibles; and the intelligible is one and being, the both-together; whereas this is One Many, and not One Being. And Plato showed the One Being to be unlimited multitude — but not the One alone. Yet the argument seeks, nevertheless, also this One Many, simply so called, and not One Being. For the one that has been determined off from substance, and rides upon substance, is itself also a unitary substance — as life is double, the one unitary, the other being-differentiated; and intellect is double, the one a henad, the other a substantial form. But the simply one — where would it be — that which is principle of the double processions, both of the unitary ones and of those called, in whatever way, substantial? Perhaps what we call One Being, and unified, as being before both, would itself be the simply one; for it too was one, in greater measure; or rather the simple one, even if it is before both; for the counter-divided members are neither being nor one; yet it is one in another manner — the manner before the division and the counter-division; and indeed simply, because it is not substance, nor life, nor intellect. And how could it still be the limit of the unified? For that is not simply unified which is not first unified; and if it is something unified, it will also be something one — if indeed it is one according to the before-both, which was the unified. In general, the argument seeks a simply one, which is only one, and not one-being; for the simply intellect is the first intellect, and the simple life the first life, and the simply substance the first substance. The first henad, then, must also be not the substantial one — for neither the vital, nor the intellectual — but the simply henad: qua henad only, and not some particular thing's one.

But perhaps the third element of the intelligible must be ranked within the intelligible, and must be made its limit; and between this and the unitary substance one must take the simply One, according to the first and simply god — if, as they say, one and god are the same — since the things before this it is not right even to call gods; and this is the One Many; whereas the unified, even though before both, was shown by the Parmenides to be One Being Many, and in this way unlimited multitude — because the differentiated belongs to the One Being. But to call this latter One Many is now in another manner: as the principle contains the things that come from the principle, and as the monad is called number; for it is through this that the procession thence takes place according to determination — because the simply One is many; and this was the source from which each of the things that proceed, according to the multitude wound up together within itself, begets from itself the multitude without. Either, then, one must in this way posit the simply one as proceeding from the particular unified — as the simply substance from the substantial henad; or that One Being must be made — if it be lawful so to speak — double-faced; for it is hymned both as limit of the intelligibles, and as fount of the intellectuals; so that, insofar as it is fount of the things proceeding after it, it is One Many, by its relation toward what comes after it — loosening the gathering of both into the subsistence of the simply one; but insofar as it is limit of the intelligible, in this respect it is something unified, and One Being — many not simply, but One Many simply. And one might adduce, for either hypothesis, testimonies from the theologies: from the Chaldaean and the Orphic, confirming the second; and from the Egyptian, and that of the Phoenicians, the former. The truth of the matter the gods themselves would know; for us, let the perplexities concerning these things stand thus far; for perhaps hereafter we shall make some inquiry into them as well.

Perhaps, then, the simply one — which is all things as one, both the unitary and the substantial — is before the unified; and the simply unified comes after it, riding upon the simply being and the simply substance, in which is gathered up every substance, both the one called unitary and the substantial one counter-divided against it — as in either of these there is some substance, the one unitary, the other substantial; whereas that simply substance is before the determination, holding in the same both the unitary and what is called substantial; wherefore one must suppose the simply substance itself, after which the particular substance is determined — here called unitary, there substantial; or better to call this latter unified, and mixed, as being what is truly opposed to the unitary; and if this should prevail, all things will be in harmony with one another — both the conclusions of the arguments, and the doctrine of the theologians; and of these matters there shall be speech a little later as well. But let us run back up to the question from the beginning: the multitude of the doubly-determined substance is either elements, or parts, or forms — to speak more commonly, of substance either unitary or unified; whereas of the substance before both — the unified and one and simply substance — there are the simply many: what Plato calls the unlimited, and artlessly undetermined, multitude — since no otherness has yet shone forth. How then are they many, if they have nowhere stood apart?
