Or rather: as the one is There according to the unified, so also the many — being, as it were, an outpouring, and as it were a relaxation, of the unified; such are the many of the unified that is before both. And if these belong to the unified, and not to the one, one must know that what is before the simply being also — the simply one according to the both-together — has the simply many; for the first principle is the many of the simply one — as it is called the Power of the Father. Simply one, then, is the prior of the two principles; simply many, the second; and the simply substance third, according to the undetermined substance; and below there sprouts off the double file of henads and of substances; and the differentiation of the many — in truth, however it may come about — begins from the otherness that has shone forth, the many being differentiated whether as elements, or as parts, or as forms. In the unified, before these, there is multitude — but, as in the unified, the one and the multitude have run together into the same. For as the one did not stand apart from being, so neither was the multitude differentiated into many; but it remained bound together with the one in the unified nature — which would be called neither one nor many, but only the both-together, as unified before both. Yet nevertheless we lead even these up from the things below, by analogy — these not being There, but being, as it were, unknowns analogous to these knowns; wherefore we call the summit of the unified mixed, and constituted from elements; the middle, whole, and from parts; and the third, a monad, and eidetic number together with the monad; and, speaking generally, the third intellect, the second life, and the first Being — from the things differentiated below indicating the wholly-complete and entire subsistence of the undifferentiated.

parts.name: Chapter 90 — Does the Unified Itself Proceed? Like Working Darkness into Light; the Gods and the Theologians Have Hymned Intelligible Triads; Athena from Athena, Athena from Zeus — Every God a Summit · pp. 272–277

lines.text: Chapter 90 — Does the Unified Itself Proceed? Like Working Darkness into Light; the Gods and the Theologians Have Hymned Intelligible Triads; Athena from Athena, Athena from Zeus — Every God a Summit · pp. 272–277

These things, then, having been thus determined for us beforehand, come, let us set in motion the discourse concerning procession — inquiring whether the unified proceeds, whether in itself or from itself; as we do seem to say that there is in it a summit, and a middle, and a last: the one as it were substance, the other as it were life, the other as it were intellect — or however else one might carry the metaphor of the names upward from below. For one might reasonably raise difficulties, turning to either side. If it is so unified as to subsist immediately after the One, and about the One — wherefore not even into one and being did any determination arise in it — what device could implant in it any differentiation whatsoever? The first of all differentiations, as it seems, is that of the one and being, since the connate growth and union of these is the first of unions; the rest are differentiated upon it, either according to the one — as the unitary number — or according to being — as the substantial. There must first appear, then, an otherness of the two monads, in order that the numbers too may be divided along with their proper monads; but where the monad is one before the two — or rather not even a monad, if the monad is determined relative to its proper number — but one nature, whole through whole unified and undifferentiated: what differentiation could there be here, into first and middle and last? It is like working darkness into the light, and a moving thing into the unmoved which is only unmoved, and the temporal into the eternal — to work any differentiation whatever into the first undifferentiated and unified. Further: if the differentiated is after the unified, and the being-differentiated proceeds from the undifferentiated and after it, then neither of the things that come from it would be within it; but first and middle and last are constituted either in the having-been-differentiated or in the being-differentiated; neither, then, would these justly be There — I forbear to say that beginning and middle and end show themselves many removes down from that order, in the limit of the differentiating nature, as the Parmenides has it — before which pre-exists the subsistence of the whole and the parts, and elder than this it declares number. But if number is not yet There, in the unified, neither is a triad; and if no triad, neither these three: first, and middle, and last.

But assuredly the gods, and the theologians, have hymned to us intelligible triads, and processions of divine principles, proceeding from the one principle of wholes. And further, the argument itself demands besides that There also some procession arise — even if, as far as may be, a unified one. For first: if you shall say that that nature is unified, being after the One — then, since it happens to be also with the many, it must somehow be multiplied as well. And if the one holds the procession back, the multitude rouses it up, and works it out. And if it is one being — because before substance and one, and because it is before either life, the unitary and the substantial, and likewise before either intellect — then the both-together intellect, a unified intellect, and a unified life, as also a unified substance: where would these be, if not in the unified all-world-order? Triply, then, even That has been world-ordered. But indeed from it proceed substance and life and intellect — this multitude coming to be outward; and surely it did not bring forth the different things according to the whole of itself. For the outer multitude is by nature begotten according to the inner — whether by cause or by existence, whether differentiated or unified. For let the inner multitude be unified — yet answering by analogy to the differentiated; for even if one should say that the many come from the one, and yet that in the one there are no many — one must know that the many of the one are, if it be lawful so to speak, the inner multitude. And if not this, yet that at least is easy to concede: that in the middle of the one, and of the multitude determined in whatever way, there must be the unified and still undifferentiated multitude. Such are the difficulties one might raise, on both sides, about the inner multitude in the intelligible.

And likewise might one raise difficulties about the outer. For either the produced multitude is like-formed to its producer — as from the one unified, many unified things: as intellects from intellect, and souls from soul; or unlike-formed — as soul from intellect, or intellect from life, or life from substance; and so, then, from the unified: substance and life and intellect. But if the latter, the unified does not itself proceed, nor does that nature suffer the procession; rather, other things proceed from it; for from the One also come the many, and the sayable things from the Unsayable; yet the nature of the One does not go forth and become many, nor does that of the Unsayable become sayable. But if the former, what differentiation could there be of the unified nature? It is like saying that the many proceed from the one like-formedly; such, too, is it to say the differentiated from the unified. And for whose sake, indeed, would it proceed unlike-formedly? For if the same form is preserved, so to speak, the end of the subsistence will be the same for firsts and middles and lasts; for perhaps it does not even proceed at all by the mere lowering of the same property — unless some difference also be added, varying the proceeding things somehow in form; for neither has it any good, that the same should be lowered, unvaryingly, in many places; nor is it possible for the same to be differentiated from itself — for why should it, if no difference and otherness be added? For not even in the case of the individuals, which differ in number only, is it easy to accept that the procession into them comes about without some form-making difference — much less in the case of commons and propers. Therefore every star, and every animal, is a common form, and is varied in form. But if the procession is such that the proceeding things have at once both something common and something proper — as man and horse are each both animal and varied — how, from the animal, which is undifferent, does the different proceed? And how is what is by nature undifferent cut into many animals — and that, the like-formed side of the procession? And still more impassable is the argument when said of the unified; for this property is destructive of all differentiation, like-formed and unlike-formed alike; so that by it is destroyed also the inner multitude that was said to be differentiated. For intellect, being a form, can perhaps be differentiated into many forms, and the whole into many parts, and the mixed into elements; but the unified — how could it be differentiated into the procession within itself? Not unlike-formedly; for whence, in the like and the same — and, to speak more greatly, the unified — nature, should come the variation by form, or by properties? In what way, then, varied? Nor yet like-formedly; for the unified wishes to be nothing other than only what it is called — unified; so that, insofar as it is begotten, it would not be differentiated; it is not, then, differentiated like-formedly. And if also inward, according to the both-together — as unified life from unified substance — both absurdities will follow at once, just as each followed severally upon the like-formed and the unlike-formed procession.

And in general this very thing too must now, perhaps, be sought: whether the procession is double, as the philosophers say — the one like-formed, as Athena from Athena; the other unlike-formed, as Athena from Zeus — or whether one nature of all procession proceeds according to the both-together. For neither would the proper proceed without something common — nor would it even subsist; nor does the common proceed, undifferent, without the proper. For Athena from Athena: a second from a first, a more partial from a more whole-like, a heavenly from a super-heavenly, as it may chance; nor do these alone vary her in form, but also a certain Athenaic peculiarity of manner, according to which every Athena is first according to her own proper nature — seeing that even of the human souls each is varied in form from every other; much more greatly, then, will the many Athenas differ from one another in form: since every god is a summit, according to his own nature. Thus the procession called like-formed shows itself to be also unlike-formed. But again, Athena from Zeus: god from god, and intellect from intellect, and demiurgic from demiurgic, and intellect-making, as it may chance, from intellect-making;
so that, being unlike-formed, it is by nature also like-formed.

Perhaps, then, everywhere every procession always comes to be as the both-together — unless it should appear that here the like dominates, and there the unlike. But this very thing too must be sought: why is the one like-formed, and the other unlike-formed — whether apart, or the both-together? For perhaps all are like-formed; or all unlike-formed. I mean this: from Zeus, we say, proceed both Zeus and Athena, and another and another — and the many would not have been begotten from one, unless the one were all of them; for always the more whole-like gathers up the more partial in itself, as the animal the many animals — man and horse and ox; for these very things the animal was, all together; and the forms that went forth apart from one another are all forms of the animal. And if Zeus from Zeus is like-formed, still he proceeds not in like manner with the others. If one attends to the names, one might well be perplexed, seeing the two processions counter-divided; but if one should consider that the partial Zeus — the second, and the third, that has proceeded — is not the same in form with the prior (for the one was all the proceeded, while the other is one of the proceeded), he will see that every procession — even the one in which all come from one — is a partition of the existence of the whole Zeus; so that each is a part of the producer, and synonymous with him: with the whole, as whole, none is the same; according to the part, in respect of which he proceeds, every one is. And if the whole produces, and the produced are not, taken as wholes, the same form — Zeus whole, and the part of Zeus, such as the second Zeus, and Athena — it is clear, again, that all are begotten unlike-formed, and other from other in form; and the communion with Zeus reaches as far as the name. And besides: even if there is a difference of the processions, what is the cause of the difference? Why, from the same, is the one like-formed and the other unlike-formed? What is the allotment of this begetting, or of that? Is it that the like-formed is accomplished according to the partition of his own proper existence, while the unlike-formed is accomplished according to the pre-taken cause of the alien one? Or rather, first: the cause is an existence of the nature that has pre-taken it — for instance, the cause of Athena, in Zeus, is something elder belonging to Zeus; either it is con-substanced with Zeus himself — and Zeus would not be without it, which is the more reverent and the truer thing to say — so that the unlike-formed procession also is accomplished according to a partition of the existence; and second: the partition of the existence will be present within Zeus, the more partial things having proceeded from him — as, for instance, the like-formed chain from him, the one called Dian; and the chain begotten from him is surely not in him according to existence, but according to cause, relative to the chain produced; and according to existence, relative to the producer of the chain. And indeed this too deserves attention: perhaps the same thing must be called the existence of one thing, and the cause of another; and there is no need to double the nature of each thing into its own so-called existence and the pre-taking of the cause of the seconds. And the same we shall say about participation: insofar as the animal in man is from elsewhere, in this respect it is participation; insofar as it fills out the man, in this respect it is an existence of the man.

Chapter 91 — How from One Come Many? The Containing Cosmoi; from Being or from Not-Being; the All-Bearing Simplicity; the Second Principle — Paternal Power, a Loosing and Unlimitedness of the One · pp. 277–282

Still higher up, one might reasonably inquire how from one thing many proceed. Why does not, from one, only one proceed? And why do the many not come from many? As it is, we say the many gods are from Zeus; but perhaps the many proceed from the things already many contained in him — whether one should wish to say according to existence, or according to cause, or even according to participation; so that many come from many. What then would proceed from one — a whole from a whole? For the produced is always more partial than the producer. Or rather: in the production called like-formed, the whole chain has proceeded all together, as from one — the whole; and in the unlike-formed, the whole chorus of the begotten, all together, as one entire, has proceeded from one — the whole. And perhaps one might say that the whole Demiurge proceeded from the whole Kronos — as one entire cosmos from one entire cosmos: the demiurgic from the titanic. Is then Zeus of equal standing with Kronos — the contained cosmos with the containing? And surely, among the bodily enclosures, the container exceeds the contained; so that it will be analogous among the bodiless: the Kronian will contain the Dian, and the Ouranian the Kronian, and the Nyktian this, and this again the simply one cosmos, world-ordered before all. Not even in this way, then, does a whole truly proceed from a whole; for Kronos would contain not the Demiurge only, but the excess as well; so that even such a procession is according to part; so that every productive cause partitions the procession from the many within her; and thus we shall be compelled, everywhere, to set the inner multitude above the outer. Since, then, all things depend from one, even this one — which we call the simply one — will have multitude in itself; for otherwise the many would not have proceeded from it; and the argument is persuaded of the unlimited.

And further, according to another manner of perplexity — something both ancient and newer: either the procession is from being — and how could that proceed which already is, and is before? — or from not-being — and what among beings could come to be from what in no way is? For there is no matter There, that from its in-potency the in-actuality might proceed; and yet nothing would be begotten in actuality from the in-potency; for the former is better than the latter, and the begotten is always needier than the begetter. Neither, then, could anything proceed from being — that which already is — nor from not-being: neither in potency, nor in actuality. Thus we say that life proceeds from substance, and intellect from life, and soul from intellect, and every bodiform form from soul. Then the seconds will be in the firsts — or they will not be, in actuality; and the latter will make the procession impossible, while the former will make it, besides, superfluous. And if one should say that they are there according to cause — we ask what ever the according-to-cause is: is it that the proceeded is the same with the producer? In form, or in number? In number is impossible; for the caused, as we say, is one thing, and the cause another; nor yet in form; for the form is everywhere one, and first; since not even this man here is the same in form with that one There: the one is an image, the other the paradigm; and the one is in matter, the other in intellect; wherefore the one in soul is a mean, other than either of the extremes. But if the same neither in form nor in number, then the cause of the begotten, in the begetter, would be nothing other than the begetter itself. And again: why is one thing the cause of another? It is like saying that not-being is the cause of being; for the begetter is itself also other than the begotten; how then is other generative of other — whether of itself, or according to another within itself? And the argument will infer an absurdity also for the things that have proceeded into matter from intellect. For nothing must be first growing up in matter; all must come from There; neither, then, is the iconic first in matter, nor the generated, nor the enmattered, nor what is dis-tended in this way and swollen; for these too are forms, differing from their opposites; neither, then, do these proceed from There — for they do not pre-exist There; and what pre-exists There cannot proceed into matter — such as the eternal and ungenerated things.

And apart from these things: from the unified, we say, the differentiated has proceeded; but these come to be according to union and differentiation — the unified, and the differentiated; and union and differentiation are shone forth together; and, universally, the opposites by one procession — the differentiated members in the differentiated. But where union is, there is the unified; and where differentiation, there what has suffered it, the differentiated; in the differentiated, then, is each of the two — both the unified and the differentiated; not, then, before the differentiated is that unified from which the differentiated proceeds. And if union is in the unified, and where she is, there is also differentiation — then the differentiated also will be in the unified. And it is still worth inquiry, what it is that has made the differentiated, instead of the unified, and after it; for how could the unified be a cause of differentiation? It is like making the contrary generative of the contrary. And if the descent differentiated, what is it that has made the descent itself? For surely not, in turn, did the excess make the descent.

And the manner of the perplexity is the same which is accustomed to be rehearsed, again and again, about the one and the many: how from one are many begotten? It is like saying that the cold proceeds from the hot. Shall we then say to this what the philosophers say — that the proceeding becomes needier than the producer; insofar, then, as the begotten steps out of the one, so far it is not one; so that it is many, of necessity? But first: the needier does not vary the form, nor the nature, of the thing; for the higher beautiful is beautiful, and the lowered also — yet each of the two is beautiful; so that each is also one, even if the one produces and the other is produced. There is, then, also a proper procession of the one — as of one proceeding into one. Second: the many will have proceeded only by accident — if it is not insofar as it is many that it is begotten, but, insofar as it is begotten, it is many. And third, the perplexity remains: why is the generation from the contrary to the contrary? Perhaps, then, it is better to say that the One is not only one, as the name shows forth, but all things, according to the one simplicity that is before all — as we say many times; wherefore it is cause of all things according to this its all-bearing simplicity: not insofar as it is one as set against the many — for it pre-exists all antithesis — but insofar as it is principle of all things, and all things; and as principle of all it so produces the things after itself: all things, as being alone; and the many, as being one; and the beings, as being supersubstantial — and yet being also the beings. For in what does it differ, that the demiurgic intellect, having pre-taken all things in himself paradigmatically, produces all things from himself iconically — and that the one principle of wholes, being simply all the things that come from her, before the things that come from her, undifferentiatedly and according to one unmultiplied nature, produces all the many from herself? The perplexity was: how, from one, the many? But now, from the principle of all, all things have shown themselves forth — because the principle also was all things, before all things.

And if the things that have proceeded are also the one that is out of all, and all things not according to the multitude of the all, one must well know that the principle also is double: the one according to the simply One that is hymned; the other according to the all — if indeed we say that she is as before all. And this latter we have long been celebrating as the many of the One — as it were its unlimited power, according to which, or together with which, That is all things, and generative of all; wherefore this principle is invoked, even by the gods, as Paternal Power. And since the first principles have grown together — and in such wise that the second is in the prior, and has proceeded from her, in her — for this reason, of the things that proceed from thence, each one, both severally and all together, is one and many at once; and the many are from the one, in the one — having proceeded, and being everywhere second to the one. Shall we then say that even in matter, after the one, are its many — and that the last of all things is not the one, but the many? As then the many will also be before all things, and the one in this way second? Or rather: the many are everywhere in the one, as things encircled by the one as by a circle; so that the one is everywhere first, and last. This, then, by a digression of the argument, stands so. But as to the original question: the many are produced by the one, because this one is called one as being simple — since it is also many, and the all, and yet greater than the all, insofar as it is one; while the many, and the all, are the second principle — being a loosing, and an unlimitedness, of the one: she who is generative of all. To seek, then, how the one produces, is the part of those ignorant of the simplicity of the one; for not yet There have existence and power and activity been counter-divided, but all is only according to the one; while the second principle first shows from beneath the generative, and what makes for the unlimited toward multitude, and the power unfolding outside the one; wherefore she has been deemed worthy of the second names; and there is nothing perplexing in the many proceeding from her — she being many, and the simply many that is before all. And we shall make the same defense also on behalf of the unified; for this is at once also multiplied; so that, being all things according to the unified, it is fittingly generative of all things, as a unified principle of all. But how were the things from her differentiated — she being unified? How, from the one, were the many differentiated? For this was the perplexity from the beginning. Or rather: the principle, being all things, was also procession, and descent, and differentiation; for each of these too is one of the all. As, then, she produces substance and life and intellect, so to speak, so together with these she co-begets the descent, and the differentiation, and the procession, and all that holds of otherness; for otherness too is differentiated together with the others; so also differentiation with the things differentiated, and procession with the things proceeding, and descent with the things descending. Not by accident, then, does anything go forth into differentiation: the generating cause both differentiates, and co-produces the differentiation itself.

parts.name: Chapter 92 — The Hierarchy of Unions: the One Form in Which All Forms Are Gathered; the Most Proper Union of the One Being, Exceptionally Hymned as the Unified; Trans-Thinking the One Summit of All Concepts · pp. 282–283

lines.text: Chapter 92 — The Hierarchy of Unions: the One Form in Which All Forms Are Gathered; the Most Proper Union of the One Being, Exceptionally Hymned as the Unified; Trans-Thinking the One Summit of All Concepts · pp. 282–283

Toward the second from the end we shall say: there is the union of the same rank as differentiation — and things of the same rank are together; and there is the union which is the one com-paction of the same matter of the antithesis, as with dyads; and elder than this, again, is the union that gathers together all such unions, or monads — being itself a monad of all the monads, and of the whole single-form number itself: being the one form, in which all the forms are gathered up. And before this one must conceive the union of the whole simply, in which the simply parts are embraced; and before this, again, the union of the elementated — being a gathering of all the elements, being the unified substance, as con-being with this union: the unitary; of which we have shown one union before both, the most proper, that of the One Being — which we exceptionally hymn as the Unified. In this, then, are all things; so that even differentiation is in it according to union, like the rest; and from this proceeds the being-differentiated, and upon this the differentiated. Whence, then, did it become unified, if not through union — as differentiated through differentiation? But these two are shone forth together. Or does it subsist by dominance — above, union; below, differentiation? Then above there is also the differentiation; so that even That is differentiated, though in lesser measure. And indeed, where the one of two opposites rules, there is also the other: where sameness, there also otherness; and where rest, there also motion; for the two are shone forth together. There is, then, another signified sense of that union, and of that differentiation — these too being opposed in a manner, yet not as things of the same rank, but as cause and caused. Or better to say: all things we conceive and name as determined — union and differentiation along with the rest — and from these we give indication also concerning the undetermined. We do not, then, give the unified its form according to union, nor the whole differentiated according to the part-wise differentiation; for intellect is unified and differentiated at once; and what, within intellect, part is to part, this the whole intellect is — as differentiated — toward substance as unified; or, to speak more properly, toward the both-together, one and being, the unified before both. We make use of the names of the determined things — whether by themselves, or according to interweaving — wishing to indicate something concerning the wholly undetermined: of which we have neither an articulated concept nor a name, because of the great partition of our thinking; for we must gather all our concepts together into one, and trans-think the one summit of all concepts, if we are ever to lay hold of some trace of that gathered nature.

Chapter 93 — Images and Paradigms: First as Such Here, as Forms Last of All; the Impartible Swollen; Being from Being and Not-Being from Not-Being; Dionysus from Zeus — All Things Numbered from the One, the Unlimited from the Second · pp. 283–287

And indeed, toward the third of the aporiai, this one thing must first be determined, concerning the images and the paradigms: the argument which says that the genera must pre-exist in the ungenerated things requires that all the forms, and the properties, begin from intellect and the eternals; then proceed into soul, and the middle substance; then also into matter, at the last; for the enmattered are not self-sufficient, nor first, nor truthful in their eidetic existence — being, as they are, con-kneaded with not-being and with the formless; not, however, that the first things are con-kneaded and enmattered, but only that the con-kneaded are not the first forms; so that the swollen, too, and the dis-stanced, insofar as they are forms, have those pre-existing, and those first; but as generated, and enmattered — and such as we see them to be — they are first, and alone, as such, here; while as forms — which they are said to be — they are last of all things. Who, then, will claim that, even as last, these forms are first? Rather, as forms only, they shone forth first There; and the opposites rule equally There — sameness and otherness, motion and rest, one and many; all the antitheses alike — but in the one place ungeneratedly, all of them, and eternally, which is the same as to say impartibly; and in the other, generatedly and temporally, which is the same as to say partibly. And the partible and the impartible would not be said as certain forms; for each of the two would be at home on either side; but in another manner: we name the whole from some part, not having a name significant of the commonness. For neither, when we call the all cosmos, do we call it this from the common nature that embraces all things, but from one property — its being ordered; for the chorus, too, is named from dancing only, and the army from campaigning; and man, from looking up at what he has seen; and horse, from rushing with its feet; for each thing, being one and many, has been called from one of the many that are within it. Is then the whole not a common name, as it is a common thing? Or rather, all names are such — even the whole: it has been named from what gathers the parts; for it is called holon because it is, as it were, in a heap and in plenty; what is seen massed together has been called whole. Thus, then, partible is the whole-and-all that is enmattered; and impartible the whole-and-all that is ungenerated — neither of the two according to the form, but according to the said manner of indication. Wherefore all the forms are both in intellect and in matter; and the same form is impartible and partible, insofar as they are forms; but here according to existence, and there according to participation; and here first, and there last; and yet these too — the first, I mean, and the last, and the existence and the participation — are as forms on either side.

Since, then, some are paradigms and others images — are these too forms, and on either side? And how could they not be? If indeed the image is a likeness, and the likeness an accomplishment of likeness; and likeness is on either side; and the paradigm is an archetype of likeness; and There one thing is likened to another, and here likewise; for Socrates, too, is a paradigm of his own image. The properties, then, are on either side; but if we call image that which is only image — such as the enmattered form — then the iconic would not be in intellect; and if paradigm that which is an ungenerated and eternal form, and what accords with the first existence — then the nature of paradigm would not be here. So then the swollen also, as a form There, is an impartible swollen; while here it is a swollen which is a form indeed, yet partible nevertheless — a swollen as partible. The property, accordingly, is common to either side; but the first and the last subsistence is proper to either side — that of the generated, and that of the ungenerated; that of the enmattered, and that of the immaterial; that of the temporal, and that of the eternal; and these not as the properties, but as begotten and begetter, and as existence and participation — and however one may be able to determine generation and substance: not as common properties, but as proper subsistences, being above, and proceeding to what is below.

This, then, I determine thus; and another point we shall determine in the same way, concerning everything produced and producing — as the whole other-moved cosmos proceeding from the self-moved, and the self-moved from the unmoved: all things that are in the first unmovedly, are in the second self-movedly, and in the third other-movedly; so that beings proceed from beings, and from things in activity; and nothing absurd follows; for the producer and the produced are not simply the same, nor in the same way, but thus the same, and thus not; for the other-moved beautiful is from the self-moved, and the self-moved from the unmoved; so that you might even say: being from being, and not-being from not-being. For there is a way in which it is the same, and a way in which it is not; and this holds for the procession that seems to be like-formed; for beautiful comes from beautiful. But if the beautiful also comes from the Good, or the other-moved itself from the self-moved, that comes from the unmoved as from what, in one way, is, and in another way is not: being according to cause, and not being according to existence; for by nature the one is cause, and the other caused — and this latter is pre-taken in that, in a certain manner which the argument will state as it goes forward. And likewise all things are in the unified, and all in the differentiated; and these proceed from those: beings from beings, in the one way of taking each, and not-beings, in the other way of taking each, varied; or, if you wish to say it so: beings from not-beings, and not-beings from beings. For in activity all things are in all; and again, in activity, nothing is anywhere: in this way nothing, in that way all things; and the perplexity has no place — neither the one that derives the in-activity from what is not in potency, nor the one that derives being from not-being; for nothing There has anything in potency, nor is it not-being in the way we mean when we raise the perplexity; but because the manner of the subsistence is other, in this respect it is not-being; and because things are by nature begotten, others out of others, in this respect in potency.

Further, then, to the fourth from the last: to those climbing up from the lasts of all things, it will appear easily dissolved, according to the like manner of method. For that many proceed from one is no wonder, if the one be generative of all things, or of many — whether according to its own all-bearing simplicity, or according to the multitude embraced within it in whatever manner. For all things were, as we said, even the one — not in potency, but in activity; yet not determined, like this cosmos, or any cosmos at all; nor unified, according to the unified; but one only — all things according to the one; and according to the unified, all things — but by undifferentiated union; and the differentiated is all things — but now in a certain determination. These things standing so, it makes no difference to say that many come from one — a one of such a kind, and so constituted — and that many, again, come from many: from the things subsisting according to the one, or standing together according to the unified, or standing apart according to the being-differentiated and the differentiated. And you could say this more clearly, if you should say that the second principle proceeds from the first, as one-many from one; and from her, the unified — at once also multiplied; and from this, little by little, the subsistence of the many, being differentiated off into multitude; so that nothing is wonderful: both that from one partless principle one whole multiplied order proceeds — as from the one cause all things together, even as one all-great cosmos — and that from many the many proceed: from the things subsisting according to one, the things not subsisting according to one. For the same thing — thus one, and thus many — one might both see and say.

Either, then, one proceeds from one — as Dionysus from Zeus; or many from one — as from Zeus the many gods; or one from many — as when the soul is said to proceed from all the things before her, and always the begotten from all the elder causes; or many from many — as we say the sensibles from the intelligibles. But nevertheless each of the two is everywhere — the one and the multitude — even if in the one place the multitude is according to the one, and in the other the one according to the multitude; and surely each is also, by itself, both one and multitude. We shall not, then, go on to infinity, seeking always, before the many one, the unmultiplied one; for this very thing — the simply one — is cause of all the many; for, being one, it is nevertheless all things, because it is before all things; yet not some one of the all, nor one made out of all, but really one — and one in this way: as all things together, according to the very One. And the second principle is herself also all things — but according to her being the many; for she was the many of that one; since every multitude subsists about the one, as every power about its proper substance. As from many, then — the all — we go up to this principle; and as from one — of the all — to the One. And in what way is each of the two of all things? The one, as the all together; the many, as the all insofar as many. And perhaps: all things, as already numbered, proceed from the One; and many, as still unlimited and undetermined and not yet at their end, from the second principle. Let so much be said about this perplexity as well.

Chapter 94 — Whole Cosmoi from Whole Cosmoi — Nothing Sterile Remains Above; All Things Are, but Intelligibly, Says the Oracle; the Successors of the Paternal Kingships; Dionysus According to the Whole; the Sevenfold Demiurge, Twice-Beyond, Among the Chaldaeans · pp. 287–291

Toward the things said next in order, higher up than what has been discussed, we say this one thing before all: that if a cosmos proceeds from a cosmos, whole from whole — as the demiurgic from the titanic, or the titanic from the connective, or the intellectual from the intelligible — then the whole prior goes forth into the second, such as it proceeds, and nothing exalted remains above, in the prior; or else, on this showing, the remainder will be sterile, and wholly without procession; so that, in this manner at least, the former will not exceed the latter by being something There which is not also here. For the contrary supposition lies ready to hand: that something shines forth in the seconds which is not yet of a nature to be differentiated in the firsts. But neither is this true; for it is There too — gathered — the very thing that is being differentiated in this one; or else whence is it differentiated? And how do we say that all things are everywhere, even if differently and differently? And when we say that the things below are more than those above, we speak according to differentiation; since There the same things are gathered. How then do we say, elsewhere, that each shines forth according to its existence? Where each thing furnishes to all its timely activity, there, surely, it differentiates its proper nature from the others; and this is what is called the first existence of each — the existence of each, first differentiated off from the other properties. Or rather, this too is true; for not everywhere are all things in the same way, but here unified, there being-differentiated; yet all things are, nevertheless, in every cosmos — in the intelligible: for all things are, but intelligibly, says the Oracle; and in the sensible; and, plainly, in the means.

How then do we always say that the higher cosmos is more whole-like than the one beneath it — and that this is contained, while that contains — if there is no excess of that over this, all things being in either, and all things of necessity equal to all? Or rather: even if equal in multitude, the one can contain the other by magnitude — and the one, sometimes, the many; as the sphere of the fixed stars contains all the spheres that follow; and the Kronian will contain the Dian, even if it be equal to it in the multitude of its forms — by its embrace, and its aspect, and, as it were, by the majesty of its nature. And next one must consider this: that since the higher always give subsistence to, and beget, all the things after themselves, it will follow that more are begotten from those than from these; thus the intelligible cosmos produces all those after itself together — the intellectual, the hypercosmic, the encosmic; the intellectual, only the two; and the hypercosmic, one only, the sensible — or into however many more cosmoi one may cut the proceeding things. The intelligible, then, is most whole-like, because embracing of all; and the sensible — or at any rate the sublunar — most partial, because it is last, and contains only its own parts; while the middles, in proportion, both contain and are contained. And in the same way, upon each chain, one would see the fore-ranked member more whole-like, and the sub-ranked more partial.

Further, let us say another thing about the same matters: that if one should say the whole demiurgic cosmos proceeded from the titanic, the accounts just now stated about the cosmoi will fit; but if one should derive Zeus from Kronos, we know that Zeus is begotten from Kronos together with many others — both among the Greeks and among the barbarians; as Kronos, again, from Ouranos together with others; and again, from Zeus, Dionysus. And if some, dividing the whole father among themselves, each take him by parts, while others have proceeded single-form from the whole — wherefore these latter are established as successors of the paternal kingships — this in no way shatters the truth of the account. For Zeus — let us say — having brought forth from himself the many gods by parts, upon this whole-complete partition brought forth the partitive wholeness, and the many gods ranked beneath her. Or did not Zeus beget even the Titans, in his own world-order, according to the Orphic tradition? So too Kronos, after many a generation before, brings forth at the last the whole one who leads off the other kingship; and the like account is handed down of Ouranos: that he gives subsistence to Kronos last, after the other Ouranids; and for this reason one must say that the produced counter-exceed one another: those that are in the father, and beside the father, being nevertheless more partial; while those that step out of the paternal property — set beside the more common nature — are wholes, and keep, toward the things begotten from themselves, the analogy of their own begetters; for the seconds answer in proportion to the wholes; yet the second kings do not stand at an equal counter-position to the first. So much, then, from the accounts.

Further, upon these things, let us say this, toward the inquiries lying before us: that the begetter — Zeus, for instance — both produces one from himself, and produces also many; but each of the two either according to the whole, or according to something of those within him: by himself, as one; the many, again, all together, according to the so-many and so-many differentiated within him; and each severally, according to some one of those within him. Thus, then, one comes from one, because according to the many embraced in him; the chorus of the many, again, according to the differentiated whole plenitude of himself; and Dionysus according to the whole alone; so that at these things one would not reasonably wonder; for from one comes one — both the whole according to the whole, and each part according to a part — and many from one, but as from one multiplied: the chorus, according to the whole; and the several many, according to the several many within him. But how is the one procession like-formed, and the other unlike-formed? Because Zeus, according to his own property, produces a certain like-formed chain; while according to the cause pre-taken within him, he produces Dionysus, and the other hetero-named gods.

What then — does he not beget Dionysus according to the whole of himself, and the many gods according to his own parts? But both the whole and the parts, at once, are his; why then is not the procession of both like-formed — as having come to be according to the existence, and, through this, synonymous? Yet it is not; for the many gods are not Zeuses; nor is Dionysus these things, though he is one. And what, indeed, is the existence according to which the chain proceeds from Zeus synonymously? Not according to the whole; for it stands counter-divided against the chains proceeding from his other parts; nor according to all the parts together, through the same cause; and if it too proceeds according to some one of the things contained in him, how does it alone share the name with the whole? And the perplexity would be interwoven fourfold. For if the produced be produced according to the whole: sometimes it is synonymous with the producer — as the sevenfold-proceeding whole Demiurge among the Chaldaeans; for each of them is hymned as twice-beyond, and has gathered up in himself all things, the very things the first also has, even if he is more partial by the descent of his rank; and sometimes it is hetero-named, like Dionysus. Or if it be produced according to some part: again, sometimes the production is synonymous — as the chain, if so it chance, of Zeus, from the whole Zeus; and sometimes hetero-named — Athena, from Zeus.

Chapter 95 — The Double Partition of the Producer, by Depth and by Breadth; the Heliac, Apolloniac, and Asclepiac Founts; the Aphrodisian Intellect and the Intellect of Dikē; the Elders of the Perplexities — Existence and Cause · pp. 291–293

Perhaps, then, the partition of each producer is double — and that of the things produced: the one by depth, belonging to the whole chain that flows off according to descent; the other by breadth, belonging to the forms contained within it, or to its unlike-parted parts. For the partition pre-taken in it by depth is like-parted, wherefore also synonymous; while the other is unlike-formed, whence the generation according to it is hetero-named. For the first and the second Zeus proceed from the all-complete one according to the whole of him — wherefore each shares his name; while the fount that is set over divinations proceeds according to some one of the unlike parts. And likewise each of the so-called partial founts, of which each leads off a proper like-formed chain, through the like-parted partition, by depth, in its turn. And if, within some one of these, there should be contained some unlike-parted fount by breadth — as in the heliac fount the Apolloniac, and in this the Asclepiac — assuredly the begetting of these also is unlike-formed.

And in the philosophic manner: from the simply intellect proceeds the like-formed begetting by depth, everywhere co-introducing the whole embrace of the forms by breadth. But if intellect produces soul, or nature, or body, it will produce unlike-formedly — according to something of what is contained within it. So that even if it produce according to the beautiful, or the good, or the just, even so the procession is unlike-formed. What then is the begotten beautiful, or just? Either an intellect, or a soul; or in one of these; or in each. Why then are soul, and intellect, and body, each a thing by itself, and each self-complete, while the beautiful, and the just, and each of the genera, are not such? For what is the allotment? And why did matter go forth to meet all the forms, and received all — while each of the others did not receive all? Or rather, first: the simpler of the forms — those holding the rank of elements — having grown together with one another always, refuse the separated subsistence by themselves; for they have their nature, unified with one another, more complete than the dis-stance that has been differentiated into self-completeness. And second: the beautiful, and rest, and motion, made their procession simply into all things; the beautiful, for instance, has made room for itself in every form; wherefore it has also gone forth along every procession.

And third: the simply intellect, according to each form of those contained within it, begets first an intellect, then a soul, then also a certain enmattered nature, given its form by that very form according to which it proceeds — so that one might say: by the beautiful, the aphrodisian intellect; by the just, the intellect of Dikē; by the good, the intellect of the good daimon, so to speak; and according to another of the forms, another intellect, standing there. For perhaps the whole depth is partitioned, and the whole breadth — varied by the dominance, in each case, of ever some one form; and one must suppose that the breadth, too, has its proper order: a first within it, and a middle, and a last, being differentiated — namely, the genera; then the more whole-like forms that come from these; then the more partial, down to the most partial — which, for all their great composition, seem to be self-complete, and to subsist upon themselves; and these, again, are deepened in yet another manner; for after the intellectual subsistence comes the psychic, and after this the nature-like; whence this procession also is unlike-formed, because it belongs to breadth — and to its procession — the breadth itself being deepened into the begetting of the lower unlike-formed things. But these matters, perhaps, exceed the measure.

And perhaps, having gone round a great circuit, we have accomplished nothing; for we seem to be saying again the thesis from the beginning: that some things proceed according to the existence, like-formedly; and others according to the pre-taken cause, unlike-formedly. What, then, is the cause? And how is another nature pre-taken in another? For why is the existence of one thing not the cause of another? For we have now come to the very elders of the perplexities. And I say, first, that the existence of the begetter is one thing, and the cause of the begotten another — above all, of the unlike-formed. For if what the in-potency is, in the world below, beside the existence — as Aristotle showed clearly — then assuredly the according-to-cause, also, is something other beside the existence. Further: if there is only the existence of the begetter, and it begets from itself and by itself, how will it ever beget anything unlike-formed, when nothing else is mixed within it beside itself? For begetting by its very being, it will give subsistence to the begotten by transmission of its proper nature; there must, then, be pre-taken some cause, also, of the unlike-formed — according to which, being something else, it will beget something else. Further again: if simply other is generative of other, without any pre-taken cause, why does not any chance thing proceed from any chance thing — since each has some existence, the one, on this showing, without a cause?

lines.text: Chapter 96 — Cause as Existence Inclined toward Otherness; the Unfolding of the Producer's Gathering; the Twice-Beyond Demiurges; Whole and Partial Founts; All Drunk Down in the Summit of the Intelligible; No Paradigms of Individuals — the Light of the Sun; Each Thing Proceeds Remaining · pp. 293–303

These, then, are the considerations that persuaded the ancient philosophers to derive all the things produced from what pre-exists according to cause. But the argument is a strange one, if a man says that the cause is pre-taken, being in something whose existence it is not. For first: whence was this cause itself begotten? If from another cause, we shall go on to infinity; and if from the existence — how is the cause unlike-formed to it, and the cause of an unlike-formed offspring? Next: if it is by its being that a thing begets, and the being of each thing is its proper existence, plainly the unlike-formed also is begotten from the proper existence; so that what is called the cause was, after all, a part of the existence. And indeed the first of the earlier arguments serves well for the contrary conclusion: for the in-potency present in a thing is a part of its existence; since its form is said to be by nature toward another, and to be in potency — as the bronze is a statue in potency; for the bronze is by nature easily moulded, and the easily-moulded is, as it were, a part of the bronze's nature. But if existence and cause are the same, how is the one generation like-formed, and the other unlike-formed? Or rather: so much as proceeds according to the existence simply, like-formed; and so much as proceeds not simply, but according to the existence that has inclined toward the generation of another, unlike-formed? For perhaps the cause is nothing else than existence inclined toward otherness, and become, for this reason, other-making; while the existence that remains upon itself is same-making. And yet even the like-formed would not be begotten, if the simple existence should not incline; for it is as inclined that the begetter is cause of the begotten. What difference, then, is left to the cause — if every cause is an inclination of the begetter toward the begotten?

Perhaps, then, it is better to call existence threefold: the one according to the like-parted partition; another according to the unlike-parted partition; and another according to breadth. For all the things that proceed from it are embraced in the producer according to one gathering — which there is no necessity to posit as its existence. For as many things as each is, so many does it project from itself; and the things produced are, all of them, an unfolding of the producer's gathering — as every number is a forth-stepping of the monad; for it is in this way that we call the one whole-like, and the others more partial: all those that distribute among themselves, by parts, the embrace of the whole. For how is it not necessary that the simply animal embrace all the things that are animals — not only according to depth, such as the heavenly, the aerial, the watery, and the chthonic animal, but also according to breadth, such as man, and ox, and horse? So too the existence of intellect embraces not only the depth gathered within it, but also the many-formed breadth of the forms — just as in the Dian intellect, and in Zeus the god himself, all things are according to existence: both those that proceed whole-completely, according to the gathered depth — who go forth complete, and synonymous with the whole, as the twice-beyond demiurges among the theurgists — and those that proceed by part, distributing the whole's distribution, stepping out of the begetting nature, and becoming hetero-named toward her: begotten from her, indeed, but according to something of the things that fill out her existence, and not according to the whole of her. Thus the unlike-formed also proceeds from the existence — from the existence that has been divided, and according to some one of the things divided within it.

But the chain of Zeus — how does it proceed from Zeus, being one of the many founts that flow off from him? Or rather: every synonymy is produced from its producer taken as whole; and for this reason it is synonymous with the whole, even if it leans somewhat aside, through being more partial; for every Zeus is father of all the gods, even if it has proceeded rather according to some one of the gods within him. For the twice-beyond is everywhere whole; but if he too be called Zeus, then one also of the partial founts within him is a Zeus — as another is a Helios, and another an Athena; for the partial chain of each god flows off from some partial fount. Thus, if there should be a fount called the fount of Zeus, homonymous with the whole, she too will produce from herself a partial chain. Perhaps, however, the whole fount is not named Zeus, but the partial one alone — or else the reverse; and if the name is common, let it be homonymy; for the nature of either is different: the one belongs to the whole founts, and sends off from herself a fountal chain only; while the other belongs to the partial, and proceeds into archons and archangels, and into azonic gods and zones — as is the law of the procession of the partial founts that are hymned; for already, upon other founts, whole-like and partial, the homonymy has been observed — even if a certain kinship of nature also be seen, itself furnishing the homonymy — as in the case of the iynges, and the connectives, and the teletarchs, and the archic ones. For every archon flows off from a partial fount.

Therefore each archic fount also is said to flow off from the crown — as the archic soul and the archic virtue flow from the partial founts at the girdle. And in the same way Iamblichus counts a partial fount of the Implacables in among the partial founts, as the whole one among the wholes. What wonder, then, if one should posit a partial demiurgic fount, other than the whole one — and yet embracing of all — such as they make the fount that is set over divinations, from which a proper partial chain flows off; and should carry the name of Zeus upon either, and that of the Demiurge as well: but in the one place, as counter-divided against the telesiurgic, and the guarding, and the purifying, and the other partial properties of the partial founts; in the other, calling demiurgic the whole that is embracing of all the causes engaged about matter. Such, then, are the defenses I hold up on behalf of these things.

And this must be concluded from the whole of it: that the things partitioned in the procession from one are pre-taken, wholly, in the one, according to gathering: as each chain is in its proper partial fount, as in the only thing thoroughly numbered; and as the fountal chain — the whole chain of the hebdomad — is in the whole fount; nay, the entire number of the partial founts is in their proper whole fount; for the whole-complete partition of the many parts partitioned inwardly in each fount is pre-taken before the partial founts that subsist outwardly, about the whole founts. For the cosmos that lies about the parts answers in proportion to those parts of the divine figure which are ordered by it: the girdle answers to the girded flanks of the goddess; the crown, to the temples and the forehead of the divine head. And again, this partition of the parts according to breadth belongs to the goddess, and comes from the out-flowing hebdomad — a number pre-taken in the monad according to depth, united together in the impartible and whole; and indeed the whole hebdomad of the first founts is gathered up in the triads of the elder founts; and the triads, again, in the one fount of founts; so that every partition after her — whether fountal, or more partial still — is gathered in her, single-form. And if in her the many are gathered — from which both the many founts are divided off, and the other multitudes are differentiated elsewhere — then assuredly all is drunk down in the summit of the intelligible, and the very appearance of multitude by the union.

This, then, must be believed on the strength of what has been said; and this besides: that everywhere the outer multitude, differentiated in the things begotten, grows out from the multitude gathered inwardly in the begetters; so that, conversely also, it is true to say: if many are in the begetter, assuredly these pass over into what is proximately begotten; and again, if in the begotten many are differentiated outwardly, assuredly in the proximate begetter the many show themselves forth beforehand; and the cause is that the generative power pre-exists in the begetter, and that everything which is seen in the begotten is pre-sketched, in some manner, in the begetting cause — according to that cause's own existence and gathering. And third, following upon these: all the seconds are always pre-taken in their priors, and the more partial in the more whole-like — the like-formed having their pre-taking according to depth, and the unlike-formed according to breadth.

And fourth: all things are partitioned into their proper ranks and existences; yet none the less all things are in all — but properly in each: here undifferentiated, here being-differentiated, here differentiated; and of these, again: here as elements in the elementated, here as parts in a whole, here as forms — and a number of forms — in a monad. And the outer multitude proceeds in analogy with the inner: here as a number from a monad — the many intellects from the one intellect; here as parts from a whole — as the many lives from the one life; here as elements from the elementated — as from the one substance the many substances; wherefore these last have grown together with one another as far as may be, and are unified in a manner undifferentiated; while the lives are differentiated more, and stand toward one another as parts of a whole; and the numbers — the intellects — have been differentiated into self-complete circumscriptions; whence it is the more familiar thing, that there are many intellects after the one and from the one; while that there are many self-complete lives, before the intellects, is not so familiar; and substances least of all, because of their great and elemental union. Yet even if it is not evident, one must nevertheless of necessity agree that there are both many lives and many substances — if indeed substance is an elementated, and a mixed out of elements; while life subsists according to the being-differentiated, and is a whole, and out of parts; and intellect is a form out of forms. Each, then, is one and many; and every inner multitude, as has been said, is generative of the outer; there must accordingly proceed, after the one substance, the many substances — each given its form according to some one dominating element among the many; and after the one life, the many lives must flow off, each mastered by some other property among the parts; just as, after the one intellect, the many intellects have proceeded, each mastered by some other among the many forms; for always the inner multitude is generative of the outer. Or rather, it should be put thus: the whole begets also the whole — the second whole; and the parts, by themselves, beget the parts in the second; and the whole, according to each of its parts, begets a certain more partial whole. And so too with the elementated and the elements, and with the monad and the entire number: the monad begets the monadic one of each number, and the multitude in the monad begets the multitude everywhere; the monad, indeed, according to the number within herself, begets both the whole number at once, and each number severally — each given its form according to one form, having gathered up within itself a whole multitude proper to itself.

Further, then, let us gather this in addition: that all things are gathered in the priors — as many as are differentiated over and above in the laters; wherefore all things are both in the intelligible, and in the intellectual world-order, and in the middle one; nay, in each of the lower as far as the sensible — but properly in each: in all other respects, by however much one might mark off what is proper to each; and indeed also according to the more and the less; or rather, according to the peculiar manner, in each place, of the union and of the differentiation; since they will differ from one another also by the containing and the being contained. What then? Is the procession of the seconds from the firsts not a begetting, but a shining-forth only, and a differentiation — as we say — of things determined and gathered above? Or rather: we call differentiation that which sets each thing according to its own existence — an existence which previously was not its property; for it had not yet been differentiated into a property, within the whole gathering; it was, at any rate, an existence of another — of that which, according to it, existed whole-naturedly; so that it is the same thing to say that the seconds are differentiated from the priors, and that they are begotten from them.

Are then all things gathered up in what is before them — as many as are differentiated afterward? For on this showing even the individuals of the forms will be gathered There; for the differentiation brought these forth, too, from the firsts. But this is most absurd; for either the causes of the individuals will abandon even the gathering — when the individual no longer is, or when it is not yet; and there will be something not always, in the eternal; or else the cause will be there in vain, always, the things caused not being always; and it is for this reason that we do not even make paradigms of the individuals; so that neither must we make the pre-gatherings of such things. And yet these too are assuredly begotten from the priors — though not according to any necessity that the begotten be pre-gathered in the begetter. Or rather: those things that make by their very being, and project their proper offspring from their own substance — these are the things that have pre-taken the gatherings of their begotten; while all that mould the forms outwardly, by their outward-going activities — as in the case of the artefacts — these have no longer pre-taken them. And in this way the individuals of the forms also come to be — by the outwardly extended activities of the moving causes. Whence, then, does such form-giving proceed, if it moulds outwardly — and whence does it mould, if it has not pre-taken the moulding of the thing? Or rather: it gives form to its own activities, for the moulding; and there comes to be a pre-taking of the forms not in the substances, but in the activities that stand now thus, and now otherwise. And whence are the activities given their form? From the universally pre-taken forms come the individual activities that are deployed on each occasion — being changed, and moulded now in this way and now in that, and figured; and, to say it as a whole, being given form, they become the accomplishers of the individuals; and this is the pre-taking of the individuals: the pre-taking taken up in the participated activities — itself re-fashioned, as the activities stand now in one way, and now in another.

Either, then, these matters must be determined in this way; or — if some argument should compel us to hold that the unmoved also is cause of the things that are moved: for instance, that intellect is demiurge of the individuals that come to be and perish, and, in general, the first substance, and indeed the one principle of wholes (for what would not proceed from thence? and how should the principles that preside over all not be causes of all? and what, among the seconds, is not embraced by the firsts?) — if, then, a man should be persuaded of this, as I for my part am persuaded, what shall we say to the perplexity? That the unmoved cause has gathered up, in its own unmovedness, even these — and these in the common manner of the nature that begets these also forever, as of an ever-flowing nature: the cause is all-bearing, and simply subsistence-making, of all the things that are begotten to infinity. As, then, of all such things at once — and, to speak more plainly, of the individuals that are ever recurring — it has pre-taken one cause: not the proper cause of me, nor of you; and yet a cause of me also, and of you, and of those that once were before, and of those that shall be once again; in this way, then, the individuals are gathered in that cause; and in this way they are differentiated from it — as the light of the sun both remains eternal in its own commonness, and is portioned out individually to each, because it has one cause, illuminating, of all individual eyes. Let so much be said of this perplexity also.

But this also must be added to what has been determined: that everywhere the things in each place — whether gathered or differentiated — are existence; so that the Athena in Zeus is an existence of Zeus; while she who has leapt up from his summit is, surely, Athena herself; and again, the participation in another — such as the Athena in the Korē — is an existence of the Korē. And if the philosophers say that each thing is threefold — according to cause, as Athena somehow existing in Zeus; according to existence, as she who is by herself; according to participation, as she who has come to be in the Korē — they say well; except that all must be determined as existences: the one, of Zeus, because she fills out the differentiated existence of Zeus; the one, her own, by herself; and the one, of the Korē, because she too fills out the Korē's multitude. And one might see the same more dialectically: the so-called genera of Being everywhere fill out the subsistence woven together from its causes — but substance as unified, life as being-differentiated, and intellect as differentiated; and the simply intellect according to the equal-balanced differentiation, while the more partial intellect is always according to the differentiation that leans toward these or those — of the genera, or of the parts, or of the forms — according to dominance. And, more logically: the simply man is in animal, according to the whole-natured single existence of animal, embracing of all animals; but there is also, after animal, the existence of man by himself; and in the third place, in the land-dwelling man — and in me, the individual — the simply man is present as an element, as animal is in man; according to existence, then, this also. For even if it is given in from above — and in this respect is participation — yet the very seating of it, in that into which it is given, becomes a part of the existence. So much on these matters also.

Come then, let us return from the beginning to what adjoins the original perplexities. That even in the like-formed there is something unlike-formed, and in the unlike-formed something like-formed — as the perplexing argument insisted — must of necessity be agreed; but none the less the one procession is like-formed, and the other unlike-formed: insofar as every Aphrodite, and every Athena, remains somehow within the bounds of the first Athena and the first Aphrodite — even if each is varied in form, each being a more partial instance of the same property; according, then, to what is common and remains, the communion both of the name and of the partition persists; wherefore the whole chain of Hera proceeds as from one and toward one. But if Erōs should proceed from Aphrodite, or Athena from Zeus, the procession is unlike-formed — because Erōs has stepped out of the aphrodisian bounds, and Athena of the Dian; and yet assuredly Athena has something Dian, and Erōs something aphrodisian, insofar as they have something like-formed toward their producers; but this is preserved as one strain within differing bounds — just as, in the other case, the differing shows itself within common bounds.

Not, then, in this respect are Athena and Zeus like-formed — that both are gods, and intellects, and demiurges; for these common attributes attend even the like-formed ones, for instance the many Aphrodites; for the pandemic ones among them are demiurgic, and intellects, and all of them goddesses; and indeed Erōtes and Aphrodites are, in this way, of the same genus. The like-formed must not, then, be defined by the more common genera, but by the more proper existences — upon which the proper names also are observed. All Aphrodites, accordingly, are like-formed, with a certain otherness; while Erōtes and Aphrodites are unlike-formed, with a certain sameness. And there are also more generic namings, like-formed and unlike-formed: the latter, as substance from Henad, and life from substance, and intellect from life, and soul from intellect, and the bodiform from soul; and, in another manner, from the one the unified, and from this the being-differentiated, and from this the differentiated; and, as far as these, the unmoved; then the self-moved; then the other-moved; the former, as gods from god, and substances from substance, and lives from life, and intellects from intellect, and souls from soul — and, from the one natural animal, the many animals of its kind.

Which then of the two would be the elder — the like-formed, or the unlike-formed? If the like is begotten before the unlike; and if the intelligible gods proceed from the simple god before the intelligible substances, and the same account holds for the others in order; and if, further, the one procession gives subsistence to a descended cosmos — as the intellectual-and-intelligible from the intelligible-and-intellectual, and so on in order — while the other makes a cosmos in the same manner, as Kronos begets the titanic world-order itself, and begets the demiurgic as descended: if these things are true, it is plain that the like-formed is elder than the unlike-formed. But universally, someone might say, procession is a stepping-out from the producer; and every stepping-out carries the begotten down into the unlike-formed. This unlike-formed, however, is that which attends upon the like-formed; and perhaps one will concede this to be elder. Yet neither is this true; for even before this, the like-formed must be — that upon which the unlike-formed attends; for each thing proceeds remaining; and the remaining in the cause makes the likeness and the sameness toward it. Let the argument, then, be drawn up so far upon these matters.
