One Intellect and One Soul; from the Demiurge the Apollonian, Areic, and Athenaic Intellects — an Intellect of Man and of Horse; Lives as Monads Becoming Determined; Substances That All But Flee Back into the Undifferentiated · pp. 303–306

lines.text: Chapter 97 — Beyond These Inquiries: Does the Unified Proceed? One Intellect and One Soul; from the Demiurge the Apollonian, Areic, and Athenaic Intellects — an Intellect of Man and of Horse; Lives as Monads Becoming Determined; Substances That All But Flee Back into the Undifferentiated · pp. 303–306

And next let us examine, in their turn, the things that lie beyond these investigations. For concerning the unlike-formed and the like-formed procession — what difference they have — it has been spoken before; and one must not con-fuse the processions, since either has something of the other. But concerning the unified it must now be said: whether it is receptive of any procession; and, if so, of what kind. For that there is an intellectual procession, and that many intellects go forth from the one intellect, a man will reasonably grant. Nevertheless we must inquire even into this: whether there are indeed many intellects; whether many souls. For perhaps the arguments which show that before the other-moved there must be the self-moved, and before the self-moved the unmoved, compel us to suppose one intellect before the soul — and one soul, ensouling all things, ranked after the one intellect. And if the argument shows life also to be before intellect, and substance before life, it compels us again to set one substance, and one life, in rank before the one intellect. And the same things one might say also of one henad, set in front of the one substance. Whence, then, is it plain that there are many gods, and many substances, and many lives, and many intellects, and many souls — each a number proceeding after its proper monad?

Or rather, there is one manner of demonstration — the one about which the present argument is engaged — from the inner many: these being generative, and these proceeding, the outer multitudes are forthwith multiplied, whether according to the unlike-formed procession or the like-formed — by depth, or by breadth, as was divided before. For the cause, being one and many, will beget according to the One, and according to the many, and further according to the both-together — one together with many: each single product receiving its form, by dominance, from some one of the many, while being one, and yet also being the many in this one. For thus from the simply intellect proceeds the connective intellect; and from this, the titanic; and from this again, the demiurgic. Each whole intellect is in the simply intellect; and each receives its form from some one of the many in that one — the connective form, or the titanic, or the demiurgic. And likewise with the more partial many: from the Demiurge proceed the Apollonian intellect, and the Areic, and the Athenaic; and, still more partially, it holds good that according to each form there is begotten a certain whole intellect, standing upon itself, given its form according to this form — as it might be, according to man, and according to horse; for thus, of necessity, from the inner multitude of the forms an outer multitude of intellects is produced. And it is plain that from the parts also, according to the parts, there arise many outer subsistences of parts.

And if the whole-and-parts is life — the first life, standing according to the being-differentiated, as we said in what went before — it is plain that those subsistences are certain whole-complete lives, having subsisted according to the inner multitude of the parts, and holding the rank of parts, both toward one another and toward the cause that brought them forth. How, then, are they wholes? And how is the wholeness a cause of wholes? For the wholeness is generative of parts, not of wholes. And how are the ranks of parts self-complete, receiving their form from things that are not self-complete? Or rather: insofar as they are lives of something, they are not yet circumscribed; for that belongs to intellect, and to all the differentiated; but these have their being in the being-differentiated; so that they have subsisted above the intellectual kind of self-completeness — being self-complete in another manner; and the first life, the one according to the whole and the parts, subsists, so to speak, according to the whole; thus they are wholes, as coming from a cause that is whole in this way; and they hold the rank of parts, because they have proceeded according to the nature of the parts, and are, as it were, a number of the life that is seen in the being-differentiated — like monads that have their being not in the having-been-determined, but in the becoming-determined.

Since the first mixed, also, produces the many mixeds after itself — the elementated, I mean, produces the elementateds — and the multitude of the elements contained within it, as has been said many times. And these are the many substances after the one substance, having proceeded from the one as — if one may truly say so — a number proceeding from a kind of monad: unified from unified, and substance from substance; holding the rank of elements, both toward one another and toward the begetting cause; self-complete through the great union of their blending, in some other manner — the uncircumscribed manner, which strives rather to be blended toward union. For such were the elements, according to whose multitude the procession of the many substances came about; for as the outer multitudes are begotten from the inner, so also do they receive their form according to the nature of those. And the substances rejoice in their blending, and all but flee back into the undifferentiated; the lives are differentiated just so far as parts are from the whole and from one another; while the intellects were the first to be circumscribed, from one another and from the whole — making their differentiated subsistence according to their proper circumscription.

Chapter 98 — The Simply Many Have No Proper Procession, Yet All Things Are Begotten Thence — From Hence All Things Stretch Their Rays into the Below; Orpheus's Ērikepaios, Seed of the Gods; the Hypercosmic Watchtower; Into Three the Intellect of the Father Said That All Things Be Cut · pp. 306–309

What is now gathered from all this, and said toward the matter lying before us, is the following: that wherever any multitude whatsoever is contained within its proper one, a proper multitude is also begotten without — as a certain number growing out from its proper monad; for the One must everywhere be prolific; and, being one and containing many, it must be generative both of one and of many. Do then the simply many — not the many forms, nor the many parts, nor the many elements, but those very things which are many only, and simply many, which we proved to be elder than the other manys — do these also make an outer multitude analogous to themselves? But if those are in the intelligible, there will be a procession even of the intelligible; and this was what we have been examining from the beginning: whether the unified is differentiated into the procession from itself; and what differentiation there could be of that which has been allotted its subsistence according to total union. For the things in it are not many in such wise as to differ from one another in any way whatsoever; for not yet is there otherness among those, nor any difference, nor any determination at all. And Parmenides also makes this plain — making the apparent division like-parted, and bringing in the first otherness lower down, and establishing the first number together with this otherness and through it; reasonably: for where otherness is, there is the dyad; and where this is, the number — though not the eidetic number; for neither is the determination eidetic, nor the otherness of the kind that is opposed to sameness. Or rather, neither is there sameness There along with it; nor has there come to be the otherness that makes the parts other than one another; but only that by which the elements grew apart, and became many — not simply, but many of a certain sort: many things, namely, that are eager for their mutual blending; and the of-a-certain-sort is a difference; whence, according to the difference of the elements blended within, the begotten monad of the many substances stood apart without — even if, far from that archaic nature, the many substances that have run forth still hasten toward their mutual con-natured blending.

But those many were wholly without difference, and of no particular sort, and for this reason wholly unified — being, as it were, one prolific nature, called many in this manner; wherefore those are also an unlimited multitude; for there is no limit in it: neither the so-much — for it is unnumbered, and without quantity; nor the of-such-a-sort — for it is undifferent, and without quality; nor at all were quantity and quality differentiated There; for that simplicity is unified — the simplicity which did not endure even the relation of one and being. Whence one might rightly conceive that that multitude remains within, in the intelligible, and in no way goes forth into the subsistence of an outer multitude. A proper procession, then, there would not be of it; but since it is wholly many, all things are begotten from thence, down to the very individuals — since even the unlimitedness of the individuals is from thence, as was said before, according to the one all-bearing, unlimited-begetting power of the intelligible. For from hence all things begin to stretch their rays into the below; from hence leaps forth the generation of the manifoldly-variegated matter — and whatever else of this kind the gods declare in their oracles about that order. And Orpheus too celebrated this much-honored god, the one bearing the seed of the gods, and called him Ērikepaios; and from him he makes the whole generation of the gods proceed. So that, to speak according to breadth, There all things are pre-taken seminally, as the theologian says, according to the unified embrace — which he called the seed of all things. For the unified also was all things, undifferentiatedly; wherefore all things were differentiated off from it. And what wonder — when even the simply One had pre-taken all things, according to its unitary, all-complete simplicity? But there was no depth in the One, because neither was there a multitude differing according to breadth; for in the processions, depth belongs to what differs in breadth. So too the unified multitude is undifferent, and only a multitude — each of the many not being divided off — by union, and not by blending; for blending belonged to differing elements, but union to undifferent many; wherefore the latter made for us the unified, and the former the elemental; wherefore the procession of the elementated went forth also outward, according to the differences of the elements blended within; while that of the unified remained, all of it, within — having in itself no difference of depth and of breadth for the outward procession; for, difference not being, it inclined all together into one and whole, and remained; and it is not possible for anything to proceed both from something and from itself, where there is no difference.

Even here below, all the enmattered and pericosmic things proceed from the whole Demiurge; yet he did not himself go forth into the matter, nor into the pericosmic, partible rank. Just so the intelligible god brought forth from himself all the divine world-orders, while himself remaining in his own — truly hypercosmic — watchtower; having gone forth into them only so far as to establish his own monad as queen of all. He himself, then, remains whole and impartible; and the intelligible has been co-ranked, in a manner, with the world-orders that flow forth from it; and of the most whole-like gods after him, each is either tripled in the procession, or sevenfolded, while of the more partial gods each is multiplied by other, greater numbers, and others again; but he himself is, of all the processional numbers, the truly remaining monad — or rather, being a monad, he exceeds all the monads, and the whole single-form multitude — the fountal multitude, to speak according to the theurgists. Whence also he is hymned by all as the fount of founts.

But if the unified is wholly without difference, and without procession, how then are we able to divide the intelligible in three — into first and middle and last; or into substance and life and intellect; or into Father and Power and Intellect; or however else one may choose to speak? And if we should cast the three intelligible triads into it, the unified would be divided in many ways — since Plato also has handed down to us three ranks of the intelligible, according to the Parmenides: calling the first One Being; the middle, Whole and Parts; and the third, Unlimited Multitude. And we ourselves spoke so in what went before, confessing the undifferentiated to be in the differentiated manner of speech. And does not Orpheus too bring forth from the egg, when the cloud is burst, the much-honored Phanēs — he also establishing a procession within the intelligible? Or it must be said to these things: first, that we carry these up from the things below into the intelligible, desiring to give some indication concerning it according to the analogy of the more familiar; for the one and being are differentiated outside the intelligible; and the whole and the parts Plato clearly sets in the middle of the intelligibles-and-intellectuals; and the unlimited multitude is subdivided there where differentiation also shines forth. And what wonder — when concerning the middle world-orders too we are eager to give indication from the intellectual ones; for we know all things eidetically — and perhaps, indeed, only psychically. The unified, then, is not divided — it which is not even being-divided; for it is the only and first unified. Neither, then, are there There many forms, nor parts, nor elements; wherefore neither is there procession, inward or outward, in truth; whence the triad shone forth after the intelligible. For into three, said the intellect of the Father, all things are cut — whose will nodded assent, and at once all things were cut. And perhaps for this reason the god is hymned as three-barbed: not as giving subsistence to a triad — rather as commanding the triadic division in response, but not as making it. Thus, then, stands the truly unified.

Chapter 99 — The Triad of the Intelligible an Analogy from Below; Each Cosmos Ends into Its Successor; the Intelligible Wholly Unparticipated, Seated upon the Crown of All; Iamblichus — the Intelligible Frozen Fast About the One; the Triad There Is Not Three Monads · pp. 309–312

But since it is not possible to see the unified itself, insofar as we are not one — having attempted to behold it, and being unable to gaze upon its single union — we multiplied it according to analogy, with the first multiplication of the things multiplied below; and the first multitude is the triad; wherefore we supposed That also to be triadic, by analogy; wherefore also it would proceed, like-formedly, by analogy; for the inner triad transcends the intelligible and the intellectual and the middle order, and is outwardly synonymous with them — so to hear the same names of the same things. Either, then, it must be put thus; or, slackening something of this whole accustomed usage, one must conceive the following: that every cosmos, having proceeded in itself as far as it was of a nature to proceed, thereupon furnished the beginning of subsistence to the one after it, but did not itself descend any further — as the cosmos of the psychic substance, having proceeded to a certain point, stood still, and from there the bodily cosmos took up the succession. In this way the intellectual also ended into the psychic; and indeed the intelligible into the intellectual; and, with the intellectual taking its station, the intelligible too will stand upon itself, and the intelligible-and-intellectual will take up the succession. The nature of the intelligible does not, then, proceed outside the intelligible cosmos; for neither does that of any other cosmos proceed into the sub-stepping of another. And if the firsts of what ever sub-steps are co-ranked and gathered with the priors, as vehicles to the things before them, so the lasts are released from such connection — for not all bodies hold to proper souls, nor all souls to intellects, nor, among the others, do all the seconds hold to their priors; but nothing of the intelligible proceeds into the below; else the seconds would be strung along the one co-ordering of the riders and the things ridden; rather, the intelligible is wholly unparticipated — the cause of this being, that it is the summit of all the cosmoi; so that it is seated upon the very crown of all. And either all things are in it undifferentiatedly; or it is exalted alike above all the differentiated; or it rides alike upon all; for the wholeness suffices for all; for it is not because it has been contracted into the undifferentiated that it is least; nay, it is the greatest of all the cosmoi.

And what would be the definition, and the difference, of what proceeds into a vehicle, and of what is ridden? The first ridden becomes, in turn, a vehicle of another; so that, if it should proceed so as to be ridden by the others — as intellect by soul, and soul by body — there will be vehicle upon vehicle: as the soul is for the intellect, and body for some other. Of what, then, would the intelligible be the vehicle? For in that way the first god would be participated; but everywhere the first must be unparticipated. But perhaps body is vehicle only; the intelligible, ridden only; and the means are viewed in either way. But if this too shall be divided into participated and unparticipated — and not one participated only, but several, and participated by several: the one by substance, another by life, another by intellect, another by soul, another by body — then the things ridden must differ from one another in form: as the hypercosmic differs from the encosmic god, and from this the intellectual, and from this again the intelligible-and-intellectual. What, then, this so great difference within the unified would be, and whence, it is hard even to fashion in thought; and further: the One neither proceeded in itself nor after itself; while for what comes after the intelligible — whence does the otherness arrive, in whatever manner? Both in itself, then, and after itself, the intelligible has justly remained in the middle station: having proceeded in itself, but having made, after itself, no procession at all.

And to these things this must be added: that the first ridden is the henad; and that upon which it first rides is substance; but the unified was before both — before, therefore, the carrying and the ridden; its nature, accordingly, does not admit the difference of the ridden, because it was before the one — which became the first ridden according to the very dis-stance toward being, as first toward second. And if one should also take into thought what Iamblichus says — that the intelligible subsisted about the One, and has grown together with the Good, and, by the inclination of its whole nature toward That, is as it were frozen fast — it is clear that it remains with That, both undifferentiated, and without procession toward the outside. And if, indeed, it displayed in itself, in whatever manner, some highest appearance of sub-stepping — even this is not differentiated by number, nor by multitude, nor indeed by otherness; but, as Iamblichus says again: the triad There is not three monads, nor did it supervene upon three monads; but it is only the form itself that supervenes upon monads; or rather it must be said: not even the form; for that is not yet a form There, nor anything like an element; for none of these things is There — but only the very one of the triad, and even this undetermined toward substance — the unified before both, as we call it. How, then, could such a thing be of a nature to go forth into several subsistences?

What then — are the many not There? Or rather: even before the unified there are the many, after the One — yet not so-many; but that many was an unlimited-begetting henad; and her first offspring is the intelligible multitude — become a unified instead of a one — though not yet is even this a so-many; for there is not yet any determination, not yet any otherness; but where these are, there is said to subsist also the first number, immediately after the unified — not the eidetic number, but the number according to the first determination, subsisting after the first undetermined nature, according to the first differing multitude; and this was the multitude of the first elements, where determination first subsisted — one and substance being the first things determined; or rather, not even these as having been already determined, but as still being determined — above all as things that have been allotted their being at the summit of what is differentiated below. These matters, then, it will be necessary to touch upon many times hereafter.

Chapter 100 — The Ascent from Things Under Sensation; the Question of the Many — Souls, Intellects, Lives, Substances; the Illuminationist Hypothesis of the Philosophers Before Iamblichus; the Double Illumination, Suspended and In-Grown; Vice and Ignorance — the Souls Self-Determining in Truth · pp. 312–317

But let us take in hand another manner of arguments about the same things — from the things below, and lying under sensation, going back up to the very first of the intelligibles — if the demonstration that arises from evidences, coming about by way of analysis, might furnish us some confirmation by its own truth. And the argument seeks not concerning the monads themselves, but concerning the many that are said to be ranked under each monad, and that proceed from each. That, then, before the other-moved is the self-moved; and before this the unmoved indeed, yet differentiated; and before this the being-differentiated; and still before this the undifferentiated. And in another manner also: that before body there must be the soul that moves the body and makes it live; and before soul, intellect — which knows all things at once, and not transitively; and before intellect, life; and before life, substance: let these things be laid down as having been demonstrated, and as agreed by all the most renowned of the philosophers.

But we inquire whether, after the one substance, there are many substances; and after the one life, many lives; and after the one intellect, many intellects; and after the soul, many souls. For perhaps someone might say that from one soul there come, into the many bodies, many illuminations; and that each body has the rational life that falls to it illumined from the one soul; and that the seeming multitude of the many souls is a multitude not of self-complete souls, but of psychic illuminations; and likewise that the multitude of intellects is the intellectual illuminations, those coming into each soul from each form of the forms determined in the one intellect. For one must of necessity agree that the illuminations are many, and differing in form — unless a man should wish to quarrel with the very principles; but that they are illuminations only, proceeding from the different reason-principles contained in the one soul, and from the forms determined in the one intellect; for it is easy to demonstrate that the multitude of the forms subsists before the multitude of the reason-principles, and that of the reason-principles before the bodiform and enmattered images; for it is plain that the true things come first — with the eternal and the unmoved. And in the same way a man might say that the many seeming lives also are vital illuminations, flowing off from the one subsisting life into all the living things; and that the many substances, in their turn, are in-givings by illumination from the one substance, proceeding into all the things that are. And why need one say much? — seeing that even the many gods were supposed to be such by almost all the philosophers before Iamblichus: saying that the supersubstantial god is one, and that the others are substantial, divinized by the illuminations from the One; and that the multitude of the supersubstantial henads is a multitude not of self-complete subsistences, but of the things illumined from the only god — divinizations given-in to the substances.

What I say many times over, then: the argument inquires, concerning each number that is said to be ranked under each archic monad, whether it is self-complete, or is multiplied only according to illumination. And the illumination is double: the one suspended from the illuminator, and con-being with it according to one continuity; the other growing into the illumined, and becoming its own, and subsisting in it as in a substrate. We must inquire, then, in which of the two senses a man shall suppose the illuminations, if he should accept them in place of the self-complete subsistences. And let this also be determined beforehand: that the self-complete subsistence is better than the illumination of the same rank — as the light of the sun, if it had subsisted by itself, and were not a hanging appendage of something else; and if it were a substance, and not, in a certain manner, an activity of substance; and if it stood self-sufficient upon itself, and were not con-substantiated as another's — would be agreed to be better. And it is plain, too, that the one kind of illumination is better than the other; for this one, even if it belongs to another, yet belongs to the better — to the illuminator itself; while that one belongs to the worse — for it is of the illumined; and the one is separate, the other in a substrate and inseparable; and it is clear which answers to which.

Further then, let this also be claimed in addition: that if something is in the worse, it will be in the better in far greater measure: thus, if the soul that is worse by nature is a self-complete substance, and not an illumination of either kind, assuredly the soul that is better by nature — better than the human — and the divine soul much more; so that, if the soul is such, then the intellect also, by the same account; and if the intellect, the life likewise; and if the life, the substance too; and if the substance, the One as well; for the self-complete, and self-sufficient, and seated upon itself would be in the superior things rather than in the needier; if, then, it is in these, it is also in those. And I mean by the substantified-by-itself-and-in-itself that which is predicated of the things whose nature it is to be so; and such are substance, and life, and intellect, and soul, and body; and we mark this off against the things that have their being in these — which we call elements, and parts, and forms, and the reason-principles in the soul; and the other such things of the body.

These things standing so: that the bodies are many, and stand apart from one another severally — the statement is evident even to a blind man; but as for the ensouled among them: either one soul, common to all, has reached them all; or, after the one, there are also many souls, one proper to each — each a certain self-moved substance. Now that the life of all is not one — this also is evident; for we perceive one life in one way, and another in another. The ensoulments of the severals, then, are proper to each; and these are either illuminations made proper to their substrates — descending from the peculiar-mannered reason-principles of the one soul — and coming to be in a substrate, in each of the bodies; but this is impossible: for that which itself moves itself is assuredly separate from the substrates — from the bodies that are ensouled by it. Or else the illuminations have not grown into these, nor have their being in these, but hang down from the illuminators, and belong to those — whether they be certain activities, or second substances attached to the first and flowing off from them, as the lights from the things that give light, or whatever else one might wish to call them; but in any case they will be, each of them, not their own, but as it were out-growths of one nature, or parts, or substantial reason-principles. And if this is so, what place will vice have, and ignorance, there being no longer any partial souls? These, then, will be affections of the whole soul; for if there were nothing else, beside the light of the sun, in this place here, then the being-quenched would be an affection of the solar light — if indeed even the lamp-light were that light's own; but this it is no longer lawful to say. The human souls, then, are not out-growths of the whole soul; they are therefore self-complete, and seated upon themselves, and being, in themselves, their own and not another's — which is to say, self-determining, and self-moved in truth. And if the human body has both the ensoulment rooted down within it, and, before this, the self-complete soul that breathes this ensoulment into it, and if they are ensouled somehow also by the soul of the All — assuredly the betters among the ensouled will have not only the life in a substrate, nor only the common life breathing upon them from afar, but also the proper soul of each of them; for such an ensoulment is better than the one that does not have the self-complete and proper soul. And in general: if it has the worst, according to the in-grown ensoulment, and the strongest, according to the common ensoulment of the one soul, why should it not have the one ranked in the middle of these?

And further, in yet another way: if our soul is a certain proper substance, and there is also the whole and one soul, being as it were the monad of souls, why not also the whole number that lies between the one and those partitioned to the last? For how was it possible for the most partial of all souls to proceed from the whole without the middle plenitudes? It is necessary, then, that each ensouled thing have been allotted a proper, self-complete soul. And if someone, speaking with precision, should say that the life-making which comes from the whole and one soul is double — the one fore-taking the proper soul, such as makes live even the soulless among the things in the All, this being worse than the peculiar-mannered and more partial life-making, such that the ensouled, taking it in addition, have become more vital; the other supervening upon this, the common life given in from the whole soul, according to which the partial things are made whole — even so, nevertheless, it is necessary either that all things be soulless, and that there be only the common life, which is an alien life, belonging to the All; or, if the ensouled also is something, that there be some proper soul of each, through which it will attain life in greater measure and more wholly; after the one soul of the All, then, there are the many self-complete souls — as may be gathered by reasoning from the appearances. And if the ensouled stands toward soul as the in-intellected toward intellect, it is necessary, I think, to make the same account prevail for these also. The ensouled body, then, is a body en-souled — having not an illumination of soul only, but gathered together with a self-complete soul; for this was better for it than that; and the in-intellected is a soul in-intellected — having not the intellectual illumination only, but attached, by nature, to a proper intellect, which is better for her than to have an intellectual illumination only. For surely this better form did not subsist in the worse things, and become con-substantiated with the worse, while in the betters, and for the betters, it should not have come to be — I mean: that the ensouled body should be yoked to a self-complete soul, while the in-intellected soul should not be yoked to a self-complete intellect. For this being better, how should it not belong, in greater measure, to the betters?
