lines.text: Chapter 101 — The Same Method for Intellect and Life; the Self-Complete and the Unparticipated Life; the Triple One; the Second Ascent Through Evidences — Other-Moved, Self-Moved, Unmoved; Substance Supra-Eternal, Intellect Eternal, Life as Aiōn Itself; the One Stretched Out Alongside All · pp. 317–319

But indeed the same manner of method holds also for intellect and life: for intellect confessedly lives; but this life is the intellect's own, and has subsisted in the intellect; there must, then, be before this one a self-complete life, of which intellect will participate according to attachment to her — yoked to her as to a better, as body to soul — and through which it will participate also of the unparticipated life; as the body, through its own proper soul, participates also of the soul of the one that has obtained it by lot, so to speak. And in the same way we shall ascend also from life to substance — both the participated and the unparticipated. And would not someone say this same thing also of the unified — it too being triple: the one according to the state that is in the substance; the other according to the participated subsistence; the other according to the unparticipated? And the same argument will demand that of the simply One also — the One before all things — there be a triple subsistence: one being the illumination come to be in another, according to which we call each thing, however it has subsisted, one; another according to the unparticipated existence; and another according to the middle one, the participated, through which the participants enjoy something also of the unparticipated. But this perplexity awaits us again hereafter.

And I wish, by another approach of argument, to run back up again from below upward, demonstrating through evidences that it is necessary, then, that not only the monads exist — the superior ones ever before the needier — but also the several numbers, those differentiated from their proper monads: as what I was just now saying — that many souls have come to be after the one soul, and many intellects after the one, and many lives and substances after the one life and substance; upon which the same perplexity will again be hung for us, concerning the unified and the One. That, then, it is necessary to suppose three — the other-moved, the self-moved, the unmoved — the more ancient philosophers also, I think, show sufficiently. For if the moved body is moved by another — for it is not moved by itself — then either the mover is a body, and is itself moved by another, and this to infinity; or it is moved by an unmoved; and how will this sometimes move, and sometimes not? For the other-moved is seen in change; but the unmoved could not begin change, lest it too should change; and it is supposed unmoved. If, then, these things are impossible, the self-moved will begin change — both its own, and that of the other-moved; it is necessary, then, to suppose the self-moved before the other-moved.

And indeed the first mover is wholly unmoved; for if this too should be moved, we shall come to infinity. And if someone should say that the self-moved is the first mover: insofar as it moves, it would be unmoved, and not self-moved; and if the same thing is at once moving and moved — insofar as moving, unmoved; insofar as moved by itself, self-moved — it will not be purely unmoved, but first of the moved, because moved not by another but by itself, and last of the movers, because it is not only moving, but also moved; and the unmixed toward the worse must be set before the mixed, as first; for if there must be, before the moved, the mover — which of necessity is unmoved — then what is at once moved cannot be the first mover; for neither is this properly the mover; for why is the same thing mover rather than moved? And why should it be said to belong to the unmoved rather than to the moved? For even if it changes itself, it is nevertheless changed; not, then, unmoved in truth. There must, then, be before the self-moved the unmoved — which again would be triple in its nature: for intellect can be wholly unmoved, or life, or substance: she as supra-eternal; intellect as eternal; and life as Aiōn itself. Or better, perhaps: to say that the one has been circumscribed by forms, and differentiated; that the other is uncircumscribed, and undifferentiated; and that the third holds itself in the middle in such wise as to be roused toward differentiation and circumscription, yet not yet to stand completely in the having-been-differentiated and circumscribed; and the order of these is plain; and before these there will be also, stretched out alongside all, the One; for one and unified are not the same; for the latter was the undifferentiated.

Chapter 102 — The Many Under Each Genus; Appearances as Evidences of the True — the Phaedrus; the Ensouled of Pythagoras and of Kylon, of Plato and of Kleon; the Soul and Its Organ, Which Indeed We Also Call the Vehicle; Ascend Now from the Self-Moved to the Unmoved; the Heavenly Revolutions and the First Unmoved · pp. 319–324

These things having been recalled to this extent, let our inquiry now be set before us concerning the things under each genus — for instance, the many forms — whether some argument will compel these too, in addition to the common things. And these also must be determined beforehand, in addition to what has been said: one, that the parts are co-form-given with their proper whole, and that the activity of the part must be characterized along with the activity of the whole — for instance, the opinative part is not the same in form in the divine soul, and in the daimonic, and in the human; but the one is itself also human, the other daimonic, the other divine; and likewise each reason-principle in each; and the self-moved, accordingly, is other and other in form; so that the apparent self-moved also is different in form — that which comes down from the one soul and from the other. Conversely, then, it must also be said that the appearances, being different in form, proceed from true things differing in form; so that the many apparent forms are evidences of the many true forms — since indeed the common apparent is demonstrative of the common true. If, then, we make the apparent self-moved in the other-moved, taken simply, an evidence of the true self-moved — as is shown more completely in the Phaedrus — then, if the forms of the appearances be many, many also will be the forms of the true; for each appearance becomes an evidence of its own proper true one, as each image, differing in whole form, is evidence of its proper paradigm. If, then, each ensouled thing is an apparent self-moved, and each is not the same in form, it is clear that the truly self-moved things also will be many forms: many, therefore, are the souls.

But perhaps, as the many paradigms are in the one intellect, so the many souls are the many psychic reason-principles, determined according to form in the one whole and single-form soul? But the parts of that soul are all divine, and parts of an all-complete nature, so that they too are all-complete in their part; for each is whole-like, and in very truth cosmic; whereas not every ensouled thing renders such activities, nor is such in its nature; rather, one is divine, another daimonic, another human; and one is the ensouled body of Pythagoras, another of Kylon; and one, if it so chance, of Plato, another of Kleon. It is necessary, then, that the properly self-moved souls also be other and other, with the same forms as their ensouled — and differing even more greatly than the apparent self-moveds differ. Many, therefore, are the souls after the one whole soul.

But perhaps they are not co-ranked with the ensouled bodies — being substances separate by themselves, and illumining from afar the ensoulments according to which the bodies become ensouled? Yet even if a man should suppose what is said to be true, it would be nothing against the present point; for that each ensouled thing has a proper soul — the one furnishing to it its differing apparent self-motion — this is what the argument wished to show: whether from afar, or from near, or in whatever place and manner it should accomplish this. Next: some activities of the ensouled are inseparable and animal-like; but others are of the soul herself — whether fighting against the ensouled, or ordering it and setting it in array, or withdrawing from it headlong, or not even seeming to be present, through the greatness of the separation. And these things are manifest in our own case; in the daimonic kinds less so, because of their invisibility — and yet many indeed have met with such; while in the divine it is harder to differentiate the activities of the ensouled, and those of the souls, and further those of the gods themselves, from whom the souls are hung. Yet one might nevertheless easily gather the same conclusions concerning these also; for our soul uses the ensouled as an organ — as she makes plain when at times she does not use it; and the divine soul would not move her own ensouled in that bound manner, even if she moves it always — having ever projected the separable apart from it. If, then, from each soul the ensouled is hung as an organ, it is clear that there con-exists with it, as the user with the organ, the rational soul of each — seen according to its co-ordering toward its proper organ — which indeed we also call the vehicle. Many souls, then, lead the many ensouled: souls differing in form from one another, as the ensouled differ in form from one another — the truly self-moved souls of the apparent self-moveds.

Ascend now from the self-moved to the unmoved, as you have ascended from the other-moved to the self-moved. For there is also a certain apparent unmoved — as, among the heavenly revolutions, the circling ever according to the same things and in the same manner: let it come from soul; for this too is a kind of change. But the in-the-same-manner, and the always, and all such characters, both are, and are spoken, according to the unchanging; wherefore in this respect the circular motion imitates intellect, as Plotinus says — or rather, as Plato himself, in the Laws, projected it as an image of the motion of intellect: the apparent unmoved of the true unmoved. For it is apparent in very truth, because in it the always has been blended together with the at-some-time — for it is always at this or that moment that it moves — and the in-the-same-manner with the now-thus-and-now-otherwise; for the in-the-same-manner, too, lay within the change according to number; so that, universally, the moved is blended with the unmoved. And if you should behold the image of intellect in the circular motion of souls also, you will see there too, analogously, the moved con-kneaded with the unmoved.

But perhaps someone might say that such an unmoved is an in-giving and image not of the intellectual unmoved, but of the psychic — of which the unchanging in body also is one; I mean the unchanging according to substance; for there is indeed something unchangeable according to the substantial both in the bodily forms and in the souls; for they are immortal, and admit neither addition nor any subtraction, nor change at all. For their substance is either eternal, as the philosophers for the most part will have it; or generated indeed, yet wholly unchanging; for one must agree that there is also a certain generation of this kind, and that not everything unchanging is in every way eternal; for the substance and subsistence, say, of the sun, though everlasting and unchanging, would not be eternal. For how could the body be eternal — standing apart, one part in one place and another in another, and dispersed abroad? For the eternal is impartible both according to place and according to time.

These things, then, are true, and are demonstrated by us elsewhere with greater precision. Yet the apparent unmoved does not lead us up only to this; it leads to the first unmoved; for even if it leads more proximately to that other, yet not on that account to the first and true as well; for we did not posit that unmoved — counter-dividing it against the self-moved and the other-moved — which, being generated, is unchanging; but that which is truly eternal, or even supra-eternal. For this was the truly and primarily unmoved; since the generated, even if it be unchanging, is other-moved. And this is the apparent unmoved in the other-moved; and in the self-moved, again, there is an apparent unmoved; for as the true other-moved is an apparent self-moved, so also the true self-moved is an apparent unmoved. For the substance of the soul is at once mover and self-moved; and insofar as it is moved, how is it eternal? And being at once mover and moved, it would not be properly unmoved — for the only-unmoved is not at the same time also moved. For the moved is significant of something generated; wherefore the self-moved is also interpreted as self-generated: for it is becoming — but by itself; and in this it differs from the other-moved; and its unmovedness is not true, but apparent, blended into the moved — as the apparent self-moved is at once also other-moved. As, then, the self-moved in the activities of the ensouled led us proximately to the substantial, apparent self-motion, and properly to the true one, so also that which, within the changes, holds ever according to the same things and in the same manner leads us proximately to its proper substance — which is itself an apparent unmovedness, even if more assimilated to the unmoved — while properly and truly it will lead up to the first unmoved. If, then, the self-moved is, the unmoved is before it; and if there are many self-moveds, differing in form from one another, each will carry us up, like-formedly, to its proper unmoved.

But perhaps someone might say that many forms are gathered together in one unmoved, as the paradigms in the one intellect; and that there are not, therefore, many intellects after the one, having proceeded from it. Or rather: it is not the same thing to speak of the heliac or the selenian part of the one intellect, and of the heliac or the selenian intellect; for neither is the apparent unmoved of the whole soul the same as the heliac or selenian one taken apart within a part of her, and as that of the heliac or selenian soul by herself; for neither is my own psychic apparent unmoved the same as the one pre-taken in the whole soul according to the cause of my soul. Since, then, they differ in form — my soul, if it so chance, from the pre-taking of it in the whole, my soul being viewed There as a part; and the soul of Kronos from the Kronian psychic cause pre-taken in the whole soul — it is plain that, as their apparent unmoveds also will differ from one another according to form, so the truly unmoved things, differing in form, will have us ascend, in the evidentiary manner, to causes differing in form. Not the same unmoved, then, will shine forth from the pre-taking of the soul of Kronos in the whole, and from the very soul of Kronos: from the latter we ascend to a Kronian proper unmoved intellect; from the former, to a part in the whole intellect — and this also Kronian. From there being many self-complete souls, then, after the one — even the one that has proceeded from her — it follows that there are many self-complete intellects after the one, having proceeded from it. Wherefore one must also inquire whether, answering to every apparent unmoved, we shall posit a true one as well. In that way there will be even a proper, self-complete intellect of my own soul. And why not? — someone might say — if indeed answering to each ensouled thing — that is, to each apparent self-moved — there is a certain proper, self-complete soul. But let this remain awaiting us, inquired into thus far.

Chapter 103 — Intellects Co-Ranked with Souls as with Organs and Vehicles; the Heliac and Selenian Intellects; the Gods Called Encosmic, Sensible, and Enmattered from the Henads' Own Properties — What Would Not Be an Offspring of God and of One?; the Ascent Not from Every Appearance · pp. 324–327

Now let us examine these things further in their turn: whether the argument shows not only many intellects simply, but also intellects co-ranked with the many souls, as with organs or as with vehicles. That the heliac apparent unmoved demonstrates to us a heliac self-complete intellect, and every selenian one, in its turn, a selenian — is evident. And if the one is a partial heliac intellect, and the other a selenian — the one giving in the apparent unmoved to the soul of the moon, the other to the soul of the sun, and, through the one and the other soul, giving to the natural forms what falls to them, and to these a trace or image of the unmoved — then each will be co-ranked according to kinship: the one with the soul of the sun, the other with that of the moon; and the one will use the other as an organ toward the perfecting of the third things; and it is plain which with which. This manner of demonstration, then, leads us up not to the unparticipated many intellects, as we showed just now, but — quite the contrary — to the participated. For from the ensouled we were led up, by proportion, to the souls co-ranked with these and participated by them; and how indeed was it likely that, ascending from the things given in, we should not come, upon these, to the givers? And the ensoulment is given in to the natural forms by the attached souls, those proximately mounted upon them; and the in-intellected to the souls, by the intellects yoked to them, of like manner and like form with them; for the likeness of their properties, and the symmetry of the equal measures of the partition from the wholes, join the participated to the participated.

Is then the unparticipated one, while the many are everywhere participated? Or rather, the philosophers recognize souls also that are hypercosmic, before the encosmic; and, above the hypercosmic and participated ones, the intellectual and unparticipated intellects. What, then, is the ascent from below to the unparticipated multitude? Is the manner of the method the same? Let only this be determined beforehand: that as the deity riding upon the intellect has pre-taken the property of intellect, and is a unitary intellect, so also the intellect riding upon the soul will have pre-taken the property of the soul, and would be an intellectual soul: intellect by subsistence, soul by the property. For such a henad also — the first one, presiding over these — projected the psychic peculiarity, and is a unitary soul, by the same account; for we call the god riding upon substance a unitary substance, according to subsistence; and a unitary life, the one riding upon life; so that also a nature, or a whole form both natural and bodiform, or a form simply enmattered, or a form encosmic — and the one riding upon such an animal would justly be a soul, and the intellect of this soul; and before all of them is the henad.

Of course we call the last gods, in a certain manner, gods encosmic, and gods sensible and enmattered: not, as the philosophers seem to say, as if the god were form-given from the lasts; for nothing is characterized, or named, from the worse, in justice; but because everywhere the henads, projecting their properties before them, give these in shares to their proper vehicles; so that the gods have come to be first — encosmic, and enmattered, and sensible, and bodily — in the unitary manner; then, after them, the intellects, in the intellectual manner; and after the intellects, the souls, in the self-moved manner; whereupon this very kind of form itself also went forth and was begotten — no longer according to property only, but now also according to the last subsistence — which we hold to be other-moved body, immediately graspable even by sensation. For this is what has long been noised abroad, even before the philosophers, and is here shown: each such name is, as it were, a property — a goodness coming from gods. For what would not be an offspring of god, and of one? Let this, then, really stand determined by us — showing itself useful both toward what has gone before and toward what is to come.

If, then, one must run back up from the apparent self-moved to the true self-moved, whether will the true one be that which is blended together with the property of the other-moved, and which is self-moved according to subsistence; or that which is such in both ways — self-moved in property and in subsistence alike, and similar to itself, and nothing else? Or rather, the transition is to either: but nearer, because more con-generic, to the participated; further, because truer, to the unparticipated. In this way, then, we shall ascend also from the apparent unmoved: first, to the intellect that is self-moved according to property alone, but unmoved according to subsistence; and second, to the one that is wholly unmoved, and truly such; and this is the unparticipated intellect. And it is plain that there is such a multitude of intellects, and a multitude of souls; for as the participated are many, so also the unparticipated must be many. For each participated property will have its own purified counterpart in its proper unparticipated one — more truly, and wholly of such a kind as the true, taken from the apparent, wishes to be.

But the ascent is not from every appearance, though the ascent to the unparticipated holds in any case; for surely we shall not come from the human soul to an unparticipated soul — so that there should be a soul of Plato, if it so chance, both hypercosmic and unparticipated; nor from the daimonic intellect to an unparticipated intellect. For every daimon is encosmic; so that neither shall we posit a hypercosmic soul answering to each daimon; for neither would every encosmic god have been previously hypercosmic; nor has every hypercosmic god pre-subsisted as already intellectual also; for neither would every intellectual one be intelligible-and-intellectual. Or, on that showing, we shall make all things everywhere determined — and the entire multitude of the gods differentiated at once in the intelligible; I mean the multitude of the whole properties, and that of the partial; and then it would no longer be true that the things above, compared with the things below, are gathered in quantity while exceeding in the quality of their worth. If, however, anyone raises difficulties against the stated argument, and demands that we determine from which things there is an ascent to the superior, and from which there is not — this too has been raised as a difficulty before, and we shall resolve the difficulty again hereafter, as far as may be possible.

parts.name: Chapter 104 — The Unparticipated Multitude Before the Participated; the Supra-Eidetic Life; Henads That Have Kindled Intellect from Themselves; Plato's Two Columns; Whether the One Above the Unified Proceeds — a Nature Wholly Without Difference, Not Only One, but Not Even Anything · pp. 327–330

lines.text: Chapter 104 — The Unparticipated Multitude Before the Participated; the Supra-Eidetic Life; Henads That Have Kindled Intellect from Themselves; Plato's Two Columns; Whether the One Above the Unified Proceeds — a Nature Wholly Without Difference, Not Only One, but Not Even Anything · pp. 327–330

For now I take the argument to demand only this much: why there is also an unparticipated multitude before the participated ones — both souls and intellects — seeing that the simply unparticipated must be joined to the multitude of the participated both as one set against multitude, and as unparticipated against participated; for the middle term would be that which is unparticipated indeed, and yet a multitude. And if there is a first participated, and the first participated leads a proper multitude, then the first unparticipated also will lead a multitude of its own; for every number is like-formed to its proper monad. In this way, then, we shall divide the unmoved also in three. For since intellect is something differentiated and circumscribed — both itself and the things within it — yet not utterly dispersed, but somehow gathered together, having its being in being-differentiated; and, to speak more plainly: since, being intellect, it has life, and this life is somehow intellectual, and not only unmixed life — there must, before the life that is in another, and blended together with another property, the eidetic, be the supra-eidetic life: life only, subsisting by herself, substantified in the being-differentiated alone — nay rather, herself projecting the being-differentiated.

Again: since life too has substance, and this substance is vital — being differentiated, and not simply unified, rather than substance simply — there must before her also be the truly substance: substance only, and completely unified. And it is plain that not only the monads stand thus in rank toward one another, but the multitudes also; and that the ascent is not only to the participated — climbing from the many intellects to the multitude of participated lives — but also from these to the unparticipated multitude. And likewise in the case of the substances; for the same account will fit them all. Accordingly, someone might say the same of the others too: that nothing prevents bringing the same necessity of the argument to bear upon the unified as well. There will be, then, before the participated many, many unparticipated henads; and those of them that have proceeded into substance are substantial; and those into life, vital; and indeed those that have kindled intellect from themselves, intellectual. It is necessary, then, that before the substantial gods there be many unparticipated gods — and not one only; and that there be also one, before the many: the simply god.

Who, then, would this be? And which are the unparticipated after him? For they must be unitary and substantial; yet not such as we call those before one and substance — the undifferentiated ones, unified according to the One Being of Plato. For those were not henads standing according to the One alone, counter-divided against Being according to the first otherness that appeared. For this otherness, it seems, having separated the one from substance, must set the simply One in front of all things; then the many unparticipated henads; and after these, next in order, the ones participated by substances, and lives, and intellects, and souls, and bodiform natural forms. But Plato, after the undifferentiated One Being, set against each other the two columns — of the participated henads, and of the participated substances — and, to speak generally, of the subsistences. And universally: if it is true to say that from the simply One a double multitude is produced — as from the simply substance, and the simply life, and the simply intellect, and, if you will, the simply soul — the one unparticipated, the other participated — how would a man not say, in justice, what is indeed plain: that from the simply unified too a double multitude of unifieds will show itself — the one unparticipated, and not co-stretched alongside the participants as far as the encosmic animals; the other participated, reaching down to these, just as each of the wholes does; so that there comes to be a procession of the unified also, outward, according to the inner many, the outer proceeding in two ways.

But if it is lawful, in raising difficulties, to reason the same things also about the simply One — the One above the unified — perhaps the same perplexities would arise about that as well. For why is there not also, belonging to the One above the unified, a proper procession above the unified — the one unparticipated, the other participated by the unified? Or rather: not yet, There, have the participating and the participated been differentiated; nor the participated and the unparticipated; nor the many and the one; for that nature was one only; and the second principle was called many as being one nature — cause of the things differentiated in every manner, being, of herself, a power of the One, differentiative and prolific. Such a nature, then, is not of a kind to endure the processions, of whatever sort, that come about by differentiation from one; for it wishes to be one only — even the all-various one — and before all things; from which such things appear, coming to be as seconds or thirds. And further: where all things are one, surely no difference could subsist there — not even one; there will not, then, be the one simply, and the unparticipated one, and the participated one; for these will be differences of the One's nature — which is wholly and altogether without difference. It is not, then, receptive of procession — not in any manner whatsoever: neither according to appearance, nor according to the analogy of remaining and proceeding and reverting, nor of begetter and begotten; for these too are certain differences. Further: since that nature is before all things, it is also the principle of all; it would not endure to be any of the things that proceed from it; none of these, then, would the archic nature of all things endure. And these belong to all things — indeed to the things that have already subsisted according to some differentiation. Not one of these, then, will it so much as indicate — it which we say is not only one, but not even anything at all. Further: if it has its being in being exalted above all things, and in being the common principle of all, how is that nature still common — if indeed it is proper, as a monad of the unparticipated multitude proceeding from itself? And how is its nature un-co-ranked — if indeed it has a participated multitude? For everything of that kind is co-ranked with the things that participate it.

Chapter 105 — The Unified Refuses All Procession — All Things Drunk Down into the One Union of All; Iamblichus and the One Great Intuition; the Hidden Cosmos, the Hypercosmic Abyss, the Common Birth-Pang of All Births; the Titanic Rending of Our Conceptions and the Daring of the Triad · pp. 330–335

About the first cause, indeed, why prolong the matter — seeing that it has nothing else in common with all the others save this alone: that it is exalted above all, and is cause of all — and does not even have the title cause as something determined apart from the one. But why should the unified not proceed, producing from itself a double multitude, unparticipated and participated? Or rather, the unparticipated we concede; for the intelligible is many; for we continue beholding it as triadic — that I may not also triple this triad into an ennead. It needed, then, that the participated also proceed, after the unparticipated. Or is it perhaps truer to say that not even the unparticipated proceeds? For not only does the One refuse the differentiated multitude, but the unified also — inclining together, whole, toward the One, and, as it were, given its form according to the nature of That, and willing nowhere and in no wise to subsist apart from it; for it is in this that the first unified has its being. As, then, the first in each kind must be the most true — for what could there be before it, before the very being of the kind? — so this also: assuredly it is most truly unified. In no way, then, does the unified admit any differentiation whatsoever; nor, therefore, procession — nor any such thing at all; for such it would be, in all justice, as its seeming elements also would justly be supposed to be.

For the unified — to speak from below, from the things after it and proceeding from it — is one being, simple, fore-ranked of both the one and the being. If, then, it makes these processions from itself — it which is not even either of the two, but before both — how should it not be superior even to the processional principle? And this principle is the one that differentiates the One and the Being from each other; for this differentiation showed itself first. And — to behold it from above, from the two principles — it is one and many at once, according to participation, as those were according to cause. But the One, and the many, do not proceed; for neither do the many; for it is a cause of processions, yet not itself proceeding; for neither is it many in the sense of a many in multitude, but as a One of such a kind — as it were an out-stretching of the One; wherefore it is hymned both as the power of it, and as its all-bearing, and as cause of all; for, taken as one, it is not even cause of all, but only before all. As, then, the unified proceeds from two principles of this kind — insofar as it has something of the One, unified; insofar as it shows forth something also of the many: not having remained one, but having become unified instead of one, and not each of those two — and in this way giving the manifold to appear — this came from the second principle; but not as something differentiated in any way. Such, then, being this unified, how should it be differentiated into any procession — whether in itself or from itself, whether unparticipated or participated? Or whence shall it have such differences, when nothing There stands by itself? Let there be, then, neither difference, nor otherness, nor differentiation, nor procession, nor descent, nor excess; neither begetter nor begotten; nor anything whatsoever differentiated toward another, or being-differentiated, or remaining in itself, or determined in whatever other manner such things are determined: for the nature of the unified has drunk down all things into the one union of all — as, if it be lawful to say, the One itself has drunk down all into the one simplicity of all.

That the truth stands thus, I am persuaded beyond everything; and so is Iamblichus — in many places insistent — compelling us to press our many intuitions together, as into one centre; and to make the circumference a centre; and so to approach the unified and intelligible — unifiedly, and intelligibly, with one great intuition, itself undifferentiated and intelligible. But since it is no easy thing for one who is a man to project such an intuition — above all while still dwelling upon the earth — and since we nevertheless desire, in whatever way, to behold even the things There, hidden in the depth There, and as it were con-fused, relative at least to our apprehension: having attempted, then, to compress that nature thus, as best we are able — though it is not yet gathered according to the one intuition which we called the centre of all intuitions — we split it, first, in two, about its dis-stanced union, seeing it now as unified, now as multiplied; though it is not so; for the unified of it is not one thing, and the multiplied another; rather, both of these are folded together according to the unified. Yet even so we are content to think, and to name: at one time calling it the multiplied — not the one itself; at another, again, hymning it as unified — as what has not suffered the one. But that nature is one; which, being unable to seize as one, we conceive in two ways: either as one and not one; or as neither one nor not one; or as one and many.

What then — do we speak falsely about it? Or rather: in the differentiation we speak falsely; but in the union even of these terms we speak truly — and yet we cannot, as yet, meet with this truth. Then, seeing all the cosmoi proceeding from the truly hypercosmic abyss, we have called that abyss a hidden cosmos — having gathered up in itself all the cosmoi — as being a cosmos of all the cosmoi; or rather their undifferentiated birth-pang: not yet enduring the cosmic form, and yet simply fore-travailing it. For there is — if it be lawful to say — of the cause of all, and before all things, one birth-pang, common and undifferentiated, of all the whole births that come from it, and of every birth, fore-ranked of the intelligibles; which indeed we call also the unified: the borderland of the cosmoi, as many as there are, and of the plenitudes contained within them — and, from above, of the one exalted simplicity.

Since, then, we conceived the truly hypercosmic abyss to be a cosmos at least to this extent, for this very reason an order also came running in together with this conception of ours — of firsts, and middles, and lasts — though there is no differentiation, not even of this kind, There, from any quarter; for not even in all the cosmoi after it is such a thing present; but from the limit of the intelligibles-and-intellectuals this differentiation first shows itself forth, as is said in the Parmenides. And let the triadic procession be seen, in some other manner, even in the priors; but in the intelligible even this cannot appear; rather, conceive even of this a birth-pang — the division in three that is spoken of There — and, if anything is more uniform still than the birth-pang, conceive it as it were seminally; for the seed is more partless than the birth-pang; or even beyond the seminal analogy; for it is beyond everything that is differentiated in any way whatsoever. Wishing, then, to lay hold of this — the truly undetermined, abysmal embrace of all things — we were ourselves partitioned, and partitioned about it; and fearing the rending of our conceptions — dreadful, and titanic in very truth: a rending not about some partible intellect, but, unholily and most rashly, about that which is in every way altogether impartible — we gladly caught hold of the triad, having run the risk of being dragged down into the last partition; and, contenting ourselves with this fall, we dared to predicate of the intelligible the threefold division — wishing to give rest to our conceptions, which can no longer be gathered together any further, and yet cannot be released from the contemplation of the intelligible, through longing for the archaic causes of the whole of nature.

Nevertheless, purifying these conceptions, and gathering them together as far as may be: first, we do not attempt to ascend thither from chance things, but from the things that have proceeded from There — substance, and life, and intellect. And second, not from the separated properties — as from the composite, or from the unitary — but from the one before the separation, the one before both. For as we said that the unified, simply, is before one and being, so also the life that comes from those is neither composite nor simple, but unified, before both. For thus the life too which we call intelligible is a unified life, before the unitary life and the as-it-were mixed. And thus also the intelligible intellect is neither the unitary one, nor the one counter-divided toward it as vehicle toward ridden — the substantial and composite toward the unitary and simple; but it is the one before both, and before the differentiation. Wherefore the separated intellect is each of the two — the one unitary, the other substantial (for let what is opposed to the monad, according to the Parmenides, be called, more commonly, substance); but the intelligible intellect is neither of the two simply: it is intellect simply; for that is the first intellect, from which were differentiated both the first unitary and the first substantial intellect — each being first, yet each, nevertheless, relative to something; while that one was first simply. And so too the simply life, relative to either separated one — the one separated into the unitary and the substantial — is life simply, and first. And substance, in the same manner, before either particular one, is substance simply; for according to the both-together, the one before either assuredly is; and not these only, but also the things within these, and the things differentiated from these, are all gathered up There according to the both-together: for all things are, but intelligibly, says the Oracle. Why, then, is it not also divided into all things, analogously? Or because, in truth, it is not divided even into these; yet all things are There, in the undifferentiated manner; and if something must needs shine forth There, the firsts would shine forth rather. And these would be ready, for the analogy at least: whatever things are most generic, and most simple, and most divine, and first among the things proceeding from the intelligible; for they would not have shone forth first, unless There also, in the birth-pang, they had been projected before the others — not according to any greater differentiation of themselves from one another (for they are unified most of all things), but according to their own highest perfection, a perfection in a certain manner intelligible, and for this reason sufficing to con-subsist with the intelligible, and to shine forth along with it — and not to be hidden beneath the coruscation of That, nor con-fused by the union of That — inasmuch as they themselves are substantified in being all-but unified, and, through their likeness toward it, suffer from the intelligible nothing that would gather them away.

And third upon these we bring a further purification of our conceptions, when we behold substance There, and life, and intellect: it does not stand with differentiation, as these names would suggest, but according to the one nature of the unified, projecting itself toward itself alone, according to the seeming descent. For, being one, it is everywhere itself, as Parmenides presents it — intelligible through and through, and undifferentiated; and, as in a whole that is undifferentiated, the whole was constituted out of a first bound, and a middle, and a last, of the same nature — just as if a man, beholding the nature that is in a substrate body, should see the one part separable, the other inseparable, and the third the middle of both, and yet confess the nature to be one. For the intelligible intellect would be so called not because it thinks, but because it is cause of the one that thinks. And indeed, if it thinks, the thinking too is, as it were, causal; and the life likewise: below is the life properly so called — the one according to subsistence, the composite; the other pre-taken according to property, the unitary; but the intelligible life is according to neither; for it is before both — but as the birth-pang of these. And so too it must be said of substance: that according to cause, or birth-pang, or union it possesses substance undifferentiated — this also pre-existing. The division itself, then, is an appearance of the division of the things begotten from There; while the very existence of the intelligible is the unified, and the undifferentiated, and everything of that kind. But of these things a little later also.

Chapter 106 — The Intelligible Cannot Make the Outward Procession, Which Does Not Even Proceed Inwardly; the Inner Multitude Only Multitude — of the Race of the Unlimited, the Much, and the Chaos-Like; Flee Headlong: Not Intellect but As-It-Were Intellect, Not Procession but As-It-Were Procession · pp. 335–336

But let us return to the point from the beginning: that the intelligible cannot make the outward procession — it which does not even proceed inwardly; so that it is of a nature to bring forth neither a participated multitude nor an unparticipated one — being single-form, and undifferentiated. Neither, then, is the inner multitude a multitude of forms, or of parts, or of elements — it which is not even a multitude in this way, as a multitude of certain things, but only multitude; nor is it the same as a multitude of things divided, and simply composed out of certain things; it is not of such-and-such things, but of unified things — things of that famous race: of the unlimited, and the much, and the chaos-like; wherefore it has also been called an unlimited multitude, as in the Parmenides — as if he had said also that its one form is a limited one. For as it changed over from the first principle — having become unified instead of one — so it varied also from the second: unlimited instead of unlimitedness, and one form instead of the manifold one — having become a multitude. For as it became unified from the One, so it became multiplied from the simply many; and its one-and-many it has gathered up into one nature: a nature gathered out of the two principles, and having gathered within itself the whole procession of the things after it and subsisting from it — above all according to their most generic differentiation, which has appeared as substance, and life, and intellect; of which, wishing to see the gathering There, we see, in place of that, the differentiation that comes from There. One must therefore not dwell upon it, but flee headlong — positing That not intellect, but as-it-were intellect; nor life, but as-it-were life; nor substance, but as-it-were substance; nor procession at all, but as-it-were procession.

Chapter 107 — Monad and Cosmos the Same There — the Truly Hypercosmic Abyss; the Differentiation That Refuted Itself; the Fragments of Gold; Plato's False Hypothesis and What It Accomplished; As-It-Were Forms, As-It-Were Parts, As-It-Were Elements; the Same Rides Upon All and Is Exalted Above All · pp. 336–339

And perhaps the procession that is imagined in whatever manner must be gathered into one — being the same within and without. For the intelligible and unified, according to its one nature, is both a monad — if it is fitting to call the uncircumscribed union of the intelligible a monad — and would in turn be a cosmos, if one must name the unified a cosmos — and, in real truth, the hypercosmic abyss. For it is not as in the case of intellect and life and substance, where the first substance is one thing, and the multitude differentiated from it another. There the both-together is called a substantial cosmos; and life is one, and many after the one — and the cosmos is at once the one life and the many; and intellect likewise — the first, and those partitioned from the first; and the intellectual cosmos is the one together with the many. Not so does that nature stand, the unified: rather, its multitude being con-sown within it, and not having stood apart into monad and number, the same has been established as at once monad and number; so that it would be the same thing — at once the whole cosmos, all and whole; not differentiated into whole and all, but these also as one; and the same would be one — what seems to be a multitude both within and without; and since the inner belongs to the monad, the inner and the outer are the same; for monad and cosmos are the same There. And in the same way, forms and parts and elements are the same There; for whole, and all, and the blend of the elements are the same; for none of these has been determined off There, nor anything else at all — but the One Being alone, and this unified.

But where Parmenides treats it as undifferentiated — one and being — he means it to be one name only, and one showing; where as being-differentiated, he says that the one and the being are its parts; and where as differentiated, an unlimited multitude — even if, always, the one runs together with the other. For the differentiation of the unified came to be into a one-ment, according to its own limit; so that not even the differentiation that showed itself There was able to undo the nature of the unified; rather, having made the attempt, it refuted itself in the argument as being no differentiation; for it unified rather than differentiated — or rather, it unified the more part, rather than differentiated it. At any rate, it showed the fragments of the unified to be unified — so that they are not fragments; neither, then, is it a differentiation — of which no work at all appeared in the intelligible, save the confirmation of the union. For the very things it seemed to divide, it brought back into the same union — as if a man, wishing to divide the form of gold, should find the divided parts also being no less gold; the division, then, has come to be of the quantity only, and not of the gold according to its form; but There it is of the unified only; for there is no quantity There, nor anything else beside this one nature.

But it is plain that Plato, wishing to indicate that it is indivisible, supposed a division, and found it without issue — or rather, found it to have accomplished some great thing: for it indicated the undifferentiatedness of the unified, and its remaining in the same manner even at the extremes — there where it would seem most of all to be differentiated from itself — according to the appearance pre-taken toward differentiation, or rather toward indication; and it was for this that he gave subsistence to the lying hypothesis.

Therefore the seeming fragments of the unified must not even be called forms, but as-it-were forms; nor properly parts, but as-it-were parts. And this indeed he established for us plainly, by bringing in again, somewhere below after the intelligible, the whole and the parts — after the number — making that very thing clear: that the parts and whole above were spoken of in some other manner; and by setting the multitude before the number in the unified, he is plainly conceiving this multitude as undetermined, before every determination. It is not, then, as-it-were composed out of certain things; nor yet is this multitude continuous; for the continuous comes after the determined; so that that multitude is unified — and not divided even into the first multitudes; but, as I have said many times, it is an unlimited and chaos-like multitude. Thus, then, the elements There also — as-it-were the severals differentiated from their proper monads — are even these as-it-were elements; for it has not been determined in any manner into partial and element-like differences, nor yet blended together; it has been unified before all differentiation; so that both the breadth There and the depth are wholly undifferentiated — to speak according to actuality and according to truth; but as in potency, and as according to analogy, let there be both breadth and depth, either of them gathered up equally — not into a blending, but into all-complete union.

What, then, I was just now saying: the inner and the outer multitude show themselves as the same in the intelligible. As, then, no intellect could go forth outside the whole intellectual world-order — for every intellect would be contained within it — and as no soul outside the psychic — for she too would be contained in her proper world-order — so also nothing goes forth outside the intelligible world-order. Would the intelligible itself, then, be outside it? Not, then, is the participated one thing, and the unparticipated another; for these too — being two multitudes — have been gathered up into one: the simply and unified multitude, multitude however one chooses to call it. For the same both rides upon all, and is exalted above all; for the participated has not been counter-divided against the unparticipated; rather, ranked before the counter-division, it holds the power of the both-together — before both — so as, being the same, to be both participated and unparticipated. For insofar as it is above the participated, it shows itself as unparticipated; and insofar as it belongs to all, it seems also to be participated. But concerning participation, again hereafter.

parts.name: Chapter 108 — The Simply One Separated from Substance by the Middle Otherness; as Many Fragments of Substance as of the One; May Some Mercy Steer the Argument into the Truth Itself; Where Shall We Place the Simply One?; Three Monads Together — the One, the Otherness, the Substance · pp. 339–341

lines.text: Chapter 108 — The Simply One Separated from Substance by the Middle Otherness; as Many Fragments of Substance as of the One; May Some Mercy Steer the Argument into the Truth Itself; Where Shall We Place the Simply One?; Three Monads Together — the One, the Otherness, the Substance · pp. 339–341

Now let us consider again concerning the simply One — I mean the one separated from substance according to the otherness that appeared in the middle — whether it must be posited, and, from it, an unparticipated multitude. For the participated is the many henads, from which are hung the many substances, so called in the more common manner; for Parmenides says that there are as many fragments of substance as of the one. But before this there must be another multitude — someone might say — the unparticipated; and the simply one before the multitude. For if the many henads are, there must necessarily be one before the many — the simply henad of that kind; for the unified is not henad only, but also substance, even if it is before both; and the One called beyond the unified is a one of such a kind as that unified is; for this is the principle of all henads and of all substances alike; whereas we are seeking a simply one which leads henads only — as we have the simply substance which leads the substances, and life likewise, being the first principle of all lives, and the simply intellect, monad of the many intellects. For if the one monad is substantial, another vital, another intellectual, each has something proper, and something common; whence, then, comes this common one in them all, if not from the common cause? And this will of necessity be supposed the simply one.

Further: the simply soul is hung from a particular intellect, and not from the simply intellect; and the simply intellect from a particular life, but not from the simply life; and the simply life, accordingly, from a particular substance, but not from the first. Thus, then, the simply substance also will show itself as the vehicle of a particular henad, and not of the simply one; but before the particular henad there must be the simply henad; for the unparticipated is always simply, while the participated is never simply. And if the unified, being differentiated, makes two, it ought to make the simply being and the simply one — or a particular each; for they happen to be of like rank in the union; and if we say that the one is simply, assuredly these too will be begotten simply. Persuasive, then, is the advocacy of the hypothesis; yet I do not think the matter stands so; for great also is the counter-pulling surmise; and may some Mercy, taking pity upon us, steer the onset of the argument into the truth itself.

First, then, it is better to run the risk together with Plato, who, straightway after the One Being, makes the One and Substance counter-arrayed in two columns. But perhaps, someone will say, he opposes the simply one to the simply substance, even if he yokes the particular one to her? Yet he says that substance has been minced into just as many fragments as the One. Shall we then set the simply one in front of the simply substance? Further: that unparticipated multitude, being attached besides, will not leave the fragments of substance and of the one equal in number. But the greater evidence is this: in the unified — right at the beginning of the second hypothesis — he supposes the One to participate substance, and Being to participate the one. And if, in the unified, they counter-participate each other, as appears, then assuredly, when differentiated, they will counter-participate each other also — so that the One is called substantial, and the being henized. That the foregoing, then, was not spoken according to the judgment of Plato is plain from these things.
But come, let us also attempt, from the matters themselves, to advocate the contrary argument. First, then: where shall we place the simply One?

For not in the intelligible — for that was the unified; nor in the intelligible-and-intellectual — for the of-a-certain-sort substance holds that place, according to the Socrates of the Phaedrus. Wherefore Plato also seems to me to take care, many times, not saying substance simply, but the really being — and showing it to be really being — the substance counter-divided against the one. But perhaps someone might say that, just as the intellectual world-order and the psychic each contain a multitude together with the simply — both the participated and the unparticipated — so also the intelligible-and-intellectual will establish its own summit together with the simply and the unparticipated multitude. But we cannot suppose many gods before the otherness; and the otherness, together with the henad, showed forth the substance.

And if this otherness herself is to be unparticipated before the participated one, and to have an unparticipated multitude, there will be a gathering of many more gods before substance. And if we set against the One not only the simply one but also the simply many, there will be an unparticipated procession of these many also — as it were certain many manynesses after the one. And how is it not necessary to set the simply many over against the simply one? But let these many be, as it were, a power or fertility of the One — yet the things There are already ranked apart; so that the many too will be another henad, as-it-were many-making. And perhaps that much-hymned otherness is herself the principle set against the One? But she is set also against substance; for they would then say that there are three monads together: the One, the Otherness, the Substance.

Chapter 109 — From the Manyness as from the One; the Unitary and the Substantial in Every Rank — Each a Particular, the Both-Together Simply; All Things Wound Off from the Intelligible; the Grades of the Supersubstantial; the One Most Properly Supersubstantial of All · pp. 341–344

But concerning these things it is no wayside task for an argument that seeks precision; yet this much the argument will demand: that, as from the One, so also from the Manyness there proceed many gods, both unparticipated and participated — if indeed there is a simply many. And how is there not, if there is the simply one? And how will the One beget a multitude outward, having nothing multiplied within itself, inasmuch as it is simply one? But neither are the many determined in any way within themselves, as has been shown before; that nature too is one, and itself many-making. And if someone says that the many belong to the One as the elements belong to the elementated, not even so will the one beget according to the many; for either of them is undetermined and unmultiplied, without procession both within and without — so as to speak of a like-formed procession even of a proper multitude.

Apart from these things: the one substance is composite, the other simple; and the latter is unitary, while the former is unified in a certain way, as by commixture. But if either is a substance of a certain sort, what then is either substance? The simply substance, accordingly, is the both-together before both. And life likewise: the simply life is that unified one; and intellect in the same way. Is then soul also the one unitary, the other substantial? Either is a such-and-such, and a particular. And body likewise:

the unitary, which makes the encosmic god; and the substantial, hung from the bodiform one — so called by pre-taking of the bodiform property — and either is a particular; even if of these too the simply subsistence pre-exists, according to the both-together before both, in the intelligible. Or rather, no wonder: for That is all things, but intelligibly; and this according to one union; wherefore the intelligible is said, even by the philosophers, to be the simply substance; and as from the simply and before-all One all things are begotten, so from the intelligible all things are wound off. Everywhere, then, there is the one and that upon which it rides: the one of each pair a particular, and either a such-and-such; while the both-together is the simply.

And if these things are well said, the simply Being will be the unified — which is also all being; and the simply One above the unified — for it too is supposed all One. And after the simply One and the simply Being, the particular henads and the particular substances are separated, and again co-ranked with one another as carrying and ridden, or as participating and participated; while above, these too were undifferentiated, in the intelligible. What then — is that simply One, as it were, a monad of the lower many henads, and the simply Being of the substances? Or was either of them cause of all things — and not the one of henads only, and the being of substances only? For otherwise we shall need yet another substance, the one common to all things. Or must we say that the simply One is Being neither in subsistence nor in property; and posit that the simply Being is One neither in property nor in subsistence; but that, by whole existence alone, the one is One, and the other Being? Wherefore, in justice, the one must be hymned as simply One, the other as simply Being; and this is that simply one over which our conceptions hover before the many henads; and this simply Being we claim to be before every being.

After these the otherness, appearing, separated them, and gave subsistence to the such-and-such particulars after the simplys — not being of that nature, but as it were images of it. For supersubstantial is also the participated one — but as above the substance that participates it: the substance by subsistence, counter-divided against the substance that is unitary by property alone. Supersubstantial too is the unified — but above either substance, the one by property and the one by subsistence. Supersubstantial too are the One and its many — the two principles — but above the simply substance, the one before both; and through the simply one, this is also the simply supersubstantial. Nay more, the One itself: in the one sense, as above the mixed unified, we call it supersubstantial according to subsistence; in the other, as above either mixed — the one by subsistence and the one by property, which the substantial henad pre-took; for That is one before both, higher and simpler than every one that is yoked to the participating mixed; for it is not simple as against some composite, nor yet composite by property, but before both — simple and incomposite. And the One — the one principle — is most properly so of all, because it is above even the unified that is before both, taken according to the both-together; since the unified is this firstly and most of all; and second is the mixed by property; and third the mixed by subsistence — which should rather be called a commixture of elements, if indeed both it, and the unitary mixed before it, are unified; from which, as from a whole, hangs that which comes after it, and that again from its own monad; for the participant always shares the name of the participated according to each property.

Chapter 110 — If One Must Dare to Declare It: from the Simply One Grows Out the Con-Generic Unparticipated Multitude — the Intelligible Race of the Gods, the Hidden World-Order Hymned by the Gods; the Unturned First Principle Kindled from Herself Only the Unparticipated Generation; the Triad an Indication Only of the Multitude · p. 344

If, then, one must dare to declare it — at once toward a more precise indication of what we are saying concerning nature and analogy, and at once toward the satisfaction of this truly much-laboring conception of ours — I would say that from the simply One, the first cause of all things, there grows out a con-generic multitude, the unparticipated; and that most of all assimilated to it is the intelligible race of the gods, remaining in the unity of That — and for this reason unified both toward itself and toward That — the hidden world-order accompanying us in our account; in which the gods have hymned it as undifferentiated, and as hypercosmic, ranked above all cosmic good order; but that it produces a participated multitude no longer. For this sensible heaven too, though the supra-heavenly cosmos produces it, somehow produces the multitude of the gods as participated only, and beneath the moon — but it does not produce an unparticipated one; for neither was the begetter himself the participated one. The unturned first principle, accordingly, begetting, begets all things indeed; but she kindled from herself only the unparticipated generation of the gods, holding it together into one union and one nature. And in another way too it was needful that, between the principle exalted in every way and above all things, and the principle that has its out-growing multitude both unparticipated and participated, there should be the intelligible principle, to which one multitude only is yoked — the unparticipated; such as we say the race of the intelligible gods to be. For the intelligible is One — and beheld, again, threefold: itself remaining in itself according to the One; itself, in itself and from itself, somehow proceeding according to the triad; and its triad is not a differentiation of its substances, but an indication only of the multitude — how much, and of what kind, has been unified in the intelligible.

Chapter 111 — The Hypotheses of the Ancient Theologians — the Chaldaean Most Mystic of All; Three Triads from the Theurgists, Taught by the Gods Themselves; Orpheus from Chronos to First-Born Phanēs; Plato's Three Conclusions; the Theologians Hand Down the Generations of the Gods Themselves, Not of the Vehicles; the One as Father, the Many as Power, the Unified as Paternal Intellect · pp. 344–349

But since we have at long last barely brought these matters to their completion, come, let us also survey the hypotheses of the ancient theologians — how one might understand them according to these philosophic conceptions we have set forth; and first the one confessed to be the most mystic of all, the Chaldaean. For this one seems, artlessly, to answer back most of all against our surmises — surmises which yearn, as far as may be, to gather the intelligible also into one union. For the theurgists hand down to us three triads There, taught by the gods themselves; nay, the Egyptians also, and the Phoenicians too, produce a great generation of gods in the intelligible — as a little later we shall relate. And what of the divine Orpheus? Does he not give subsistence to many gods, from Chronos down to the first-born Phanēs? And the philosopher most honored among us, Plato himself — does he not conclude three conclusions upon the One Being? Which is the same as to say: does he not hand down three intelligible divine ranks, differing from one another? So that it must be inquired how the gods, and the men near-sown of the gods, understood these things when they handed them down.

To begin, then: how have the gods delivered the intelligible triads to the theurgists? Three members, as the newer philosophers systematize it, belong to each triad: limit, the summit; the unlimited, the middle; and substance — intellect — the last; so that there are two henads, and one monad of the triad, substantial and composite. But first it is a thing to wonder at, that two henads should be participated, while that which participates is one — insofar as it has been substantified. Next: why is the limit a henad, and the unlimited, again, another henad — this one Power, that one Father — while the third, the paternal Intellect, is not himself also a third henad? For intellect too ought to begin from a henad; and life likewise, or substance also. Of course they themselves, among the intellectuals, rank the unitary intellect in front of the substantial; the same thing, then — and with far more justice — ought to have been done in the case of the intelligibles. But the theologians, whose systems they expound, hand down to us the generations and the ranks not of the vehicles, nor of the things that have proceeded from the gods, but of the gods themselves.

If, then, we hear the intelligible ranks, and the intellectual, and the hypercosmic, and the encosmic, handed down as ranks of gods, why in the world do we claim that, in the case of the intelligibles alone, the things that come from the gods are mixed in among the gods themselves? And if they say Father, or Power, we hear them as henads; but if paternal Intellect, we pass over to another kind. And yet what shall we do when the paternal Intellect is said to produce the triadic world-orderings — iynges, connectives, teletarchs — the intellectual threefold divisions, and all the cosmic ones? Shall we then derive the henads from the mixed and composite intellect, and make the superior from the worse? — as if one should derive the souls from bodies, or the intellects from souls. Or shall we suppose the iynges and the connectives and the other gods to be not unitary, but substantial? But then we shall speak against both our own selves and the gods. And if, in Orpheus, the first-born god, who bears the seed of all the gods, leapt forth first from the egg and ran upward — what device is there to expound the egg as Being, and yet to hymn as a god the first-born who leapt forth from being? And how does it stand to reason to suppose substances twofold, and lives likewise — or, failing that, intellects and souls: the one set unparticipated, the other participated — and yet to suppose all the henads participated; among whom, most of all, the unparticipated was fitting?

But on this showing we shall not make the triads thus; rather, each is a triad of three henads, from the last of which we shall hang the substance — as once seemed good also to our own guide, when I communicated to him these reflections concerning the third member: so that each triad too is single and unitary, the two henads before the third being unparticipated, and that last one participated. On this scheme, then — since the prior triad, as a whole, always leads the second whole — the unparticipated multitude will be scattered abroad, and not continuous with itself as it is in the other cases; for we should not find a participated soul in the middle of the unparticipated ones — as it were an encosmic among the hypercosmic — nor a participated intellect in the midst of the unparticipated, as it were a hypercosmic one among the intellectuals. How then, after the third henad of the first triad, which is participated, shall the first henad of the second triad be ranked? For whole comes after whole: the second after the first, and indeed the third after the second. Next, the substantial intelligible also will be torn apart along with them, and will not be whole inclined together toward whole, itself toward itself, and unified — if indeed we shall not even rank the successive henads together with one another, but parted asunder by the unparticipated. And again: out of three, how do we make one triad from three monads unlike in form — some unparticipated, and some participated? It is like as if a man should make one number out of certain hypercosmic gods and certain encosmic; or out of archic ones and archangelic; or out of these and the azonic.

Besides these things: since the multitude of the unparticipated completes a cosmos — as with souls, as with the intellects — it is plain that, of those too, the unparticipated will fill out one world-order, and the participated another. Which, then, is the intelligible cosmos — the unparticipated one?

And which will the participated number be? Of substance, presumably; yet the cosmos after the intelligible is of life, as we say. Or is the participated one the intelligible? Then what would the one before it be, the unparticipated? For the first cosmos is the intelligible, as we say. And if the both-together is the intelligible, why are not the other cosmoi also taken according to their both-together multitude — the intelligible-and-intellectual, the intellectual, the hypercosmic, the encosmic? Further: if the same property is in the henad and in the substance hung from her — and that henad is paternal Intellect — then this substance too is paternal Intellect. And if the henad fills out the triad according to this property, it is clear that the substance also fills out the same triad according to the same property; for in the other cosmoi as well, the substantial are co-ranked analogously to the unitary. How then are two monads of the triad simple, while the third is double — at once henad and substance? And apart from these things: if the paternal Intellect is a henad, and some substance is hung from him, and these are separated from each other by otherness, then the unified before both is manifest — and it will fall into the midst of the triad, and tear it apart; or else it will be before the triad — I mean even the first triad; and then we shall no longer rank the triads immediately after the one principle, as they themselves wish to say, and as the Oracles bear witness — not the newer men only, but Iamblichus also, and Porphyry; and there will appear, before these, other triads constituted according to the unified — as we shall say very shortly.

Perhaps, then, letting go of this hypothesis also, we must rather suppose the other: that the third is neither the one, nor the being, nor the one together with the being yoked to it, but the unified before both — ranked according to the paternal Intellect; and, if you will, according to the Mixed of Plato — yet intelligible, and supersubstantial; and if again you will, according to the Being of the philosophers — that Being, at least, which is undetermined toward one and being alike, and beheld before both. For That is the simply substance, as we were saying; and it would be mixed from the two principles before it; for the unified is one and not one — and, insofar as not one, multiplied. This character, then, comes to it from the second principle; while its being-unified comes from the first. Having proceeded, then, from both at once, it is com-blended and mixed. But since the principles are not determined off from one another, but subsist more excellently than according to all determination — for it is from the second that the determinative and differentiative manner flows away, and not immediately after her — the unified also was undetermined, both in itself and relative to those principles. For if unified, then also in every way undifferentiated; for these reasons, then, That must be posited neither composite, nor com-blended, nor elemented, nor from elements — save by some analogy, for the sake of clearness and of a certain indication, when our conception yearns to lay hold, most dimly, of the truth that is impracticable and truly beyond nature.

But it is simply unified, and simple altogether. For the One was supposed as the very withdrawal from all things; and the many, as the all of the One; and the unified — which a man might with good likelihood call, and surmise to be, the first one-all — as what for a while was the One; then this stood apart into its own unlimitedness, as into a kind of chaos; for it was limit alone, and the aether of all things; but the chaos, having stood together and come forth as one — as at once limited and unlimited according to one simplicity, and indicating this nature — has become a kind of one, ample on every side, in place of the ungraspable principles. This third One, then, after the second and the first, we call the unified — as unlimitedness turned back toward the limit, and as it were struck sideways; or rather, a third principle, standing as something out of both — and before both: before both of the two below, as being neither of them according to the simply; and out of both of those above, as again not according to the simply; so that it is the same toward either pair — but toward those above, as third; toward those below, the determined ones, as first. This triad, then, comes to be: the One as Father, and the many as Power, and the unified as paternal Intellect.
