lines.text: Chapter 112 — How Will He Produce the Three Triads? — Tripling the Simply One; the Powers Are Three and the Fathers Three; No Number Among Those; Which Cosmos Is the Intelligible-and-Intellectual?; the Iynges, the Connectives, and the Teletarchs Assigned to Their Orders; Time the Image of Aiōn · pp. 349–351

But if someone should suppose it thus, how will he produce the three triads? For he will need to triple both the simply one and the simply many; neither of them, then, will be simply; for the simply is everywhere one. Let the unified, indeed, be threefold within its single-form character; but how the simply one is to be also threefold is difficult even to feign. Nay, even the unified — if one makes it into monads, it will be dis-spanned from itself; for the powers are three, and the fathers three. And apart from these things, how shall the first and the second and the third be ranked? For together with the whole first triad there will be the unified also, before the second and the third father. And how could there be any number at all among those — whether in the wholly unified, or, what is harder still, in the things before the unified? There is, then, neither monad nor triad there. And again, the number will be made of unlike-formed members — if indeed it is composed of limit and unlimited and mixed (or being), or of Father and Power and paternal Intellect.

But, to leave all these things aside: the intelligible cosmos being constituted in these, which cosmos will come after it as the intelligible-and-intellectual? And which is the intellectual? For this last must be set according to the intellect in subsistence; and the one before it, according to the life in subsistence; the intelligible, then, we shall posit according to the substance — the one we call substance by subsistence. He, then, who is according to the unified — the one before substance and life and intellect — would not be intelligible, but above the intelligible. What, then, would that one have been called? Perhaps the simply cosmos — both without difference, and gathering up the others in common. But even if a man should grant this, which would the intelligible be? Plainly, it would concern the really being substance, as Plato says — the one we called, in what went before, the summit of the intelligibles-and-intellectuals. But this was the principle of the being-differentiated; and the being-differentiated was life; of life, then, this is the principle — and not of substance, nor of the undifferentiated, which we said the intelligible to be, but of the being-differentiated, which for us was the intelligible-and-intellectual.

But even if one lets this too pass, how, we shall ask, shall we bound the intelligible-and-intellectual — and how far does it reach? For who the pure intellect is, is manifest — and that from him the intellectuals begin; it remains, then, that the connective world-order, together with the teletarchic, make up the middle. And what is the triad of the middle? The teletarchs, according to the Oracle, are comprehended together with the connectives; and the connectives themselves are three — just as, before the connectives, the iynges, occupying the intelligible substance, as has been said. And perhaps one might assign to these the intelligible — even the really being substance — because of its gathering character, and because it is gathered together most of all; and to the connectives, the intelligible-and-intellectual, even the first life; for it is the proper work of life to hold together — preserving the differentiated and eidetic subsistence, and at the same time proceeding along with its differentiation; for the continuous signifies both dis-stancing and partition, and, at once, the holding-together and union of the parts; and besides, according to the hypothesis customary with the philosophers, this manner is agreed to display the very prime of life. And perhaps the time that consorts with this heaven is an image of the Aiōn that consorts with that heavenly one, and measures its revolution — since this heaven also is assuredly the truest image of that heaven; and it is plain which is image of which. And for this reason, as it seems, the first intellectual intellect both differentiates himself from the Father, and partitions that one relative to himself — because life too is partitioned by the differentiation of the forms.

And one to whom it pleases to say these things might say that the intelligible is beheld in the monad alone of the iyngic nature; and the intellectual tribe in the triad of the world-leaders — or, as the philosophers divide it, of the pure intellect, and the life-generating, and the demiurgic; while the middle plenitude, the intelligible-and-intellectual, is beheld fittingly in a dyad; for the dyad is vital, and rejoices in the processions that step out least far from their proper monad. And what is the middle dyad? The connective nature and the teletarchic: the latter determining the holding-together into beginning and term, and into the ranks between, of necessity; the former making continuous, and binding tight into one, the firsts and the middles and the lasts. Perhaps, then, as I said, a man might also order matters in this way, using such reasonings.

Chapter 113 — I Am Wary of Counterfeiting the Ancestral Hypothesis, Which Pleased Not Only the Most Renowned of Men but the Gods Themselves; In the Footsteps of Iamblichus's Much-Beholding Judgment; Not Linen to Linen; the Really Being Substance Beheld by the Steersman Alone; the Summit of Life Wishing to Be Substance; the Flowing and Seething That We Call Life · pp. 351–355

But I am wary of counterfeiting the ancestral hypothesis — which pleased not only the most renowned among men (for no one of the philosophers, up to this day, has supposed otherwise), but the gods themselves. For Orpheus, the theologian of the Greeks, made Phanēs the first who is beheld by the gods — above all by the intellectual gods, among whom is the demiurge also; and the gods who gave out the much-honored Oracles have handed down to us these first triads as intelligible — whose hypercosmic abyss, they announce, the intellectual gods know, even in their intellection. And I should feel shame, too, before the divine Iamblichus, were I to innovate anything in these matters — a man who is the best exegete of divine realities, and above all of the intellectual.

It seems good to me, then, following in the footsteps of his much-beholding judgment, to suppose the intelligible cosmos to be that unified abyss — containing not the really being substance, the one determined over against the one that rides upon it, but the simply substance: neither unitary nor mixed, but only one substance, before either. If, then, any of gods, or any of men, has given the intelligible cosmos its subsistence in substance, let him be heard as speaking of this unified substance — every one agreeing with the speakers thus far, while purifying the substance up into that simply and unified and wholly undifferentiated one. For indeed all those very men who say these things supposed the intelligible in the undifferentiated union of all, and no one disputes about this; and Iamblichus is witness — who furnishes to the intelligible a second union, after the one principle of wholes; and everywhere insists that it subsists about the One; and that it is in every way not to be torn away from the One; and who deprecates every division upon it, or doubling, or dis-stancing — making many objections of this kind against the elder.

If, then, the intelligible is truly unified, what device is there to join to the intelligible world-order the substance that is determined off from the one, and consorts with otherness, and has suffered, in whatever manner, a determination of elements? This is not, as the saying goes, joining linen to linen — it is to gather together, by our discourse, a kind of poetic meeting-of-the-glens, upon the most holy spectacles, artlessly. Let that intelligible, then, be supposed by us now, as from the beginning, in what is wholly and altogether undifferentiated; and in the being-differentiated let the intelligible-and-intellectual stand — as was said then, so now likewise. And in it the otherness begins, and makes the first dis-stancing, of being and of one: the latter standing according to its simplicity, in which it is whatever it is; the former according to the containment of all things — a containment bereft of simplicity, at least in respect of not remaining simplicity, though participating it nevertheless. Whence also that substance is the first elemented; and in it are the first elements; and the first number is There; and further, the first determination. But these things — said many times by us, and by Plato, and by the Oracles themselves — how should they belong to the intelligible?

And if the really being substance is here, and we recognize this substance as being, one cause is the summit-character of the being-differentiated, neighboring upon the undifferentiated, and still preserving safe a gathered form of substance; and a cause also is the comparison with its contrary, which renders the com-blending of the elements better known, when set against the simplicity of that one — as being not one, but rather unified. For as this one imitates the simply One — being a one of substance, while That is all things one — so also the substance, being unified relative to this one, is an imitation of what was called the simply unified, and the all-unified: this substance having been united into substance alone — or better, perhaps, to say com-blended. And upon these things: this substance is apprehended by the substantial knowledge, as the one by the unitary knowledge, and the simply intelligible by the knowledge above either; but we, as we now are, do not use even the substantial knowledge with precision — not even so much of it as reaches to the rational and human soul — but something dimmer still than this, and at a still greater distance. With good likelihood, then, the intelligible does not strike upon us; for neither does the unitary, which is seated above substance; for to see this also belongs to divine knowledge; whence we announce the highest of the things we intellect as the intelligible, and, as substance, the really being. For Plato also, leading the souls up as far as this place, supposes the being substance to be in this region, and beheld by the steersman of the soul alone — unless indeed he intimates, through saying really and being substance, that it participates also another intelligible substance lying above it; as Proclus too thought fit to understand him.

As, then, the heaven is intelligible not simply, but relative to something — for this too seems good to the philosophers — so also this substance is intelligible not simply, but relative to something: holding the first place, in the account of substance, of the vital world-order. For this substance is a substance com-blended out of elements; and every blending is somehow vital, since it is also natural — whether it be by nature, or come to be afterward, even if at the first it were constituted by art. And if we said that it is proper to life to be roused toward differentiation, this substance too would be a kind of life, according to whatever determination of its elements; while the elements themselves, in turn, press on toward union, and are eager, in a certain manner, to con-fuse the determination; for the whole elemental nature is of this kind. For these reasons, then, it settles back again into substance; but, to speak more truly, it is the summit of life — wishing to be substance rather than life — just as the completion of life has been eager to be intellect rather than life. And what wonder, if the summit of life gives the semblance of substance rather? — seeing that the summit of the intellectuals also shows forth the intellectual substance, and is intelligible, as within the whole intellectual world-order.

What then — do we not also suppose in the intelligible a life, the simply life, and intellect likewise; and indeed, first There, the simply substance — so that the simply substance is not alone the intelligible, as we were just now saying? And in general: if, after the simply intellect that is There, there is the intellect by itself — the one that thinks, and is intellect in its own right; and likewise, after the simply life, the unified one, there is the life here that is by itself, counter-differentiated toward intellect; then there must also be a substance by itself, counter-divided toward life — not being the summit of life, but another kind. Or it must be said again: the one is undifferentiated, the other being-differentiated, the third differentiated. And in this last all things have been established as differentiated — the others, and the one, and the being; for either is, as it were, a whole form — the one unitary, the other substantial; and every form has its proper circumscription, as intellect does. But in the middle all things subsisted as being-differentiated, beginning from the one and the being; wherefore nothing here is circumscribed — yet neither is it unified; rather it has suffered, as it were, a certain pouring-forth, able neither to remain, nor to be turned back into circumscription; there came to be, accordingly, a kind of flowing and seething — which we call life. But in the wholly undifferentiated, both the others, and the one of the being, are undifferentiated; whence it is wholly unmoved, having not even one seething, nor any flowing — so that it is substance only. So that, according to truth, these things have been ordered thus, and stand apart by bounds of this kind.

Chapter 114 — There Is Nevertheless, by Analogy, in Each All Things; the Very Flower of Substance; Life the Being-Differentiated Unmixed; Where the One Stands Thus Toward the Being, There the Proper Kind Subsists Simply; to Be Substance Is Just This — to Be Unified · pp. 355–357

There is nevertheless, by analogy, in each all things: as, in the undifferentiated whole, the most undifferentiated; and the being-differentiated, as in That; and the differentiated, as in a nature wholly unified. Wherefore also in the whole substance there is, as substance, the very flower of substance; and life, the middle; and intellect, the third — yet simply life, and simply intellect, because in the unified alone has the being subsisted undifferentiated from the one. And again, in the whole that is being-differentiated — being such as it is — the summit is most of all substance — the substance we so call when we counter-divide it against the henad — showing forth indeed something vital also, in keeping with its being the summit of the very being-differentiated, yet being differentiated least of all, and therefore most of all displaying beforehand the nature of substance; while the middle, at its prime in the being-differentiated, is, precisely in this respect, properly and solely life: mastered neither by the undifferentiated nor by the differentiated, but being only the being-differentiated, unmixed. And in the differentiated whole, again: in its beginning the undifferentiated somehow shows forth — wherefore this is the intellectual substance; in its midst, the being-differentiated — wherefore the intellectual life has its nature here; and in its final bounding, the differentiated — where the intellectual intellect is at his prime, and for this reason became commensurate with the world-ordering of matter.

These things having been thus determined many times over: if the doubter should demand an undifferentiated life — taking the one from the being — and an intellect of the same kind, he has them, in the manner in which these too are of a nature to be in the unified; yet let him know that he is overstepping the stated determinations; for neither can life possess the being which she is, unless the one be differentiated from the being; nor intellect, unless these be, before all things, differentiated. So that, by the most proper account: where the one stands thus toward the being, there the proper kind subsists, simply. If the substance is unified — and it is plain that then all the rest in them are unified also; if it is being-differentiated, life — for all things have now been moved toward differentiation; if it is differentiated, intellect — for now in him the rest also have been circumscribed. Simply, then, is this intellect; and simply this life; and simply this substance.

How then did we say, in what went before, that there is in this manner a life before both, and an intellect before both — each before the differentiation of the being and the one — just as we said substance is what answers to the both-together; and again a certain substance, the separated one, as we said life and intellect are — the one displaying the one, the other the being? Or these things also hold the truth aforesaid; but now, speaking with precision, we say: substance is a nature unified, and worthy to be ranked immediately after the One; and to be substance is just this — to be unified; this, then, is the simply substance. And a certain one, and relative, is whatever is spoken after these — the vital, the intellectual, the psychic, or, if one wishes so to call it, even the enmattered substance. And life simply is the one beheld in the being-differentiated; and if there is some intellectual life, or eidetic, or psychic, or enmattered, each of these would be relative, and a certain one. Likewise, then, intellect simply is the one beheld in what is first differentiated; and the one after him, whoever he may be, is a certain one, and relative. And as the life in the differentiated order is relative, and is as in that order, so too the substance in the being-differentiated: it is as in this order, and is a relative substance. Not, then, before the one and the being is the One Being that is before both; for then the life before both would have to be before either life as well; and concerning the intellect one might raise other difficulties of the same kind.

Chapter 115 — Substance Before Both, Intellect Out of Both, Life with Both; the Reversion of Intellect into Itself Comes with Otherness; the First Life, in Whom Is the Differentiation Eldest of All; the Animal Defined — a Substance Living and Knowing; the Unitary Also Divided in Three · pp. 357–358

Perhaps, then, the doctrine of the philosophers would again be truer: that the intelligible is one leading, and being following, the latter con-unified with the former as much as may be. Or rather it must be said: if they mean it undifferentiatedly, they say the same as we; for it is in life that the being-differentiated begins; but if they mean it as the one riding, and the other ridden, then the two are assuredly differentiated from one another; and this is proper to intellect; and they themselves confess it, since they everywhere hymn, surely, the reversion of intellect into himself; and the reversion into oneself comes about together with differentiation from the others, and with otherness. If, then, substance is to differ at all from intellect, she must of necessity be also undifferentiated. And if she is undifferentiated, and intellect differentiated, then life must of necessity be the being-differentiated. It is not possible, then, for life to be before both, as substance is; for neither can a substance be out of both, taken as two differentiated, or as things being-differentiated — so as to speak simply, and properly.

And perhaps the one is before both — as neither of the two, neither the one nor the being, showing forth in her by itself; and the other is out of both — as out of two that are differentiated, and only then co-ranked together; and the third is with both — as in the middle of these two states, the being-unified and the being-differentiated: still keeping something of the archaic union, yet already showing forth from beneath something of the differentiation also. And this is the first life, and the simply life — because in her is also otherness, and the differentiation that is eldest of all. And indeed these three we are accustomed to noise abroad in the mixed and substantial realm as well — knowledge, life, substance; and again intellect, and life, and substance. And, defining the animal, we say that it is a substance living and knowing — substance being one thing, and life another, and knowledge another; and the unitary is nowhere here; nay, we divide that also in three, after the same fashion, naming a supersubstantial intellect, and a life likewise, and a substance — the substance standing on either side, in the one and in the being.

Chapter 116 — The Ladder from the Soulless Form Upward — Nature Warming Substance into Seething; the Life That Truly Is, Poured Forth More Excellently Than Reversion; the Principles by Nature Nameless, Named from Their Parts; the Nature Remaining in the Untrodden Places, Surmised by Us from Afar · pp. 358–360

How then are we now constrained, positing by our argument that substance is only the undifferentiated of one and of being? Or rather: each of these is said in many ways, and everywhere preserves the same analogy of each toward each. For the last substance — the soulless form — is unmoved by itself. But if this too should be moved naturally, a kind of life comes to be for it — nature herself; who does not allow it to remain undifferentiated, chilled fast upon itself, but warms the substance out into her own activity, rendering it a seething substance; and the more complete life, added on, made the plant; and upon this, sensation made the animal — sensation, which differentiated and articulated life into its proper bound, so that it is separated as far as may be from the others, judging by pain and pleasure toward what is its own. And another substance and life and knowledge is the self-moved: this also a kind of eidetic one, and nothing other than form, in which the being, the living, and the knowing are differentiated from one another, even if blended together in another respect; but so much as is gnostic in the soul stands differentiated, and is differentiative of its knowables according to proper bounds; while so much as is vital grows together toward union out of the differentiation, and is a kind of flowing, ever continuous toward itself; wherefore it furnishes to bodies also a certain holding-together — dimensional, and yet, in some manner or other, real.

And before these is the unmoved substance of intellect, and a like life, and a knowledge holding in the same manner — these too all eidetic; for they are differentiated from one another; but to the gnostic nature this belongs by nature — wherefore this knowledge is first, and the simply: inasmuch as it form-gives intellect, and is form-given, according to the differentiated. But the life in intellect is not simply — because it is a vital form, and not the first and simply life; nor, then, is the substance there simply — far more greatly not; but as-it-were substance, and as-it-were life; while all is intellect, and all belongs to intellect. But before this is the life that truly is — being life only, and not, in addition to this, a form as well; nor circumscribed according to the reversion into herself, but poured forth more excellently than according to reversion. And elder still than she is the substance: which endures no pouring at all, neither the upward flowing nor the downward, but is most firmly compacted, altogether, in the undifferentiated; differentiated neither toward life, nor toward intellect, nor toward any other of the things that have proceeded from her; for neither is she differentiated from what comes after her; rather she stands thus toward both of these: that life is being-differentiated only, while substance, remaining in the undifferentiated, differs by this alone from the things that go forth. These things, then, have been determined somewhere before as well.

But now to the difficulty: whenever we behold substance and life and intellect (or knowledge), we see their eidetic peculiarities counter-divided toward one another, and we take them as three forms — just as if one should take the eidetic one, or the eidetic being, or the limit, or the unlimited: not the first principles, but certain parts taken apart, homonymous with the principles — from which we also name the principles, which are by nature nameless. Thus, I think, we conceive substance also, and life, and knowledge — all of them eidetic, and for this reason of a nature to be named, or defined. And perhaps not even the unmoved ones, but certain self-moved — or, it may chance, even other-moved and opinable ones — we think we must use to conceive and define those as well; whereas one ought not merely to name those homonymously, but rather to indicate them alongside, according to analogy — the supra-eidetic from the eidetic.

What, then, this substance is toward this life, and this life toward this knowledge — that, in the first subsistences, is what the wholly unmoved-toward-differentiation is toward what is being moved into it, and this toward what has been moved. And what has been moved into differentiation is the simply intellect; what is being moved, the simply life; what is unmoved toward it, the simply substance. And the simply intellect and the simply form are the same; but the simply life and the eidetic life are not the same — for the simply life is supra-eidetic; and the substance is, simply, above the eidetic substance and above the vital; wherefore it is simply. So that, from what has now been divided, we are able more truly to determine each simply one, and the certain one that comes after the simply. Let no one, then, demand that the simply ones be such as certain ones characterized by the analogy, and consorting with their own truth; nor let him be led up from the readier conceptions to that manner which is more supernatural than all habituation; but let him hear, when we say substance, and life, and indeed intellect also, the true one — spoken according to indication, from the familiar — of the nature that remains in the untrodden places, and is surmised by us from afar. Yet it is true also — and a thing reaching to the summit of contemplation — to see the three in each, because each is all things: doubling the analogy upward, and using what was indicated before for the indication of others more precise.

But toward the last of the difficulties these things too are perhaps sufficient; and after this, if need be, we shall say something toward it again; and need there assuredly will be, when we inquire where the Animal-itself must be laid away; and one may surmise, even from what lies before us, that — being sated full of life, and holding the second rank after her — it will everywhere be ranked analogously to her; as being, however, the first paradigm.
