lines.text: Chapter 117 — No Number in the Intelligible — What Is the Hymned Ennead?; Not Three Monads, as Iamblichus Also Says; the One That Blossoms Upon the Forms; One, Many, All — Father, Power, Paternal Intellect; the Centre, the Flowing, and the Circumference — More Naturally a Sphere; Let Us Not Count the Intelligible on Our Fingers, but Open the One and Greatest Eye of the Soul; the One Untriaded and Unmonaded · pp. 360–366

Come now, let us also re-examine the other difficulties — whether what they say is anything sound, or rotten. To begin with: we shall say that number is not in the intelligible — neither a number of like-formed members, nor of unlike-formed; for the nature of the determined is not There at all; nor that of the continuous; nor any difference, nor otherness, nor differentiation — in the simply unified, at least. What, then, is the hymned ennead in the intelligible? Does it signify only the all-complete perfection of the triad There? — which, being unable to gather together by our reasoning, we set apart in three: its everywhere-perfect; and its all-containing, which leads forth every multitude; and its generative of every triad, wherever and however subsisting; and its commanding of every procession down to the last; and the unmasterable character of its prolific power; and everything else of this kind — or rather, the unified of all such intuitions, one after-intuition; and this while wishing to conceive of that triad according to indication alone. What, then, is this triad? Not three monads — as Iamblichus also says — but not even the form. For what circumscription could there be in the unified? Is it then the one itself, which is the flower of the form? Yet not even this One — the one that is of a nature to blossom upon some one of the forms, as upon the triad, the form alone, immaterial, beheld without the monads; nor yet, surely, the one upon all the forms together — for that belongs to the differentiated one; so that neither is it the one of the being-differentiated. It would be, then, the one of the undifferentiated triad. But the triad signifies, again, the beginning of the unified, and the middle, and the end — yet these also unified.

Further: the one, taken simply, was not arithmetical, but made plain the one simplicity of all things; and the dyad after the one — the one called undetermined — was not a dyad set upon two monads; rather, through her was made plain the cause of the one, generative of all things; and according to both, he was a Father able to beget all things; and indeed, third from these, the unified — as it were an activity having proceeded from power; and from such a monad, then, and such a dyad, there subsisted a triad having the unified by nature: being a dyad turned back toward the one, and for this reason paternal Intellect. But in saying these things we make three. Or is the Father — being able, and begetting all things after himself — himself the whole triad? The triad, then, is a monad; and a monad that is not the principle of number, but cause of monad and of all number; nor is it in any circumscription, like a form set apart alone, but is the single-form simplicity of all things.

Are the three, then, the same — or other? A triad, or a monad? Or none of these, according to truth? For nothing of such things is There: not sameness, not otherness, not triad, not monad — the monad, I mean, that is set against the triad; for there is no antithesis in the intelligible. Is then the unified the very thing the one is? Or the one, what the many are? Or the many, what the unified is? I shall certainly not say so. How then are the all not three? Because they are none the less one: for the one is many, and the many all; we speak of nothing as one thing and then another. For the one is not one property, but such as all things; and the all are not all in that fashion, but as one; and the many likewise — since the one too is not-one, and the all are many that have been determined. For if earlier we said that the all signify the second principle — as being the all of the One — yet now, shifting a little, we shall say it better: that all and many are not the same; rather, the many, taking determination in addition, became all; for the many, insofar as many, are still unlimited. Therefore the Father is one; and the undetermined power of the One is many; and the Intellect of the Father is all. Further: the all were the many, determined by one according to reversion; and you see that the many stand by nature between the one and the all; and the one is simplicity only, while the all are at once the union of all things. According to the unified, then, intellect was constituted; and as in the intellectual all things are circumscribed according to form, so in the unified all things are gathered up according to one, uncircumscribedly.

A monad, then, is this nature — being simple, and many; for its simplicity is containing of very many things, even of unlimited ones; and further it is all, because its many have been determined by the one — since indeed they were the many of the one. Is it then a monad in its substrate, having three peculiarities? It is we who divide, being unable to comprehend one thing that gathers the three; for in this way, wishing to define the other things also, we say many in place of one — running around the elements instead of the elemented. But as, in those cases, we think fit to behold the form that is before the elements, or that supervenes upon the elements, being led up to it from the elements, so here too, far more greatly, we must let go the determined peculiarities, and lead up to one simple nature, from which the partition of these is partitioned lower down. Let the common of the three, then, be conceived — as of a triad — according to the one of the triad: not the arithmetical triad, but that whole one which we just now gave subsistence to in our discourse, the triad of the supreme principles; since the monad too was not arithmetical, but the monad of all, in which all things are pre-taken — as every number is in the monad.

And, to speak simply: as we use the eidetic for indication of the supra-eidetic, so also the arithmetical peculiarities, as symbols of the numberless and the altogether undetermined. And besides, for the showing forth of what we wish to say — even if we cannot say it — that other image must be taken up: that the one is the centre of all things; and the dis-stancing from the centre is the second principle, being a flowing of the centre; and the surround, the last circumference after the dis-stancing — being a kind of reversion toward the centre — is the paternal Intellect; and the whole is one circle — or, to say it more naturally, a sphere. And it is plain that it is not a form, but a nature more uniform than every form. And what more could one say of it than the very one? For it is this that form-gives that immaterial circle.

And, to say it once for all: let us not count the intelligible upon our fingers, nor touch it with determined conceptions; but, gathering together all our intuitions at once, and closing them — opening the one and greatest eye of the soul, by which nothing differentiated is beheld (for by it is seen not even the one itself, in real truth, but only the unified; and not even this insofar as it is set against the differentiated, but that which has gathered up this also) — with such an eye, then, looking Thither, even if from afar, and as it were from the last things, we shall nevertheless see the intelligible: that it is wholly undifferentiated, and wholly numberless. Save that, even standing so, there will be imaged in us — if one must speak thus — its simplicity, its manyness, its allness; for the intelligible is one many all, so that the one nature is traversed in three ways. And how is the nature one, if one and many? Because the many are the unlimited-in-power of the one. And how one and all? Because the all are the all-holding activity of the one. Yet neither must activity be spoken of as an out-stretching of the power toward what is outside, nor power as an out-stretching of the existence remaining within — for that, again, is to say three instead of one. For, it being one, one name suffices for the showing of those things, as we have testified many times. Are they then without difference? And whence comes this? It is easy to surmise: for we say the principles are three, and next to one another — Father, and Power, and paternal Intellect; but these, according to truth, are neither one nor three, nor one and three at once; it is by us that they must needs be shown through such names and such intuitions — by poverty of those that befit them; or rather, by eagerness for showings that in no way befit them. For as we call it one, and many, and all; and Father, and Power, and paternal Intellect; and again limit, and unlimited, and mixed; so too monad, and undetermined dyad, and the triad constituted out of both of these. And as those, so also these: purifying our conceptions, as far as may be, we disallow that they fit those realities. Let the intelligible triad, then, be called — so far as is possible — a triad in this way: as the one of the triad; and of that triad which seems to be constituted from the three first principles. Concerning that union itself, indeed, we could never say anything that comes near it.

But concerning the order of the three triads: if a man, having set this stated triad according to the one of the intelligible triad — as it would come to be — should see this one also as being all-complete, and as subsisting wholly triadic to itself — the triadic being present even in each of the three monads (for in the numbers also the monads of each are not without difference toward those of the others, but those of the triad are somehow triadic, and those of the tetrad tetradic) — if a man, as I said, should suppose the monads of that all-great triad also to be of this kind, so that these too are not simply monads, but monads of a triad, of their own peculiar manner, perhaps in the one of that triad he would comprehend also the whole procession of the intelligible into three triads, not even thus departing from its proper union. And indeed, in this way, neither will the unified be before the second one — the prior — as the argument seemed to find difficult; for each monad will have the triadic in its own rank, being upon itself; for the one will appear triadic before the others, and the many second, and third upon these the unified; and the whole Father will be co-ranked with the whole intelligible through the whole Power as middle — the one through the one to the one; and again the triple with the triple through the triple; nor indeed will the unified be dis-spanned from itself into three monads; for it remains unified in the same manner, even if it should show forth the triadic within itself; and far more greatly does the one remain — unified — one holding-three; and the Power likewise, even if she should shine forth three-natured.

And how shall the one be triple? Because, being one, it nevertheless presides over the triple of the unified; for let this be a triple unified, as has been said, holding a certain tripleness; but the one turns this tripleness back toward itself, so that the one, according to the one, holds the triple as shown forth within it. And indeed the Power also — inasmuch as she is a dyad — being carried along with the one becomes one-formed; while with the unified she is co-imaged as triple. She is a dyad, then, in the middle of the one and the triad; for the unified, as third, is by nature a triad; while the things before it are such in a more supernatural manner. It is not, then, wonderful, nor hard, to conceive the one as thus triadized: not that it is numbered, or determined, but that it has pre-taken in itself the tripleness of the unified, and that it is one as the triadic in the whole triad. Or — whatever of this kind a man can conceive, let him conceive it rather than a differentiation of the one; unless indeed it be more commensurate to suppose even a certain sub-stepping from it: so that there is both one Father and three — the same being one and three-formed; or rather one, yet showing forth from beneath something triadic also; I mean not what is partitioned in three, but the impartible one of the triad. But if the one is triadic, how is it simply one? — for the argument earlier raised this too, with justice. Or rather: having supposed the one simply, and the many simply, and the all simply according to the unified, out of these simply monads we made, as we thought, the simply triad; so that the triadic also belongs to the one simply — insofar as the simply one has pre-taken that whole triad, and was, as it were, initiated into it, and was counted together with the other simply principles, as first principle leading the second and the third. For let the simply one be, in real truth, the numberless — and, if one must speak more plainly, the untriaded and the unmonaded; for it is not even monadic, seeing that it is not even one according to truth, but is so called according to indication alone; and such also is the simply unified; nay, the many too, in the middle of these, are such in the manner called simply — without all determination, and all addition.

Chapter 118 — Three They Must No Longer Be Called; As the Gods Speak to Egyptians, Syrians, and Greeks in Their Own Tongue, So to Men in Human Dialect; the Lightning-Flash About Our Eyes; the Discourse That Disparages Itself; the Rainbow of the Single-Colored Sun; the Triad in the Forecourt of the One in the Philebus; Pre-Appearance, Pre-Cause, Pre-Analogy · pp. 366–369

Three, then, they must no longer be called — as though they had suffered the being-three, when nothing else has shown itself forth There. Save that we, conversing humanly about the most super-divine of principles, cannot otherwise either conceive or name them than thus — constrained as we are to use words concerning the realities that rise up into what is beyond the all, and beyond life, and beyond substance. Since the gods also do not teach us — at times, and some among us — such things about these matters, or about others, as they themselves intellect, nor in the manner in which they intellect; but as they converse with Egyptians, or Syrians, or Greeks, using the speech proper to each — else they would have uttered themselves to them in vain — so also, being earnest to deliver to men what is their own, they will justly use the human dialect; and this is composed not only of such-and-such verbs and nouns, but of intuitions also, answering to these and fitted upon them.

If, then, we even deviate from that truth — for, searching through the intelligible abyss, how great and of what kind it is, we are carried aside toward the things below and partial, drawn along with, or dragged down with, the necessity of our small-fashioned nothingness — nevertheless there is need of the carrying-aside, and of the deviation; for otherwise it is not possible, conditioned as we now are, to conceive anything about them; and we must be content, even from afar, and barely, and most dimly, somehow to touch upon them sideways, or to surmise alongside them some trace — like a lightning-flash suddenly about our eyes; and even if the lightning be roused from somewhere within, from the soul herself — being small, and not shining very much — it nevertheless becomes for us a token, by way of analogy, of that super-brilliant and super-vast one. And this much also in the present discourse must be praised: that it disparages itself, and confesses that it is abashed, and cannot look back against that light — the unified and intelligible.

In this way, then, we speak of the triad There: as signifying an undifferentiated multitude; and of the dyad again, in turn, as the cause of that multitude; and of the monad besides these, as the one itself, which is beyond this multitude. And this is the much-hymned intelligible triad — which, wishing to paraphrase now in one way and now in another, we escape our own notice setting it forth still more variegated in our discourses; and most of all when we make it an ennead: reckoning out its all-completeness, and its commanding of all things from the firsts to the lasts; and, in the third — which is by nature three-formed — beholding the principles before it as in a mirror, imaged triadic, shining down upon his three forms on every side: as, in a cloud holding three mirror-like dimensions, the single-form color of the sun is shown forth as the imaged, many-colored rainbow.

Therefore Socrates also, in the Philebus, not being able to look full against that One, made known instead — for this very reason — the triad ranked, as he says, in its forecourt: assuredly because, gazing upon the unified, he saw the triad glittering in the one ray of the henad. And in general, as with the other things, so also the triad we lead up There according to indication. And as the first principle is a monad, and the second an undetermined dyad, and the third a triad — because this last was beheld according to reversion, and the one before her according to remaining — so also the whole triad composed of these is not, as it seems, a triad of three monads; rather, there is one all-complete union, the same remaining, and proceeding, and turning back; and these not as some three, but as one before the three, having power for the three.

Are the Fathers, then, three — or one? Or rather neither three nor one: above every triad; so that also above the whole one which we counter-distinguish toward these, as one toward two and three. And the Power, accordingly, is neither one nor three; and the Intellects according to the unified likewise; for in the unified the one and the two and the three have not been determined; rather, as the things There are above all determination, so also above the eldest determination of all — and this is the determination of one, and of two, and of three.

But even if it should stand thus — as that nature does stand, according to truth — nevertheless let us lead up to it, for the sake of clearness, and of commensurateness toward men, the most august of the things that have proceeded from it and after it: such as the one, the many, the unified; the Good, the cause of all things; the limit, the unlimited, the mixed; and whatever else is of this fashion; and indeed, of the determined order, the all-complete and what subsists all-completely — the very things which the triad There holds, and the procession of the triad. And all of these, according to subsistence, have their standing after the intelligible; but according to appearance, or cause, or analogy, they are in the unified; and in what is above it, nothing other than pre-appearance, or pre-cause, or pre-analogy — as if a man should descry, in the multitude that is before all number, a certain unarticulated — nay rather, even undifferentiated — pre-subsistence of the numbers, as in the formless matter that of the forms. And at a third step upward, one ascending from the chaos will surmise that these things are pre-taken in the aether of the simplicity of all — insofar as there consorts with it, and belongs to it, both the chaos-like unlimitedness, and the unified, undifferentiated com-paction of all things.

Chapter 119 — Since We Dare to Number the Numberless — How the Division Must Be Made; Each Monad Divided in Three, Lest the Triads Be Scattered; the One Father Who Is Also Power and Intellect; the One Snatching the Principles into His Unspeakable Union; No Seeming Triad Is Truly a Triad — Every Determination Drunk Down in the One · pp. 369–372

But since we do dare, in whatever way, both to number the numberless, and to order what is above all order, and nevertheless to world-order the truly hypercosmic abyss — come now, let us say these very things: in what direction, and in what manner, it must be done. As, then, the intelligible cosmos, and the intellectual, and the intelligible-and-intellectual upon these, happened to be divided in the first instance; and as we then divided each of these three sections in three, according to analogy with the orders that come after, carrying over from these to that one the indication of the differentiation — namely, that as great as the intellectual was in its having-been-differentiated, so great is the intelligible-and-intellectual in its being-differentiated, and as great as this last is in its having-been-differentiated, so great is the intelligible in its own undifferentiated — and in an establishment no less all-full: in this way then, as I said, beholding in that one also the everywhere-perfect, we divided it into Father and Power and Intellect, and each of these we divided further in three again. And how, then? For we divided the Father into three fathers, and the Power into three powers, and the Intellect into three intellects; and then we fitted and co-ordered each to each — the kindred to the kindred, rank answering to rank. Or will the triads in this way be scattered abroad —

if each is to be constituted out of the first and the second and the third, and the first triad will not be whole, nor the second whole, nor the third whole? For each will then contain members unlike in rank, and unlike in form.

And indeed, in the case of the worlds after these, it is not done so: for, the whole iyngic nature being paternal in the middle order, and the connective being of power, and the teletarchic intellectual, we do not fill up each triad out of the three; rather, we divide each nature separately in three, according to form, as far as the whole division: the iyngic into father and power and intellect; the connective into the same; and the teletarchic likewise. So too, then, let us divide each monad of the intelligible triad in three — for instance, the paternal into father and power and intellect; for this one whole is Father; insofar as he is by himself, he is father only; but insofar as the power is carried along with him, and he himself shares in common with her, in a certain manner he becomes power; and insofar as he is father of the intellect, and the intellect is his, in this respect he becomes intellect. Thus, then, even being one, he nevertheless shows forth the triad of his own simplicity. In the same manner the Power also is established as a triad — both remaining by herself, and carried along with either of the extremes. And third in order, the Intellect likewise is tripled: so much of him as has been turned back toward the Father becomes paternal within his own third triad; so much as grows together with the Power is brought to completion as intellectual power; and so much as remains upon himself, unmixed relative to his betters — that much is handed down as the intellect proper of the triad.

And in this way the monads of each triad are like-formed and like-ranked; and in this way also the triads can be gathered up into monads — according to the one beheld in each triad, not according to its multitude. Nay, even these three wholes — monads, as it were — will not be set apart from one another by differentiation; rather, above every monad that is united toward herself, those will be united toward one another: the simply One bracing his own first one-making power upon the principles that are continuous with him up to himself, and snatching them up into his own unspeakable union — whose excess over the union of a monad is so great that even the third from the One, the one we called the unified, even this, by its own nature, and before the unmanageable simplicity of the One, has its standing above monadic analogy. For every monad is a form; or, if not a form, then something determined; or, if not that, then at least the principle of a determined constitution; but the unified is above form, and above all determination, and above all substance beheld according to otherness; and it is not the principle of number, but simply of all things after itself; and it does not hold within itself a multitude of many numbers coiled together, but is wholly numberless and undifferentiated — this very thing alone which is called unified.

No triad, then, that seems to be is, in real truth, a triad; for the three do not remain determined off from one another — the unified, the many, the one; rather, the unified is poured back up into the many, according, at least, to the dominance of the power; and the power — together with that one, when it has been poured abroad into power — is folded back up into the one, letting go her own pouring, and running back up into the simplicity of the One; the one, then, has seized all things, not allowing the determination of the triad to appear, but declaring all things to be the One — just as the power, in her turn, shows even the intellect to be an unlimited chaos, flying in the undetermined of the power. And the intellect — in so far as, by himself, he falls short of the elder principles, by so much only does he appear intellect.

How then is it really a triad? For in every triad the monads are lesser than the whole of it; and yet no monad makes its own triad to vanish — on the contrary, it even helps to constitute it. But here the one is the most masterful of all, and there is nothing before it; so that neither is this whole a triad; for then the many would be before the one. Further: the one even makes the triad vanish; for in it every determination is drunk down. Wherefore in the one, even the so-called triad is one alone; and in the many, even the triad is a dyad — for it is power; while in the unified there would be a certain clear showing-forth of the triad, because it is the first to have suffered both the one and the many; and the triad too is the first number out of one and two — and this is unified-and-multiplied, monadic-and-dyadic.

parts.name: Chapter 120 — Existence, Power, Activity — the Oracles' Names for the Three, as the Great Iamblichus Also Beholds It; Do Substance and Existence Differ? — I for My Part Do Not See Such a Difference; the Father Only Father, Cause of Being but Not Himself Being; Not Even in Potency, but Having Snatched Himself Away Even from Aptitude; the First Powerless and Actless, If It Be Lawful to Say · pp. 372–375

lines.text: Chapter 120 — Existence, Power, Activity — the Oracles' Names for the Three, as the Great Iamblichus Also Beholds It; Do Substance and Existence Differ? — I for My Part Do Not See Such a Difference; the Father Only Father, Cause of Being but Not Himself Being; Not Even in Potency, but Having Snatched Himself Away Even from Aptitude; the First Powerless and Actless, If It Be Lawful to Say · pp. 372–375

Of such things, then, let this be enough for us — for when should we cease, contending with discourse, beyond our nature, toward the intellection of the hymned intelligible triads? Let us turn our thought instead to those inquiries which busy themselves about the very nature of the monads — the paternal, the dynamic, and the one called intellectual. Is it then the case — as the middle one plainly indicates — that this one takes her stand according to power, and is beheld as principle of all powers; and the paternal as existence, of which the power also is said to be; and the intellectual as activity, proceeding from power, and being the activity of the existence? For the proportion which substance holds toward power, and power toward activity — this, one might say, the paternal peculiarity holds toward the dynamic, and the dynamic toward the intellectual. And the principles which different men have wished to indicate through different things — as the Pythagoreans through monad and dyad and triad, or Plato through the limit and the unlimited and the mixed, or we ourselves, earlier, through the one and the many and the unified — this the Oracles of the gods have indicated through existence and power and activity. The Father, at any rate, they clearly name existence; and the power they hand down by no other name either.

But if the Father is existence, and the power the middle, how should the third not both be, and be called, activity? And indeed the great Iamblichus also beholds this matter in this way; and perhaps the intellect too has been named from intellecting — that is, from activity — whatever 'to intellect' may signify: whether the knowing, or the turning back toward the Father, or the longing after him. And perhaps the Father would exist only; while the Power, besides the existing, would put forward also the being-able; and the Intellect, besides these, the activity as well. And such an indication would preserve much of the union of the first principles — if indeed, being three, they are nevertheless united toward one another thus: as power toward existence, and as the activity of the existence. And it is plain that the principles are united toward one another even more greatly than the one nature is toward herself — the nature that exists and is able and acts, being one and three-formed.

Should we then conceive them so — and, taking our start from this third peculiarity, posit the simply substance as the third, which is the unified? How could we say that the Father is sketched according to substance, if indeed substance and existence are the same? Or do they say they are not the same? — rather, existence would be said of gods, and substance of the things hung from them; for thus the philosophers are accustomed, in many places, to distinguish. But even if this were true, the being has not yet been determined off, among those, from the one; nor is the unified a being; nor, then, is the Father the one; but perhaps the Father is as the simply one, and the unified would be the simply being, spoken in another manner — and neither of the two is the one strictly, as has been said often before. And it would be possible to speak thus, if it were true that substance and existence differ.

But as it is, I for my part do not see such a difference: for to be and to exist we say of the same thing — if ever, indeed, we should say that being obtains; for with the ancients this is altogether customary. And if it be urged that being must pre-exist before everything else — before the being-able, and the acting, and the faring-well or being-well, and almost all the others; for in the genera of being also the being leads the others — if, then, for these reasons being rules, and in a certain way stands under (for after the one we conceive the being), then to exist and to be would even so be the same; save that being, as ranked before the others, and as furnishing being to the others, would on this account be called also existing. If, then, substance and existence are the same, and the simply substance is the third, what reason could there be to carry this over to the Father? And does not the paternal peculiarity itself wish to be the cause of being for another — and not to be itself, insofar as it is paternal?

The first Father, then — the simply Father — not being something else first and then father, but father only: he would not himself be; but he will be cause of being to others, and first of all to the simply being, the being before all things; so that in this way also the Father is before all existence and substance. Likewise too the paternal Power — inasmuch as she is bringing-forth of substance — would be ranked before it. Was the third, then, the paternal activity? — so that the activity too is before the substance, inasmuch as it is bringing-forth of substance, and is a paternal activity. The unified, then, is not the simply substance — if indeed it is a paternal activity, begetting the beings; unless the activity runs together with what is activated. And the paternal activity, insofar as it holds to the one and the father, is unified, according to the reversion toward that which is called the One There; but insofar as it has gathered up in itself the things that are being separated and begotten from it, in this way also the simply substance is before the determined substance, just as has been said before.

Or must it be said that the third principle answers, by analogy, to the first activity: that, having taken together the acting, the being-able, and the paternal and generative peculiarity, it has become substance simply? — for we call substance, and being, that which both acts and is able, and which has subsisted first; so that by herself she is substance, while relative to the Father she is called the activity of the Father. Or perhaps it must be beheld in that other way: the third principle is substance, and existence already in actuality and according to activity; while the second is still in potency — and it is this that the Power makes plain? For the things that are in the lower orders in a worse manner are There taken in a better; so stands, then, the in-potency toward the in-actuality. But the Father is not even in potency yet; rather, he snatched himself away even from the aptitude toward substance, in whatever manner conceived — since among the things here also, the one of matter is beyond the in-potency, though on the worse side. For the in-potency has already been pre-determined, by its aptitude toward the form.

But perhaps it is more natural to say this: that existence makes plain the subsistence only — as power the being-able only, and activity the acting only; while substance is the whole, and has taken the three together; whence that which subsists but is able for nothing, or that which is able but acts nothing, we say either is not at all, or is in vain. And again, we hold it right that nothing be in vain. In the third, then, the three have run together; in the second, the two alone; in the first, the one alone — truly: whence this first is existence only, and subsistence — as it were powerless and actless, if it be lawful to say so, being conceived according to what is better than power and than activity; and the second principle is existence together with power, yet acting nothing, and being before activity — and supplying to all things what is before activity, as the first supplies what is before power; and the third, taking the acting in addition, has become substance: a nature subsisting, and being-able, and acting. In this way, then, will existence differ from substance: as the being alone, by itself, from the being that is beheld together with the others; for existence is an element of substance, and has been taken up for the indication of the simplest principle — what is said in this way would have some reason.

Chapter 121 — Hyparxis, as the Name Shows — a Foundation, or as It Were a Floor, Laid Down Beforehand; Cause of All Substance but Not Yet Substance; One and Hyparxis and Father Come to the Same; the Power That Wishes to Be Only a Pouring of the One; the Eldest of All Reversions, Which Is Union Rather Than Reversion · pp. 375–377

And existence seems to me to be determined most of all in this manner: as the name shows, it makes plain the first principle of each subsistence — as it were a certain foundation, or as it were a floor, laid down beforehand for the whole, and for all the building-upon. Wherefore he who gave the name also set the preposition in front of 'beginning' (archē), because he wished to make plain a principle pre-supposed for whatever things are said, in any way whatever, to be. And this is the simplicity before all things, to which all composition accrues; and this is, surely, the very one that lies beyond all things, pre-underlying: which is cause of all substance, but not yet substance; for every substance is composite — whether by union, or by blending, or in whatever other manner; but that was the one itself, alone. And there is need — if there is to be any composition at all — that the one and simple be pre-underlying, and pre-existing, artlessly; since without this nothing else would come forth into subsistence. The existence, then, of all substance is the one — even the first ground laid down. And if it be supposed before substance, according to its proper simplicity, it would be productive of substance; so that the existence is also, assuredly, paternal. To the same point, then, come for us one, and existence, and father.

And upon this first ground and existence there accrues a certain second supposal — being as it were a multitude of that one, and as it were a dis-stancing of it, when the one willed to be all things before all things; which indeed we call, by analogy, power — because power too was an out-stretching of substance. And upon this the third principle goes forth, gathering together, as it seems, the most complete and all-perfect form: as it were standing apart in three, and united into substance in place of existence; wherefore the paternal Intellect is made like to his own father, and has been turned back toward him — as the unified toward the one, and substance toward existence. Yet they are not the same; and the power is another thing, a middle: having stepped out from the paternal simplicity, and in this respect carried along with the one, yet not yet circumscribed into a union, but wishing to be only a pouring, and an unlimitedness, of the one; wherefore she also consorts with the father — as a one being poured with a one that remains. Whence the second principle is not yet unified, but still one — even if become, in a certain way, truly into chaos.

In what way, then, existence differs from substance, let so much be said. And it is plain that the henad, separated from substance, will everywhere be separated analogously, as existence. For if the simply one is existence, the simply unified also is substance. And if the one that is counter-divided toward the being — as hung from it according to otherness — is existence, then the being also, relative to this existence, is substance; though according to its own simplicity it too is existence; while the simply one is existence only — as also the simply many; and the first power is nothing other than the many. And now the unified also — which is a mixture of the one and the many taken simply, and for this reason is itself the simply being; and the simply being is called unified because, everywhere, that which is so called is what has suffered the one and yet nevertheless is not one — as Plato shows in the Sophist. Rightly, then, is the one the Father of the triad — because he is before the being, and begetter of the being; and the power of the Father is the many — because she is the out-stretching of the one toward the begetting of the being; and the paternal Intellect is the unified and the being, beheld according to the reversion toward the paternal one.

Not, surely, the gnostic reversion — for knowledge is not yet differentiated There; nor the vital — for neither has life been in any way differentiated among those; but the substantial: for substance is counter-divided toward these after the unified. And this substantial reversion, which is the eldest of all reversions, is not turned back into substance, but into the simply One; wherefore — this being before all things — the reversion also is surpassing of all the reversions; wherefore this is reversion simply, and not a certain reversion — such as the gnostic toward a knowable, or the appetitive toward a desirable (for this latter is rather vital); nor even as toward the being of the unified — for that would be a certain, and a relative, reversion; but the reversion toward the simplest of all, and itself simplest of all: that of the unified toward the One, of the first toward the first; and standing thus in respect of differentiation — or rather, of undifferentiated excess — that it is a union rather than a reversion.

But nevertheless the analogy will both declare it to be a reversion, and will name intellect the one who subsists according to it — because reversion is proper to intellect. And if the differentiated belongs to intellect, as was said before, then in this way also the unified is intellect — because third from the Father; however one may discourse, it will be so called according to some analogy, and an indication supernatural in its greatness. But so far as speaking in common goes, let it have been said thus.

Chapter 122 — The Threefold Division of the Unified — One-Being, Whole-and-Parts, Unlimited Multitude, as Plato Divided; the Many Before All Number; the Fragments in Which the Many First Appeared; the Uncarved Once-Beyond Intellect, the Both-Ways-Shining Hecate, and the Twice-Beyond Flashing with Intellectual Severings; the Father of the Fathers · pp. 377–380

But the more particular manner must now be told, according to the threefold division of the unified: in which its summit is wholly undifferentiated; its middle already, in a certain way, being-differentiated — as compared with that; and its bound differentiated — so far as one may speak at all of a differentiated of the unified. For Plato also, having differentiated this into one and being, nevertheless found either of them becoming the both-together; and the middle he made a whole out of parts — out of the one and the being; and this was the property of the being-differentiated; while the summit is in every way one being — both the one of the being, and the being of the one. And should one say something further still, he will say rightly: that the summit holds the being mastered by the one; the last, conversely, the one mastered by the being; and in the middle, either is of equal weight.

Or again, as Plato has it: the first is one-being; the next, whole and parts; the third, unlimited multitude. This last, then, answers by analogy to intellect, according to the multitude already differentiated; the middle, according to the being-differentiated; and the first, according to the unified.

Wherefore the summit is only one being; the middle is already beginning a certain partition; and the third has been divided into many — as intellect, we say, into the forms, so this into the many: the many which we say are many before all number; whence also the unlimited multitude — because it is numberless by nature, and before every arithmetical bound; for number does not admit the unlimited — not even according to those who assert it — but the multitude does: that of which there was an unlimited multitude, a matter, as it were, of number, needing an arithmetical limit — or rather, neither matter, nor needing a limit, but beyond the subsistence of all the numbers.

These many, then, are the many of the unified one — as the many before the unified are many according to the second principle, which, as we said, is simply of the one: those are many as one; these, many as unified. And of these there pre-exists, in the middle of the intelligible, neither the many nor the unlimited multitude, but parts and whole — the many still held fast in the one, and only beginning to be differentiated from it; whence the whole has come to be in place of one, and the parts in place of impartibles gathered up by their proper one. But when it was differentiated with the complete differentiation — as great and of such kind as was of a nature to come to be of the unified — so many and such fragments coming to be, in this third member the many appeared at once; and the whole is unlimited multitude; and this whole unlimited multitude will answer, by analogy, to intellect and to the forms in intellect; wherefore it has been hymned as the intelligible intellect of the whole intelligible.

And the middle answers to the middle order — the one that obtained even the same name — in the second world-order after the intelligible; and the summit to the first elemented, com-blended from elements — being itself the unified moment of the whole unified cosmos. And again, in the third world-order, the intellectual: the uncarved intellect, the once-beyond, is likened to the summit of the unified, the wholly unified; while the both-ways-shining Hecate, appearing whole and many-parted, resembles the middle of the unified. And what, in this order, the twice-beyond intellect is — flashing with intellectual severings — that, There, is the intelligible and unified intellect: flashing, he also, if it be lawful to say it, with intelligible severings.

But indeed — whether there are certain such differences in the unified, or pre-appearances of differences, or pre-causes, or however one should choose to say it (for more has been said about these things before) — the unified was the paternal Intellect: insofar as he is one, whole; but insofar as he is thus divided in three, it is plain how, by the same account, we shall divide along with him both the complete Power into three powers, and the one Father into three fathers. For the one will be father of the unified moment in the unified intellect; another, of the moment beheld as whole-and-parts; another, of the one taken according to the unlimited multitude; whence this last was called, in the paternal triad, the paternal intellect; the middle one, power; and the first, the father of the fathers. Likewise the powers also will be taken in three ways, carried along with the three on either side — with the fathers, I mean, and with the paternal intellects; for the powers are always both-ways-shining, and commensurate toward either distance; nevertheless, within the triad of the powers also, the first holds paternal worth relative to the others; the middle is the power of the powers; and the third, the intellect of the first. And so again also in the unified and intellectual triad, the final bounding of the intelligible world-order: the first is father of the intellects; the middle, power; and the third, the unified intellect — even that of the unified father.

Let so much, now said concerning the Chaldaean triads, suffice for present purposes — we having in no way pried into the holy rite handed down by the Oracles concerning them; for the examination of those things did not yet belong to the present occasion.

Chapter 123 — The Traditions of the Other Theologians; the Orphic Rhapsodies — Time, Aether and Chaos, and the Egg from Which Phanēs Leaps Forth; Mētis, Ērikepaios, Phanēs; the Theogony of Hieronymus and Hellanicus — Water and Earth, the One Left Unspoken, the Winged Serpent Named Unaging Time and Heracles, with Necessity Who Is Adrasteia; Aether, Unlimited Chaos, Misty Erebos; the Egg and the First-Born God Called Zeus and Pan · pp. 380–382

But since we have made mention of these things, in whatever way, for the sake of the setting-forth concerning the intelligibles, and of the thorough purification of our own conceptions — come now, let us relate alongside, in due measure, the traditions of the other theologians also concerning the intelligible world-order: if from these too we are able to take up a reverence still greater — and, so far as may be, greatest — of that surpassing union.

In these current Orphic Rhapsodies, then, the theology concerning the intelligible is this — which the philosophers also interpret: setting Time in place of the one principle of wholes; in place of the two, Aether and Chaos; and in place of the being, simply, reckoning the Egg — and making this the first triad. And to the second triad belongs either the Egg conceiving and conceived — the god — or the silvery tunic, or the cloud, because from these leaps forth Phanēs; for at different times they philosophize different things about the middle. This, then — whatever it may be — they take as the intellect; while as father and power they conceive in addition certain other things in no way belonging to Orpheus; and the third triad they take to be Mētis as intellect, Ērikepaios as power, and Phanēs himself as father.

And perhaps the middle triad must also be set according to the three-formed god, while still being conceived in the egg; for the middle, too, always images forth the both-together of the extremes — as this also is at once both egg and three-formed god. And you see that the egg is the unified; and the three-formed — and in real truth many-formed — god is the differentiated of the intelligible; while the middle is, according to the egg, still unified, but according to the god, already differentiated — and, to say the whole of it, being-differentiated. Such, then, is the customary Orphic theology.

But the theology current under Hieronymus and Hellanicus — if indeed he is not the same man — stands thus. Water was, he says, from the beginning, and matter, out of which the earth was compacted; positing these two principles first — water and earth: the latter as scatterable by nature, the former as gluing her together and holding her together; but the one before the two he leaves unspoken; for the very fact of not even speaking about it indicates its unsayable nature. And the third principle after these two was begotten of them — of water, I say, and earth — and is a serpent, having heads of a bull and of a lion grown upon it, and in the middle the face of a god, and having wings also upon the shoulders; and the same has been named Unaging Time, and Heracles. And with him consorts Necessity — being the same nature as Adrasteia also — incorporeal, stretched arm-wide through the whole cosmos, touching its bounds. This, I think, is said to be the third principle, standing according to substance; save that he gave it subsistence as male-and-female, for indication of the cause that is generative of all things.

And I take it that the theology in the Rhapsodies, letting go the two first principles — together with the one before the two, the one handed down in silence — set up its beginning from this third principle after the two, as being the first that holds anything speakable, and commensurate to the hearing of men. For this was the much-honored Unaging Time in it — the father of Aether and Chaos. And indeed, according to this theology too, this Time, the serpent, begets a triple offspring: Aether, he says, intellectual, and Chaos unlimited, and third upon these, Erebos misty. This second triad he hands down as analogous to the first — being dynamic, as that one was paternal; wherefore its third member also is misty Erebos; and the paternal, summit member is Aether — not simply, but intellectually; and the middle, of itself, unlimited Chaos.

But indeed, among these, as he says, Time begot an Egg — this tradition too making it the offspring of Time, and born among these, because from these also the third intelligible triad goes forth. What then is this triad? The Egg; and the dyad of the two natures within it, male and female, together with the multitude of the all-various seeds in the middle; and third upon these, a god without body, having golden wings upon his shoulders, who had, grown upon his flanks, heads of bulls, and upon his head a monstrous serpent, presenting the semblance of all manner of shapes of beasts. This one, then, must be taken as the intellect of the triad; and the middle kinds — the many, and the two — as the power; and the Egg itself as the paternal principle of the third triad; and the third god of this third triad this theology hymns as Prōtogonos, and calls him Zeus, the disposer of all things and of the whole cosmos — wherefore he is also called Pan. So much does this genealogy too set forth concerning the intelligible principles.

parts.name: Chapter 124 — The Theology Recorded by Eudemus the Peripatetic — Orpheus Keeping the Whole Intelligible in Silence and Beginning from Night; Homer, in Whom Even Zeus Stands in Awe of Swift Night; Hesiod's Chaos, Earth, Tartaros, and Erōs; Acusilaus — Erebos and Night, Then Aether, Erōs, and Mētis; Epimenides — Aēr and Night, the Two Titans, and the Egg; Pherecydes the Syrian — Zas, Chronos, and Chthonia, and the Five Recesses · pp. 382–384

lines.text: Chapter 124 — The Theology Recorded by Eudemus the Peripatetic — Orpheus Keeping the Whole Intelligible in Silence and Beginning from Night; Homer, in Whom Even Zeus Stands in Awe of Swift Night; Hesiod's Chaos, Earth, Tartaros, and Erōs; Acusilaus — Erebos and Night, Then Aether, Erōs, and Mētis; Epimenides — Aēr and Night, the Two Titans, and the Egg; Pherecydes the Syrian — Zas, Chronos, and Chthonia, and the Five Recesses · pp. 382–384

But the theology recorded in Eudemus the Peripatetic, as being that of Orpheus, kept silence about the whole intelligible — as altogether unsayable and unknowable in the manner of discursive traversal and announcement; and it made its beginning from Night — from whom Homer also sets up his beginning, even if he has not made his genealogy continuous. For Eudemus is not to be accepted when he says that Homer begins from Okeanos and Tethys; for Homer appears to know Night also as a goddess so great that even Zeus stands in awe of her — for he dreaded, says the poet, to do things displeasing to swift Night. So let Homer too, himself, begin from Night.

And Hesiod, when he relates that Chaos came to be first, seems to me to have called the incomprehensible and wholly unified nature of the intelligible Chaos, and to bring forth Earth first from thence, as a certain principle of the whole generation of the gods. Unless indeed Chaos is the second of the two principles, and Earth and Tartaros and Erōs are the triple intelligible: Erōs in place of the third, as beheld according to reversion — for Orpheus also, in the Rhapsodies, names it thus; Earth in place of the first, as being first compacted in a certain solid and substantial establishment; and Tartaros in place of the middle, as already, in a certain way, stirred aside toward differentiation.

And Acusilaus seems to me to suppose Chaos as the first principle, as wholly unknown; and the two after the one: Erebos the male, and the female Night — the latter in place of unlimitedness, the former in place of limit; and from these, mingled together, he says, came to be Aether and Erōs and Mētis — these three intelligible subsistences: making Aether the summit one, and Erōs the middle, according to the natural middleness of love, and Mētis the third — by now the much-honored intellect itself. And besides these he brings forth, from the same, a great number of other gods also, according to the history of Eudemus.

And Epimenides supposed two first principles, Aēr and Night — plainly honoring with silence the one before the two — from which Tartaros was begotten: the third principle, I take it, as a certain mixed one, com-blended out of the two. And from these came two Titans — so calling the intelligible middleness, because it stretches out toward both, the summit and the bound; and these being mingled with one another, an Egg came to be — this very thing, the intelligible animal in real truth — from which, again, another generation came forth.

And Pherecydes the Syrian says that Zas always is, and Chronos, and Chthonia — the three first principles: the one, I mean, before the two, and the two after the one; and that Chronos made, out of his own seed, fire and breath and water — the triple nature, I take it, of the intelligible; from which, divided in five recesses, another numerous generation of gods was constituted — the one called five-recessed; which is perhaps the same as to say, the five-cosmosed. But concerning these things another occasion will perhaps show itself.
Such, then, and so many — for the present — let the suppositions conveyed through Greek myths stand as taken up by us; there being many others besides.

Chapter 125 — The Theologies of the Barbarians — the Babylonians: Tauthe and Apasōn, the Mother of the Gods, the Only-Begotten Mōymis, and Bēlos the Demiurge; the Magi and the Areian Race: Place or Time, Ōromasdēs and Areimanios; the Sidonians: Time, Desire, and Mist; the Phoenicians of Mōchos: Oulōmos, Chousōros the Opener, and the Egg Burst into Heaven and Earth; the Egyptians: the Unknown Darkness Thrice Proclaimed, and the Three Kamēphis · pp. 384–386

Of the Barbarians, the Babylonians seem to pass over the one principle of wholes in silence, and to make two, Tauthe and Apasōn — making Apasōn the husband of Tauthe, and naming her the mother of the gods; of whom was begotten an only-begotten son, Mōymis — being itself, I take it, the intelligible cosmos, brought forth from the two principles. And from the same parents another generation came forth, Lachē and Lachos. Then again a third from the same, Kissarē and Assōros — from whom came to be three, Anos and Illinos and Aos; and of Aos and Daukē was born a son, Bēlos, whom they declare to be the demiurge.

And the Magi, and the whole Areian race — as Eudemus also writes this — some call the whole intelligible and unified Place, and others Time: out of which were differentiated either a good god and an evil daimon — or light and darkness before these, as some among them say. These too, then, themselves, after the undifferentiated nature, make the twofold column of the better beings to be differentiated: of the one column Ōromasdēs is the leader; of the other, Areimanios.

And the Sidonians, according to the same writer, suppose before all things Time, and Desire, and Mist; and from Desire and Mist mingled, as two principles, came to be Aēr and Aura — making known by Aēr the unmixed summit of the intelligible, and by Aura the living pre-figuration of the intelligible, moved out of it. And again, from both of these an Egg was begotten — answering, I take it, to the intelligible intellect.

But outside of Eudemus we find the mythology of the Phoenicians according to Mōchos: Aether was the first, and Aēr — these two principles, from whom is begotten Oulōmos, the intelligible god — itself, I take it, the summit of the intelligible; from whom — coming together with himself — he says was begotten Chousōros, an opener first, and then an Egg: this latter, I take it, they call the intelligible intellect, and the opener Chousōros the intelligible power, inasmuch as it first differentiated the undifferentiated nature. Unless rather, after the two principles, the summit is the Wind, the one; and the middle the two winds, Lips and Notos — for they make these too, in a certain way, before Oulōmos — and Oulōmos himself would be the intelligible intellect; and the opener Chousōros the first order after the intelligible; and the Egg, the heaven; for it is said that, when it was burst into two, heaven and earth came to be — each of the two halves.

But of the Egyptians Eudemus relates nothing accurate. The Egyptians, however, who in our own time have become philosophers, brought forth their hidden truth, having found it in certain Egyptian discourses: that, according to them, the one principle of wholes is hymned as Unknown Darkness — and this proclaimed three times as such; and the two principles are water and sand, as Heraïscus says — or, as Asclepiades, his elder, has it, sand and water — from which, and after which, was begotten the first Kamēphis; then a second, from him; and then, from this one, the third — by whom the whole intelligible world-order is filled up. Thus far Asclepiades. But the younger Heraïscus says that the third Kamēphis — named from his father and his grandfather — is the sun: which is surely the intelligible intellect. But the precise account of these matters must be taken from those men themselves.

And this also must be known concerning the Egyptians: that they are dividers, in many places, of the things that subsist according to union — since they have divided even the intelligible into the properties of many gods, as those who wish may learn by meeting with their writings: I mean the record of Heraïscus, written for Proclus the philosopher as a complete account of the doctrine of the Egyptians, and the Concord of the Egyptians with the Other Theologians, which Asclepiades began to write.

Chapter 126 — Of Participation in the First Principles and the Whole Intelligible; What the Name Signifies — the Sun Participated According to the In-Given Light; Protagoras and Lycophron, Who Sever All Things from One Another; the Argument That Destroys Even Itself; the Soul That Becomes Pythagorean or Platonic; Motion Must Stand and Rest Must Move; the Beautiful and the Just Counter-Participate — Here the Text, as Transmitted, Breaks Off · pp. 386–390

Upon these things we must treat of the participation of the first principles and of the whole intelligible — that which we say is the unified: whether these are participated by all the things that are second, or are not participated; or in one way are, and in another are not. For that substance is twofold — the one participable, the other unparticipated — and life and intellect in the same manner, has been said before, and determined in due measure. Yet about these things too there must be further inquiry; and about the individuals — whence there is any subsistence of them; and whether participation reaches even to the things that come to be and perish.

First, then, it must be said what the name 'to participate' signifies, and what we mean by participation. Does it wish to make plain a having — but a having after another, and from another? — a having in the second place, and not first? — a having of another being, after that one, which is other than that in which it is not? — and that participation is of something whose existence it is not, as of an original and prototype? — so that the same form is itself by itself, but is participated by proceeding into another from another. And the participated is twofold: the one, that which gives; the other, the given itself — according to which the giver is participated. For according to the given, the sun in heaven is, as it were, participated — according to the light in-given by it to our eyes; yet the given itself also is participated; and we say the participant participates of either: of the one, as of what proceeds upon another, after another, and from another; of the other, as of what gives to another its own property, after itself. So much, then, concerning the name.

But that there is some such thing also among the realities — and that one thing does participate of another, and that each does not stand by itself, isolated from the others, and called only that which it is — as Protagoras attempts to suppose, and Lycophron declared outright — the argument will make plain, when moderately tested. For what, they will say, would the beautiful be, other than beautiful? And what the just, other than just? Then neither must the beautiful be called just, nor the just beautiful. And what then of saying that the beautiful is? Nay, the beautiful is not a being, but only beautiful. And the just is not — for the 'is' is proper to the being. Nothing, then, of the others is, besides the being; nor does anything else stand, besides the standing; nor is anything moved, besides the moving; everything, then, is without share of everything; and one name only must be predicated of each — that of its proper peculiarity; and they enjoin that we must not interweave, nor make a sentence, as said truly of one nature. For the man too is man only — neither animal, nor rational, nor mortal; for he is none of these things — only that very thing which is man.

Further, they say: the participant — that is, what remains — is said to participate of another; but if it remains the same, the very thing it was before, what more has it got, in that it participated of the other? And the participated itself also remained upon its own peculiarity, the very thing it was from the beginning; so that it too must be held worthy of the same name as before. And third: one thing consorts with another either according to union, or according to com-blending, or according to juxtaposition; and which of these modes of consorting we shall say participation is, must be sought. Not juxtaposition — for things lying beside one another are unaffected by one another, while participation comes with some affection. Nor according to union — for the participated and the participant must be set apart; but union makes the two one, and there no longer remains a participant and a participated. But neither according to com-blending — which seems the most plausible; for com-blending is of two members of like rank, and of elements both belonging to one existence — not of the one as participant and the other as participated. Accordingly, one would not say that the white body is a com-blending of whiteness and body, in the way that body is a blend of the three-dimensioned elements. For the participant always wishes to be the substrate of the participated; and this latter, to be as in that substrate. These things, then, and the like, would be said by those who raise difficulties against participation, and hold it right that nothing participate of anything else.

But truly terrible is the argument, if it shall make all things dis-spanned from one another, and sharing in common in no one thing — not even in the one itself, since the same argument will fit concerning the one as well. And it will abolish many of the acknowledged forms besides: sameness, likeness, equality, union as a whole — nay, wholeness itself; for each of the parts must participate of one wholeness. And it overturns all science too — if indeed it is not admissible to predicate one thing of another, whether speaking or thinking; so that the argument will destroy even its very self. For it will not be permitted to it to say that the realities are separated from one another; for then all things will plainly participate of the same thing — of the separation toward one another. And indeed, to those who look at the realities themselves it is manifest that some things participate of others, and certain things of the same things. For the forms in matter appear to stand thus: the elements participate of one another, and the things made of elements participate both of the elements themselves, and they too of one another; for our body is warmed, and is chilled, and further is nourished from plants and from the other fruits.

And the senses — are they not form-given by their sensibles? And appetite and spirit — are they not altered both toward the worse and toward the better? And the rational soul — is she not educated, taking over the educator's culture? Does she not become Pythagorean by philosophizing — or Platonic? And there is that saying of Socrates: how would one man have recognized another's affection, were there not something common between them? — and it is plain that the common is always from one. And what — do the worse not manifestly participate of the higher, as matter of the forms? The wood, at any rate, has been shaped, and cut by the saw, and formed into a throne; and does the body not live, and is it not moved from within — not in the way the soulless is moved, from without? And this air, and the whole sublunary realm — is it not lit by the heavenly light? And do the immaterial not supply to all the enmattered their unceasing power? And, to speak more logically still: man and horse — each is a form, each an animal, each a being, each one; and all things are common, except the peculiarity of each; and the common things are, as it were, elements of the peculiarity — even of that one — yet are not upon themselves. For that which is not of itself and by itself — and first, itself — of this there is participation, having come from another into another, as we were saying. But these things, perhaps, are agreed.

But how shall we free ourselves from the contrary arguments? It must be said, surely, that the forms are not even of a nature to subsist apart from one another, each upon itself alone; for motion must stand, and rest must move; otherwise, neither will motion remain in that in which it is, nor will rest be active, in so far as it is. Likewise also the beautiful and the just counter-participate one another: the beautiful of the just, in order that it may act its proper activity, and be unconfused toward the others; and the just of the beautiful, in order that it may be lovely, and dear, and worthy of praise. And we shall be at no loss to say the like in most cases. The forms, then, as I said, must of necessity participate of one another; and it is the peculiarities — conceived by themselves, though they are not by themselves — that work the difficulties for us; since, according to truth, neither — —
Telos
